Many species possess high cellulolytic activity [16–18] and/or are symp-tomless parasites of plants (endophytes) [19]. A brief review of the nutritional versatility of Trichoderma spp. is given in Supporting Information S1 Text. Genus-wide studies of the nutri-tional traits of Trichoderma have revealed that shifts from ancestral mycoparasitism to phyto-phagy and back again occurred several times during Trichoderma evolution [16]. The best available explanation for such inter-kingdom (fungi <–> plants) nutritional jumps is the host-habitat hypothesis [20], which posits that sympatric cohabitation increases the chance of host/substrate shifts. For Trichoderma, a widely accepted theory proposes that ancestral species could parasitize fungal hyphae growing in decaying wood and, thus have evolved the ability to degrade plant biomass [21]. However, the mechanisms underpinning this transition are not known. Interestingly, the genome analysis of another mycoparasitic hypocrealean fungus, Escovopsis weberi, (which feeds on cellulolytic fungal gardens of leaf-cutting ants and therefore lives in proximity to lignocellulose) did not reveal any enrichment for genes encoding cellu-lases and xylanases [22]. This finding challenges the host-habitat hypothesis and shows that parasitism on a lignocellulolytic host does not necessarily result in an enhancement of lignocel-lulolytic machinery.
To understand the evolutionary mechanisms that lead Trichoderma to grow on plant bio-mass and, thereby expand its nutritional range, we performed a phylogenetic analysis of the plant cell wall-degrading carbohydrate-active enzymes and auxiliary proteins encoded in the genomes of nine species of Trichoderma that are members of three major infrageneric clades [23] plus twelve other Hypocreales fungi. Our gene tree / species tree reconciliation analysis revealed massive lateral transfer of genes (LGT) encoding plant cell wall-degrading enzymes to Trichoderma from plant-associated Ascomycota hosts. The results suggest that LGT from other ascomycetes was likely facilitated by expansion of Trichoderma mycoparasitic host range to these fungi, and this genetic phenomenon has been an important event in the evolution of this trait.
Results All Trichoderma spp. can feed on plant and fungal biomass To assess Trichoderma nutritional preferences with respect to plant and fungal biomass, we compared nine species belonging to the three major infrageneric groups (T. reesei, T. pararee-sei, T. longibrachiatum and T. citrinoviride from section Longibrachiatum; T. harzianum, T.
guizhouense, T. virens from section Pachybasium; and T. atroviride and T. asperellum from sec-tion Trichoderma, Supporting Information S1 Table) with mycoparasitic E. weberi (Hypo-creales, Ascomycota) and the cellulolytic and endophytic Pestalotiopsis fici (Xylariales, Ascomycota [24]). To approximate conditions in nature, we used (i) cell walls of fungus Gano-derma lucidum (Polyporales, Basidiomycota) and (ii) epiphyte-free dried leaves and biologi-cally pre-degraded wood for the species Shorea johorensis (Dipterocarpaceae, Plantae). G.
lucidum and S. johorensis were selected as sources of biomass because of the tropical occur-rence of T. reesei, E. weberi, and P. fici, while other fungi were considered cosmopolitan. Also, we tested a diversity of plant-related substrates, such as coniferous commercial wood, micro-crystalline cellulose, wheat straw, and pectin (Supporting Information S1 Fig). All fungi grew well on the cell walls of G. lucidum. Aside from this substrate, E. weberi only formed a small amount of biomass on leaves. Trichoderma spp. and P. fici grew equally well on all substrates that consisted of plant biomass. In general, the nine Trichoderma spp. showed remarkable Massive interfungal LGT of plant cell wall-degrading enzymes PLOS Genetics | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1007322 April 9, 2018 3 / 33 similarities in their ability to feed on plant biomass. In contrast, E. weberi did not exhibit this nutritional versatility.
Trichoderma and Escovopsisform a monophyletic clade and share a common ancestor with entomoparasitic fungi Considering the abundance of plant-associated fungi in the order Hypocreales, we hypothe-sized that the phytophagy of Trichoderma was maintained during its evolution, whereas E.
weberi may have lost this ability over the course of its specialization that allowed it to parasitize on Agaricales mushrooms cultivated by ants [22]. To test this hypothesis, we reconstructed the evolutionary history of Trichoderma. We used 21 whole-genome sequences for fungi of the order Hypocreales, including E. weberi [22], five newly sequenced genomes of Trichoderma (T.
longibrachiatum, T. citrinoviride, T. harzianum, T. guizhouense, and T. asperellum), and previ-ously published genomes of T. reesei [25], T. virens [26], T. atroviride [26], and T. parareesei [27] (Supporting Information S1 Table). We selected 100 orthologous, neutrally evolving, unlinked genes encoding proteins required for a diversity of cellular functions (Supporting Information S2 Table). We reconstructed their individual phylogenies based on both nucleo-tide and amino acid sequences (Data deposited at http://itol.embl.de/shared/druzhininaetal).
Each gene was tested for a neutral evolution using Tajima’s D test (Supporting Information S2 Table) and concatenated into an alignment of 47,726 amino acids in length (Supporting Infor-mation S2 Table). The details of the phylogenetic analyses are given in Supporting Information S2 Table. This analysis revealed that the monophyletic family Hypocreaceae, represented here by the Escovopsis and Trichoderma genera, shared a last common ancestor with fungi from the families Cordycipitaceae, Ophiocordycipitaceae, and Clavicipitaceae, which are dominated by extant entomoparasitic fungi (Fig 1A). The branch leading to the plant-associated Nectriaceae family diverged earlier in the course of the evolution of the Hypocreales.
The Trichoderma pcwdCAZome is distinct from that of other hypocrealean fungi The evolutionary history of Trichoderma explains its ability to efficiently derive nutrition from living and dead fungi ([4], see above) and its interactions with animals [4]. If the ability of Tri-choderma to degrade plant biomass was inherited via vertical gene transfer, its phytophagy should resemble that of other Hypocreales fungi, especially those of the phytoparasitic family Nectriaceae. To test this, we identified all genes of the nine Trichoderma species that encode car-bohydrate-active enzymes (CAZome, as defined at http://www.cazy.org/Genomes.html) in Tri-choderma and selected those that are known to be involved in the plant cell wall degradation (pcwdCAZome). We retrieved proteins from all glycoside hydrolase (GH) families, which are active in hydrolysis of cellulose, the xylan backbone, other hemicelluloses and hemicellulose side chains, and pectin and its side chains. This search resulted in a total of 32 GH families. The PL1 family of pectate lyases and two accessory protein families (the AA9 lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases and the expansin-like protein swollenin) were included comprising a total of 746 proteins from the nine Trichoderma spp. genomes (Supporting Information S3 Table).
For this comparison, we counted genes encoding enzymes for 29 of the GH families in other Hypocreales genomes [22, 28–36] (Supporting Information S3 Table). The unrelated polyphagous fungi, Neurospora crassa [37] and Chaetomium globosum [38] (both Sordariales, Ascomycota), were used as outgroups. A comparative analysis of these fungi showed that the pcwdCAZomes of phytoparasitic Fusarium and Nectria spp. are significantly larger than those of the entomoparasitic and mycoparasitic lineages, including Trichoderma. However, the clus-ter analysis revealed similarities between the pcwdCAZome composition of the mycoparasitic Massive interfungal LGT of plant cell wall-degrading enzymes PLOS Genetics | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1007322 April 9, 2018 4 / 33 E. weberi and that of the entomoparasites, but not that of Trichoderma (Fig 1B). The latter genus possessed a pcwdCAZome that was more than twice as large as that of E. weberi. A prin-cipal component analysis (Fig 2) separated the pcwdCAZomes of Trichoderma spp. from those of E. weberi and the entomoparasites. Interestingly, the pcwdCAZomes were also separated from the phytoparasitic Nectriaceae. The Trichoderma pcwdCAZome exhibited closest simi-larity to the taxonomically distant fungi N. crassa and C. globosum. These data, therefore, do not support the hypothesis that the composition of Trichoderma pcwdCAZome is the ancestral state. Instead, it is likely the evolutionarily derived state.

LGT events are not reflected in the clustering of pcwdCAZymes in Trichoderma genomes LGT has frequently been shown to involve the transfer of large genomic fragments containing several genes [43]. Since a third of the T. reesei pcwdCAZome occurs in 20 discrete, loose clus-ters [25, 44], we tested whether these clusters are the consequence of LGT. An analysis of the synteny of the chromosomal loci of the above clusters in T. reesei with that in the other Tricho-derma spp. showed that the clusters were highly syntenic (>80% of all gene positions were conserved), and this pattern was independent of their chromosomal location [45]. Thirty-three of the pcwdCAZymes of T. reesei were organized into a total of 16 clusters (Supporting Information S5 Table), but only 13 of these pcwdCAZyme genes had been acquired by LGT.
In addition, the pcwdCAZyme genes in individual clusters were obtained from different donors. Therefore, we reject the hypothesis that the LGT-derived genes may have given rise to the origin of the CAZyme clusters proposed for Trichoderma [25].
Alloparasitism of Trichoderma is complemented by parasitism on closely related Pezizomycotina, including adelphoparasitism on Hypocreales Our analysis showed that Trichoderma phytophagy is indeed an apomorphic character that did not result from the convergent evolution of individual species or clades. Instead, it was obtained over the course of evolution through incidence of large-scale LGT. Putative donors include phytoparasitic fungi phylogenetically close to Trichoderma and possibly even neigh-boring groups. Interfungal interactions between Trichoderma and filamentous Ascomycota are rarely observed in nature [4]. However, the successful application of Trichoderma-based biofungicides against plant-pathogenic Ascomycota and respective studies of the roles of indi-vidual genes in mycoparasitism [46–55] support the hypothesis that such interactions take place alongside alloparasitism (parasitism on unrelated hosts) on Basidiomycota.
The possible cellular mechanisms for the uptake and incorporation of foreign DNA by fungi include conjugation, viral transduction, and conidial and hyphal fusion [56]. Although LGT between eukaryotes with cell walls has rarely been reported [57, 58], mycoparasitism has been viewed as a possible mechanism that could be linked to it [55, 59].
All fungi from the Hypocreaceae family are known to be aggressive alloparasites and they are common on sporocarps of Basidiomycota fungi in situ [4] (Fig 8A), Trichoderma spp. are effective against phytoparasites from Basidiomycota (for example [15, 26]), and the cause of the green mold disease on mushroom farms [60, 61]. In dual confrontation assays with colo-nies of Lentinula edodes (Agaricales, Basidiomycota), all Trichoderma spp. were able to parasit-ize this host, while E. weberi showed neither parasitism nor antagonistic reactions (Supporting Information S3 Fig). Similarly, all Trichoderma species were substantially more aggressive compared to E. weberi when confronted with its host fungus Leucoagaricus gongylophorus (Agaricales, Basidiomycota) (Supporting Information S3 Fig).
The evolutionary analysis of the pcwdCAZome of Trichoderma revealed LGT biased towards relatively close fungi (filamentous Pezizomycotina, Ascomycota). This selectivity could be explained by the ability of Trichoderma to parasitize Ascomycota fungi, which, in turn, is considered to be the major trait that sets Trichoderma apart from the other mycopara-sitic Hypocreaceae fungi, such as Escovopsis, Hypomyces, and Sphaerostilbella, which parasitize Basidiomycota [16]. To test this hypothesis, we investigated the interactions of Trichoderma spp. with several model phytoparasitic Ascomycota. We investigated interactions between T. reesei and the lignocellulolytic P. fici [24], which was several times identified as one of the putative LGT donors (Fig 6). P. fici was also selected because it has been isolated from the same ecosystem where T. reesei is common (the phyllo-sphere of Shorea sp., Borneo) and it has comparable growth rates in vitro (Supporting Informa-tion S1 Fig). In dual confrontation assays on agar plates, T. reesei overgrew a colony of P. fici, but did not kill it (Fig 9A). Microscopic examination revealed a tight association between the hyphae, suggesting endoparasitism of P. fici by T. reesei (Fig 9B). Confocal microscopy revealed that cords of P. fici hyphae were penetrated and colonized by the thinner hyphae of T.
reesei (Fig 9C). This experiment shows that Trichoderma hyphae can grow inside hyphae of at least some extant putative Ascomycota donors. Dual confrontation assays with a set of ran-domly selected Eurotiales fungi showed that Trichoderma is capable of attacking these fungi as well (Supporting Information S3 Fig). However, endoparasitism was not observed, possibly because the hyphae of the tested Eurotiales fungi were comparable in size with Trichoderma spp., making internal penetration difficult.
A surprising finding of this study was the detection of four cases of LGT of cellulolytic enzymes from other Hypocreales. Interestingly, Trichoderma is also capable of parasitizing fungi belonging to its very close phylogenetic neighbors (adelphoparasitism [62]), including Fusarium [55, 63]. To investigate the range of Trichoderma adelphoparasitism, we confronted different Trichoderma strains with fungi from the same genus, family, and order (Fig 10). The microscopic study revealed numerous cases of hyphal fusion that may be linked to self/non-self-recognition mechanisms in Trichoderma species and only in part to parasitism. Therefore, evidence for adelphoparasitism was only accepted when one colony overgrew the other. Our results showed that T. harzianum might attack its sister species, T. guizhouense (Fig 10A, see Fig 1 for phylogenomics). Any of the nine Trichoderma species can parasitize E. weberi (Fig 10B for T. atroviride), while the latter fungus did not attack Trichoderma. The majority of Tri-choderma strains attacked and/or killed Fusarium spp. (Fig 10C) [55, 63], although individual strains of the latter host fungus resisted Trichoderma infections. A similar interaction was observed in a confrontation with Emericellopsis alkalina, which belongs to an Acremonium species complex in Hypocreales (Fig 10D). Our results show that all species of Trichoderma studied are capable of adelphoparasitism in the strictest sense of this term (parasitism on organisms belonging to the same genus or family [62]), and this property extends to intera-ctions with other filamentous Ascomycota. Along with the unique ability to perform adel-phoparasitism, Trichoderma maintains its alloparasitic properties (Supporting Information S3 Fig).
Discussion LGT as an evolutionary shortcut to achieving nutritional versatility In this work, we uncovered a possible evolutionary process that contributed to the develop-ment of the nutritional versatility of Trichoderma. Phylogenomic analysis showed that the genus shared a last common ancestor with entomoparasitic hypocrealean fungi (Cordycipita-ceae, Ophiocordycipitaceae, and Clavicipitaceae). Since then, Trichoderma evolution has been directed towards mycotrophy. Although this path has also been taken by a number of other fungi of the family Hypocreaceae [20,55], Trichoderma is the most taxonomically diverse mycoparasitic fungus, harboring at least 260 molecularly defined species [64] found world-wide (NCBI Taxonomy browser, Nov. 2016). Trichoderma can also interact with animals [65], Massive interfungal LGT of plant cell wall-degrading enzymes PLOS Genetics | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1007322 April 9, 2018 15 / 33 Massive interfungal LGT of plant cell wall-degrading enzymes PLOS Genetics | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1007322 April 9, 2018 16 / 33 Fig 9. Hyphal interactions observed using light microscopy (400x magnification). C. Confocal image showing endoparasitism of T. reesei on hyphae of P. fici on a glass slide prepared as shown in S3 Fig. D. Hyphae of P. fici TUCIM 5788 and a fluorescent chlamydospore of T. reesei. E. T. reesei TUCIM 4817 mycelium. Scale bar on C–E—40 μm.
https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1007322.g009 Fig 10. Adelphoparasitism of Trichoderma on members of the same genus (A), same family (B), and same order (C, D). Parasites were inoculated on the right side of each plate, and hosts are on the left side. Images were taken after 10 days of incubation at 28˚C in the dark. Parasitism is assigned as a function of active overgrowth of the opponent colony. NCBI accession numbers for the DNA barcodes for fungi are given in Supporting Information S6 Table. Note to A: In this experiment, the host fungus T. guizhouense NJAU 4742 did not produce conidia (see other images in Supporting Information S3 Fig).
https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1007322.g010 Massive interfungal LGT of plant cell wall-degrading enzymes PLOS Genetics | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1007322 April 9, 2018 17 / 33 although the evolutionary state and mechanisms are not understood (see also Supporting Information S1 Text). It is known that the evolutionary history of some hypocrealean fungi involved the emergence of mycotrophy from a entomoparasitic/sarcophagic background. For example, Elaphocordyceps spp., deriving from the mainly entomoparasitic order Cordycipita-ceae, are parasites of false truffles of the genus Elaphomyces (Eurotiales) [66].
Nikoh and Fukatsu [20] invoked the host-habitat hypothesis for such a “jump” from feeding on cicada nymphs to parasitism on truffles.
Due to the chemical composition of animals and fungi, the host shift from feeding on arthropods to feeding on fungi does not appear to be a difficult metabolic transition. Instead, it would only require a fine-tuning of ecological adaptations for specific hosts in one or another kingdom (i.e., mechanisms for recognition, defense, and overcoming the host). In contrast, feeding on plant biomass is an evolutionary challenge for any fungus specialized for feeding on insects or fungi. Our comparative analysis of the pcwdCAZome of hypocrealean fungi revealed that members of entomoparasitic families have a relatively poor repertoire of genes required for degradation of plant biomass compared to those of the hypocrealean phytopara-sites. This paucity is also present in the Escovopsis weberi, a parasite of Agaricales and the clos-est phylogenetic neighbor of Trichoderma for which genome information is available [22].
The reduced number of pcwdCAZymes of E. weberi contradicts the predictions of the host-habitat hypothesis (see above) because the habitat of this fungus is directly linked to plant biomass, which is used by ants to cultivate E. weberi’s host fungus Leucoagaricus spp. The pcwdCAZome of the nine Trichoderma spp. investigated here was found to be of intermediate size between entomoparasitic and phytoparasitic Hypocreales fungi. We demonstrate that the abilities of Trichoderma to feed on plant and fungal biomass are equally developed in the studied species. Consequently, nutritional extension—not shifts or “jumps”—results in nutri-tional versatility and provides the basis for the general environmental opportunism of this genus [4].
Trichoderma gained pcwdCAZymes from filamentous Ascomycota hosts Our data suggest that nearly half of the genes encoding pcwdCAZymes have been obtained by LGT from other fungi. Gene duplication, which has been described as a major source of gene innovation in fungi [67] and other organisms [68] apparently played only a minor role in the evolution of the Trichoderma pcwdCAZome. It has been reported that 0.1–3% of the genes in a given Pezizomycotina genome were derived by LGT, usually indicating interdomain exchanges [43, 67]. When this estimation is applied to the 122 proteins of the pcwdCAZome of Trichoderma, maximally five genes would be expected to have originated from LGT. This sug-gests that the frequency of LGT in pcwdCAZome is an exceptional case. Surprisingly, we did not detect any transfer event from prokaryotes, and we also did not observe LGT events from Basidiomycota fungi. Marcet-Houben and Gabaldon [69] and Savory et al. [59] reviewed LGT events between bacteria and fungi, and listed T. reesei as one of the fungi comprising the high-est number of bacterial-derived proteins. However, the genes transferred encoded arsenite reductases, catalases, different racemases and enzymes of peptidoglycan metabolism, but no pcwdCAzymes. Because the transfer of bacterial glycoside hydrolase genes to ciliates [70] or rotifers [71] has been demonstrated to have shaped their adaptation to polysaccharide-rich environments, we expected to find such cases for Trichoderma. However, none of the 50 LGT events detected in this study involved a bacterial donor.
The only example of non-fungal putative LGT to Trichoderma was that of the gene encod-ing the auxiliary protein swollenin [72, 73]. The plant expansins were described to have under-gone at least two LGT events to other organisms, including one event that gave rise to Massive interfungal LGT of plant cell wall-degrading enzymes PLOS Genetics | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1007322 April 9, 2018 18 / 33 amoebozoa expansins and fungal swollenins and another that gave rise to the bacterial expan-sins [73]. Our data are in accordance with these findings and further suggest that Trichoderma was among the first fungal genera to undergo LGT from plants (either directly or through other fungi).
Which features of Trichoderma mycoparasitism may be linked to LGT?
Historically, LGT between eukaryotes containing cell walls has been considered to be rare and linked to phagotrophy [74]. However, nearly two decades ago, Wo ¨stemeyer et al. [56] hypothe-sized that hyphal fusion mycoparasitism might offer nearly ideal conditions for interfungal DNA exchanges. They demonstrated the transfer of genes in vitro from the Mucoromycotina mycoparasite Parasitella parasitica to its Mucoromycotina host, Absidia glauca [75]. This has not occurred in other Hypocreaceae (Escovopsis, Hypomyces, Sphaerostilbella, etc.) that feed on Basidiomycota. args.summary:
This research article (published April 9, 2018, in PLOS Genetics) investigates the evolutionary origin of the nutritional versatility of Trichoderma fungi—molds that can parasitize other fungi, attack animals, and degrade plant biomass. 

**Methods:** The researchers conducted a phylogenomic analysis of 23 hypocrealean fungi (including nine Trichoderma spp. and the related Escovopsis weberi), using whole-genome sequences including five newly sequenced Trichoderma genomes. They analyzed 122 gene families encoding plant cell wall-degrading carbohydrate-active enzymes (pcwdCAZome) using gene tree/species tree reconciliation (NOTUNG analysis) to distinguish between gene duplication, gene loss, and lateral gene transfer (LGT).

**Key Findings:**
- Trichoderma evolved from an ancestor with limited cellulolytic capability that fed on fungi or arthropods, sharing a last common ancestor with entomoparasitic fungi (Cordycipitaceae, Ophiocordycipitaceae, Clavicipitaceae).
- Nearly half (41%, 50 of 122 phylogenetic groups) of the Trichoderma pcwdCAZome was obtained via LGT from plant-associated Ascomycota fungi, including Eurotiomycetes (16 cases), Leotiomycetes (7), Sordariomycetes (15), and Dothidiomycetes (2).
- No LGT was detected from Basidiomycota (despite these being common hosts of Trichoderma) or from prokaryotes.
- The only non-fungal LGT was for the auxiliary protein swollenin, putatively from green plants.
- Trichoderma is capable of endoparasitism and adelphoparasitism (parasitism on closely related fungi, even within the same genus/family), which may have facilitated LGT from phylogenetically related Ascomycota donors.
- Escovopsis weberi, a close relative that parasitizes Basidiomycota, showed no such nutritional versatility or LGT events, challenging the host-habitat hypothesis.
- Four GH families (GH6, GH26, GH51, GH62) appear entirely derived from LGT events.
- The study suggests LGT from plant-associated fungi allowed primarily mycotrophic Trichoderma to evolve into decomposers of plant biomass—an unprecedented degree of lateral gene transfer for fungal pcwdCAZyme genes.

**Conclusion:** The authors propose that LGT is linked to Trichoderma's unique ability to parasitize taxonomically related fungi (Ascomycota), and that lateral transfer of genes resulted in profound nutritional expansion, contributing to the emergence of a generalist capable of feeding on organic matter of any origin.

## [RNAi from plants to nematodes](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167779907000236)

[2007, Trends in Biotechnology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/trends-in-biotechnology)Godelieve Gheysen, Bartel Vanholme

### A host plant engineered to become resistant to the four major root-knot nematode species

The paper by Huang _et al._[7] is a good illustration of how fundamental research into the nematode genes that are possibly involved in parasitism might lead to the engineering of crop plants that are resistant to nematodes. The parasitism gene _16D10_ of _[Meloidogyne incognita](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/meloidogyne-incognita "Learn more about Meloidogyne incognita from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ encodes a conserved [RKN](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/meloidogyne "Learn more about RKN from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") peptide, which stimulates [root growth](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/root-growth "Learn more about root growth from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") when expressed in _A. thaliana_ and functions as a ligand for a putative plant transcription factor. This peptide is secreted from the subventral glands of _M. incognita_ into plant roots and is thought to have an important role in the early signaling that occurs during feeding-site formation (Box 1). Expression of a [dsRNA](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/double-stranded-rna "Learn more about dsRNA from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") directed against this gene (using the 35S promoter) resulted in _A. thaliana_ plants with a 69–93% reduction in the number of RKN eggs after infection, compared with the empty-vector control. This result was obtained in agar plate assays with each of the four major RKN species (_M. incognita_, _M. javanica_, _M. arenaria_ and _M. hapla_). RNA blot analysis showed that _16D10_ dsRNA was produced and processed to [siRNAs](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/small-interfering-rna "Learn more about siRNAs from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") in the transgenic lines. This range of resistance is unique and cannot be obtained by any natural RKN resistance gene.

The results of this study raised several key questions: how convincing is the evidence that [RNAi](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/rna-interference "Learn more about RNAi from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") is active from plants to nematodes? does it mean that this technique can now be efficiently used for high-throughput gene function analysis? are crop plants that are resistant to all kinds of nematodes within our reach?

The answer to these questions is certainly not an unequivocal yes, and cautious optimism is warranted.

## [Host delivered-RNAi of effector genes for imparting resistance against root-knot and cyst nematodes in plants](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0885576522000170)

[2022, Physiological and Molecular Plant Pathology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/physiological-and-molecular-plant-pathology)Ila Joshi, ... Pradeep K. Jain

### 5 Effector genes silenced in root-knot nematodes by HD RNAi

[RKNs](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/meloidogyne "Learn more about RKNs from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") include _[Meloidogyne](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/meloidogyne "Learn more about Meloidogyne from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ species which have a wide host range and cause major crop losses. Main target effector genes that have been studied are from _M. incognita_ which is one of the most devastating among all RKNs (Table 1). One of the major effector proteins widely studied among _Meloidogyne_ spp is 16D10. Structurally 16D10 has been confirmed as a [secretory protein](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/secretory-protein "Learn more about secretory protein from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") and is involved in induction of [giant cell](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/foreign-body-giant-cell "Learn more about giant cell from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") formation. It interacts with scarecrow-like plant transcription factors. _[Arabidopsis](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/arabidopsis "Learn more about Arabidopsis from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ plants harboring [dsRNA](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/double-stranded-rna "Learn more about dsRNA from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") construct of 16D10 exhibited 63–90% reduction in number of galls [40] further highlighting its involvement in the formation of [giant cells](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/syncytium "Learn more about giant cells from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). Host delivered silencing of _Mc16D10L_ gene in [transgenic](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/transgenics "Learn more about transgenic from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_Arabidopsis_ and potato led to 68% reduction in number of [egg masses](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/egg-mass "Learn more about egg masses from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") of _M. chitwoodi._ [46,47].

[Calreticulin](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/calreticulin "Learn more about Calreticulin from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), another effector protein, is a [calcium binding protein](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/calcium-binding-protein "Learn more about calcium binding protein from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") having a putative role in cell cycle. It acts as calcium binding chaperone and modulates the storage of calcium in plant cells. The signalling process of plant cells is modified by Calreticulin protein and includes [cell adhesion](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/cell-adhesion "Learn more about cell adhesion from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), gene expression, and [immune regulation](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/immunoregulation "Learn more about immune regulation from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") through calcium binding or direct interaction with other signalling proteins. Manipulation of cell cycle is done to create permanent feeding sites [48]. Knock-down of _Mi-CRT_ gene in pre-parasitic infective juveniles led to reduced ability of nematodes to parasitize plants and induce galls on tomato [49]. Transgenic _Arabidopsis_ with [RNAi](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/rna-interference "Learn more about RNAi from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") construct for _Mi-Crt_ was evaluated against _M. incognita_ and reduction in number of galls in transgenic lines was found on infection with _M. incognita_. Along with HD-RNAi transgenics of _Mi-Crt_ gene, overexpression lines for gene were also evaluated against _M. incognita_ infection. The over expression lines were found to have increased susceptibility for [nematode infection](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/nematode-infection "Learn more about nematode infection from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") with increased number of galls [50]. Another effector gene, _8D05,_ from _M. incognita_ is expressed in the sub-ventral esophageal gland cells throughout the nematode [life cycle](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/life-cycle "Learn more about life cycle from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). This gene is involved in interaction with [tonoplast](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/tonoplast "Learn more about tonoplast from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") intrinsic protein 2 (TIP2) of host plant for parasitization. In transgenic _Arabidopsis_ lines overexpressing _Mi8D05,_ an increase in susceptibility to _M. incognita_ infection was observed. Furthermore, change in plant phenotype was also observed in terms of accelerated [shoot growth](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/shoot-growth "Learn more about shoot growth from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") and [flowering](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/anthesis "Learn more about flowering from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). However, the phenotype of the plant after complete growth was found to be normal. A significant reduction, up to 90%, in number of galls was observed in HD-RNAi lines of _Mi8D05_ [51].

A novel dorsal gland secretory protein, Misp12 (_M. incognita_ putative esophageal gland cell secretory protein 12), was found to be active during adult female stage with the possible function of maintenance of the permanent feeding sites of nematodes. It has been found to be involved in modulation of plant defense mechanisms [52]. The expression studies showed up-regulation of _Misp12_ at the J3/4 and female stages, which suggested that the plant cell defense mechanisms, were controlled at the mature stages to maintain the giant cells for nutrients. Salicylic acid pathway proteins, PR1 and PAL5, were up-regulated in the RNAi lines of _Misp12_ plants and down-regulated in the _Misp12_ over-expressing plants. Furthermore, up-regulation of [jasmonic acid](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/jasmonate "Learn more about jasmonic acid from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (JA) and salicylic acid (SA) pathway defense-related genes in the virus-induced silencing of _Misp12_ plants, and down-regulation of SA pathway defense-related genes in _Misp12_-expressing plants indicated the gene might be associated with the suppression of the plant defense response. Two of the proteins of JA [signalling pathway](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/signal-transduction "Learn more about signalling pathway from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") namely, proteinase inhibitors (_Pin2_) and _β-thionin_ genes were up-regulated in virus induced _Misp12_ gene silencing lines. Silencing lines had reduced number of galls and eggs than control plants. The reduction in number of J3/J4s was 65% and similarly 69% reduction in number of the mature female was observed [52].

Niu et al. [53] reported successful silencing of _Mimsp40_, another effector, in transgenic Arabidopsis plants. In expression studies on different developmental stages, the expression was found to be more in case of parasitic J2s while it decreased in subsequent adult sedentary stages suggesting the function of _Mimsp40_ gene in early onset of parasitism and formation of permanent feeding sites. Furthermore, _Mimsp40_ was localized in sub-ventral esophageal glands confirming its functionality in early parasitism stages. In _Mimsp40_ HD-RNAi _Arabidopsis_ lines, evident reduction was observed in the number of galls produced. _A. tumefaciens_ strain GV3101 cells containing _Mimsp40_ constructs when used to infect tobacco plants suppressed cell death associated with both PTI (PAMP-triggered immunity) and ETI (effector-triggered immunity) responses. One of the major features of PTI response in Arabidopsis plants i.e. [callose](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/callose "Learn more about callose from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") deposition, was found to be reduced in case of _Mimsp40_ over expression lines. It interferes with the innate immune response triggered by elf18 protein. Evident reduction in susceptibility to _M. incognita_ infection was observed in RNAi lines. Infection was found to be decreased in terms of reduction in number of galls in one of the transgenic lines by up to 50%. _Mi msp4_ 0 has been reported to fight the plant defense system initially at the time of invasion [53].

Two other nematode effector proteins _msp-18_ and _msp-20_ secreted in dorsal and sub-ventral glands respectively, have been reported to be silenced in [eggplant](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/eggplants "Learn more about eggplant from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") [54]. The 47% reduction in _M. incognita_ infection was reported in terms of number of galls in case of both _msp-18_ and _msp-20_. HD-RNAi of _Mi-msp-1_ sub-ventral gland gene in egg plant was reported to reduce the nematode infection. The reduction in number of galls was 33.78–46.92% and reduction in egg masses was observed to be up to 41.05–51.16% [55]. Recently _Mi-msp2_ gene was employed to confer resistance against _M. incognita_ in _Arabidopsis_ lines via HD-RNAi. Significant reduction in infection was observed in terms of galls (52–54%) and females (60–66%). Drastic reduction in number of egg masses was observed ranging from 84 to 95%. Moreover, the reduction in _Mi-msp2_ transcript levels was also observed to be up to 85% correlating it well with the reduction in infection [56]. In a detailed study on conferring resistance against _M. incognita_, reduction in number of galls was observed in the RNAi lines of the effector genes _Mi-msp3_ (89%), _Mi-msp5_ (78%), _Mi-msp18_ (86%), and _Mi-msp24_ (89%) [57].

## [Horizontal gene transfer between bacteria and animals](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0168952511000163)

[2011, Trends in Genetics](https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/trends-in-genetics)Julie C. Dunning Hotopp

### Other bacteria-to-animal HGT events

Bacteria–animal HGT is not limited to endosymbiont interactions. _Hydra_ are simple freshwater animals that can reproduce asexually by budding. The _Hydra magnipapillata_ genome contains 71 candidates for HGT that show a closer relation to [bacterial genes](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/bacterial-gene "Learn more about bacterial genes from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") than [metazoan](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/animal "Learn more about metazoan from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") genes, and 70% of these are supported by [expressed sequence tags](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/expressed-sequence-tag "Learn more about expressed sequence tags from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (ESTs) [33]. Many of these 71 genes are strong candidates for HGT because they only have bacterial homologs [33].

In [bdelloid rotifers](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/bdelloid-rotifer "Learn more about bdelloid rotifers from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), which are also small freshwater asexual animals, DNA from bacteria, fungi and plants are concentrated in telomeric regions along with [mobile genetic elements](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/mobile-genetic-elements "Learn more about mobile genetic elements from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")[34]. Although some of the genes resulting from HGT are not functional, others are transcribed. Two genes for bacterial [peptidoglycan](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/peptidoglycan "Learn more about peptidoglycan from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") synthesis are transcribed with the splicing of introns not present in bacteria [34]. One of these proteins was overexpressed in _E. coli_ and found to be a functional [enzyme](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/enzyme "Learn more about enzyme from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")[34].

These two asexual animal genomes show evidence of extensive HGT from diverse organisms including bacteria. This might suggest a correlation between asexuality and the presence and/or persistence of DNA resulting from HGT. This is consistent with Muller's ratchet, which suggests that in the absence of recombination through sexual reproduction, asexual organisms will accumulate mutations in an irreversible manner [35–37] including DNA from HGT. The contribution of asexuality to HGT in animals can be examined using _[Wolbachia](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/wolbachia "Learn more about Wolbachia from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ and the reproductive phenotypes it induces, which include asexuality through parthenogenesis (Box 2).

Numerous HGT events have also occurred during the evolution of plant [parasitic nematodes](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/parasitic-nematodes "Learn more about parasitic nematodes from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_._ It is thought that such transfers allowed the free-living ancestors of these nematodes to exploit plants as a new ecological niche. Sixty genes for six protein families in the _[Meloidogyne incognita](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/meloidogyne-incognita "Learn more about Meloidogyne incognita from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ genome were found to be the result of HGT from diverse bacterial sources followed by subsequent [gene duplication](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/gene-duplication "Learn more about gene duplication from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") and expansion [38]. These include [cellulases](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/cellulase "Learn more about cellulases from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), [pectate lyases](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/pectate-lyase "Learn more about pectate lyases from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") and expansin-like proteins not typically found in other animals but that are involved in degrading or modifying the plant cell wall [38]. The proteins have been biochemically characterized, are secreted into plant tissues, and are involved in parasitism [38]. Another [plant parasitic](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/parasitic-plant "Learn more about plant parasitic from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") nematode _[Heterodera glycines](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/heterodera-glycines "Learn more about Heterodera glycines from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ contains a biosynthetic pathway for [vitamin B6](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/vitamin-b6 "Learn more about vitamin B6 from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") of bacterial origin [39]. Despite the apparent prokaryotic origin of these genes, they contain introns, have polyadenylated transcripts, and map to the nematode chromosome [39]. Phylogenetic analysis places them closest to _Protochlamydia amoebophila_, an endosymbiont of [amoeba](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/amoeba-life-cycle-stage "Learn more about amoeba from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")[39].

Given that there are many more [bacterial cells](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/bacterial-cell "Learn more about bacterial cells from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") relative to eukaryotic ones and that [eukaryotic cells](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/eukaryotic-cell "Learn more about eukaryotic cells from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") are frequently in proximity to bacterial cells, it is not surprising that HGT is increasingly described between bacteria and animals. For example, the human body contains more bacterial cells than [human cells](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/human-cell "Learn more about human cells from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (for review see [40]), and many of these bacteria are in intimate contact with human mucosal cells. In addition, many of these same bacteria have mechanisms, such as the [type IV secretion system](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/type-iv-secretion-system "Learn more about type IV secretion system from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), to transfer DNA to the environment and to other organisms. Therefore, there are many opportunities and avenues for HGT from bacteria to animals. This type of HGT is of interest because it has the potential to provide novel functions to animals, allow adaptation to novel niches, and affect their evolution. Such transfers from the [human microbiome](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/human-microbiome "Learn more about human microbiome from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") also have the potential to induce [somatic cell](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/somatic-cell "Learn more about somatic cell from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") mutations, and thereby be important to human health (Box 3).

Box 3
Bacteria-to-human HGT and the microbiome

During the original public effort to sequence the human genome, an analysis of the inheritance patterns of exons [57] refuted a previous analysis describing 223 human proteins arising from bacterial HGT [55]. Yet, in this analysis 40 genes were found to be shared exclusively between bacteria and humans [57], as would genes resulting from bacteria HGT. A subsequent phylogenetic analysis of human proteins for HGT [60] overlooked comparisons with prokaryotes. Additionally, the HGT of units smaller than a gene [61] would be obscured in both analyses. All of these points might suggest further analysis is warranted that does not focus solely on whole exons or genes and makes use of the many bacterial genomes sequenced subsequently.

Overall, it seems clear that inherited HGT is not ubiquitous from bacteria to humans. However, with the enormous size of the human microbiome, is there an equally enormous opportunity for HGT to somatic cells that could have profound effects in human health and disease? Such somatic cell mutations would largely be overlooked in whole genome assemblies.

The American Cancer Society reports that 15–20% of cancers worldwide and 10% of cancers in developed countries are linked to viral, bacterial or parasite infections. Although chronic inflammation is increasingly implicated as a mechanism for cancer development (for a review, see [62]), proto-oncogene disruption by bacterial DNA could provide yet another mechanism. Another avenue for disease following HGT would be through the transcription and expression of bacterial DNA. _A. tumefaciens_ induces the production of a plant tumor through the expression and transcription of bacterial DNA [10,63,64]. It, therefore, seems plausible that the expression and transcription of bacterial DNA could induce tumors in animals.

Although disadvantageous outcomes of HGT are easy to conceptualize, is there room for advantageous outcomes? Bacteria in the digestive tract are associated with the fermentation of nondigestible dietary residues and with the production of vitamin K (for a review, see [65]). Could HGT in our intestinal cells allow for the gain of these properties? With the decreasing costs of human genome sequencing, we might soon be able to compare the DNA content of individual cells in frequent contact with bacteria with those from more sterile portions of the body to address these highly speculative questions.

## [The invisible life inside plants: Deciphering the riddles of endophytic bacterial diversity](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0734975020301166)

[2020, Biotechnology Advances](https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/biotechnology-advances)Jakub Papik, ... Ondrej Uhlik

### 4.5 Microbe-microbe interactions within a holobiont

The overwhelming number of interconnections among microorganisms and the host plant, which together form an ecological unit, have been recently discussed in terms of their mutually inclusive development (Occhipinti, 2013; Vandenkoornhuyse et al., 2015). This has led to the concept of the hologenome which defines the multicellular organism and its associated microorganisms as a unique entity where evolutionary selection occurs not only on the level of the host and its [microbiota](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/microflora "Learn more about microbiota from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), but also within associated microbes (Hassani et al., 2018; Vandenkoornhuyse et al., 2015). Generally, microorganisms react more rapidly to environmental changes than their host organism, and thus are likely to play a crucial role in the evolution of the entire [holobiont](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/holobiont "Learn more about holobiont from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (Rosenberg and Zilber-Rosenberg, 2016). A study by Egamberdieva et al. (2017) demonstrated this phenomenon by showing that mutualistic interaction between the salt-tolerant endophyte _[Bacillus](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/bacilli "Learn more about Bacillus from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ _subtilis_ and non-tolerant _[Mesorhizobium ciceri](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/mesorhizobium-ciceri "Learn more about Mesorhizobium ciceri from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ improved the symbiotic performance of _M. ciceri_ and plant growth under [saline soil](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/saline-soil "Learn more about saline soil from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") conditions.

Endophytic bacteria are able to antagonize microbial phytopathogens (Furnkranz et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2009; Khalaf and Raizada, 2018; Zhao et al., 2018), and in turn pathogenic infection impacts the composition of endophytic communities as well. For instance, the diversity of bacterial endophytes in potato (_[Solanum](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/lycopersicon "Learn more about Solanum from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ _tuberosum_ L.) stems was increased in plants infected by the bacterial pathogen _[Erwinia carotovora](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/pectobacterium-carotovorum "Learn more about Erwinia carotovora from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ subsp. _atroseptica_ in contrast to healthy plants (Reiter et al., 2002). Another study demonstrated a shift in bacterial root endophytic community composition in tomatoes upon infection by the root-knot nematode _Meloidogyne incognita_, leading to an enrichment of the endophytic _[Sphingobacteriales](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/sphingobacteriales "Learn more about Sphingobacteriales from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_, _[Flavobacteriales](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/flavobacteriales "Learn more about Flavobacteriales from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_, and nematode-associated _Rhodocyclales_ and _[Enterobacteriales](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/enterobacteriales "Learn more about Enterobacteriales from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ (Tian et al., 2015). In contrast, Bulgari et al. (2011) observed a decrease in endophytic bacterial diversity in grapevine (_[Vitis](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/vitis "Learn more about Vitis from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ _vinifera_ L.) leaves upon [phytoplasma](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/phytoplasma "Learn more about phytoplasma from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") infection, but at the expense of enriching _[Burkholderia](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/burkholderia "Learn more about Burkholderia from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ and _Bacillus_, endophytic taxa that are more resistant to reactive oxygen species and able to induce a plant defence response, possibly leading to plant recovery.

Interactions between fungi and bacteria also take place in the endosphere and have been shown to be crucial for the [life cycle](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/life-cycle "Learn more about life cycle from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") development of plant-associated fungi. Such relationships extend beyond plant-microbe and microbe-microbe interactions and highlight the complexity of a holobiont, since they occur among the host plant, its microbial inhabitants and their [endosymbionts](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/endosymbiont "Learn more about endosymbionts from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). Evidence has been found that endofungal bacteria can enhance the production of phytohormones by a fungus (Hoffman et al., 2013) or produce [phytotoxins](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/phytotoxin "Learn more about phytotoxins from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") responsible for the pathogenic nature of their host. The latter is the case for rhizoxin produced by _Burkholderia rhizoxinica_, the endosymbiont of the pathogennic fungus _[Rhizopus microsporus](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/rhizopus-microsporus "Learn more about Rhizopus microsporus from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ that causes rice seedling blight (Partida-Martinez and Hertweck, 2005). Endofungal colonization has also been speculated to benefit the survival of [plant pathogens](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/plant-pathogens "Learn more about plant pathogens from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") in soil; the globally distributed phytopathogenic bacterium _[Ralstonia solanacearum](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/ralstonia-solanacearum "Learn more about Ralstonia solanacearum from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ produces a secondary metabolite, ralsolamycin, which on the one hand facilitates the invasion of the bacterium into the fungal hyphae and induces [chlamydospore](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/chlamydospore "Learn more about chlamydospore from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") formation of the plant-associated fungus on the other. This interaction enhances the survival of the fungus, which in turn provides a specific niche for [bacterial colonization](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/bacterial-colonization "Learn more about bacterial colonization from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (Spraker et al., 2016). As for mutualistic interactions among [endophytic fungi](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/endophytic-fungus "Learn more about endophytic fungi from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") and bacteria, Salvioli et al. (2016) showed that the obligate bacterial endosymbiont ‘_Candidatus_ Glomeribacter gigasporarum’ of the [arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/arbuscular-mycorrhiza "Learn more about arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_[Gigaspora margarita](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/gigaspora-margarita "Learn more about Gigaspora margarita from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ increased the rate of [sporulation](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/sporogenesis "Learn more about sporulation from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") of the symbiotic fungus and enhanced its ATP production and detoxification of reactive oxygen species. At the same time, the bacterium enhanced the fungal responsiveness to [strigolactones](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/strigolactone "Learn more about strigolactones from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), plant-derived signal molecules crucial for establishing the mutualistic association. Such an interaction led to improved fungal ecological fitness and its symbiotic capacity (Salvioli et al., 2016).

Cooperative microbe-microbe interactions often take place in biofilms, and plant-associated habitats are not an exception. While biofilm production contributes to the colonization of plant surfaces, such as [phyllosphere](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/phyllosphere "Learn more about phyllosphere from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), [rhizosphere](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/rhizosphere "Learn more about rhizosphere from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), or spermosphere, as reviewed by Ramey et al., 2004, it is still unknown to what extent the processes associated with biofilm development determine the endophytic lifestyle. The previously mentioned production of EPSs, an important trait for endophytic colonization, is required for the biofilm formation and determines the conditions of microbial life in biofilms (Flemming et al., 2007; Meneses et al., 2011; Smol'Kina et al., 2012). It is also possible that the ability to produce EPSs and to form biofilms might serve as a protective mechanism of survival during transient hostile conditions _in_ _[planta](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/plantae "Learn more about planta from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ (van Overbeek and Saikkonen, 2016). Importantly, biofilms are hotspots of horizontal gene transfer. While recent studies suggested that there is a natural barrier to horizontal gene transfer from prokaryotic to eukaryotic [lineages](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/lineages "Learn more about lineages from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), i.e. from bacteria to the host plant (Ku and Martin, 2016; Wickell and Li, 2020), the transfer of [genetic](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/genetics "Learn more about genetic from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") material between [prokaryotes](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/prokaryote "Learn more about prokaryotes from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") remains an important yet unexplored evolutionary mechanism in bacterial endophytes (for a recent review see Tiwari and Bae (2020)). Although only a few studies have aimed to explore the role of horizontal gene transfer between prokaryotes in relation to endophytism so far, they have suggested its importance in the adaptation and survival of both endophytes and the host plant (Gu et al., 2018; Taghavi et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2010; Weyens et al., 2009).

Overall, our knowledge of these multitrophic interactions within the plant holobiont are relatively fragmental, and we have practically no complex insight into these interactions. Only recently, several studies applied the [keystone species](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/keystone-species "Learn more about keystone species from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") concept to plant-associated microbiota (Liu et al., 2019; Macedo-Raygoza et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019). By definition, keystone species are organisms, including microbes, that have an immense impact on a specific ecosystem; in this case, a holobiont. Such species influence the community structure and diversity and are essential for the ecosystem's functioning (Paine, 1966). Identifying keystone endophytic taxa of particular crops and solving their unique roles in plants would significantly contribute to the development of the above-mentioned agricultural applications of endophytes and also deepen our knowledge of microbial assembly in the endosphere.

### 2 Taxonomy, botanical description and production

Chayote is taxonomically classified within _[Embryophytes](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/embryophyta "Learn more about Embryophytes from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_; class _[Magnoliopsida](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/magnoliopsida "Learn more about Magnoliopsida from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_; order _Violales_; family _[Cucurbitaceae](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/cucurbitaceae "Learn more about Cucurbitaceae from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ (along with bitter apple, gourd, cucumber, melon, and pumpkin); genre _Sechium_ and species _[Sechium edule](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/sechium-edule "Learn more about Sechium edule from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ Jacq Sw. (Lim, 2012; Saade, 1996). There are few reports available regarding the [genetic diversity](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/genetic-divergence "Learn more about genetic diversity from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") of chayote (Cadena-Iñiguez et al., 2007; Machida-Hirano et al., 2015). _Sechium edule_ species presents a wide variation regarding the form and colour of fruits, many of which are only known on local markets. There are ten species currently accepted to exist, eight of which are wild (_S. Chinantlense_, _S. compositum_, _S. hintonii_, _S. talamancense_, _S. panamense_, _S. pittieri_, _S. venosum_ and _S. vilosum_) and two cultivated (_S. tabaco_ and _S. edule_) (Saade, 1996). Despite the large variety of _Sechium edule_ commercially cultivated, only the _Viren levis_, called “smooth green”, has been utilized for large-scale exploitation. Mexico has been the main producer and exporter of “smooth green” chayote worldwide (Cadena-Iñiguez et al., 2007).

Botanically, chayote plant grows from a single thick root, which produces adventitious tuberous roots (Fig. 1). The stems are several metres long, slightly compressed and longitudinally furrowed. The flowers are unisexual and the leaves are slightly [lobate](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/clobetasol-propionate "Learn more about lobate from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") (with three to five angular lobes) and have minutely denticulate margins and three to five divided [tendrils](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/tendril "Learn more about tendrils from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). The fruits are pear shaped and grow either individually or in pairs on a shared [peduncle](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/peduncle "Learn more about peduncle from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"). They are fleshy or fleshy-fibrous, may have longitudinal ridges or [furrows](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/furrows "Learn more about furrows from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages"), and come in many different shapes (globose, ovoid, subovoid, pyriform), sizes (4.3–26.5 cm long, 3–11 cm wide), number and type of spines, and colours (white and yellowish or pale green to dark green). The fruit is highly perishable and, unlike other cucurbits, contains only a single seed, which is compressed, smooth and can germinate and send out a shoot within thirty days of harvesting. In cultivated plants, the seed germinates when the fruit is still on the plant, while in wild plants only once the fruit becomes detached (Aung, Ball, & Kushad, 1990; Bermejo & León, 1994; Saade, 1996; Cadena-Iñiguez et al., 2007).

This ScienceDirect topic page provides an AI-generated overview of Meloidogyne incognita, a species of root-knot nematode (RKN) harmful to chili plants and other crops. The page compiles chapters and articles on resistance research, particularly focusing on RNA interference (RNAi) strategies to engineer nematode-resistant plants.

Key findings from the articles include:

**RNAi-Based Resistance (2007, 2022):** The parasitism gene 16D10 of M. incognita encodes a conserved RKN peptide secreted from subventral glands that stimulates root growth and functions as a ligand for plant transcription factors during feeding-site formation. Transgenic Arabidopsis plants expressing dsRNA against 16D10 showed 69-93% reduction in RKN eggs across the four major RKN species (M. incognita, M. javanica, M. arenaria, M. hapla) — a resistance range unattainable with natural RKN resistance genes. A 2022 review documents host-delivered RNAi (HD-RNAi) targeting multiple effector genes with significant reductions in galls and egg masses, including: 16D10 (63-90% gall reduction), Mi-CRT calreticulin, 8D05 (up to 90% gall reduction), Misp12 (65% reduction in J3/J4s, 69% in mature females), Mimsp40 (up to 50% gall reduction), msp-18 and msp-20 (47% reduction), Mi-msp-1, Mi-msp2 (52-54% galls, 60-66% females, 84-95% egg masses), and Mi-msp3 (89%), Mi-msp5 (78%), Mi-msp18 (86%), Mi-msp24 (89%).

**Horizontal Gene Transfer (2011):** Sixty genes across six protein families in the M. incognita genome resulted from HGT from bacterial sources, including cellulases, pectate lyases, and expansin-like proteins involved in degrading plant cell walls — facilitating the nematode's exploitation of plants as a new ecological niche.

**Endophytic Interactions (2020):** M. incognita infection shifts bacterial root endophytic community composition in tomatoes, enriching Sphingobacteriales, Flavobacteriales, Rhodocyclales, and Enterobacteriales.

**Nematode Secretions (2008):** Describes how nematode esophageal gland cell secretions, including cell-wall modifying proteins, chorismate mutase, CLE peptides, and ubiquitin-pathway proteins, are released through the stylet to form specialized feeding cells.

<webpage_content>
Agri Articles (e-Magazine for Agricultural Articles) Volume: 05, Issue: 03 (MAY-JUNE, 2025) Available online at http://www.agriarticles.com Agri Articles, ISSN: 2582-9882 Agri Articles ISSN: 2582-9882 Page 258 Interactions between Plant Parasitic Nematodes and Bacteria: Now and Then *Banajit Baishya Master’s Research Scholar, Department of Nematology, College of Post Graduate Studies in Agricultural Sciences, Umiam, Meghalaya, India *Corresponding Author’s email: banajit7372@gmail.com ased on genome-to-genome analyses of gene sequences obtained from plant-parasitic, root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.), it seems likely that certain genes have been derived from bacteria by horizontal gene transfer. Strikingly, a common theme underpinning the function of these genes is their apparent direct relationship to the nematodes’ parasitic lifestyle. Phylogenetic analyses implicate rhizobacteria as the predominant group of ‘gene donor’ bacteria. Root-knot nematodes and rhizobia occupy similar niches in the soil and in roots, and thus the opportunity for genetic exchange may be omnipresent. Further, both organisms establish intimate developmental interactions with host plants, and mounting evidence suggests that the mechanisms for these interactions are shared too. We propose that the origin of parasitism in Meloidogyne may have been facilitated by acquisition of genetic material from soil bacteria through horizontal transfer, and that such events represented key steps in speciation of plant-parasitic nematodes. To further understand the mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer, and also to provide experimental tools to manipulate this promising bio-control agent, we have initiated a genomic sequence of the bacterial hyper parasite of plant parasitic nematodes, Pasteuria Penetrans. Initial data have established that P. penetrans is closely related to Bacillus spp., to the extent that considerable genome synteny is apparent. Keywords: Horizontal gene transfer; Meloidogyne; Pasteuria penetrans; Rhizobia; Root-knot nematode; Synteny. Introduction Nematodes are the most abundant and speciose metazoans, and account for up to 80% of the kingdom’s members. Not surprisingly, nematodes have evolved to occupy diverse ecological niches. Like the model organism Caenorhabditis elegans, most are free-living and graze on microbes or detritus, and as such, have no obvious direct impact on humans. Others however, are adapted as parasites and are responsible for such widespread problems as debilitation of livestock, human disease, and crop damage. Not surprisingly, C. elegans and animal- and human-parasitic species have been studied disproportionate to their numbers. In this short article, we will report on recent findings in plant-parasitic nematodes with a particular emphasis on the role that acquisition of bacterial genes by ancestral plant-parasitic forms might have played in evolution of plant-parasitism. Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) has previously been suggested for individual nematode genes and indeed, an explicit model of HGT in nematode evolution has been proposed. A recent comprehensive genomic analysis revealed a surprising number of nematode genes as being candidates for having arisen via HGT from bacteria. Because these data suggest that associations between nematodes and bacteria may have been extensive in the evolutionary past, we have become interested in extant interactions between bacteria and plant parasitic nematodes. Collectively, genome-wide analyses of plant-parasitic nematodes and their bacterial pathogens will likely shed B Baishya (2025) Agri Articles, 05(03): 258-261 (MAY-JUNE, 2025) Agri Articles ISSN: 2582-9882 Page 259 considerable light on the function and evolution of these pathogens, and further, will likely suggest new strategies for nematode control. Mode of Action 1. Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT): Certain genes in Meloidogyne spp. appear to have been acquired from bacteria via horizontal gene transfer. These genes are directly related to the parasitic lifestyle, aiding nematodes in host plant invasion, such as those encoding cellulases, pectate lyases, and Nod factor-like proteins. The likely bacterial donors include rhizobacteria (e.g., Rhizobium, Pseudomonas, Bacillus), which share ecological niches with nematodes. 2. Pasteuria penetrans: Pasteuria is a bacterial hyper parasite that infects and kills plant-parasitic nematodes, and its mode of action includes: Attachment of endospores to the nematode cuticle. Germination and penetration of the nematode after it infects a plant root. Colonization of the nematode’s body, particularly reproductive tissues, preventing egg production. Sporulation inside the nematode, eventually killing it and releasing new endospores into the soil. 3. Biocontrol Implications: Pasteuria's species-specificity and spore durability make it a promising biological control agent. Genomic sequencing of Pasteuria reveals a close relation to Bacillus subtilis, helping model its biology and improve bio control strategies. Some interaction Between Nematode and bacteria and their Economic importance Different sorts of interactions can be found between nematodes and bacteria. It may be neutral if no one is harmed. In obligate mutualistic interactions, such as between entomopathogenic nematodes (EPNs) and their symbiotic bacteria, both parties gain. In case of a disease complex, protocooperation is noticed. Commensalism is uncommon, although it does occur. Both get injured during competition. Nematodes suffer when natural enemies attack them. WhIn case of obligate parasitic interaction, nematodes suffer during interacting. (Table 1) Nematode-induced physiological changes to the host plant: Different sedentary endoparasites form galls (giant cells) or syncytia, i.e., nutrient-rich cells, which act as a substrate for bacterial colonization. Nematode-induced physiological changes to the host plant: Different sedentary endoparasites form galls (giant cells) or syncytia, i.e., nutrient-rich cells, which act as a substrate for bacterial colonization.(table2) Baishya (2025) Agri Articles, 05(03): 258-261 (MAY-JUNE, 2025) Agri Articles ISSN: 2582-9882 Page 260 Animal parasitic nematodes-bacteria interaction: Wolbachia is a widespread intracellular bacterial symbiont of arthropods and common in insects. One of their more exotic and unexpected hosts is the filarial nematodes, parasites responsible for several severe maladies, such as- onchocerciasis (river blindness), lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis) and dirofilariasis (heartworm). It is a tri-partite symbiotic interaction where three different biological entities are involved. They are 1) The host reservoir (Humans and other mammals, like- dogs, cats and monkeys, etc., having complex digestive system making them ideal to host parasites and endosymbionts), 2) Parasite (Filarial nematodes: thread-like adults reside in lymphatic/subcutaneous tissues. Microfilariae circulate in the blood or migrate through tissues), 3) Endosymbiont (Wolbachia: bacteria which infects arthropods and some nematodes. In some cases, the host cannot reproduce, or even survive, without it). Wolbachia is obligate, Rickettsia-like, endosymbiotic, maternally inherited, intracellular α-proteobacteria, round with a diameter of 0.5μm, enclosed in a double trilaminate membrane with a cytoplasm containing ribosomal-like granules. Endosymbionts and PPNs: Endosymbiotic bacteria have major effects on virulence and biology of associated PPNs. Cardinium, Wolbachia, Xiphinematobacter and Burkholderia are four major endosymbionts who arise from quite divergent phyla (Bacteroidetes, Verrucomicrobia, Alphaproteobacteria and Betaproteobacteria) and found to be associated with PPNs. Wang and Wu in 2017 explained simultaneous evolution of PPNs with their associated endosymbiont. Early plant feeding nematodes are mainly ectoparasites and have limited efficiency in feeding and inducing parasitism. But sometimes, they may acquire endosymbionts from interacting soil eukaryotes that make them fit to digest plant cells or synthesize essential nutrients which have limited supply in roots, e.g., Xiphinematobacter (endosymbiont) may synthesize essential amino acids to supplement Xiphinema americanum (nematode)’s diet of root phloem. Abundant carbon assimilation from newly accessible plant matter or bacteria-supplied nutrients (e.g., heme, lipoate and amino acids) increase the efficiency of nematodes. Nematodes achieve cell wall degrading capacity (e.g., cellulases, glucanases and pectinases) by acquiring additional endosymbionts, like- Wolbachia-like Rickettsiales ancestor. They also keep evolving with symbionts until the HGT occurs because after that these enzymes will be no longer needed from symbionts’ end. Nematodes with ability to support symbionts are more rapidly colonized by new endosymbionts. It may be called as symbiont facilitation or replacement, possibly in case of Cardinium- or Burkholderia- like symbionts. Conclusion The interactions between plant parasitic nematodes (PPNs) and bacteria are complex and significantly influence plant health and disease progression. In the past, nematodes and bacteria were studied in isolation, but recent research has shown that they often act together, either synergistically or antagonistically. PPNs can damage root systems, creating entry points for pathogenic bacteria and promoting co-infections. Conversely, certain bacteria can inhibit nematode activity through antagonistic interactions or by triggering plant defense mechanisms. Beneficial bacteria, such as plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR), have emerged as promising biocontrol agents against nematodes, offering an environmentally friendly alternative to chemical treatments. With the help of molecular and genomic tools, researchers are now better able to unravel the mechanisms behind these interactions and develop targeted management strategies. Understanding the dynamic relationships between PPNs and bacteria is vital for improving crop productivity and sustainability. A holistic, integrated approach that combines biological, ecological, and technological insights will be key to managing these pests effectively in the future. References 1. David McK.
