From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Transfer of genes from unrelated organisms

"HGT" redirects here. For other uses, see [HGT (disambiguation)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HGT_(disambiguation) "HGT (disambiguation)").

This article is about the natural process. For artificial gene transfer, see [Gene delivery](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_delivery "Gene delivery").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Tree_Of_Life_%28with_horizontal_gene_transfer%29.svg/250px-Tree_Of_Life_%28with_horizontal_gene_transfer%29.svg.png)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tree_Of_Life_(with_horizontal_gene_transfer).svg)

Tree of life showing vertical and horizontal gene transfers

**Horizontal gene transfer** (**HGT**) or **lateral gene transfer** (**LGT**)[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) is the movement of genetic material between [organisms](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organism "Organism") other than by the ("[vertical](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertical_transmission "Vertical transmission")") transmission of [DNA](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") from parent to offspring ([reproduction](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproduction "Reproduction")).[[4]](#cite_note-4) HGT is an important factor in the evolution of many organisms.[[5]](#cite_note-Gyles_2014-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) HGT is influencing scientific understanding of higher-order evolution while more significantly shifting perspectives on bacterial evolution.[[7]](#cite_note-Ochman_2005-7)

Horizontal gene transfer is the primary mechanism for the spread of [antibiotic resistance](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antibiotic_resistance "Antibiotic resistance") in bacteria,[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[5]](#cite_note-Gyles_2014-5)[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) and plays an important role in the evolution of [bacteria](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteria "Bacteria") that can degrade novel compounds such as human-created [pesticides](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bactericide "Bactericide")[[11]](#cite_note-11) and in the evolution, maintenance, and transmission of [virulence](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virulence "Virulence").[[12]](#cite_note-Keen_2012-12) It often involves [temperate](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperateness_(virology) "Temperateness (virology)") [bacteriophages](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteriophage "Bacteriophage") and [plasmids](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasmids "Plasmids").[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) Genes responsible for antibiotic resistance in one species of bacteria can be transferred to another species of bacteria through various mechanisms of HGT such as [transformation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformation_(genetics) "Transformation (genetics)"), [transduction](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transduction_(genetics) "Transduction (genetics)") and [conjugation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacterial_conjugation "Bacterial conjugation"), subsequently arming the antibiotic resistant genes' recipient against antibiotics. The rapid spread of antibiotic resistance genes in this manner is becoming a challenge to manage in the field of medicine. Ecological factors may also play a role in the HGT of antibiotic resistant genes.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

Horizontal gene transfer is recognized as a pervasive evolutionary process that distributes genes between divergent prokaryotic lineages[[17]](#cite_note-Zhou_2021-17) and can also involve eukaryotes.[[18]](#cite_note-Sieber_2017-18)[[19]](#cite_note-Gabaldón_2021-19) HGT events are thought to occur less frequently in eukaryotes than in prokaryotes. However, growing evidence indicates that HGT is relatively common among many eukaryotic species and can have an impact on adaptation to novel environments. Its study, however, is hindered by the complexity of eukaryotic genomes and the abundance of repeat-rich regions, which complicate the accurate identification and characterization of transferred genes.[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)

It is postulated that HGT promotes the maintenance of a universal life biochemistry and, subsequently, the universality of the genetic code.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Horizontal_gene_transfer&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[Griffith's experiment](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Griffith's_experiment "Griffith's experiment"), reported in 1928 by [Frederick Griffith](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Griffith "Frederick Griffith"),[[23]](#cite_note-23) was the first experiment suggesting that bacteria are capable of transferring genetic information through a process known as [transformation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformation_(genetics) "Transformation (genetics)").[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-25) Griffith's findings [were followed by research](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avery–MacLeod–McCarty_experiment "Avery–MacLeod–McCarty experiment") in the late 1930s and early 1940s that isolated [DNA](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") as the material that communicated this genetic information.

Horizontal genetic transfer was then described in Seattle in 1951, in a paper demonstrating that the transfer of a viral gene into *[Corynebacterium diphtheriae](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corynebacterium_diphtheriae "Corynebacterium diphtheriae")* created a virulent strain from a non-virulent strain,[[26]](#cite_note-26) simultaneously revealing the mechanism of [diphtheria](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diphtheria "Diphtheria") (that patients could be infected with the bacteria but not have any symptoms, and then suddenly convert later or never),[[27]](#cite_note-27) and giving the first example for the relevance of the [lysogenic cycle](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysogenic_cycle "Lysogenic cycle").[[28]](#cite_note-28) Inter-bacterial gene transfer was first described in Japan in a 1959 publication that demonstrated the transfer of antibiotic resistance between different species of [bacteria](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteria "Bacteria").[[29]](#cite_note-29)[[30]](#cite_note-30) In the mid-1980s, Syvanen[[31]](#cite_note-31) postulated that biologically significant lateral gene transfer has existed since the beginning of life on Earth and has been involved in shaping all of evolutionary history.

As Jian, Rivera and Lake (1999) put it: "Increasingly, studies of genes and genomes are indicating that considerable horizontal transfer has occurred between [prokaryotes](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prokaryote "Prokaryote")"[[32]](#cite_note-32) (see also Lake and Rivera, 2007).[[33]](#cite_note-33) The phenomenon appears to have had some significance for unicellular [eukaryotes](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eukaryote "Eukaryote") as well. As Bapteste et al. (2005) observe, "additional evidence suggests that gene transfer might also be an important evolutionary mechanism in [protist](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protist "Protist") evolution."[[34]](#cite_note-34)

Grafting of one plant to another can transfer [chloroplasts](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloroplast "Chloroplast") ([organelles](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organelle "Organelle") in plant cells that conduct [photosynthesis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis "Photosynthesis")), [mitochondrial DNA](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitochondrial_DNA "Mitochondrial DNA"), and the entire [cell nucleus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_nucleus "Cell nucleus") containing the [genome](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genome "Genome") to potentially make a new species.[[35]](#cite_note-35) Some [Lepidoptera](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lepidoptera "Lepidoptera") (e.g. [monarch butterflies](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarch_butterflies "Monarch butterflies") and [silkworms](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silkworm "Silkworm")) have been genetically modified by horizontal gene transfer from the wasp [bracovirus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bracovirus "Bracovirus").[[36]](#cite_note-36) Bites from insects in the family [Reduviidae](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reduviidae "Reduviidae") (assassin bugs) can, via a parasite, infect humans with the [trypanosomal](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trypanosoma "Trypanosoma") [Chagas disease](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chagas_disease "Chagas disease"), which can insert its DNA into the [human genome](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_genome "Human genome").[[37]](#cite_note-37) It has been suggested that lateral gene transfer to humans from bacteria may play a role in cancer.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

Aaron Richardson and [Jeffrey D. Palmer](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_D._Palmer "Jeffrey D. Palmer") state: "Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) has played a major role in bacterial evolution and is fairly common in certain unicellular eukaryotes. However, the prevalence and importance of HGT in the evolution of [multicellular](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multicellular "Multicellular") eukaryotes remain unclear."[[39]](#cite_note-39)

Due to the increasing amount of evidence suggesting the importance of these phenomena for evolution (see [below](#Importance_in_evolution)) molecular biologists such as Peter Gogarten have described horizontal gene transfer as "A New Paradigm for Biology".[[40]](#cite_note-Gogarten_2000-40)

## Mechanisms

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Horizontal_gene_transfer&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Mechanisms")]

There are several mechanisms for horizontal gene transfer:[[5]](#cite_note-Gyles_2014-5)[[41]](#cite_note-Todar_2012-41)[[42]](#cite_note-Maloy_2002-42)

* [Transformation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformation_(genetics) "Transformation (genetics)"), the genetic alteration of a [cell](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_(biology) "Cell (biology)") resulting from the introduction, uptake and [expression](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_expression "Gene expression") of foreign genetic material ([DNA](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") or [RNA](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RNA "RNA")).[[43]](#cite_note-Stearns_2005-43) This process is relatively common in bacteria, but less so in eukaryotes.[[44]](#cite_note-44) Transformation is often used in laboratories to insert novel genes into bacteria for experiments or for industrial or medical applications. See also [molecular biology](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_biology "Molecular biology") and [biotechnology](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biotechnology "Biotechnology").[*[citation needed](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]
* [Transduction](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transduction_(genetics) "Transduction (genetics)"), the process in which bacterial DNA is moved from one bacterium to another by a virus (a bacteriophage, or [phage](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phage "Phage")).[[43]](#cite_note-Stearns_2005-43)
* [Bacterial conjugation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacterial_conjugation "Bacterial conjugation"), a process that involves the transfer of DNA via a plasmid from a donor cell to a recombinant recipient cell during cell-to-cell contact.[[43]](#cite_note-Stearns_2005-43)
* [Gene transfer agents](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_transfer_agent "Gene transfer agent"), virus-like elements encoded by the host that are found in the [alphaproteobacteria](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphaproteobacteria "Alphaproteobacteria") order [Rhodobacterales](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodobacterales "Rhodobacterales").[[45]](#cite_note-McDaniel_2010-45)

### Horizontal transposon transfer

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Horizontal_gene_transfer&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Horizontal transposon transfer")]

A [transposable element](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transposable_element "Transposable element") (TE) (also called a transposon or jumping gene) is a mobile segment of DNA that can sometimes pick up a resistance gene and insert it into a plasmid or chromosome, thereby inducing horizontal gene transfer of antibiotic resistance.[[43]](#cite_note-Stearns_2005-43)

Horizontal transposon transfer (HTT) refers to the passage of pieces of DNA that are characterized by their ability to move from one [locus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_locus "Gene locus") to another between genomes by means other than parent-to-offspring inheritance. Horizontal gene transfer has long been thought to be crucial to prokaryotic evolution, but there is a growing amount of data showing that HTT is a common and widespread phenomenon in [eukaryote](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eukaryote "Eukaryote") evolution as well.[[46]](#cite_note-Schaack_2010-46) On the transposable element side, spreading between genomes via horizontal transfer may be viewed as a strategy to escape purging due to purifying selection, mutational decay and/or host defense mechanisms.[[47]](#cite_note-Dupeyron_2014-47)

HTT can occur with any type of transposable elements, but [DNA transposons](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_transposon "DNA transposon") and [LTR retroelements](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retroelement "Retroelement") are more likely to be capable of HTT because both have a stable, double-stranded DNA intermediate that is thought to be sturdier than the single-stranded RNA intermediate of [non-LTR retroelements](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retroelement "Retroelement"), which can be highly degradable.[[46]](#cite_note-Schaack_2010-46) [Non-autonomous elements](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transposable_element "Transposable element") may be less likely to transfer horizontally compared to [autonomous elements](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transposable_element "Transposable element") because they do not encode the proteins required for their own mobilization. The structure of these non-autonomous elements generally consists of an intronless gene encoding a [transposase](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transposase "Transposase") protein, and may or may not have a promoter sequence. Those that do not have promoter sequences encoded within the mobile region rely on adjacent host promoters for expression.[[46]](#cite_note-Schaack_2010-46) Horizontal transfer is thought to play an important role in the TE life cycle.[[46]](#cite_note-Schaack_2010-46) In plants, it appears that [LTR retrotransposons](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LTR_retrotransposons "LTR retrotransposons") of the Copia superfamilies, especially those with low copy numbers from the Ale and Ivana lineages, are more likely to undergo horizontal transfer between different plant species.[[48]](#cite_note-Aubin_2023-48)

HTT has been shown to occur between species and across continents in both plants[[49]](#cite_note-Baidouri_2014-49) and animals (Ivancevic et al. 2013), though some TEs have been shown to more successfully colonize the genomes of certain species over others.[[50]](#cite_note-Ivancevic_2013-50) Both spatial and taxonomic proximity of species has been proposed to favor HTTs in plants and animals.[[49]](#cite_note-Baidouri_2014-49) It is unknown how the density of a population may affect the rate of HTT events within a population, but close proximity due to [parasitism](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasitism "Parasitism") and cross contamination due to crowding have been proposed to favor HTT in both plants and animals.[[49]](#cite_note-Baidouri_2014-49) In plants, the interaction between lianas and trees has been shown to facilitate HTT in natural ecosystems.[[48]](#cite_note-Aubin_2023-48) Successful transfer of a transposable element requires delivery of DNA from donor to host cell (and to the germ line for multi-cellular organisms), followed by integration into the recipient host genome.[[46]](#cite_note-Schaack_2010-46) Though the actual mechanism for the transportation of TEs from donor cells to host cells is unknown, it is established that [naked DNA](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naked_DNA "Naked DNA") and RNA can circulate in bodily fluid.[[46]](#cite_note-Schaack_2010-46) Many proposed vectors include arthropods, viruses, freshwater snails (Ivancevic et al. 2013), endosymbiotic bacteria,[[47]](#cite_note-Dupeyron_2014-47) and intracellular parasitic bacteria.[[46]](#cite_note-Schaack_2010-46) In some cases, even TEs facilitate transport for other TEs.[[50]](#cite_note-Ivancevic_2013-50)

The arrival of a new TE in a host genome can have detrimental consequences because TE mobility may induce mutation. However, HTT can also be beneficial by introducing new genetic material into a genome and promoting the shuffling of genes and TE domains among hosts, which can be co-opted by the host genome to perform new functions.[[50]](#cite_note-Ivancevic_2013-50) Moreover, transposition activity increases the TE copy number and generates [chromosomal rearrangement](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromosomal_rearrangement "Chromosomal rearrangement") hotspots.[[51]](#cite_note-Wallau_2012-51) HTT detection is a difficult task because it is an ongoing phenomenon that is constantly changing in frequency of occurrence and composition of TEs inside host genomes. Furthermore, few species have been analyzed for HTT, making it difficult to establish patterns of HTT events between species. These issues can lead to the underestimation or overestimation of HTT events between ancestral and current eukaryotic species. [[51]](#cite_note-Wallau_2012-51)

## Methods of detection

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Horizontal_gene_transfer&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Methods of detection")]

Main article: [Inferring horizontal gene transfer](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inferring_horizontal_gene_transfer "Inferring horizontal gene transfer")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Xenology.svg/250px-Xenology.svg.png)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Xenology.svg)

A speciation event produces [orthologs](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ortholog "Ortholog") of a gene in the two daughter species. A horizontal gene transfer event from one species to another adds a [xenolog](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xenolog "Xenolog") of the gene to the receiving genome.

Horizontal gene transfer is typically inferred using [bioinformatics](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioinformatics "Bioinformatics") methods, either by identifying atypical sequence signatures ("parametric" methods) or by identifying strong discrepancies between the evolutionary history of particular sequences compared to that of their hosts. The transferred gene ([xenolog](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xenolog "Xenolog")) found in the receiving species is more closely related to the genes of the donor species than would be expected.[*[citation needed](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

One demonstrated method to find HGT events is through Shotgun Metagenomics; breaking down then sequencing DNA in a sample by its contiguous regions and looking for phylogenetic mismatches, which can be inferred as instances of Horizontal Gene Transfer.[[52]](#cite_note-Yang_2024-52)

## Viruses

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Horizontal_gene_transfer&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Viruses")]

See also: [Chimera (virus)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimera_(virus) "Chimera (virus)")

The [virus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virus "Virus") called *[Mimivirus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mimivirus "Mimivirus")* infects [amoebae](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amoebae "Amoebae"). Another virus, called *[Sputnik](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_(virus) "Sputnik (virus)")*, also infects amoebae, but it cannot reproduce unless mimivirus has already infected the same cell.[[53]](#cite_note-La_Scola_2008-53)

> Sputnik's [genome](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genome "Genome") reveals further insight into its biology. Although 13 of its genes show little similarity to any other known genes, three are closely related to mimivirus and [mamavirus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamavirus "Mamavirus") genes, perhaps cannibalized by the tiny virus as it packaged up particles sometime in its history. This suggests that the [satellite virus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_virus "Satellite virus") could perform horizontal gene transfer between viruses, paralleling the way that bacteriophages ferry genes between bacteria.[[54]](#cite_note-54)

## Prokaryotes

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Horizontal_gene_transfer&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Prokaryotes")]

Horizontal gene transfer is common among bacteria, even among very distantly related ones, and also between bacteria and archaea.[*[citation needed](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] This process is thought to be a significant cause of increased [drug resistance](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_resistance "Drug resistance")[[5]](#cite_note-Gyles_2014-5)[[55]](#cite_note-Barlow_2009-55) when one bacterial cell acquires resistance, and the resistance genes are transferred to the other species.[[56]](#cite_note-Hawkey_2009-56)[[57]](#cite_note-Francino_2012-57) Transposition and horizontal gene transfer, along with strong natural selective forces have led to multi-drug resistant strains of *[S. aureus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staphylococcus_aureus "Staphylococcus aureus")* and many other pathogenic bacteria.[[43]](#cite_note-Stearns_2005-43) Horizontal gene transfer also plays a role in the spread of virulence factors, such as [exotoxins](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exotoxin "Exotoxin") and [exoenzymes](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exoenzyme "Exoenzyme"), amongst bacteria.[[5]](#cite_note-Gyles_2014-5) A prime example concerning the spread of exotoxins is the adaptive evolution of [Shiga toxins](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiga_toxin "Shiga toxin") in *E. coli* through horizontal gene transfer via transduction with *[Shigella](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shigella "Shigella")* species of bacteria.[[58]](#cite_note-58) Strategies to combat certain bacterial infections by targeting these specific virulence factors and mobile genetic elements have been proposed.[[12]](#cite_note-Keen_2012-12) For example, horizontally transferred genetic elements play important roles in the virulence of *[E. coli](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escherichia_coli "Escherichia coli")*, *[Salmonella](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmonella "Salmonella")*, *[Streptococcus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streptococcus "Streptococcus")* and *[Clostridium perfringens](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clostridium_perfringens "Clostridium perfringens")*.[[5]](#cite_note-Gyles_2014-5)

In prokaryotes, restriction-modification systems are known to provide immunity against horizontal gene transfer and in stabilizing mobile genetic elements. Genes encoding restriction modification systems have been reported to move between prokaryotic genomes within [mobile genetic elements](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_genetic_elements "Mobile genetic elements") (MGE) such as [plasmids](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasmid "Plasmid"), [prophages](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophage "Prophage"), insertion sequences/transposons, integrative conjugative elements (ICE),[[59]](#cite_note-59) and [integrons](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integron "Integron"). Still, they are more frequently a chromosomal-encoded barrier to MGE than an MGE-encoded tool for cell infection.[[60]](#cite_note-Oliveira_2014-60)

Lateral gene transfer via a mobile genetic element, namely the integrated conjugative element (ICE) *Bs1* has been reported for its role in the global DNA damage [SOS response](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SOS_response "SOS response") of the gram positive *Bacillus subtilis*.[[61]](#cite_note-61) Furthermore, it has been linked with the radiation and desiccation resistance of *Bacillus pumilus* SAFR-032 spores,[[62]](#cite_note-62) isolated from spacecraft cleanroom facilities.[[63]](#cite_note-63)[[64]](#cite_note-64)[[65]](#cite_note-65)

Transposon insertion elements have been reported to increase the fitness of [gram-negative](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram-negative_bacteria "Gram-negative bacteria") *[E. coli](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escherichia_coli "Escherichia coli")* strains through either major transpositions or genome rearrangements, and increasing mutation rates.[[66]](#cite_note-66)[[67]](#cite_note-67) In a study on the effects of long-term exposure of simulated microgravity on non-pathogenic *E. coli*, the results showed transposon insertions occur at loci, linked to SOS stress response.[[68]](#cite_note-68) When the same *E. coli* strain was exposed to a combination of simulated microgravity and trace (background) levels of (the broad spectrum) antibiotic ([chloramphenicol](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloramphenicol "Chloramphenicol")), the results showed transposon-mediated rearrangements (TMRs), disrupting genes involved in bacterial adhesion, and deleting an entire segment of several genes involved with motility and [chemotaxis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemotaxis "Chemotaxis").[[69]](#cite_note-69) Both of these studies have implications for microbial growth, adaptation to and antibiotic resistance in real time space conditions.

Horizontal gene transfer is particularly active in bacterial genomes around the production of secondary or specialized metabolites.[[70]](#cite_note-Ginolhac_2005-70) This is clearly exhibited within certain groups of bacteria including *P. aeruginosa* and *actinomycetales*, an order of *Actinomycetota.*[[71]](#cite_note-71) [Polyketide synthases](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyketide_synthase "Polyketide synthase") (PKSs) and [biosynthetic gene clusters](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolic_gene_cluster "Metabolic gene cluster") provide modular organizations of associated genes making these bacteria well-adapted to acquire and discard helpful modular modifications via HGT.[[72]](#cite_note-72) Certain areas of genes known as [hotspots](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recombination_hotspot "Recombination hotspot") further increase the likelihood of horizontally transferred secondary metabolite-producing genes.[[73]](#cite_note-Gross_2009-73) The promiscuity of enzymes is a reoccurring theme in this particular theatre.[*[citation needed](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

### Bacterial transformation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Horizontal_gene_transfer&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Bacterial transformation")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Transformation_HGT_in_Bacteria.svg/250px-Transformation_HGT_in_Bacteria.svg.png)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Transformation_HGT_in_Bacteria.svg)

1: Donor bacterium 2: Bacterium who will receive the gene 3: The red portion represents the gene that will be transferred. Transformation in bacteria happens in a certain environment.

[Natural transformation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformation_(genetics) "Transformation (genetics)") is a bacterial adaptation for DNA transfer (HGT) that depends on the expression of numerous bacterial genes whose products are responsible for this process.[[74]](#cite_note-Chen_2004-74)[[75]](#cite_note-Johnsborg_2007-75) In general, transformation is a complex, energy-requiring developmental process. In order for a bacterium to bind, take up and recombine exogenous DNA into its chromosome, it must become [competent](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_competence "Natural competence"), that is, enter a special physiological state. Competence development in *[Bacillus subtilis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacillus_subtilis "Bacillus subtilis")* requires expression of about 40 genes.[[76]](#cite_note-Solomon_1996-76) The DNA integrated into the host chromosome is usually (but with infrequent exceptions) derived from another bacterium of the same [species](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species "Species"), and is thus homologous to the resident chromosome. The capacity for natural transformation occurs in at least 67 prokaryotic species.[[75]](#cite_note-Johnsborg_2007-75)

[Competence](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_competence "Natural competence") for transformation is typically induced by high cell density and/or nutritional limitation, conditions associated with the [stationary phase](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacterial_growth#Phases "Bacterial growth") of bacterial growth. Competence appears to be an adaptation for DNA repair.[[77]](#cite_note-77) Transformation in bacteria can be viewed as a primitive sexual process, since it involves interaction of homologous DNA from two individuals to form [recombinant DNA](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recombinant_DNA "Recombinant DNA") that is passed on to succeeding generations. Although transduction is the form of HGT most commonly associated with [bacteriophages](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteriophage "Bacteriophage"), certain phages may also be able to promote transformation.[[78]](#cite_note-Keen_2017-78)

### Bacterial conjugation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Horizontal_gene_transfer&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Bacterial conjugation")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Conjugation_HGT_in_Bacteria.svg/250px-Conjugation_HGT_in_Bacteria.svg.png)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Conjugation_HGT_in_Bacteria.svg)

1: Donor bacterium cell (F+ cell) 2: Bacterium that receives the plasmid (F- cell) 3: Plasmid that will be moved to the other bacterium 4: Pilus and T4SS. Conjugation in bacteria using a sex pilus; then the bacterium that received the plasmid can go give it to other bacteria as well.

 [![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Bacterial_conjugation.png/250px-Bacterial_conjugation.png)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bacterial_conjugation.png)

*E. coli* cells going through conjugation and sharing genetic information. F-pilus is reaching towards other cell.

As mentioned before, [conjugation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacterial_conjugation "Bacterial conjugation") is a method of horizontal gene transfer through cell to cell contact.[[43]](#cite_note-Stearns_2005-43) Through the process of conjugation, [type IV Secretion Systems](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_IV_secretion_system "Type IV secretion system") (T4SS) are used to passage on DNA from the donor cell to the recipient cell.[[79]](#cite_note-79) These T4SS encoded within the plasmid carry other proteins and genes that help supplement the cell in conjugation. Research has shown that there are Single Binding DNA Binding proteins (SSBs) also encoded within the conjugative plasmid may help with conjugation and cell viability.[[80]](#cite_note-80) This is thought to be the case because SSBs naturally are expressed to help with stabilizing single-stranded DNA (ssDNA).[[81]](#cite_note-81) SSBs will also recruit other proteins like RadD or RecA expressed in events of DNA recombination, repair, and replication.[[82]](#cite_note-82)[[83]](#cite_note-83) Further showcasing their possible role in conjugation. Although it may help, studies have also shown for proteins like SSB to not be essential in conjugation. For example, the plasmid pCF10 from *[Enterococcus faecalis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enterococcus_faecalis "Enterococcus faecalis")*, a gram-positive bacterium, has a SSB like-protein called PrgE and was classified for not being required for conjugation.[[84]](#cite_note-84) More work needs to be done on why proteins that bind to ssDNA are encoded into conjugative plasmids.

Conjugation in the case of microbiomes and symbioses is very important. From this process new genes are acquired that lead to increasing [genetic diversity](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_diversity "Genetic diversity") and evolution such as the acquisition of antibiotic resistance genes. *[Mycobacterium tuberculosis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycobacterium_tuberculosis "Mycobacterium tuberculosis")* is a species that has evolved through methods like conjugation while gaining antibiotic resistance.[[85]](#cite_note-85)[[86]](#cite_note-86) This evolution or increase in genetic diversity is also seen in many other species.[[87]](#cite_note-87) Due to this, there is a huge concern on how impactful conjugation or horizontal gene transfer can be on human health and your microbiome as pathogenic microbes can become more pathogenic. Studies have shown that even our own microbiome has a plethora of antimicrobial genes which if transferred to pathogenic microbes could be detrimental.[[88]](#cite_note-88)

[Conjugation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacterial_conjugation "Bacterial conjugation") in *[Mycobacterium smegmatis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycobacterium_smegmatis "Mycobacterium smegmatis")*, like conjugation in *[E. coli](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escherichia_coli "Escherichia coli")*, requires stable and extended contact between a donor and a recipient strain, is [DNase resistant](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deoxyribonuclease "Deoxyribonuclease"), and the transferred DNA is incorporated into the recipient chromosome by [homologous recombination](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homologous_recombination "Homologous recombination"). However, unlike *E. coli* [high frequency of recombination conjugation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacterial_conjugation#Mechanism "Bacterial conjugation") (Hfr), mycobacterial conjugation is a type of HGT that is chromosome rather than plasmid based.[[89]](#cite_note-Gray_2013-89) Furthermore, in contrast to *E. coli* (Hfr) conjugation, in *M. smegmatis* all regions of the chromosome are transferred with comparable efficiencies. Substantial blending of the parental genomes was found as a result of conjugation, and this blending was regarded as reminiscent of that seen in the meiotic products of sexual reproduction.[[89]](#cite_note-Gray_2013-89)[[90]](#cite_note-Derbyshire_2014-90)

### Archaeal DNA transfer

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Horizontal_gene_transfer&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Archaeal DNA transfer")]

[Haloarchaea](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haloarchaea "Haloarchaea") are aerobic [halophiles](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halophile "Halophile") thought to have evolved from anaerobic [methanogens](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methanogen "Methanogen"). A large amount of their genome, 126 composite gene families, are derived from genetic material from bacterial genomes. This has allowed them to adapt to extremely salty environments.[[91]](#cite_note-91)[[92]](#cite_note-92)

The [archaeon](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaea "Archaea") *[Sulfolobus solfataricus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfolobus_solfataricus "Sulfolobus solfataricus")*, when [UV](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraviolet "Ultraviolet") irradiated, strongly induces the formation of [type IV pili](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilus#Type_IV_pili "Pilus") which then facilitates cellular aggregation.[[93]](#cite_note-Fröls_2008-93)[[94]](#cite_note-Allers_2011-94) Exposure to chemical agents that cause DNA damage also induces cellular aggregation.[[93]](#cite_note-Fröls_2008-93) Other physical stressors, such as temperature shift or pH, do not induce aggregation, suggesting that DNA damage is a specific inducer of cellular aggregation.[*[citation needed](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

UV-induced cellular aggregation mediates intercellular chromosomal HGT marker exchange with high frequency,[[95]](#cite_note-Ajon_2011-95) and UV-induced cultures display recombination rates that exceed those of uninduced cultures by as much as three orders of magnitude. *S. solfataricus* cells aggregate preferentially with other cells of their own species.[[95]](#cite_note-Ajon_2011-95) Frols et al.[[93]](#cite_note-Fröls_2008-93)[[96]](#cite_note-Fröls_2009-96) and Ajon et al.[[95]](#cite_note-Ajon_2011-95) suggested that UV-inducible DNA transfer is likely an important mechanism for providing increased repair of damaged DNA via homologous recombination. This process can be regarded as a simple form of sexual interaction.

Another [thermophilic species](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermophile "Thermophile"), *[Sulfolobus acidocaldarius](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfolobus_acidocaldarius "Sulfolobus acidocaldarius")*, is able to undergo HGT. *S. acidocaldarius* can exchange and recombine chromosomal markers at temperatures up to 84 °C.[[97]](#cite_note-Grogan_1996-97) UV exposure induces pili formation and cellular aggregation.[[95]](#cite_note-Ajon_2011-95) Cells with the ability to aggregate have greater survival than mutants lacking pili that are unable to aggregate. The frequency of recombination is increased by DNA damage induced by UV-irradiation[[98]](#cite_note-Wood_1997-98) and by DNA damaging chemicals.[[99]](#cite_note-Reilly_2002-99)

The [*ups* operon](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfolobales#The_ups_operon "Sulfolobales"), containing five genes, is highly induced by UV irradiation. The proteins encoded by the *ups* operon are employed in UV-induced pili assembly and cellular aggregation leading to intercellular DNA exchange and [homologous recombination](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homologous_recombination "Homologous recombination").[[100]](#cite_note-Wolferen_2013-100) Since this system increases the fitness of *S. acidocaldarius* cells after UV exposure, Wolferen et al.[[100]](#cite_note-Wolferen_2013-100)[[101]](#cite_note-van_Wolferen_2015-101) considered that transfer of DNA likely takes place in order to repair UV-induced DNA damages by homologous recombination.

## Eukaryotes

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Horizontal_gene_transfer&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Eukaryotes")]

"Sequence comparisons suggest recent horizontal transfer of many genes among diverse species including across the boundaries of [phylogenetic](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phylogenetic "Phylogenetic") 'domains'. Thus determining the phylogenetic history of a species can not be done conclusively by determining evolutionary trees for single genes."[[102]](#cite_note-102)

### Organelle to nuclear genome

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Horizontal_gene_transfer&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Organelle to nuclear genome")]

* Analysis of [DNA sequences](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_sequence "DNA sequence") suggests that horizontal gene transfer has occurred within eukaryotes from the chloroplast and [mitochondrial genomes](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitochondrial_genome "Mitochondrial genome") to the [nuclear genome](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_genome "Nuclear genome"). As stated in the [endosymbiotic theory](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endosymbiotic_theory "Endosymbiotic theory"), [chloroplasts](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloroplast "Chloroplast") and [mitochondria](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitochondria "Mitochondria") probably originated as bacterial [endosymbionts](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endosymbiont "Endosymbiont") of a progenitor to the eukaryotic cell.[[103]](#cite_note-103)

### Organelle to organelle

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Horizontal_gene_transfer&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Organelle to organelle")]

* [Mitochondrial genes](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitochondrial_gene "Mitochondrial gene") moved to parasites of the [Rafflesiaceae](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafflesiaceae "Rafflesiaceae") plant family from their hosts[[104]](#cite_note-104)[[105]](#cite_note-105) and from chloroplasts of a still-unidentified plant to the mitochondria of the bean *[Phaseolus](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phaseolus "Phaseolus")*.[[106]](#cite_note-106)

### Bacteria to fungi

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Horizontal_gene_transfer&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Bacteria to fungi")]

* Horizontal transfer occurs from bacteria to some [fungi](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fungi "Fungi"), such as the yeast *[Saccharomyces cerevisiae](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saccharomyces_cerevisiae "Saccharomyces cerevisiae")*.[[107]](#cite_note-107)

### Bacteria to plants

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Horizontal_gene_transfer&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Bacteria to plants")]

* Agrobacterium, a pathogenic bacterium that causes cells to proliferate as crown galls and proliferating roots is an example of a bacterium that can transfer genes to plants a

args.summary:
This is the Wikipedia article on Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT) or Lateral Gene Transfer (LGT), defined as the movement of genetic material between organisms other than by vertical transmission (parent to offspring). HGT is the primary mechanism for the spread of antibiotic resistance in bacteria and plays an important role in bacterial evolution, including the degradation of novel compounds like human-created pesticides and the evolution, maintenance, and transmission of virulence. It involves temperate bacteriophages and plasmids, with mechanisms including transformation, transduction, and conjugation.

HISTORY: Griffith's experiment (1928) first suggested bacterial transformation. Horizontal genetic transfer was described in 1951 in Seattle, showing transfer of a viral gene into Corynebacterium diphtheriae created a virulent strain. Inter-bacterial gene transfer was first described in a 1959 Japanese publication demonstrating transfer of antibiotic resistance between different bacterial species. Syvanen (mid-1980s) postulated lateral gene transfer has existed since the beginning of life. Molecular biologists such as Peter Gogarten have described HGT as "A New Paradigm for Biology."

MECHANISMS include: (1) Transformation – uptake/expression of foreign DNA; (2) Transduction – bacterial DNA moved by bacteriophages; (3) Bacterial conjugation – transfer via plasmid during cell-to-cell contact using Type IV Secretion Systems; (4) Gene transfer agents – virus-like elements encoded by the host found in alphaproteobacteria.

HORIZONTAL TRANSPOSON TRANSFER (HTT): Transposable elements (jumping genes) can carry resistance genes between genomes. HTT is increasingly recognized as common in eukaryotes as well as prokaryotes. DNA transposons and LTR retroelements are more likely to undergo HTT due to stable double-stranded DNA intermediates. In plants, LTR retrotransposons of the Copia superfamilies (specifically Ale and Ivana lineages with low copy numbers) are more likely to transfer horizontally. Proposed vectors include arthropods, viruses, freshwater snails, and endosymbiotic bacteria. Spatial and taxonomic proximity favor HTT.

DETECTION: HGT is typically inferred using bioinformatics (parametric methods identifying atypical sequence signatures, or identifying discrepancies in evolutionary history). Shotgun metagenomics can identify phylogenetic mismatches indicating HGT. Transferred genes are called "xenologs."

VIRUSES: The Sputnik satellite virus can perform horizontal gene transfer between viruses, as some of its genes are closely related to mimivirus and mamavirus genes, paralleling how bacteriophages ferry genes between bacteria.

PROKARYOTES: HGT is common among bacteria and between bacteria and archaea. It is a significant cause of increased drug resistance and spread of virulence factors like exotoxins and exoenzymes. Examples include multi-drug resistant S. aureus, Shiga toxins in E. coli via transduction with Shigella. Restriction-modification systems provide immunity against HGT. Horizontally transferred elements play roles in virulence of E. coli, Salmonella, Streptococcus, and Clostridium perfringens. HGT is active around secondary/specialized metabolite production. The integrated conjugative element (ICE) Bs1 plays a role in the SOS response of Bacillus subtilis.

BACTERIAL TRANSFORMATION: A complex, energy-requiring developmental process requiring about 40 genes in Bacillus subtilis. Competence is induced by high cell density or nutritional limitation and appears to be an adaptation for DNA repair. It occurs in at least 67 prokaryotic species. It can be viewed as a primitive sexual process.

BACTERIAL CONJUGATION: Uses Type IV Secretion Systems (T4SS). Single-strand DNA binding proteins (SSBs) encoded in conjugative plasmids may aid conjugation though some (like PrgE in pCF10 of Enterococcus faecalis) are not essential. Conjugation is important in microbiomes, contributing to genetic diversity and evolution, including antibiotic resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Mycobacterial conjugation (in M. smegmatis) differs from E. coli: it is chromosome rather than plasmid based.

ARCHAEAL DNA TRANSFER: Haloarchaea derived 126 composite gene families from bacterial genomes, allowing adaptation to salty environments. Sulfolobus solfataricus and S. acidocaldarius undergo UV-induced pili formation, cellular aggregation, and high-frequency DNA exchange/recombination for DNA repair via homologous recombination. The ups operon (five genes) is highly induced by UV and employed in these processes, increasing fitness after UV exposure.

EUKARYOTES: HGT has occurred within eukaryotes from chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes to the nuclear genome (per endosymbiotic theory). Mitochondrial genes moved to Rafflesiaceae parasites from hosts, and from chloroplasts to mitochondria of Phaseolus beans. Horizontal transfer occurs from bacteria to fungi like Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Agrobacterium can transfer genes to plants (causing crown galls). Monarch butterflies and silkworms have been genetically modified by HGT from wasp bracovirus. The trypanosomal parasite causing Chagas disease (transmitted by assassin bugs/Reduviidae) can insert DNA into the human genome.

## Summary

Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is the transfer of genetic material between distantly related organisms. While most genes in prokaryotes can be horizontally transferred, HGT events in eukaryotes are considered as rare, particularly in mammals. Here we reported the identification of HGT regions (HGTs), which are genomic sequence fragments indicating the occurrence of HGT events, in human, mouse, cow, lizard, frog, zebrafish, fruit fly, nematode, Arabidopsis and yeast. By comparing the genomes of these 10 representative eukaryotes with 1,496 eukaryotic genomes, 16,098 bacteria and 11,695 viruses, we found between 10 and 243 non-redundant HGTs per species, and most of these HGTs were previously unknown. These HGTs have transformed their host genomes with various numbers of copies and have impacted hundreds, even thousands of genes. We listed several examples of HGTs and proposed some possible routes that HGT events occurred. Further analysis showed that the majority of the 1,496 eukaryotes with full length genome sequences also contain HGTs. Our findings reveal that HGT is widespread in eukaryotic genomes, and HGT is a ubiquitous driver of genome evolution for eukaryotes.

## Background

Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is the transfer of genetic material between organisms that is not from parent to offspring, and it is a major driver of genome evolution in bacteria and archaea[[1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-1), [2](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-2)]. On average, 81% of genes in bacteria were involved in HGT[[3](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-3)]. Recent evidence has shown that HGT events also exist in eukaryotes. For example, HGT regions (HGTs) have been reported from soil bacteria to the common ancestor of _Zygnematophyceae_ and _embryophytes_, which increased its resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses during terrestrial adaptation[[4](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-4)]. HGT of a plant detoxification gene BtPMaT1, made whiteflies gain the ability to malonylate a common group of plant defense compounds[[5](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-5)]. Besides, 1,410 genes were acquired via 741 distinct transfers from non-metazoan donors in 218 insects and males lacking LOC105383139 which was transferred from bacteria courted females significantly less in diamondback moths[[6](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-6)]. Another remarkable example of HGT is a ∼1.5Mb fragment of _Wolbachia spp._ DNA integrated into the pill bug _Armadillidium vulgare_ genome, resulting in the creation of a new W sex chromosome[[7](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-7)]. HGTs have been observed in genomes of five parasitic plants in the _Orobanchaceae_ family[[8](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-8)], several unicellular pathogens[[9](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-9)] and blood-sucking parasites[[10](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-10)–[12](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-12)]. It has been proposed that only unicellular and early developmental stages of eukaryotes are vulnerable to HGT[[13](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-13)], while some argue that HGT events in eukaryotes may be limited to those derived from endosymbiotic organelles[[14](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-14), [15](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-15)]. Mechanisms for the transfer of DNA into eukaryotic genomes have been described for viral infection, transposons, conjugation between bacteria and eukaryotes, or from endosymbionts (not only plastids and mitochondria)[[16](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-16)]. Some behaviors, such as predation, and life-styles, such as parasitism, have been reported to promote DNA transfer in eukaryotes[[17](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-17)]. Therefore, while the prevalence of HGT may be rare in eukaryotes, compared to bacteria and archaea, it does occur. However, the scale and impact of HGT events in eukaryotes are unknown.

We presented here a fast identification method for HGTs in eukaryotes using both sequence composition bias and genome comparison. We evaluated the method by a simulated dataset and a dataset of HGT regions reported previously for whitefly. We applied this method to 10 representative organisms with high quality genomes which were at different positions in phylogenetic tree of eukaryotes. Many bacterial and viral genomes were also compared to reveal the potential media organisms or vectors for HGT in eukaryotes.

## Results

### A Fast HGT identification method and its evaluation

We created a fast identification pipeline for HGTs in eukaryotes by combining sequence composition filtering and sequence alignment (Figure S1; see Methods). In brief, we first identified genomic regions most different from the rest of the genome based on their k-mer frequencies and then we aligned these selected genomic regions to other genomes. Before sequence alignment, we divided all genomes into three different groups based on their taxonomic information, including self group (SG), closely related group (CRG) and distantly related group (DRG). The genomic regions were considered as candidate HGT regions if their sequence conservation levels were discordant to the phylogenetic tree of relevant species. Specifically, genomic fragments were determined as HGT sequences occurred in the common ancestor of organisms listed in SG if they had higher identity percentage with species in DRG than that in CRG. To further evaluate the accuracy of our HGT identification pipeline, we evaluated it with a simulated dataset and a real dataset (HGTs reported in whitefly).

We evaluated the pipeline with a genome containing simulated HGTs (see Methods). Since our HGT identification pipeline has two main steps (sequence composition-based filtering and sequence alignment), the evaluation was done for the two steps. While top 1% fragments were input to the pipeline, 20.6% correct results would be identified after sequence composition-based filtering and 17.77% correct results identified after sequence alignment (Figure S2A; Table S1). When the percentage of fragments input was up to 20%, 58.9% and 57.1% correct results were identified after two steps respectively and it can be seen that the precision of prediction was higher than 90% for all cases (Figure S2A; Table S1). This indicates that we may have underestimated the number of HGTs (low recall rate) but majority of the identified HGTs are reliable.

We also evaluated our pipeline on the 170 HGTs previously reported for whitefly [[6](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-6)] (see Methods). While only top 20% genome fragments were input to our pipeline, 71.8% of the 170 HGTs would be identified after sequence composition-based filtering, indicating that the first step is effective to keep candidate HGTs, and 32.4% of the 170 HGTs would be identified after sequence-alignment-step (Figure S2A), indicating that our nucleotide sequence comparison based HGT identification method is different with existing methods. Overall, 131 HGTs were identified by our pipeline, 47.3% of which (62 HGTs) were overlapped with reported HGTs while 52.7% of which (69 HGTs) were not reported (Figure S2B; Table S2). Among 69 HGTs not reported previously, 36 HGTs did not overlap with protein-coding sequences, which made them invisible to the previous reported HGT identification methods limited to protein coding regions. The remaining 33 newly found HGTs did overlap with protein-coding regions, but the coverage of these protein coding regions by HGTs was less than 25% of their corresponding total protein, which might be the reason why they were not identified by previous method (Figure S2B). For the 115 HGTs reported previously but missed by our method, 48 HGTs were left out by sequence composition-based filtering step and the remaining 67 HGTs were not identified by our pipeline. Among them, 35 had more similar sequences with genomes in CRG than that in DRG while the other 32 had similarity lower than 50% with genomes in DRG (Figure S2B).

The comparison with previously reported HGTs show that our results are reliable and our method could identify some novel HGT events because it broke the restriction of identifying HGT regions involving protein coding regions only.

### Widespread of HGT events among eukaryotes

We applied our HGT identification method to identify HGTs in 10 representative organisms with high quality genomes, including 1 primate, 2 mammals, 3 non-mammalian vertebrates, 2 invertebrates, 1 plant and 1 fungus. We identified between 10 and 243 non-redundant cross-kingdom eukaryotic HGTs for these 10 representative organisms ([Figure 1A](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F1); Table S3). The number of HGTs found in nematode, an invertebrate, was the smallest, while the number for Arabidopsis was the largest ([Figure 1A](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F1)). HGT events occurred to the common ancestors of organisms contained in self groups (SGs) of each representative organism. The HGTs of nematode mostly occurred at species level, while the HGTs of fruit fly and yeast mostly occurred at order level; human, mouse and Arabidopsis had more HGTs at class level, while cow, lizard, frog and zebrafish had more HGTs at phylum level ([Figure 1A](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F1)). The cross-kingdom species having the most similar sequence with the target organism was identified as the HGT related organisms. Overall, the HGT related organisms of these 10 representative species were distributed in 6 different kingdoms (bacteria: 196/745 [26.3%], metazoan: 168/745 [22.6%], protozoa: 154/745 [20.7%], plants: 153/745 [20.5%], fungi: 66/745 [8.9%], viruses: 8/745 [1.1%]) ([Figure 1B](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F1); Table S4). Bacteria, metazoan, plants and protozoa occupied the highest proportion of HGT related organisms in mammals (human, mouse, cow), non-mammalian metazoan (lizard, frog, zebrafish, fruit fly and nematode) and non-metazoan eukaryotes (yeast and Arabidopsis) respectively ([Figure 1B](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F1)). Especially, the _Actinomycetes_ of bacteria, the _Insecta_ of metazoan, the _Magnoliatae_ of plants, the _Aconoidasida_ of protozoa and the _Sordariomycetes_ of fungi contained prevalent HGT related organisms (Figure S3). Besides, most of the identified HGTs in the 10 representative organisms were previously unknown compared with reported HGTs[[11](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-11), [18](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-18)–[25](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-25)] ([Figure 1C](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F1)).

To determine the frequency of HGT in eukaryotes, we calculated an HGT-appearance number N AB for a representative organism A and another eukaryotic organism B, which was defined by the frequency with which organism B appeared in the phylogenetic trees of non-redundant HGTs of representative organism A. For instance, among the 92 non-redundant HGT trees for Homo sapiens, Pan troglodytes was found in 89 of them, therefore the HGT-appearance number N AB between Homo sapiens and Pan troglodytes was 89. The distribution of HGT-appearance numbers N AB between the 10 representative organisms and 1496 eukaryotes was shown in [Figure 1D](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F1) and Table S5. The HGT-appearance numbers of organisms having the same taxonomic classification were higher ([Figure 1D](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F1)), indicating that most HGTs identified by our pipeline were transferred before the divergence of model organisms and their sibling lineages. This also implies that these HGTs may have important functions since they have survived during the evolution[[1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-1)]. By using this metric, we determined that 90.2% of eukaryotes (1349 of 1496) hosted HGTs ([Figure 1D](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F1), 1E), revealing widespread of HGT events across eukaryotes.

### Duplications of HGTs and their impact on their host genomes

We compared the non-redundant eukaryotic HGTs we identified with their host genomes to further elucidate the impact of HGTs on their host genomes. Overall, 77.2% of HGTs (575 of 745) have a single copy in their host genomes, and the rest (22.8%, 170 of 745) have multiple copies. Especially, 6 HGTs have more than 100 copies ([Figure 2A](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F2); Table S3). In particular, HGT region “NC_037357.1:83623202-83624198” related to BovB in the cow genome had 36,868 copies (with a total length of 36.3 Mbps), which was consistent with a previous study that BovB were present as many copies[[10](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-10)]. In newly identified HGTs, zebrafish HGT region “NW_018395302.1-126431-127344” had 126 copies and occupied 18 Kbps.

These HGT copies had affected many genes as well. In total, 93% of HGTs (693 of 745) had influence on 8,910 gene regions and 75.8% of them were overlapping with protein coding genes ([Figure 2B](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F2) and [2C](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F2)). Especially, almost all HGTs impacted genes in Arabidopsis, yeast, nematode and fruit fly. There were 16 HGTs, each of which impacted more than 10 genes in their host genome (Table S3). For example, the zebrafish HGT region mentioned above and its copies overlapped (at least 1bp) with 52 protein-coding genes ([Figure 2D](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F2)), which was a huge impact on the zebrafish genome functions. HGTs with similar (but different degree of) impact on genome can also be found for most of the 10 representative organisms. Gene ontology (GO) analysis of genes affected by HGTs in different organisms shows that some were associated with ion channel (cow), synaptic membrane (human), actin cytoskeleton (mouse), thioester biosynthetic process (fruit fly), organic hydroxy compound metabolic process (yeast), biosynthetic process (Arabidopsis), etc. (Figure S3; Table S6). The genes impacted by HGTs in the remaining 4 of the 10 representative species have no enriched functions.

The genes mentioned above were affected by HGTs in different genetic elements. As a whole, only 5.2% (495/8.905) of genes overlapped by HGTs were affected in their CDS regions, with the rest were affected in the intron, upstream, downstream and exon regions ([Figure 2E](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F2)). This was because HGTs with a large copy numbers were mostly affected the intron regions of the genes (Figure S5), which might conform a rule for the occurrence of HGT, ‘first do no harm’[[1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-1)]. In details, 75.3% (354/470) of genes affected by single-copy HGTs were affected in their CDS regions, while this proportion dropped to 0.2% (141/8435) for multi-copy HGTs and 70.9% (5984/8435) of genes affected by multi-copy HGTs were affected in their intron regions. Besides, the distribution of gene elements affected by copies of HGTs was different in different organisms ([Figure 2E](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F2)). Most copies of HGTs overlapped with introns in vertebrates, while in invertebrates, fungi and plants, most of the HGT regions overlapped with CDS regions.

### Repetitive sequence composition of HGTs

We compared the non-redundant HGTs detected in 10 representative organisms with the repetitive sequences annotated in their reference genomes. Between 0∼77% of their HGTs overlapped with interspersed repeats (excluding simple repeats) ([Figure 3A](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F3); Table S7), revealing significant species and repeat-specificity. The types of repeats overlapping with HGTs showed significant correlation with overall genomic repeat composition. Long interspersed nuclear elements (LINEs) retrotransposons were common in HGTs detected in mammals, frog and lizard, while long terminal repeat (LTR) retrotransposons were common in HGTs detected in fruit fly, yeast and Arabidopsis, consistent with their frequencies in their host genomes ([Figure 3B](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F3) and S6). In comparison, the distribution of LTR in zebrafish HGTs was not consistent with their distribution in the host genomes, as seen the LTR in frog HGTs and the satellite in cow HGTs ([Figure 3B](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F3) and S6). In the zebrafish genome, LTR appeared in as many as 37 non-redundant HGTs (60.7%), while that repeat only accounted for 4.2% of repeats in the genome.

BovB and L1 retrotransposons are the two most abundant transposable elements (TEs) in eukaryotes and replicate via an RNA intermediate[[26](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-26)]. The horizontal transfer of BovB is known to be widespread in animals[[11](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-11)] and horizontal transfer of L1 has been shown in plants, animals and several fungi[[18](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-18)]. In total, 4 of our non-redundant HGT events overlapped with BovB retrotransposons in cow (Table S8), supporting previous results for horizontal transfer of BovB[[11](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-11), [18](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-18)]. Furthermore, 119 L1 horizontal transfer events were identified in human, mouse, cow, lizard, frog and zebrafish (Table S8), providing more evidence that L1 elements are horizontally transferred[[18](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-18)].

All HGTs that overlapped with BovB retrotransposon were associated with the intracellular pathogen _Babesia bigemina_ while one of them was also associated with the blood-sucking parasite _Cimex lectularius_ (bed bug) (Table S8), both of which were the reported possible intermediary species[[12](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-12)]. _Babesia bigemina_ is an Apicomplexan parasite that infects red blood cells [[27](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-27)], which infects livestock worldwide, including wild and domestic vertebrate animals. _Cimex lectularius_ is known to feed on animal blood and can host over 40 zoonotic pathogens[[28](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-28)], thus transmitting many infectious diseases[[29](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-29)]. [Figure 3C](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F3) showed the tree of cow HGT region “NC_037344.1: 42095551-42096199” and its homologs. In addition to the two candidate vector species, this HGT tree also included 5 bovid mammals and 10 non-mammalian vertebrates (3 fishes, 3 amphibians, 4 reptiles) ([Figure 3C](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F3); Table S9), which were clearly clustered in distinct branches. Like in other parasites[[10](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-10)], it appears that _Cimex lectularius_ and _Babesia bigemina_ transfer DNA between the hosts it feeds on.

A considerable number of genes of intracellular pathogens have been acquired through HGT, including Apicomplexans[[30](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-30), [31](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-31)]. Our analysis identified 76.5% (91/119) HGTs overlapped with L1 retrotransposons were associated with Apicomplexan intracellular pathogens, including _Babesia bigemina_ and _Plasmodium vivax_ (Table S8). For example, the tree of human HGT region “NC_000004.12:121865648-121866285” ([Figure 3D](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F3); Table S9) had shown the transfer between _Babesia bigemina_ and mammals, including 26 primates, 11 Artiodactyls, 11 Carnivores, 9 Rodents, 8 Chiropterans, 1 Eulipotyphl, 1 Lagomorph and 1 tree shrew.

Gypsy LTR retrotransposons are widely distributed among eukaryotes and have been found in plants, fungi and vertebrates[[32](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-32)]. The HGT of Gypsy is well known in Drosophila[[33](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-33)] and plants[[34](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-34)], and has been found between fungi and non-seed plants[[35](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#ref-35)]. In our results, 73 HGTs overlapped with Gypsy were identified in zebrafish, Arabidopsis, lizard, frog, fruit fly and yeast, which further supported previous reports. The Arabidopsis HGT region “NC_003076.8:12073716-12073960” showed the horizontal transmission of Gypsy LTR retrotransposons took place among 105 magnoliopsida plants and 14 insects ([Figure 3E](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F3); Table S9). Some HGTs overlapping with repeat sequences of other 6 representative organisms were in Figure S7.

### HGTs overlapping with non-repeating sequences

The above examples were mainly HGTs related to transposons and occurred in protozoa and eukaryotes. There were also 490 HGTs not overlapped with repetitive sequences ([Figure 3A](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F3); Table S7), and 433 HGTs (88.4%) of them overlapped with 530 protein coding genes (Table S10) while 90.9% (482/530) of protein coding genes affected by 433 HGTs were affected in CDS regions ([Figure 4A](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.07.26.501571.full#F4); Table S10). Gene ontology (GO) analysis of protein coding genes affected by HGTs in different organisms showed that some were associated with aldo−keto reductase activity (human), lipid oxidation (mouse), organic hydroxy compound metabolic process (yeast), organophosphate biosynthetic process (Arabidopsis), etc. (Figure S8; Table S11). We did not find enriched functions for the protein coding genes impacted by HGTs in the remaining 6 of the 10 representative species.

args.summary:
This is a bioRxiv preprint (doi: 10.1101/2022.07.26.501571) titled "Widespread of horizontal gene transfer events in eukaryotes" by Kun Li, Fazhe Yan, Zhongqu Duan, David L. Adelson, and Chaochun Wei, from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and the University of Adelaide. The study challenges the long-held view that horizontal gene transfer (HGT) events are rare in eukaryotes, particularly mammals.

**Methodology:** The authors developed a fast HGT identification pipeline combining sequence composition filtering (k-mer frequency analysis) and sequence alignment. Genomes were divided into self, closely related, and distantly related groups based on taxonomy, and regions with sequence conservation discordant with phylogenetic expectations were identified as candidate HGTs. The pipeline was validated on simulated datasets and 170 previously reported whitefly HGTs, achieving >90% precision.

**Key Results:**
- Comparing 10 representative eukaryotes (human, mouse, cow, lizard, frog, zebrafish, fruit fly, nematode, Arabidopsis, yeast) against 1,496 eukaryotic genomes, 16,098 bacteria, and 11,695 viruses, the researchers identified between 10 and 243 non-redundant HGTs per species (745 total).
- Most HGTs identified were previously unknown.
- 90.2% of the 1,496 eukaryotes (1,349 total) hosted HGTs, revealing HGT is widespread across eukaryotes.
- HGT-related organisms spanned 6 kingdoms: bacteria (26.3%), metazoan (22.6%), protozoa (20.7%), plants (20.5%), fungi (8.9%), viruses (1.1%).
- 77.2% of HGTs had a single copy in host genomes; 22.8% had multiple copies, with 6 HGTs having more than 100 copies. One cow HGT region related to BovB had 36,868 copies (36.3 Mbps).
- 93% of HGTs (693/745) influenced 8,910 gene regions, with 75.8% overlapping protein-coding genes.
- 490 HGTs did not overlap repetitive sequences; 88.4% of these (433) overlapped 530 protein-coding genes.

**Transposable Element Analysis:**
- BovB and L1 retrotransposon horizontal transfers were confirmed. All BovB-associated HGTs were linked to the intracellular pathogen Babesia bigemina and the bed bug Cimex lectularius (blood-sucking parasites), which may serve as transfer vectors.
- 76.5% (91/119) of L1 retrotransposon HGTs were associated with Apicomplexan intracellular pathogens (Babesia bigemina, Plasmodium vivax).
- 73 HGTs overlapping Gypsy LTR retrotransposons were found across zebrafish, Arabidopsis, lizard, frog, fruit fly, and yeast.

**Conclusion:** The findings reveal that HGT is widespread in eukaryotic genomes and is a ubiquitous driver of genome evolution for eukaryotes, not just bacteria and archaea.

# Insects Carry 1,410 Horizontally-Transferred Microbial Genes: Study

Jul 19, 2022 by  [News Staff](https://www.sci.news/author/scinews)

[« Previous](https://www.sci.news/medicine/alzheimers-disease-gastrointestinal-tract-disorders-genetic-link-11010.html)

|

[Next »](https://www.sci.news/biology/three-desmognathus-species-11019.html)

**In new research, a team of scientists from Zhejiang University and Vanderbilt University examined horizontal gene transfer — an important evolutionary force shaping prokaryotic and eukaryotic genomes — in high-quality genomes of 218 insect species, including butterflies and moths, and found that they acquired 1,410 genes exhibiting diverse functions via 741 distinct transfers from microbes. The researchers argue that these genes might have been essential for insect evolution by allowing them to develop beneficial traits in mating behavior, nutrition, growth, and adaptation to environmental changes.**

![Li et al. systematically examined horizontal gene transfer in 218 high-quality genomes of diverse insects and found that they acquired 1,410 genes exhibiting diverse functions, including many not previously reported, via 741 distinct transfers from non-metazoan donors. Image credit: Li et al., doi: 10.1016/j.cell.2022.06.014.](https://cdn.sci.news/images/2022/07/image_11011-Insect-Genes.jpg)

Li *et al*. systematically examined horizontal gene transfer in 218 high-quality genomes of diverse insects and found that they acquired 1,410 genes exhibiting diverse functions, including many not previously reported, via 741 distinct transfers from non-metazoan donors. Image credit: Li *et al*., doi: 10.1016/j.cell.2022.06.014.

Horizontal gene transfer is fairly common between microbes. For example, bacteria use this mechanism to transmit antibiotic-resistance genes between species.

But scientists more recently have been systematically looking at the phenomenon between insects and microbes or plants.

“Previous studies have shown that horizontal gene transfer may have contributed to insect biodiversity, but nobody knew how large a role it plays in this process,” said Dr. Xing-Xing Shen, an evolutionary biologist at Zhejiang University.

“Since there are a lot of high-quality insect genomes available for our analysis, I thought that now is a good time to systematically investigate how prevalent horizontal gene transfer is in insects.”

For their study, Dr. Shen and colleagues gathered 218 high-quality insect genome samples representing 11 of 19 species-rich orders of insects.

With these data, they were able to draw an evolutionary tree, identify out-of-place genes that are more commonly found in non-animal genomes, and examine what factors contribute to the fate of horizontal gene transfer in insects.

“There were horizontal gene transfer events everywhere we looked,” Dr. Shen said.

“However, we don’t know whether these transfers of genes are beneficial to the insects, or even the functions for most of these genes.”

The authors then decided to validate the function of the most prevalent foreign gene without known functions in insects: [*LOC105383139*](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/?term=LOC105383139).

“*LOC105383139* was horizontally introduced into nearly all moths and butterflies from a donor in the bacterial genus [*Listeria*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listeria),” they said.

“This gene has persisted in the genome since the time of moths’ and butterflies’ common ancestor more than 300 million years ago.”

In diamondback moths, males lacking *LOC105383139* courted females significantly less.

“Surprisingly, we saw those moths lacking this gene cannot produce many viable eggs,” said Dr. Jianhua Huang, also from Zhejiang University.

“Then, we found that the gene influences the male courtship behavior.”

The [results](https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(22)00719-X) were published in the journal *Cell*.

Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) was first described in microorganisms in the late 1940s1, and around 20 years later it was speculated to have a role in the adaptation of multicellular eukaryotes — specifically plants2. Since then, methods to detect HGT have improved, and these have revealed the surprising extent and relevance of HGT to the variation of viral, prokaryotic and eukary­ otic gene content. Many apparent gene duplications, for example, are now known to be the result of HGT, not autochthonous gene duplication, resulting in a ‘web of life’ rather than in a steadily bifurcating tree3,4.
For a transferred gene to survive in the recipient lineage for long periods of time, the gene usually needs to provide a selective advantage either to itself (in the case of a selfish genetic element) or to the recipient, and research on HGT initially focused on such genes. However, it is now known that many of the genes that have been identified as transferred through comparative genomics between close relatives have neutral or nearly neutral effects in the recipient in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms5. One rule for transferred genes seems to be ‘first do no harm’ — genes that are suc­ cessfully integrated into a recipient are often expressed at low levels and encode functions at the periphery of metabolism6. These neutral acquisitions, however, can later provide novel combinations of genetic material for selection to act on — in some cases, the transferred material becomes domesticated over time and pro­ duces a beneficial phenotype. In other cases, when the imported genes remain neutral and there is no obvious benefit associated with their retention, the genes are likely to be lost over time.
HGT has long been recognized as an important force in the evolution of bacteria and archaea. However, the exchange of genetic information between prokaryotic symbionts and their eukaryotic hosts, and even between eukaryotes, signifies that HGT in eukaryotes occurs more frequently than previously thought7,8. Often these transfers involve gene donations to unicellular eukary­ otes9 and are frequently associated with bacterial endo­ symbionts10 (known as endosymbiotic gene transfer (EGT) or intracellular gene transfer (IGT)). However, bacterial genes can also be transferred to multicellular eukaryotes8. Recent interest in the human microbiome has reinvigorated the search for HGTs from symbionts into the human genome. Although transfers of bacte­ rial genes into the human germ line11,12 have not be con­ firmed, evidence is accumulating of HGT from bacteria to human somatic cells13. These findings demonstrate the enduring influence of HGT on the evolution of all parts of the web of life, eukaryotes included.
In this Review, we present an overview of how HGT has contributed to innovation throughout the web of life by providing novel combinations of gene sequences for selection to act upon, thus shaping the evolution of species ranging from single-celled microorganisms to multicellular eukaryotes. Advances in the understand­ ing of mechanisms of HGT, methods of identifying HGT events and the growth of genome databases have facilitated these insights.

Horizontal gene transfer: building the web of life Shannon M. Soucy1, Jinling Huang2 and Johann Peter Gogarten1,3 Abstract | Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is the sharing of genetic material between organisms that are not in a parent–offspring relationship. HGT is a widely recognized mechanism for adaptation in bacteria and archaea. Microbial antibiotic resistance and pathogenicity are often associated with HGT, but the scope of HGT extends far beyond disease-causing organisms. In this Review, we describe how HGT has shaped the web of life using examples of HGT among prokaryotes, between prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and even between multicellular eukaryotes. We discuss replacement and additive HGT, the proposed mechanisms of HGT, selective forces that influence HGT, and the evolutionary impact of HGT on ancestral populations and existing populations such as the human microbiome.
