--- SOURCE 1: Horizontal gene transfer in bdelloid rotifers is ancient, ongoing and more frequent in species from desiccating habitats ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4632278

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article from BMC Biology (published November 4, 2015, doi:10.1186/s12915-015-0202-9) by Eyres et al., investigating horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in bdelloid rotifers. The authors hypothesized that bdelloids incorporate foreign DNA during chromosome repair following desiccation-induced double-strand breaks, which might contribute to species divergence and adaptation.

METHODS: The researchers sequenced transcriptomes of four congeneric Rotaria species from different habitats—two from permanent aquatic habitats (R. magnacalcarata and R. socialis, obligate epibionts on freshwater waterlice) and two from desiccating habitats (R. sordida from terrestrial moss and R. tardigrada from ephemeral pools). They identified putative foreign genes using the HGT index (h_U ≥30) and validated transcriptome results using a draft whole genome assembly of R. magnacalcarata.

RESULTS: All four species contained many genes matching non-metazoan genes more closely than metazoan genes. Transcript assemblies contained 60,542–121,350 contigs per species. The proportion of foreign genes (h_U ≥30) was 10.4% in R. magnacalcarata, 9.5% in R. socialis, 12.8% in R. sordida, and 14.1% in R. tardigrada—exceeding the 9.7% found in A. ricciae. Desiccation survival experiments confirmed habitat differences: none of the aquatic species survived desiccation, while 80.6% of R. sordida and 50% of R. tardigrada recovered after dehydration. There was a significant negative relationship between desiccation survival and proportion of HGT.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Nearly half of foreign genes were shared between all four species and the Adineta outgroup, indicating acquisition in a common ancestor predating the divergence of bdelloid families over 60 million years ago.
- Many hundreds of foreign genes were unique to particular species, indicating HGT is ongoing.
- Using a dated phylogeny (Rotaria's most recent common ancestor dated to 29 Mya), they estimated an average of 12.8 gains versus 2.0 losses of foreign genes per million years. The desiccating clade (R. sordida + R. tardigrada) had a threefold higher rate of gain and sixfold lower rate of loss than the aquatic clade.
- Differential loss of ancestral foreign genes associated with desiccation protection (glutathione and trypanothione metabolism enzymes) was found in the two non-desiccating species.
- Foreign genes came primarily from eubacteria (40.7% of transcripts), with fungal (19.2%), protist (28.7%), plant (10.0%), and archaeal (1.5%) origins. Most foreign genes were enzymes involved in catabolism of complex polysaccharides and stress responses.
- Genome validation showed 85% of R. magnacalcarata-unique foreign genes were present in its genome scaffolds, confirming transcriptome results and ruling out contamination (71% of unique foreign genes were on scaffolds also containing native metazoan genes).

CONCLUSIONS: Nearly half of foreign genes were acquired before bdelloid family divergence over 60 Mya, but HGT is ongoing and contributes to functional differences among species. The findings support the desiccation hypothesis: desiccating habitats promote HGT, though species from permanently aquatic habitats still possessed hundreds of foreign genes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We found that 9.5–14.2% of transcripts had h_U ≥30 in the four Rotaria species examined... Finding evidence of a high proportion of HGT in species from multiple families demonstrates that abundant HGT is not unique to Adineta species... but is a feature of bdelloid rotifers more widely, even those from permanently aquatic habitats.", "Nearly half of foreign genes were acquired before the divergence of bdelloid families over 60 Mya. Nonetheless, HGT is ongoing in bdelloids and has contributed to putative functional differences among species. Variation among our study species is consistent with the hypothesis that desiccating habitats promote HGT.", "Using a dated phylogeny, we estimate an average of 12.8 gains versus 2.0 losses of foreign genes per million years.", "The proportion of foreign genes (h_U ≥ 30) differs significantly among Rotaria species... R. tardigrada has a higher proportion of HGT (0.141 ± 0.004) than R. sordida (0.128 ± 0.004)... which in turn has a higher proportion than R. magnacalcarata and R. socialis (0.104 ± 0.004 and 0.095 ± 0.004...)", "The proportion of animals surviving desiccation differed significantly across species: no R. magnacalcarata and R. socialis from freshwater ponds survived, whereas 80.6% of R. sordida individuals from moss on trees and 50% of R. tardigrada individuals from a temporary pond recovered after dehydration."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: [PDF] Bdelloid rotifers deploy horizontally acquired biosynthetic genes ... ---
URL: https://www.pure.ed.ac.uk/ws/files/459018389/s41467-024-49919-1.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in Nature Communications (2024, vol. 15, article 5787), investigates how bdelloid rotifers use horizontally acquired genes against a fungal pathogen. The authors (Nowell, Rodriguez, Hecox-Lea, Mark Welch, Arkhipova, Barraclough, and Wilson) tested whether horizontally transferred genes show enrichment in response to fungal infection in two bdelloid rotifer species with different pathogen resistance levels.

**Key methods:** RNA-seq was used to identify differentially expressed genes when rotifers were exposed to the fungal pathogen Rotiferophthora globospora. Two host species were compared: Adineta ricciae (resistant, 18% mortality) and A. vaga (susceptible, 71% mortality), which differ by a factor of four in resistance. Gene expression was measured at 7 and 24 hours post-exposure, and results were compared to desiccation stress responses.

**Key findings:**
1. **Bdelloid genomes contain ~10-11.5% HGT genes** (an order of magnitude greater than other animals), mostly from bacteria, fungi, and plants.
2. **Horizontally acquired genes were 2-3x more likely to be upregulated** during pathogen exposure (23-32% of upregulated genes were HGT candidates vs. ~11.5% background), a stronger enrichment than for desiccation stress.
3. **NRP/PKS biosynthetic gene clusters resembling bacterial antibiotic-producing pathways** were the most markedly overrepresented upregulated genes. The most enriched GO term was 'phosphopantetheine binding' (a key cofactor in NRP/PKS synthesis).
4. **Expression differed strikingly between species:** The resistant A. ricciae upregulated 11 NRP/PKS gene models with fold-changes nearly 10 times stronger than A. vaga (which only upregulated 2). A. ricciae has at least 6 copies of an orthologous PKS-NRPS hybrid cluster (vs. 2 in A. vaga) encoding a predicted cyclic heptadepsipeptide similar to tyrocidine A (an antifungal compound) and hymenamide J.
5. **Other shared HGT-encoded responses** included RNA ligases (for RNA repair) and glucanases (possibly for attacking fungal cell walls).
6. **Most pathogen-induced HGTC were inherited from a common ancestor** (94% of A. ricciae's upregulated HGTC at T24 showed evidence in other bdelloid genomes), rather than being recent independent acquisitions.
7. These mechanisms may compensate for the challenges asexual reproduction poses against pathogens (Red Queen Hypothesis).

The study concludes that by acquiring, domesticating, and expressing non-metazoan biosynthetic pathways, bdelloids may have evolved antimicrobial mechanisms absent from other animals, providing a potential explanation for their long-term diversification despite obligate asexuality.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"When rotifers were challenged with a fungal pathogen, horizontally acquired genes were over twice as likely to be upregulated as other genes — a stronger enrichment than observed for abiotic stressors."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: The Bizarre Biology of Bdelloid Rotifers – Biological Recording ---
URL: https://biologicalrecording.co.uk/2025/09/23/bdelloid-rotifers

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Biological Recording (biologicalrecording.co.uk) is a blog article titled "The Bizarre Biology of Bdelloid Rotifers" by Joss Carr, featuring a Q&A with Dr. Chris Wilson, a Lecturer in Biology at the University of Oxford. 

Key points covered:
- Bdelloid rotifers are tiny filter-feeding animals living in freshwater habitats worldwide (ponds, streams, lakes, moss, soil, puddles, ice sheets), among the most resilient of all animals.
- All bdelloid rotifers are females—no males have been observed in 300 years since discovery. Mothers lay eggs that hatch into genetic copies of themselves without sex, sperm, or fertilisation.
- They steal DNA from other organisms via horizontal gene transfer, with about 1 in 10 genes (approximately 10% of their genomes) copied from bacteria, fungi, and even plants.
- They have stolen dozens of antibiotic recipes from bacteria, which they use to fight off their own diseases—potentially leading to shortcuts in developing drugs against antibiotic-resistant infections in humans.

Q&A Highlights with Dr. Chris Wilson:
1. Species definition: Despite asexual reproduction, rotifers can be defined into discrete species based on morphology (consistent clustered forms), supplemented by DNA sequencing that corroborates distinct genetic clusters.
2. Gene stealing from animals: Very hard to determine; plant DNA is obvious in rotifer genomes but animal DNA would be less detectable. Dr. Wilson guesses they are almost certainly stealing genes from other animals.
3. Species identification difficulty: Very difficult because bdelloid rotifers are soft-bodied with diagnostic parts (wheel organs) tucked internally; must minimize time between field sampling and microscope viewing. The only identification key is in German and ~50 years old. Only a handful of people worldwide are skilled at identifying them to species level.
4. Horizontal gene transfer consistency: Generally consistent within species because most HGT occurred long ago—estimated at only once every ~100,000 years. Some genes are unique to particular species (more recent arrivals), and clusters appear consistent among individuals within species.
5. Mechanism of HGT: Unknown. No one has witnessed it; experiments to make rotifers "eat" DNA have failed. Hypotheses include DNA incorporation during desiccation-repair (though some non-desiccation-surviving rotifers still have horizontal genes) and "jumping DNA" (transposons). This remains an active research area.

The page also includes links to literature references (Wilson et al. 2024, Wilson and Sherman 2010) and information about the entoLIVE webinar programme delivered by the Biological Recording Company, sponsored by the British Entomological & Natural History Society, Royal Entomological Society, and Amateur Entomologists' Society.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Unlike other known animals, all bdelloid rotifers are females, with no sightings of males in the 300 years since they were discovered — rotifer mothers lay eggs that hatch into genetic copies of themselves, without sex, sperm or fertilisation."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>

The study investigates how horizontally transferred fungal carotenoid genes in the pea aphid (*Acyrthosiphon pisum*) enable light-driven ATP synthesis that promotes cold adaptation.

**Methods:** Green morph aphids were reared on broad bean (Vicia faba) at controlled conditions. 6. The P.aerivorus/P.pacifica comparison of three genes in 24 natural isolates revealed copy number variations: Ppa-cel-1 and Ppa-cel-2 were found in all 24 isolates, but Ppa-cel-3 only in 16, suggesting recent duplication from Ppa-cel-2.

8. Evidence of intron gain after HGT: putative donor cellulase genes in slime molds (Dictyostelium discoideum and Polysphondylium pallidum) contain only 1-2 introns, while P. pacificus cellulase genes possess 13-16 introns (14-452 bp), including several introns below 50 bp typical of P. pacificus.

CONCLUSION: The study demonstrated that functional assimilation, remarkable gene turnover, and positive selection are key features of horizontal gene transfer events in nematodes. Five key notions support functional integration: transcription of cellulase genes, detection of peptides by mass spectrometry, demonstration of secreted cellulase enzymatic activity, intron gain in phase with functional open reading frames, and high turnover dynamics with selection. The authors speculate that HGT represents a major source for evolutionary innovation in nematodes, helping them invade diverse ecosystems including as parasites of plants and animals.
</summary>

"We could demonstrate functional integration of acquired cellulase genes into the nematode's biology as predicted by theory. Thus, functional assimilation, remarkable gene turnover and selection might represent key features of horizontal gene transfer events in nematodes."

--- SOURCE 17: Meloidogyne ---
URL: http://nemaplex.ucdavis.edu/taxadata/g076.aspx

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page is an entry in the Nemaplex database (UC Davis) providing a comprehensive overview of the root-knot nematode genus Meloidogyne (Goeldi, 1892), the type species of which is Meloidogyne exigua. It covers taxonomy, morphology, distribution, economic importance, feeding/host-parasite interactions, symptoms, hosts, life cycle, damage, and management.

KEY POINTS:

Classification: Rhabditida → Tylenchina → Tylenchoidea → Meloidogynidae → Meloidogyninae. The name derives from Greek words meaning "apple-shaped" and "female."

History: The International Meloidogyne Project (J.N. Sasser, US-AID, ~1975-1985) advanced species separation using host range tests, chromosome counts (Triantaphyllou), juvenile head structure (Eisenback), protein gel electrophoresis, and DNA patterns. The North Carolina Differential Hosts Test distinguishes four common species (M. incognita races 1-4, M. arenaria races 1-2, M. javanica, M. hapla) using cotton, tobacco, pepper, watermelon, peanut, and tomato. There are about 100 described species (2021); 68 were listed in 1988 by Luc, Maggenti et al.

Morphology/Anatomy: Females have 2 prodelphic ovaries, are swollen, deposit eggs in a matrix secreted by six rectal glands (eggs not retained in the body), have an excretory pore usually anterior to the metacorpus, do not form cysts, and have fingerprint-like perineal cuticular striations. Males have 1-2 testes, no caudal alae, and a characteristic half-twist of the body. They are sedentary obligate root parasites that usually form galls; parthenogenesis predominates.

Distribution: Worldwide distribution; most widely recognized plant-parasitic nematode due to characteristic galling symptoms.

Economic Importance: In California's Nematode Pest Rating System, unencountered potentially hazardous species are A-rated; limited-distribution species like M. naasi and M. chitwoodi are B-rated; widespread species are C-rated. The "major" species (M. arenaria, M. hapla, M. incognita, M. javanica) were recognized since Chitwood's 1949 characterization. Emerging species (M. chitwoodi, M. fallax, M. minor, M. enterolobii, M. exigua, M. paranaensis) are increasingly recognized via biochemical/molecular methods; M. floridensis is a growing concern in California for overcoming Nemaguard rootstock resistance in Prunus.

Host-Parasite Interactions: J2 larvae are attracted to root tips (zone of elongation), lateral root emergence sites, and by CO2 (possibly via lowered pH from carbonic acid). They penetrate mechanically (stylet thrusts) and chemically (cellulase, pectinase), migrating between cortical cells toward the apex, then back to the vascular cylinder. Subventral glands (prominent in J2, atrophying in adults) are linked to giant cell initiation. The dorsal esophageal gland (DEG) secretions (packed in 800nm secretory granules) stimulate multinucleate giant cells; if the nematode is removed, giant cells atrophy. Giant cells form via acytokinetic mitosis (karyokinesis without cytokinesis / endoreduplication), while syncytia in Heterodera/Globodera form via repeated S-phase endoreduplication. Over 50 genes are upregulated in feeding cell development. Chorismate mutase from nematode esophageal glands suppresses pathogen-triggered immunity (salicylic acid pathway). The nematode also induces hyperplasia (galling), higher auxin and cytokinin levels in galled tissue, and systemically induces transcriptome/spliceome reprogramming (9064 splicing events in 2898 genes).

Symptoms: Yellowing, mid-day wilting, water/nutrient stress symptoms, gall formation, root branching, sometimes death with interacting organisms.

Hosts: Parasites of over 3,000 host plants as a genus; Jensen et al. (1977) listed 874 crop species for 7-8 species in the western U.S. M. incognita is extremely polyphagous (up to 3,000 plant species), while M. megatyla and M. pini are restricted to Pinus spp.

Life Cycle: J2 penetrate roots, migrate intercellularly to the vascular cylinder, induce feeding sites, become sedentary, molt through J3 and J4 (which pass within the J2 cuticle, do not feed), then molt to females which lay 400-500 eggs (up to 2,800) in a gelatinous matrix. Most growth occurs during the second stage. Cellulases in the egg-mass matrix (possibly acquired via horizontal gene transfer from bacteria) help digest a hole to the root surface. Sex reversal can occur under adverse conditions. Body weight increases ~250-fold (0.11 ug J2 to 300 ug female+egg mass); total energy demand = 1 calorie. Comparison table: Meloidogynidae have multinucleate giant cell feeding sites (vs. syncytium in Heteroderidae), wide host range, mainly parthenogenic reproduction, eggs in egg mass, no cyst, hatching from favorable environmental conditions, and acytokinetic mitosis + endoreduplication cell cycle.

Management (Host Plant Resistance): Resistance may be pre-infection (preventing entry) or post-infection (preventing egg-laying stage). The Mi gene (single dominant gene near centromere of chromosome 6) confers resistance to M. incognita, M. javanica, and M. arenaria, and also against potato aphid (Macrosiphum euphorbiae) and whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). It was transferred from wild Solanum peruvianum via embryo rescue techniques (Smith, 1944). The Aps-1 acid phosphatase isozyme marker (Rick and Fobes, 1974) aided breeding. The gene was cloned and sequenced in Dr. Valerie Williamson's lab at UC Davis and transferred to susceptible tomato via Agrobacterium. Resistance breaks down at soil temperatures >28°C and with repeated single-source resistance use in California, aggressive nematode strains are being selected (Kaloshian et al. 1996). A table shows vegetable cultivars with resistance: M. incognita has the most (109 total, including 43 tomato, 30 cowpea), with only 3 resistant cultivars for M. hapla.
</summary>

"The 'major' species, M. arenaria, M. hapla, M. incognita and M. javanica, have been recognized and well-studied since Chitwood's characterization of the genus in 1949... some species of root-knot nematodes, e.g., M. chitwoodi, M. fallax, M. minor, M. enterolobii (=M. mayaguensis), M. exigua, and M. paranaensis, have been recognized with the advent of biochemical and molecular methods,"

--- SOURCE 18: Widespread horizontal gene transfer between plants and their microbiota ---
URL: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.08.25.505314.full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a bioRxiv preprint (DOI: 10.1101/2022.08.25.505314) titled "Widespread horizontal gene transfer between plants and their microbiota" by Shelly Haimlich, Yulia Fridman, Hitaishi Khandal, Sigal Savaldi-Goldstein, and Asaf Levy (from Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Technion-Israel Institute of Technology). It has since been published in ISME Communications (doi: 10.1093/ismeco/ycae073).

**Objective & Hypothesis:** The authors hypothesized that the spatial proximity and long-term relationships between plants and their microbiota promote cross-kingdom horizontal gene transfer (HGT). They tested this using Arabidopsis thaliana and its extensively sequenced microbiome.

**Methodology:**
- Compared A. thaliana genes against 582 fully sequenced commensal bacteria isolated from Arabidopsis (plant-associated, PA), covering 1,051 genomes total (including 441 non-plant-associated bacteria, plants, fungi, archaea, and other eukaryotes).
- Used BLASTP with threshold of at least 35% amino acid identity across at least 80% of both proteins.
- Filtered out 'trivial hits' shared with organelles (mitochondria and chloroplast, which originate in bacteria).
- Constructed gene trees from multiple sequence alignments to detect phylogenetic evidence of HGT (where gene trees and genome trees were inconsistent).

**Key Results:**
- Identified 767 Arabidopsis proteins mapped to 60,850 bacterial proteins as potential molecular mimicry candidates.
- Detected 180 unique cross-kingdom HGT events: 84 genes likely transferred from plants to bacteria, and 96 genes from PA bacteria to plants.
- Additionally found 161 genes transferred between PA bacteria and the eukaryotic domain (source unclear), 65 genes with unclear inheritance patterns, and 361 genes with no HGT patterns.
- Rejected DNA contamination by confirming no homologous pairs exceeded 76% amino acid identity.

**Functional Enrichment:**
- Genes transferred from plants to bacteria are enriched in secreted proteins, carbohydrate catabolism enzymes (pectin esterase, glycosidase), and include chitinases (CHI, AT2G43570), endo beta mannanase (XCD1), and pectin lyases (PME5) — enabling bacteria to exploit plant-derived sugars.
- Genes transferred from bacteria to plants are enriched in redox homeostasis and cytoplasmic proteins, including many auxin biosynthesis YUCCA genes and nucleoside metabolic processes. 69/96 (72%) of such genes are found in all dicots and monocots, suggesting ancient HGT events.

**Taxonomic Patterns:**
- Bacteroidetes were enriched as gene acceptors from plants, while Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria were depleted as either acceptors or donors.
- Rhizobiales and Hyphomicrobiales (Proteobacteria) and Micrococcales (Actinobacteria) showed significantly fewer HGT events than expected.
- In most cases the donor/acceptor taxonomy remained "unknown" (multiple phyla involved).

**Recent HGT Examples:**
- The plant CHI (chitinase) gene is present in only 7 PA Streptomyces genomes (patchy distribution), with protein structures very similar (RMSD=0.791).
- The bacterial DET2 homologue (steroid-5-alpha-reductase, key in brassinosteroid biosynthesis) is nearly specific to plant-associated Leifsonia genus (Actinobacteria), located downstream of a tRNA gene; protein structures highly similar (RMSD=0.727) despite less than 50% sequence identity.

**Functional Validation (Proof-of-Concept):**
- The authors tested whether the Leifsonia DET2 homologue (lfDET2) could functionally replace the Arabidopsis DET2 gene. Arabidopsis DET2 is 46% identical to Leifsonia Det2 (similar to identity shared with rice and barley homologues).
- Expression of lfDET2 (driven by 35S or Arabidopsis DET2 promoters) in the Arabidopsis det2 mutant background rescued the dwarf phenotype and root meristem defects, restoring normal plant growth.
- lfDET2 localized to the endoplasmic reticulum, matching atDET2 localization.

**Conclusion:** The results suggest cross-kingdom HGT is relatively frequent and shaped the genomes of plants and their microbiota by adding adaptive traits. The transferred genes likely participate in molecular mimicry between hosts and their commensal microbiomes. Key author correspondence: alevy@mail.huji.ac.il.
</summary>

"We detected 180 unique genes that were horizontally transferred between plants and their microbiota. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Smithsonian Magazine article (published around December 2015, authored by Maris Fessenden) reports on a scientific controversy regarding tardigrade genomes. Tardigrades (also called moss piglets or water bears) are microscopic aquatic invertebrates known for surviving extreme conditions like the vacuum of space, desiccation, and freezing.

The controversy began when a University of North Carolina (UNC) team, led by researchers including Thomas Boothby and Bob Goldstein, published research in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences reporting that the tardigrade species Hypsibius dujardini carries about 6,600 genes acquired through horizontal gene transfer from other organisms (mostly bacteria, but also fungi, plants, viruses, and archaea). They claimed this foreign DNA made up about 17.5 percent of the tardigrade's genome, and suggested these genes might explain the creatures' resilience to extreme conditions.

About a week later, a rival group from the University of Edinburgh, led by Mark Blaxter (including Sujai Kumar), challenged these findings. They had also sequenced the same species and found only between 36 and 500 horizontally transferred genes—a much smaller proportion. The Edinburgh group published their contradictory findings on the preprint server bioRxiv.org before formal peer review. They suspected the UNC group had mistakenly sequenced DNA from bacteria living alongside the tardigrades, confusing microbial genes with tardigrade genes. Blaxter noted that some DNA fragments were too rare to biologically belong to the same genome.

The UNC researchers acknowledged the possibility of contamination but defended their methodology, stating they were aware of the potential problem and would conduct additional analysis before further comment. They appreciated that their rivals published contradictory results quickly on bioRxiv.

The article highlights this back-and-forth as demonstrating how science can self-correct rapidly in the digital age—what took nine days in this case would have taken months in the past. Both teams praised the fast publication times and data sharing. As of publication, the jury was still out on how much of the tardigrade's genome comes from foreign sources.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"What is evident is the amazing new ability of science to self correct rapidly," Blaxter tells Yong.
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Science News article (published December 2015, by Tina Hesman Saey) reports on a scientific dispute over claims that tardigrades (water bears) are prolific gene borrowers through horizontal gene transfer. A previous study led by Bob Goldstein at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (published November 23, 2015, in PNAS) claimed that tardigrades (Hypsibius dujardini) obtained about 17 percent of their genes from bacteria and other organisms.

However, researchers in evolutionary biologist Mark Blaxter's lab at the University of Edinburgh conducted a new analysis (posted online December 1 on BioRxiv.org) concluding that the bacterial DNA in the reported tardigrade genome is mostly contamination, not genuine horizontal gene transfer. The Edinburgh team estimated that about 30 percent of the DNA in the North Carolina group's tardigrade genome may be contaminants, and that foreign genes may account for less than 1 percent of the tardigrade genome. Blaxter's team was able to confirm only 54 of the more than 6,600 proposed borrowed genes as genuinely embedded in the tardigrade genome.

Goldstein and coauthor Thomas Boothby acknowledged in a written comment that the new analysis "raises some reasonable concerns about contamination" in their paper, noting they had considered contamination as the most likely initial explanation.

Context for the discrepancy: Only 107 of the alleged foreign genes underwent close scrutiny in the original study, with results extrapolated to the rest. Salzberg (Johns Hopkins) noted the tardigrade genome's size of more than 212 million bases—more than twice what Goldstein's group previously reported—raised red flags. Tardigrades contain only about 1,000 cells, so scientists must pool many animals to get enough DNA, inevitably mixing in DNA from the microbiome and ingested algae. The assembled genome sits in thousands of small pieces.

University of Cambridge molecular cell biologist Chiara Boschetti cautioned that it's not yet established that the Edinburgh analysis is correct, noting they "may have over-cleaned their data." She framed the dispute as a positive example of scientific self-correction: "Such quick testing of extraordinary claims is how science should work... Let's find out where the truth is."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We said, 'This is so different from our assembly, something must be wrong,'" Blaxter recalls.

--- SOURCE 1: Multiple lateral gene transfers and duplications have promoted plant parasitism ability in nematodes - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2955110

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in PNAS (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) on October 12, 2010 (doi: 10.1073/pnas.1008486107, PMID: 20876108, PMCID: PMC2955110), authored by Etienne G.J. Danchin and colleagues from INRA Sophia-Antipolis (France) and CNRS Marseille (France). The article is titled "Multiple lateral gene transfers and duplications have promoted plant parasitism ability in nematodes."

MAIN TOPIC: The study investigates the evolutionary origins of plant cell wall-degrading/modifying enzymes found in plant-parasitic nematodes. These enzymes are generally absent from animals but show similarity to bacterial homologs, suggesting acquisition via lateral gene transfer (LGT).

KEY FINDINGS:
- The analysis demonstrates that multiple independent LGT events from different bacterial sources gave rise to six gene families involved in plant cell-wall modification in clade IV plant-parasitic nematodes (root-knot nematodes and cyst nematodes).
- The plant-parasitic nematode genome of Meloidogyne incognita contains more than 60 genes covering six different protein families for cell wall degradation—an unprecedented repertoire in animals, including cellulases, xylanases, polygalacturonases, pectate lyases, candidate arabinanases, and expansin-like proteins.
- The six gene families and their closest bacterial relatives include: GH28 polygalacturonases (closest to Ralstonia solanacearum), PL3 pectate lyases (closest to Actinomycetales like Clavibacter michiganensis), GH43 arabinanases (closest to Actinomycetales), GH5 cellulases (closest to Bacteroidetes and some insects), GH5 xylanases (closest to Clostridium acetobutylicum), and EXPN expansin-like proteins (closest to Actinomycetales).
- Multiple potential bacterial donors are plant pathogens or symbiotic soil bacteria that share plant hosts with nematodes, satisfying the criterion of sympatry for LGT to occur.
- Massive gene duplications following LGT acquisition account for the abundance and diversity of these multigenic families.
- Genes feature multiple introns (with at least one intron position shared across lineages), indicating early intron gain after LGT; GC content and codon usage of LGT-acquired genes are indistinguishable from other nematode genes, supporting ancient transfer.
- Four groups of bacteria may serve as potential donors; notably, Clavibacter michiganensis (which shares hosts with nematodes) possesses the PL3 most closely related to those of root-knot and cyst nematodes.

--- SOURCE 13: Horizontal gene transfer ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horizontal_gene_transfer

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Wikipedia article on Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT) or Lateral Gene Transfer (LGT), defined as the movement of genetic material between organisms other than by vertical transmission (parent to offspring). HGT is the primary mechanism for the spread of antibiotic resistance in bacteria and plays an important role in bacterial evolution, including the degradation of novel compounds like human-created pesticides and the evolution, maintenance, and transmission of virulence. It involves temperate bacteriophages and plasmids, with mechanisms including transformation, transduction, and conjugation.

HISTORY: Griffith's experiment (1928) first suggested bacterial transformation. Horizontal genetic transfer was described in 1951 in Seattle, showing transfer of a viral gene into Corynebacterium diphtheriae created a virulent strain. Inter-bacterial gene transfer was first described in a 1959 Japanese publication demonstrating transfer of antibiotic resistance between different bacterial species. Syvanen (mid-1980s) postulated lateral gene transfer has existed since the beginning of life. Molecular biologists such as Peter Gogarten have described HGT as "A New Paradigm for Biology."

MECHANISMS include: (1) Transformation – uptake/expression of foreign DNA; (2) Transduction – bacterial DNA moved by bacteriophages; (3) Bacterial conjugation – transfer via plasmid during cell-to-cell contact using Type IV Secretion Systems; (4) Gene transfer agents – virus-like elements encoded by the host found in alphaproteobacteria.

HORIZONTAL TRANSPOSON TRANSFER (HTT): Transposable elements (jumping genes) can carry resistance genes between genomes. HTT is increasingly recognized as common in eukaryotes as well as prokaryotes. DNA transposons and LTR retroelements are more likely to undergo HTT due to stable double-stranded DNA intermediates. In plants, LTR retrotransposons of the Copia superfamilies (specifically Ale and Ivana lineages with low copy numbers) are more likely to transfer horizontally. Proposed vectors include arthropods, viruses, freshwater snails, and endosymbiotic bacteria. Spatial and taxonomic proximity favor HTT.

DETECTION: HGT is typically inferred using bioinformatics (parametric methods identifying atypical sequence signatures, or identifying discrepancies in evolutionary history). Shotgun metagenomics can identify phylogenetic mismatches indicating HGT. Transferred genes are called "xenologs."

VIRUSES: The Sputnik satellite virus can perform horizontal gene transfer between viruses, as some of its genes are closely related to mimivirus and mamavirus genes, paralleling how bacteriophages ferry genes between bacteria.

PROKARYOTES: HGT is common among bacteria and between bacteria and archaea. It is a significant cause of increased drug resistance and spread of virulence factors like exotoxins and exoenzymes. Examples include multi-drug resistant S. aureus, Shiga toxins in E. coli via transduction with Shigella. Restriction-modification systems provide immunity against HGT. Horizontally transferred elements play roles in virulence of E. coli, Salmonella, Streptococcus, and Clostridium perfringens. HGT is active around secondary/specialized metabolite production. The integrated conjugative element (ICE) Bs1 plays a role in the SOS response of Bacillus subtilis.

BACTERIAL TRANSFORMATION: A complex, energy-requiring developmental process requiring about 40 genes in Bacillus subtilis. Competence is induced by high cell density or nutritional limitation and appears to be an adaptation for DNA repair. It occurs in at least 67 prokaryotic species. It can be viewed as a primitive sexual process.

BACTERIAL CONJUGATION: Uses Type IV Secretion Systems (T4SS). Single-strand DNA binding proteins (SSBs) encoded in conjugative plasmids may aid conjugation though some (like PrgE in pCF10 of Enterococcus faecalis) are not essential. Conjugation is important in microbiomes, contributing to genetic diversity and evolution, including antibiotic resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Mycobacterial conjugation (in M. smegmatis) differs from E. coli: it is chromosome rather than plasmid based.

ARCHAEAL DNA TRANSFER: Haloarchaea derived 126 composite gene families from bacterial genomes, allowing adaptation to salty environments. Sulfolobus solfataricus and S. acidocaldarius undergo UV-induced pili formation, cellular aggregation, and high-frequency DNA exchange/recombination for DNA repair via homologous recombination. The ups operon (five genes) is highly induced by UV and employed in these processes, increasing fitness after UV exposure.

EUKARYOTES: HGT has occurred within eukaryotes from chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes to the nuclear genome (per endosymbiotic theory). Mitochondrial genes moved to Rafflesiaceae parasites from hosts, and from chloroplasts to mitochondria of Phaseolus beans. Horizontal transfer occurs from bacteria to fungi like Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Agrobacterium can transfer genes to plants (causing crown galls). Monarch butterflies and silkworms have been genetically modified by HGT from wasp bracovirus. The trypanosomal parasite causing Chagas disease (transmitted by assassin bugs/Reduviidae) can insert DNA into the human genome.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific review article, "Horizontal gene transfer: building the web of life" by Soucy, Huang, and Gogarten (published in Nature Reviews Genetics, August 2015, Volume 16), provides a comprehensive overview of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) — the sharing of genetic material between organisms not in a parent-offspring relationship — and its role in shaping evolution across all domains of life.

**Key mechanisms of HGT in prokaryotes:** The three most recognized mechanisms are conjugation (transfer via physical contact through a conjugation pilus), transformation (uptake of exogenous DNA from the environment), and transduction (gene delivery through phage predation, with generalized and specialized subtypes). More recently described mechanisms include gene transfer agents (GTAs) — phage-derived systems carrying random host DNA fragments — and cell fusion (bidirectional gene exchange, observed in archaea such as Haloferax and Sulfolobus).

**HGT in eukaryotes:** Gene exchange became more complicated with the evolution of the nucleus, but mechanisms include endosymbiotic gene transfer (EGT), introgression (gene flow from hybridization followed by backcrosses), the "you are what you eat" ratchet (gene acquisition through phagotrophy in protists), and the weak-link model (weakly protected unicellular or early developmental stages as entry points for foreign genes into multicellular eukaryotes).

**Detecting HGT:** Methods rely primarily on phylogenetic conflict (conflicting branching patterns between gene and species trees), gene composition analysis (codon usage and oligonucleotide composition), and pan-genome analysis. The pan-genome consists of the core genome (genes in all members) and accessory genome (genes in only some members). An analysis of 61 E. coli genomes revealed only 6% of gene families were present in all genomes.

**Evolutionary impact:** HGT is more frequent between closely related organisms — in haloarchaea, over 90% of HGTs were integrated through homologous recombination, and HGT frequency decreases exponentially with phylogenetic distance. HGT drives metabolic innovations (e.g., the methylaspartate cycle in haloarchaea, over 1,000 bacterial genes imported into haloarchaea enabling the move to aerobic environments) and shapes holobiont evolution. In human microbiomes, HGT is 25-fold more frequent between human-associated organisms than between organisms from different hosts or environments.

**Key examples of HGT effects:**
- Gut bacteria in Japanese people acquired seaweed-digesting enzymes from parasites of marine algae
- The moss Physcomitrella patens acquired genes from fungi, bacteria, viruses, and aquatic animals
- The basal flowering plant Amborella trichopoda acquired at least four whole mitochondrial genomes from mosses and green algae
- Type II antifreeze protein genes were transferred among herring, smelt, and sea raven, aiding adaptation to icy water
- C4 photosynthesis was acquired by Alloteropsis grasses multiple times through gene transfers from other C4 grasses
- Genes from archaic to modern humans (brain development allele via introgression)
- Chlamydial genes found in photosynthetic eukaryotes, suggesting involvement in plastid establishment

**Conclusions:** While mechanisms of prokaryotic gene exchange are well understood, mechanisms in multicellular eukaryotes (weak-link model, sperm-mediated transfer, introgression) remain less clear. The review emphasizes that HGT creates a "web of life" rather than a simple branching tree, and that transferred genes range from beneficial to neutral, with neutral acquisitions sometimes later becoming domesticated and producing beneficial phenotypes.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 17: Horizontal Gene Transfer – Microbial Genetics (Dr.B) ---
URL: https://open.maricopa.edu/microbialgenetics/chapter/horizontal-gene-transfer

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is Chapter 5 of the open educational textbook "Microbial Genetics (Dr.B)" by Graham Boorse (2025), published on the Maricopa Open Digital Press platform. It covers Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT or lateral gene transfer) in bacteria, a key driver of bacterial evolution and adaptability that allows bacteria to acquire new genetic material from other bacteria (even distantly related ones) within the same generation, distinct from vertical gene transfer (parent to offspring).

The chapter identifies three primary mechanisms of HGT:

1. **Transformation**: Bacteria take up free or "naked" DNA released from lysed (burst) cells in the environment. Requires the recipient cell to be in a state of "competence" for DNA binding, uptake, and integration (often via homologous recombination). This was famously demonstrated by Frederick Griffith in 1928, providing early evidence that DNA is the carrier of genetic information. It is a cornerstone laboratory technique, including the educational use of transforming E. coli with the pGLO plasmid, which carries genes for ampicillin resistance and Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP), allowing fluorescence under UV light.

2. **Transduction**: Bacterial DNA is transferred via a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria). During phage replication, bacterial DNA can be mistakenly packaged into new phage particles. Generalized transduction transfers any bacterial gene, while specialized transduction transfers genes located near the phage integration site. It can occur between different bacterial species susceptible to the same phage.

3. **Conjugation**: Direct transfer of DNA through cell-to-cell contact, likened to bacterial "mating." Typically requires a conjugative plasmid (such as the F-plasmid or fertility factor in E. coli), which codes for a sex pilus that initiates contact and a mating bridge for DNA transfer via rolling circle replication. High-frequency recombination (Hfr) cells, with the plasmid integrated into the chromosome, can also transfer chromosomal DNA. This mechanism is highly efficient and can even transfer genes across broader taxonomic groups.

The chapter emphasizes that HGT is a cornerstone of bacterial evolution, enabling rapid acquisition of new functions (antibiotic resistance, virulence, metabolic capabilities) and posing a major global health challenge through the spread of antibiotic resistance genes. Understanding HGT is critical for developing strategies to combat infectious diseases, for bioremediation, and for biotechnological applications. The content is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology (authored by Vincent Daubin and Gergely J. Szöllősi) examines horizontal gene transfer (HGT) as a major evolutionary force and explores its implications for reconstructing the tree of life.

MECHANISMS: The paper reviews the three well-documented mechanisms of HGT: Transformation (uptake of free DNA from the environment, as first demonstrated by Griffith in 1928 with pneumococcus bacteria), Conjugation (one-way DNA transfer via a "sexual pilus" carried by conjugative plasmids or bacteriophages), and Transduction (transfer via bacteriophages, including defective phages called "gene transfer agents"/GTAs). Once inside a cell, DNA may be destroyed, persist as plasmids, or integrate into the host chromosome via homologous recombination or insertion.

DETECTION METHODS: Three approaches identify horizontal transfers: (1) Gene repertoire comparison, which reveals gene content differences between strains/species; (2) Gene composition analysis based on G+C content and codon usage differences; (3) Phylogenetic methods comparing gene trees to species trees, which are the most general and sensitive but require accounting for duplication, transfer, and loss events as well as phylogenetic uncertainty. The adaptive role of HGT is well established through pathogenicity/symbiosis "islands." Ancient transfers even touched fundamental functions (e.g., reverse gyrase in hyperthermophiles, tRNA synthetases). The "complexity hypothesis" suggests proteins with more molecular interactions are less likely to be transferred.

Only about 60 genes are common to all living genomes (insufficient to perform universal functions). Gene repertoire differences arise from duplication, gene loss, HGT, saturation of homology signal, and new gene origins.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (Annu. Rev. Phytopathol. 2000, by U. Liane Rosewich and H. Corby Kistler) examines the role of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in fungal evolution. The authors define HGT as stable transfer of genetic material between individuals not attributable to vertical (meiotic or mitotic) processes. They note that although HGT evidence in eukaryotes remains largely anecdotal, fungi may have experienced more HGT than other eukaryotes, making them well-suited model systems because HGT can be tested experimentally.

The authors outline indirect evidence for HGT, including character-state discordance between element and organismal phylogenies, high similarity between elements in distantly related organisms, irregular distribution patterns, habitat-associated gene sharing, and genomic inconsistencies (G+C content, codon usage). Alternative explanations (erroneous phylogenies, paralog comparisons, ancestral retention, introgressive hybridization) must be considered. Phylogenetic tests include bootstrapping, maximum likelihood, T-PTP tests, and incongruence length differences.

The review organizes potential HGT cases by element type:
1. PLASMIDS: Fungal plasmids (usually 1-21 kb, linear, often mitochondrial) show discordant phylogenies, random global distribution patterns (e.g., 7 Neurospora plasmid groups among 225 isolates), and experimental transfer. Horizontal transfer was demonstrated experimentally by co-culturing unrelated strains (e.g., pAI2 from Ascobolus immersus to Podospora anserina; kalilo between Neurospora species).
2. MYCOVIRUSES: Lacking an extracellular phase, these transfer via cytoplasmic mixing. Some RdRp similarities between distant species suggest possible HGT.
3. INTRONS: Group I introns (nuclear, mitochondrial, and rRNA) and group II introns (organellar only) can move via homing and transposition. The best-substantiated case involves horizontal transfer of a group I intron from fungi to the angiosperm Peperomia. The cox1 intron i4 of Agrocybe aegerita showed 90.5% amino acid identity with the homologous intron in P. anserina, strongly supporting recent HGT. Intron phylogenies are often incongruent with species phylogenies.
4. TRANSPOSABLE ELEMENTS: Sporadic distribution patterns (e.g., grasshopper retrotransposon in Magnaporthe grisea, Fot1 in Fusarium oxysporum) suggest HGT, though stochastic loss is an alternative explanation. Vectors (symbionts/parasites) are proposed but unproven.

The authors conclude that HGT in fungi may be a more important evolutionary factor than in other eukaryotes, particularly for introns and plasmids, which may need periodic horizontal transfer for long-term persistence.

![PLOS](/resource/img/logo-plos-full-color.svg)

## Figures

![Figure 1](/plosbiology/article/figure/image?size=inline&id=10.1371/journal.pbio.0040005.g001)
![Figure 2](/plosbiology/article/figure/image?size=inline&id=10.1371/journal.pbio.0040005.g002)
![Figure 3](/plosbiology/article/figure/image?size=inline&id=10.1371/journal.pbio.0040005.g003)
![Table 1](/plosbiology/article/figure/image?size=inline&id=10.1371/journal.pbio.0040005.t001)
![Figure 4](/plosbiology/article/figure/image?size=inline&id=10.1371/journal.pbio.0040005.g004)
![Figure 5](/plosbiology/article/figure/image?size=inline&id=10.1371/journal.pbio.0040005.g005)

## Abstract

The majority of well-documented cases of horizontal transfer between higher eukaryotes involve the movement of transposable elements between animals. Surprisingly, although plant genomes often contain vast numbers of these mobile genetic elements, no evidence of horizontal transfer of a nuclear-encoded transposon between plant species has been detected to date. The most mutagenic known plant transposable element system is the *Mutator* system in maize. *Mu*-like elements (MULEs) are widespread among plants, and previous analysis has suggested that the distribution of various subgroups of MULEs is patchy, consistent with horizontal transfer. We have sequenced portions of MULE transposons from a number of species of the genus *Setaria* and compared them to each other and to publicly available databases. A subset of these elements is remarkably similar to a small family of MULEs in rice. A comparison of noncoding and synonymous sequences revealed that the observed similarity is not due to selection at the amino acid level. Given the amount of time separating *Setaria* and rice, the degree of similarity between these elements excludes the possibility of simple vertical transmission of this class of MULEs. This is the first well-documented example of horizontal transfer of any nuclear-encoded genes between higher plants.

**Citation:** Diao X, Freeling M, Lisch D (2006) Horizontal Transfer of a Plant Transposon. PLoS Biol 4(1):
e5.
https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.0040005

**Academic Editor:** Robert Martienssen, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, United States of America,

**Received:** April 19, 2005; **Accepted:** October 31, 2005; **Published:**  December 20, 2005

**Copyright:**  © 2006 Diao et al. This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original author and source are credited.

**Competing interests:**  The authors have declared that no competing interests exist.

**Abbreviations:**BLAST,
Basic Local Alignment Search Tool; bp,
base pair; MULE,
*Mu*-like element; NCBI,
National Center for Biotechnology Information

## Introduction

Horizontal transfer can be defined as the process by which genes can move between reproductively isolated species. It is far more frequent than was once thought, particularly among prokaryotes [[1](#pbio-0040005-b001)], to the extent that it has complicated analysis of bacterial evolution [[2](#pbio-0040005-b002)]. Like many transfers between bacteria, most well-documented transfers detected to date between higher eukaryotes involve movement of transposable elements [[3](#pbio-0040005-b003)]. The best-documented examples involve the transfer of *P* [[4](#pbio-0040005-b004)] and *mariner* elements [[5](#pbio-0040005-b005)] between animal species. In contrast, no case of horizontal transfer of a nuclear-encoded plant gene has been reported. Recently, systematic analysis of mitochondrial genes and group I mitochondrial introns has revealed that they have been subject to frequent horizontal transfer between plant species [[6](#pbio-0040005-b006)–[8](#pbio-0040005-b008)], suggesting that there is no fundamental barrier to gene flow between reproductively isolated plant species. Interestingly, despite the vast numbers of transposable elements found in most plant nuclear genomes and the demonstrated propensity of these elements to move between animal species, no evidence for horizontal transfer of nuclear-encoded plant transposons has been detected. This is in part due to the lack of comprehensive surveys of these elements in a large number of plants. However, extensive phylogenetic analysis of *haT* [[9](#pbio-0040005-b009),[10](#pbio-0040005-b010)] and *mariner* [[11](#pbio-0040005-b011)] transposons in a variety of plant species has been consistent with vertical, rather than horizontal, transmission of these elements in plants. The same appears to be the case for
CACTA elements [[12](#pbio-0040005-b012)] and the *Ty1-copia* group of retrotransposons [[13](#pbio-0040005-b013)] as well. The case of *mariner* elements is particularly surprising given that *mariner* elements in metazoans are particularly prone to horizontal transfer, to the extent that such transfer has been hypothesized to be an integral part of the success of this class of elements [[14](#pbio-0040005-b014)].

*MuDR* is an unusually active and mutagenic maize class II (DNA intermediate) transposon. It is the autonomous member of a family of transposable elements in maize, all of which share the same 200–base pair (bp) terminal inverted repeats, but each of which contains a unique internal sequence. *MuDR* encodes two genes: *mudrA,* the putative transposase, and *mudrB,* a helper gene; these are translated into two proteins: MURA and MURB, respectively [[15](#pbio-0040005-b015)]. *Mu*-like elements (MULEs) containing *mudrA* homologs and long terminal inverted repeats are widespread among both monocot and dicot angiosperms [[16](#pbio-0040005-b016)–[20](#pbio-0040005-b020)]. Any given species can have multiple, distinct subfamilies of MULEs [[17](#pbio-0040005-b017)].

Previous analysis of DNA gel blots and the sequences of a portion of MULEs from a number of grass species revealed a distinct lack of congruence between species phylogenies and that of their MULEs [[17](#pbio-0040005-b017)], consistent with horizontal transfer. However, given the presence of multiple MULE subfamilies in most grass genomes, a lack of congruence between host and MULE phylogenies would be expected if particular MULE subfamilies were lost from some plant lineages but not from others. Thus, although suggestive, incongruence between transposon and host species phylogenies cannot be expected to conclusively demonstrate horizontal transfer. Our criteria for unequivocal evidence of horizontal transfer of MULEs require that sequences from two species be too similar in noncoding regions to be reasonably expected to have diverged at the same time as their respective host species. Based on such evidence, we report horizontal transfer of a nuclear-encoded transposable MULE between two Gramineae (grass) lineages: the Panicoid and the Bambosoid subfamilies. Extensive phylogenetic and paleontologic evidence suggests that these subfamilies diverged between 30 and 60 million years ago [[21](#pbio-0040005-b021)–[23](#pbio-0040005-b023)]. The degree of similarity in noncoding and synonymous sequence between MULEs in these groups is inconsistent with this divergence time.

## Results

We have isolated portions of MULEs from several species of *Setaria* (millets of the tribe Panicoideae) and compared them with those in publicly available databases and with sequences we have previously obtained [[17](#pbio-0040005-b017)]. Some of these sequences are unexpectedly similar to a small group of rice MULEs. The observed degree of similarity in noncoding and synonymous sites is much higher than one would predict given the time separating *Setaria* and rice.

A total of 27 sequences from eight species of the genus *Setaria* were obtained. All 27 sequences encoded potential products with similarity to the MURA protein from maize (data not shown). Nineteen nonredundant sequences were subjected to more detailed analysis. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that all of the sequences fell into previously defined class II or class III groups of the *MuDR* family of MULEs ([Figure 1](#pbio-0040005-g001)). These classes of elements are phylogenetically distinct from the other known functional MULEs such as *Jittery* in maize [[17](#pbio-0040005-b017)] and *AtMu1* in Arabidopsis [[24](#pbio-0040005-b024)]. As has been previously observed with other species, a single species of *Setaria* may have elements from more than one class of MULEs, consistent with previous observations that multiple, paralogous families of MULEs can exist within a single genome [[15](#pbio-0040005-b015)].

MULE sequences from *Setaria italica* (foxtail millet, not shown) and the closely related *Setaria faberi* (giant foxtail, “sf” in [Figure 1](#pbio-0040005-g001)) are strikingly similar (approximately 90% identical over 585 bp) to an element present on Chromosome 5 of the nuclear genome of *Oryza sativa* ssp. *japonica*. This element is designated *Os493.* A nearly identical element (98.9% nucleotide identity) is also present in *O. sativa* ssp. *indica*. Based on the observation that the sequences flanking the transposon insertion in both of these *O. sativa* ssp. are the same, we conclude that this element is present at the same position in each of these subspecies. *Os493* has similarity to MURA from maize from amino acid 37 to amino acid 730 of the 823–amino acid maize protein. *Os493* is flanked by the 9-bp direct repeats typical of *Mu* transposon insertions. A second, truncated element, *Os072,* is located on Chromosome 1 in *japonica* and is also present at the same position in the *indica* genome. Counting indels as single events, this element is 96% identical to *Os493.* Like the full-length elements, this element is flanked by the same 9-bp flanking duplications in both subspecies. A final truncated element on Chromosome 5, *Os408,* is present in the *japonica* genome but is absent in sequences available from the *indica* genome. This element is 94% identical to *Os493.* These are the only rice elements with significant (>80% nucleotide identity over 585 bp) similarity to the *Setaria* elements. blastn (Nucleotide-Nucleotide Basic Local Alignment Search Tool [BLAST]; National Center for Biotechnology Information [NCBI], Bethesda, Maryland, United States) searches using the full-length element from rice reveal that all other significant blast hits (e value <10−4) to *Os493* that are not members of the genus *Oryza* are to sequences from maize, sorghum, or sugarcane, all of which, like *Setaria,* are Panicoid grasses of the tribe Andropogoneae. To confirm the presence of this class of elements in our rice sample, we used primers specific to *Os493* to amplify several of them. One product was identical over 794 bp to *Os072,* a close relative of *Os493*. A second product was 98% identical to *Os493* (data not shown).

To understand more fully the overall distribution of this class of MULEs within the grasses, Southern blot hybridization was employed using a portion of the *mudrA* homolog from one *S. faberi* element (designated *Sf3*) as a probe to a wide variety of species representing the major subfamilies of the grasses ([Figure 2](#pbio-0040005-g002)). Hybridization and washing of the probe were performed at high stringency (see [Materials and Methods](#s4)); we have empirically determined that this degree of stringency will not detect sequences less than 87% identical to the probe (see below). The results revealed a strikingly discontinuous distribution of this class of elements. As expected based on our sequencing and database searches, it is present in a subset of the Panicoideae, with the strongest hybridization occurring with DNA from *Setaria* sp., although some species, such as *Setaria sphacelata,* hybridized poorly to the probe. Note that the probe did not detect any MULEs in *Setaria anceps,* which has an element that is 87% identical to the probe, thus defining the limit of detection for this probe. At this level of stringency, we did not detect signal from any species of the subfamilies Chloridoideae or Pooideae and only weak signal from Panicoid grasses such as sorghum and maize. As expected, DNA from rice hybridized well to the probe, and the size of the BamHI fragment is that expected for *Os072* (the predicted size of the *Os493* fragment would be too large to transfer onto this blot). Two other Oryzoids, *Ehrharta erecta* and *Zizania latifolia,* did not hybridize. Interestingly, three species of bamboo indigenous to East Asia (*Shibateae kumasaca, Fargesia nitida,* and *Phyllostachys vivax*) hybridized well to the probe, but three species of bamboo indigenous to Central America (*Chusquea montana, Chusquea quila,* and *Otatea acuminata*) did not. Primers designed from the *Setaria* element were used to amplify sequences from *Shibateae kumasaca* and *Fargesia nitida;* sequencing of these products confirmed that they are highly similar to both the rice and the *Setaria* sequences. Indeed, each was 93% identical over 641 bp to the *Setaria Sf3* element and 95% identical to rice *Os493.* Despite the higher similarity of these sequences to those in *Setaria,* we focused our analysis on a comparison between rice and *Setaria* because of the availability of the fully sequenced rice genome.

To extend our analysis to include both coding and noncoding sequences, we obtained most of the complete sequence of a single MULE from *S. faberi.* Using PCR primers designed from the rice MULE terminal inverted repeats, it was possible to amplify and sequence a complete copy of a *Setaria* element with the exception of the 20 bp on both ends that were used as primers. This nearly complete element is designated *Sf4. Sf4* differs from the *Setaria* elements obtained in the first round of amplifications, but it retains significant similarity to *Os493* (see [Figure 1](#pbio-0040005-g001)). The presence of frameshift and/or stop codons in both the *Setaria* and rice MULEs ([Figure 3](#pbio-0040005-g003)) suggests that neither element is currently functional. However, both sequences contain long terminal inverted repeats (approximately 176 bp) and clear nucleotide similarity to the *mudrA* gene of *MuDR.* A region near the 5′ terminal inverted repeats (nucleotides 222–560 in *Os493*) has a number of deletions or insertions in one of the two elements, including a 41-bp deletion in the *Os493* element. A second region near the 3′ terminal inverted repeats (nucleotides 3350–3568 in *Os493*) has reduced homology (only 58% identity). Not counting these two regions and counting indels as single events, overall nucleotide identity of the two MULEs is 88% over 3.8 kb. This is a degree of similarity comparable to that of a well-conserved host gene. For example the *waxy* gene from *S. italica* shares 88% identity over 1.6 kb of open reading frame with *waxy* from rice ([Table 1](#pbio-0040005-t001)).

Due to the long period of time separating *Setaria* and rice (roughly 50 million years), high sequence similarity over more than 3 kb can only be due to selection or horizontal transfer; the species are distantly related such that long sequences not under selection are no longer recognizably homologous [[25](#pbio-0040005-b025)]. Further, conservation of noncoding sequences is far lower in plants than it is in animals, despite very similar neutral mutation rates [[26](#pbio-0040005-b026)].

In order to directly compare genes from *Setaria* and rice, we have examined several nuclear-encoded genes from these two species. Only a few such genes have been sequenced from the genus *Setaria,* mostly from *S. italica.* We have obtained the complete sequence of two nuclear-encoded cDNAs from *S. italica* that have clear homologs in rice: acetyl-coenzyme carboxylase *(acc1)* and oxidoreductase *(o. reductase)* ([Table 1](#pbio-0040005-t001)). The total cDNA coding sequence available was 7,765 bp ([Table 1](#pbio-0040005-t001)). The total untranslated upstream and downstream sequence (sequences immediately adjacent to the start and stop codons) from these genes was 1,203 bp (data not shown). When comparing rice with *S. italica,* these genes show an overall average identity of 76% in coding sequences ([Table 1](#pbio-0040005-t001)) and only 40% in the untranslated sequences after alignment (data not shown). The corrected frequency of nonsynonymous substitutions for these genes ranges from 0.41 to 1.17, and the corrected frequency of synonymous substitutions ranges from 0.05 to 0.16. Importantly, the ratio of synonymous to nonsynonymous substitutions per site (dS/dN) for these genes was 7.2 and 8.0, consistent with selection for function at the amino acid level ([Table 1](#pbio-0040005-t001)). The dissimilarity of the untranslated sequences immediately upstream and downstream of the coding sequences as well as the divergence of synonymous sites is consistent with the absence of selection on these sequences during the roughly 50 million years since the divergence of the *Setaria* and rice lineages. Very little genomic sequence is available for any *Setaria.* However, the complete genomic copy of *S. italica waxy* gene is available. The exons of this gene were 88% identical to the rice *waxy* gene over 1,584 bp. In contrast, the introns shared only 52% identity over 1,243 bp ([Table 1](#pbio-0040005-t001)), which is comparable to the frequency of substitutions in UTR and synonymous sites in this gene and the cDNA sequences (data not shown).

Unlike other genes in rice and *Setaria*, the high degree of homology of the MULEs is not the result of selection at the level of amino acid sequence. This can be inferred from analysis of both introns and synonymous sites.

Because the horizontal transfer hypothesis rests heavily on the analysis of the MULE introns, we will describe them in some detail. The MULEs in rice and *Setaria* contain three predicted short introns at the same locations in each element ([Figure 4](#pbio-0040005-g004); see also [Figure 3](#pbio-0040005-g003)). The first predicted intron represents an insertion relative to *mudrA* in maize, which lacks this sequence. The intron is 82 bp long in the rice element and 78 bp long in the *Setaria* element. Successful splicing of this putative intron would maintain the reading frame of the rice element and precisely remove the insertion from both MULEs ([Figure 4](#pbio-0040005-g004)A). Left unspliced, the intron in both MULEs would result in the introduction of two stop codons and would alter the reading frame of the putative transcript of the rice element. Although no homologous cDNAs are available, an exon trap database, in which genomic sequences are expressed to examine splicing patterns, reveals that this intron can be precisely spliced from *Os493.*

The second intron is in the same position as is the third intron of *mudrA* (see [Figure 2](#pbio-0040005-g002)). This intron is 71 bp in both the *Setaria* and rice elements. Unspliced, this intron would introduce a frameshift and several stop codons to both the rice and the *Setaria* elements. Successful splicing of this intron in the *Setaria* and rice MULEs would result in expression of a short additional region of conservation between the proteins encoded by these elements and MURA ([Figure 4](#pbio-0040005-g004)B). This region includes a previously identified nuclear localization signal [[27](#pbio-0040005-b027)]. The blastn searches identify a maize EST (AW067488) with high similarity to *Os493* and *Sf4* (78% and 77% nucleotide identity, respectively, in this region). It is much more similar to *Os493* and *Sf4* than it is to *MuDR* and is presumably related by vertical transmission to the MULE in *Setaria.* A nearly identical (99% nucleotide identity) genomic version of this cDNA, designated *Zm890,* is also available. A comparison of the genomic to cDNA sequence reveals that this intron in this maize element is spliced precisely at sites predicted for the second intron of *Os493.* A comparison of the maize cDNA to the genomic version of the sequence also reveals the presence of a third intron in this region that is also predicted to be spliced from *Os493* and *Sf4.* This intron is 74 bp in the rice *(Os493), Setaria (Sf4),* and maize *(Zm890)* MULEs. Unspliced, this intron would introduce a frameshift and at least one stop codon in all three elements. The *mudrA* gene from *MuDR* in maize lacks this intron.

When we compare the *Setaria* and rice MULEs, we find that the degree of conservation is as high in these three putative introns (89% identity over the 227-bp total in the three introns) as it is in the rest of the transposon ([Figures 4](#pbio-0040005-g004) and [5](#pbio-0040005-g005)). For comparison, we can use a portion of the similar element in maize *(Zm890)* for which we have both genomic and cDNA sequences. Although the exon sequences are quite similar to the rice and *Setaria* MULEs, the intron sequences retain only limited similarity ([Figures 4](#pbio-0040005-g004) and [5](#pbio-0040005-g005)). Overall, in the region depicted in [Figure 4](#pbio-0040005-g004)B that compares the maize and *Setaria* elements, which includes 348 bp of exon sequence and 145 bp of intron sequence, exon sequences are 92% identical (319 of 348) in comparing the rice and the *Setaria* elements. Together, the last two introns are 88% identical (128 of 145). In contrast, when the maize MULE *Zm890* is compared to *Os493,* although the exon sequences are 78% identical (270 of 348), the intron sequences are only 58% identical (85 of 145), consistent with selection on exon but not intron sequences.
