args.summary:
This is a BioEssays perspective article by Jinling Huang (East Carolina University, USA; Kunming Institute of Botany, China) arguing that horizontal gene transfer (HGT) has been widespread and significant throughout eukaryotic evolution, proposing a "weak-link model" to explain its mechanisms in multicellular eukaryotes.

Key arguments:
1. Many bacterial genes in eukaryotic genomes cannot be explained solely by organellar gene transfer (OGT) from mitochondria or plastids. These organelles represent fixed gene pools that have been progressively depleted through gene loss, so OGT cannot account for all or most bacterial genes. Strong phylogenetic signals exist for various proteobacterial groups (16.7%) and other bacteria (13.8%) in eukaryotic genomes beyond cyanobacteria and alpha-proteobacteria.

2. No insurmountable barriers to HGT exist, even in complex multicellular eukaryotes. Recent HGT events have been reported in cnidarians, mites, insects, nematodes, fish, and land plants. Isolated germ cells are barriers but not absolute ones.

3. HGT has occurred continually throughout eukaryotic evolution. Foreign genes were introduced at major historical stages during evolution of primary photosynthetic eukaryotes. Acquired genes account for 4-5% of genomes in some unicellular eukaryotes (rumen ciliates, Galdieria sulphuraria), over 3% of nematode genomes, and 8-9% of gene content in bdelloid rotifers—likely underestimates due to loss of phylogenetic signal.

4. The weak-link model proposes that unicellular eukaryotes and early developmental stages (spores, zygotes, embryos) of multicellular eukaryotes are the most likely entry points for foreign genes, since nuclear DNA is relatively exposed during these stages. Once incorporated, foreign genes spread through cell proliferation/differentiation to germ cells and are transmitted to offspring.

Specific predictions of the model: (i) frequent HGT in unicellular eukaryotes; (ii) foreign genes in multicellular eukaryotes with exposed early developmental stages; (iii) frequent HGT in asexual multicellular eukaryotes; (iv) many anciently acquired genes in multicellular eukaryotes inherited from unicellular ancestors.

The article contrasts HGT (an open system) with OGT (a closed system that approaches a dead end as transferable gene pools deplete), argues that HGT may be underestimated because patchy gene distributions are often attributed to gene loss or artifacts rather than HGT, and calls for careful investigation of HGT cases with independent lines of evidence. The author concludes that "as long as vertical inheritance remains the null hypothesis, HGT in eukaryotes will likely be underestimated."

You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
Insights & Perspective Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes: The weak-link model Jinling Huang1)2) The signiﬁcance of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in eukaryotic evolution remains controversial. Although many eukaryotic genes are of bacterial origin, they are often interpreted as being derived from mitochondria or plastids.
Because of their ﬁxed gene pool and gene loss, however, mitochondria and plastids alone cannot adequately explain the presence of all, or even the majority, of bacterial genes in eukaryotes. Available data indicate that no insurmountable barrier to HGT exists, even in complex multicellular eukaryotes.
In addition, the discovery of both recent and ancient HGT events in all major eukaryotic groups suggests that HGT has been a regular occurrence throughout the history of eukaryotic evolution. A model of HGT is proposed that suggests both unicellular and early developmental stages as likely entry points for foreign genes into multicellular eukaryotes.
Keywords: .endosymbiosis; eukaryotic evolution; gene acquisition; genome evolution; organellar gene transfer Introduction About a decade ago, Doolittle et al.
raised a question about the number of bacterial genes in protists, speculating that many bacterial genes should have accumulated in genomes of protists through feeding activities [1, 2]. Back then, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) had been documented widely as a mecha-nism to gain foreign genetic materials in prokaryotes, but remained largely an exotic concept in eukaryotes, with little substantial evidence. It is now clear that HGT has occurred in all major eukaryotic lineages. Horizontally acquired genes are not only frequent in unicellular eukaryotes [3–5], but also found in various multicellular eukaryotes, in-cluding cnidarians [6, 7], mites [8], insects [9–12], nematodes [13–15], ﬁsh [16], and land plants [17–22]. Although reports of HGT in eukaryotes are still frequently met with skepticism, evi-dence for HGT throughout eukaryotic evolution is abundant and increasing.
In this paper, I discuss issues related to HGT in eukaryotes. Because most foreign genes reported in eukaryotes thus far are from bacteria, I will focus on bacterial genes. I argue that many bacterial genes in eukaryotes cannot be explained simply as gene transfers from mitochondria or plastids; rather, HGT in eukaryotes should be widespread and expected. Further, I propose a mecha-nism for integration of foreign DNA into eukaryotic genomes during unicellular or early developmental stages, when their nuclear DNA is relatively exposed to potential sources of HGT.
No barrier to HGT in eukaryotes is insurmountable To understand the scale of HGT in eukaryotes, it is important to consider the presumed barriers to gene acquisi-tion. Historically, protists were thought to be more likely to acquire genes than multicellular eukaryotes [1, 3]. Many protists are intimately associated with bacteria or microbial eukaryotes, which serve as food sources, pathogens, or symbionts. Certain species (e.g. Acan-thamoeba sp.) can harbor a wide range of bacterial endosymbionts; in effect, they are training camps for bacterial adaptation to the intracellular environ-ments of eukaryotic hosts [23, 24].
Although mitochondria and plastids – derived from a-proteobacterial and cyanobacterial endosymbionts, respec-tively – often receive the most DOI 10.1002/bies.201300007 1) Department of Biology, East Carolina University, Greenville, NC, USA 2) Key Laboratory of Biodiversity and Biogeography, Kunming Institute of Botany, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Kunming, China Corresponding author: Jinling Huang E-mail: huangj@ecu.edu Abbreviation: HGT, horizontal gene transfer; OGT, organellar gene transfer.
868 www.bioessays-journal.com Bioessays : 868–875,  2013 The Author. Bioessays Published by WILEY Periodicals, Inc. This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs License, which permits use and distribution in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited, the use is non-commercial and no modifications or adaptations are made.
Think again prominent recognition, their bacterial ancestors likely represented only a portion of microbial diversity present within their ancient host cells. Tempo-ral, transient, or obligate endosym-bionts occur in many organisms [25], and differences between obligate endo-symbionts and organelles can be mar-ginal. For example, there has been heated debate over whether Prochlor-ococcus-related cyanobacterial endo-symbionts (chromatophores) in Paulinella should be considered organ-elles [26–28]. Although not to the same extent as in mitochondria and plastids, chromatophore genomes are highly reduced [29], with some essential genes transferred to the nucleus [30]. Translo-cation machinery also has evolved to re-import the protein products of trans-ferred genes back into chromato-phores [31, 32].
Relative to protists, HGT is often assumed to be rare in complex multi-cellular eukaryotes because the physi-cal isolation of germ cells from somatic cells may prevent foreign genes from being transmitted to offspring [33, 34].
Despite this assumption, recent HGT events have been frequently reported in both animals and plants [8, 11, 19–21, 35, 36]. Some of these horizontally acquired genes in animals and plants are derived from symbionts, either inside or outside germ cells [7, 10, 36], whereas others are from free-living organisms [16]. The magnitude of HGT from obligate bacterial endosymbionts to their insect hosts can be staggering [10]. In some other cases, genes even were acquired from other sources to help maintain obligate endosymbionts [37]. HGT appears to be particularly frequent in plant mitochon-dria [38–40], which often harbor mito-chondrial genes from distantly related plants. It has been speculated that the acquisition of foreign genes in plant mitochondria was mediated through parasitism, transfer agents (e.g. insects, pathogens, or viruses), illegitimate pol-lination or other mechanisms [38, 41].
In any case, these foreign genes must ultimately pass through germ cells to be transmitted to the mitochondria of offspring.
These data suggest that, although isolated germ cells may indeed be barriers to HGT in animals and plants, they are not insur-mountable.
Bacterial genes in eukaryotes: How many are of organellar origin?
Given that barriers to HGT clearly are not insurmountable, we can examine available data to contemplate the num-ber of HGT-derived genes in eukaryotes.
It is well known that eukaryotic genomes contain many bacterial genes [42]. Because of the a-proteobac-terial and cyanobacterial origins of mitochondria and plastids, respectively, these genes are often presumed to predominantly be mitochondrial or plastid derivations [43–45]. Indeed, a supertree analysis of 185 genomes from all three domains of life revealed that the strongest phylogenetic signals among eukaryotic genes come from cyanobacteria, a-proteobacteria, and archaebacteria. Presumably these are attributable to plastids, mitochondria and an archaeon that was likely in-volved in the origin of eukaryotic cells [46]. However, strong signals also exist for different proteobacterial groups (16.7%) as well as for various other bacteria (13.8%), raising the question: how many of these remaining bacterial genes are indeed of mitochon-drial or plastid origin?
It can be argued that all these bacterial genes are possibly derived from mitochondria or plastids. Prokary-otic genomes are ﬂuid and shaped by constant gene acquisition and gene loss [47, 48]. Over time, such ﬂuidity could erase the a-proteobacterial or cyanobacterial signal of an organellar gene [45, 49, 50]. This scenario is not unlikely, particularly if the ancient progenitor of mitochondria or plastids was phylogenetically basal to extant a-proteobacteria or cyanobacteria; a sin-gle homologous replacement in either the endosymbiotic ancestor or its sister taxon could completely obliterate the true phylogenetic identity of an organ-elle-derived gene.
Fluid prokaryotic genomes, however, appear not to be a signiﬁcant issue for identifying plastid-derived genes. The majority of function-al genes in plastid genomes are either closely related or highly similar to cyanobacterial sequences [51], despite evidence for HGT to the cyanobacterial progenitor of plastids [52]. Similarly, cyanobacterial signal remains the stron-gest for all bacterial genes in eukaryotes [46], even though some plastid-derived genes might have evolved rapidly as a result of functional decoupling from plastids [53]. There-fore, it is doubtful that the ﬂuidity of prokaryotic genomes could account for all or the majority of genes of other bacterial origins.
The argument that all or most bacterial genes in eukaryotes are of organellar origin is inherently linked to the dynamic process of DNA transfer from organelles to the nucleus [43, 54, 55]. During the evolution of mitochondria and plastids, many organellar genes were either gradually lost or transferred to the nucleus. I here call the latter process organellar gene transfer (OGT) to distin-guish it from endosymbiotic gene transfer (EGT), which also frequently involves other endosymbionts. Indeed, OGT has led to the incorporation of numerous genes of organellar origin into the nuclear genome. However, it is rarely mentioned that the transfer of functional genes from mitochondria or plastids to the nucleus is constrained by the gene pool of these organelles. Genes acquired from mitochondria and plastids in any eukaryotic genome must be fewer in number than the original gene contents of the a-proteobacterial and cyanobacte-rial progenitors of two organelles. Al-though ongoing DNA transfer from organelles to the nucleus has been demonstrated experimentally [56, 57], functional genes are rarely involved.
Conversely, frequent gene loss events during organellar evolution, occurring independently or as a result of OGT, led to increasingly reduced transferrable gene pool in organellar genomes [54, 58].
Major reductions of genomes are com-mon features of many endosymbionts, bacterial, or eukaryotic [58, 59]. Although the scale of gene loss versus transfer to the nucleus is not entirely clear, the loss of organellar genes can be signiﬁcant in some organisms [60, 61]. For instance, the tremendous loss of organellar genes is particularly evident in apicomplexans, both the plastid and mitochondrial genomes of which are highly reduced or completely lost [62, 63]; their nuclear genomes, with genes presumably derived from ﬁve genomes (including plastid, mitochondrial, and nuclear genomes of an algal endosymbiont), sometimes con-tain less than 4,000 genes [62, 64, 65].
.....Insights & Perspective J. Huang 869 Bioessays : 868–875,  2013 The Author. Bioessays Published by WILEY Periodicals, Inc.
Think again Once a gene has been lost from the organellar genome, it is likely gone forever unless a homolog is acquired again from another source, a very rare phenomenon. Over time, the gene pool available for OGT becomes increasingly smaller. In this sense, the process of OGT represents a closed system; it will eventually approach a dead end when the transferable gene pool is depleted.
While this does not diminish the signiﬁ-cance of OGT in eukaryotic genome evolution, it also suggests that mitochon-dria and plastids should not be granted unbound power to explain all bacterial genes in eukaryotes.
Compared to OGT, HGT represents an open system, one theoretically allowing genes to be acquired from virtually unlimited sources. Given the ultimate constraint on OGT, many genes of other bacterial origins may at least be equally explained by HGT. Importantly, the large numbers of proteobacterial and cyanobacterial genes in eukaryotes are also consistent with the observation that proteobacteria and cyanobacteria are the most common endosymbionts in many eukaryotic groups (e.g. amoe-bae [23, 66], fungi, [67], plants [68], insects, nematodes, and other ani-mals [69, 70]). In particular, Wolbachia and Rickettsia are not only common endosymbionts, but also potentially closely related to the bacterial ancestor of mitochondria [43, 71].
In many respects, they are similar to mitochon-dria in having reduced genomes result-ing from both gene loss and transfer to the nucleus [72, 73]. In other cases, they might have been secondarily lost, leaving only their genes in the host nucleus [74]. If similar proteobacterial endosymbionts existed during early eukaryotic evolution, it would be nearly impossible to distinguish their phyloge-netic signal from that of mitochondria.
HGT occurs continually in major eukaryotic lineages There are many straightforward cases of HGT in eukaryotes that involve recently acquired genes [10, 18, 36, 75, 76].
Because phylogenetic signal from their donors remains clear, these recently acquired genes can be readily identiﬁed.
There are also cases of convergent gene acquisitions or recurrent transfers of the same genes. For instance, acquisi-tion of genes encoding enzymes for plant cell wall degradation occurred independently in multiple major line-ages [15, 77, 78]. Recurrent HGT events involving bacteria as ultimate donors have been observed in plants, choano-ﬂagellates, amoebae, and others [17, 78, 79]. Not only can HGT lead to acquisi-tion of individual genes, but also entire metabolic pathways [11, 14, 76, 80, 81].
The proﬁciency of some eukaryotes in acquiring foreign genes is further evi-denced by their stunning ability to recycle plastids [82, 83]. In some cases, protein products of horizontally ac-quired genes function in permanently established plastids [84, 85]; in others, transient plastids were stolen from algal prey and genes were acquired for plastid maintenance [86]. These observations showcase HGT as a dynamic process in eukaryotes, and one that is usually under-appreciated.
The dynamic nature of HGT is also reﬂected in its continual occurrence over time. Although complex multicel-lular eukaryotes appear to have fewer recently acquired genes than protists, this does not diminish the possibility that they acquired many genes more anciently. Unicellularity is the most common form of eukaryotic life, and it is known that unicellular eukaryotes are prone to HGT [3, 4]. In fact, acquired genes can be found in numerous unicellular eukaryotes including many obligate intracellular parasites [76, 87–89], which often have streamlined genomes and retain fewer foreign genes. The fact that all multicellular eukaryotes de-scend from unicellular ancestors points to potentially more frequent ancient HGT [20, 90]. Indeed, foreign genes were introduced regularly at major historical stages during the evolution of primary photosynthetic eukar-yotes [17, 20, 91–96]. In some unicellular eukaryotes such as rumen ciliates and red alga Galdieria sulphuraria, acquired genes account for 4–5% of the total genome [77, 96]; similarly, HGT has contributed to over 3% of the nematode genome [97] and at least 8–9% of the gene content in bdelloid rotifers [98].
These numbers may still be under-estimations because of the loss of phylogenetic signal in many anciently acquired genes.
Tracing this dynamic process back to the inception of eukaryotic evolution leads to the following conjecture. If the ancestral eukaryote was indeed chime-ric and derived from a symbiosis of bacteria and archaea as often sug-gested [99, 100], then we should expect that the earliest eukaryotes were similar to extant prokaryotes in proﬁciency of DNA uptake. Thus, they probably ac-quired many genes from external sour-ces. Similarly, if the host cell or the ancestral eukaryote was able to engulf the proteobacterial progenitor of mito-chondria, it might engulf other bacteria or bacterial DNA as well. Assuming the nucleus or other unique eukaryotic features did not appear in a sudden event, speciﬁc barriers to HGT now present in eukaryotic cells would have evolved gradually. Therefore, HGT dur-ing early eukaryotic evolution might occur as frequently as in modern bacteria and archaea, allowing foreign genes to trickle into early eukaryotes continually. Even with a low ﬁxation rate, many foreign genes could have accumulated in extant eukaryotes over a long evolutionary time period [1, 2].
This process theoretically is open-ended and could have introduced miscella-neous genes independently in different lineages through time.
Conceivably, genes acquired later from other sources might have replaced mitochondria- or plastids-derived homologs in the nucle-us, explaining in part the observation that many proteins of non-organellar origin function in organelles in various lineages [84, 85, 94].
The assumption that organelles are the sole or primary source of bacterial genes not only contradicts many appar-ent cases of HGT in eukaryotes [3–5, 35], but also provides little explanation for eukaryotic adaptation to diverse hab-itats. Adaptation to shifting environ-ments is often accompanied by acquisition of new genes and loss of others [47, 101]. Bacteria and archaea are able to adapt to their environments by sampling from a large global gene pool and maintaining ﬂuid genomes [47, 48]. If novel genetic information cannot be achieved, the adaptability of any eukaryote with a limited gene pool will be hampered. Particularly for early eukaryotes, the task for surviving in various niches and further diversifying into major lineages was probably J. Huang Insights & Perspective.....
870 Bioessays : 868–875,  2013 The Author. Bioessays Published by WILEY Periodicals, Inc.
Think again daunting. Given the fact that point mutation, recombination, gene duplica-tion, and genome rearrangement only operate on pre-existing genes, it would have been disadvantageous for early eukaryotes to completely abandon their ability to acquire ready-to-use genes from other sources.
The weak-link model explains frequent HGT in eukaryotes One of the most popular models for HGT in eukaryotes is the gene ratchet mechanism proposed by Doolittle [1, 2].
Under this model, bacteria phagocytized by protists as food sources are lysed within host cells, allowing their DNA to be incorporated into host genomes.
Though elegant, this model does not explain the widespread existence of foreign genes in eukaryotes that do not engage in phagocytosis. Given the occur-rence of HGT in eukaryotes with miscel-laneous lifestyles [3–5, 35], I here offer a different perspective on HGT mecha-nisms in eukaryotes.
For any foreign gene to be acquired and stably inherited by a recipient organism, it must (i) enter recipient cells, (ii) be integrated into the recipient genome, and (iii) be transmitted to offspring. Foreign genes could enter cells of the recipient organism at any weakly protected stage of the lifecycle in natural environments.
This process could be facilitated if the recipient and donor organisms maintain an intimate physical association through symbiosis, parasitism, infection, or other known forms of contact [18, 35].
For unicellular eukaryotes, the HGT process could be similar to the gene ratchet mechanism proposed by Doolittle [1], but does not speciﬁcally require feeding activities for foreign genes to enter recipient cells. Once inside the cell, integration of foreign genes into recipient genomes does not appear to be particularly difﬁcult, given the still frequent movement of organ-ellar DNA fragments into the nucleus in different organisms [56, 57]. Even if the initial attempt to integrate into the nuclear genome fails, as long as foreign genes can enter recipient cells without signiﬁcant difﬁculties, successive attempts may eventually lead to suc-cessful integration of foreign genes into the recipient genome [1]. Subsequently, transmission of integrated foreign genes to offspring can be accomplished simply through mitosis in these unicellular organisms (Fig. 1A).
For complex multicellular eukar-yotes such as plants and animals, foreign genes must be passed through specialized reproductive cells (germ lines) to be transmitted to offspring.
Therefore, the isolation of germ cells from somatic cells is often considered to be the major barrier to HGT in animals and, to a lesser extent, higher plants [33, 34]. Overcoming this barrier is certainly not easy, but possible. For example, the close association of Wol-bachia with germ cells of arthropods or acquisition of bacterial endosymbionts during embryonic development could promote stable HGT from these endo-symbionts to their hosts [9, 10]. Similar-ly, if a plant or an animal is exposed to and readily incorporates foreign DNA during its very early developmental stages, subsequent cell proliferation and differentiation will spread these foreign genes to other tissues, including germ cells (Fig. 1B). For instance, in nonvascular and seedless vascular plants, female gametes are weakly protected in archegonia and exposed to external environments during fertili-zation, and male gametes generally are exposed completely prior to reaching an oocyte. External fertilization occurs in animals inhabiting aquatic environ-ments, meaning gametes and zygotes are, likewise, freely exposed to foreign sources of DNA. Structurally internal-ized gametes in seed plants and animals in terrestrial environments may be protected from mechanical damages, but not necessarily foreign DNA from symbiotic bacteria, pathogens, or other microbes [8, 10, 19, 38]. Foreign genes introduced during zygotic or embryonic development will be propagated through mitosis into germ cells and, therefore, next generation. Propagation of foreign genes also is possible through gene transfer among neighboring cells, as demonstrated in natural plant grafts [102, 103]. In these respects, the entry points in early developmental stages represent the weak link in recipient organisms for initiating for-eign gene transfer; as such, they ultimately control the transmission of foreign genes to offspring. Once foreign genes are passed onto offspring, they can be ﬁxed in the population through drift or positive selection on newly acquired functions.
This model of gene acquisition critically depends on the presence of weak or unprotected points for foreign genes to enter recipient cells. Other than early developmental stages (e.g.
zygotes, embryos, or spores) of multi-cellular eukaryotes, weak-link entry points for foreign genes include all lifecycle stages in unicellular eukar-yotes. In multicellular eukaryotes with complex sexual reproduction, the prop-agation of foreign genes through cell proliferation and differentiation does not require direct contact between the donor and differentiated reproductive tissues of the recipient (Fig. 1B). In multicellular eukaryotes with asexual reproduction, this process allows for-eign genes to be transmitted directly to offspring by mitotic propagation of cells carrying these genes (Fig. 1C). Because foreign genes are expected to decay into pseudogenes if not selectively advanta-geous to the recipient organism, the actual number of acquired genes should vary among organisms of different life-styles. However, given the potential role of HGT in allowing organisms to explore new resources and niches [47, 48, 101, 104], foreign genes with novel functions could be ﬁxed more frequently in recipients under resource limitation or in shifting environments.
This model also makes the following speciﬁc predictions regarding the oc-currence or overall frequency of HGT in eukaryotes of different lifestyles: (i) Frequent HGT in unicellular eukar-yotes.
Since all developmental stages of unicellular eukaryotes represent weak-link entry points, there are ample opportunities for foreign genes to be integrated and, therefore, transmitted to offspring.
(ii) Occurrence of foreign genes in multi-cellular eukaryotes with fully exposed unicellular or early developmental stages (e.g. spores, zygotes, or embry-os) in their lifecycles (see above).
(iii) Frequent HGT in asexual multicel-lular eukaryotes. The absence of speciﬁc germ cells means that any cell carrying foreign genes may .....Insights & Perspective J. Huang 871 Bioessays : 868–875,  2013 The Author. Bioessays Published by WILEY Periodicals, Inc.
Think again propagate them into offspring. The frequency of HGT should be even higher if bacterial endosymbionts exist in asexual structures, such as spores and hyphae in fungi [67].
(iv) Existence of many anciently ac-quired genes in multicellular eukaryotes. Because multicellular eukaryotes are ultimately derived from unicellular ancestors, it is expected that many foreign genes acquired by their unicellular ances-tors remain in the genomes of their multicellular descendants.
HGT may still be underestimated in eukaryotes Despite potentially frequent HGT in many eukaryotes, identiﬁcation of ac-quired genes often is complicated.
Although foreign genes may gradually accumulate in recipient genomes, their phylogenetic signal tying them to spe-ciﬁc source taxa may be muted or completely erased by substitutions over time. Additionally, HGT from unculti-vated or extinct bacterial lineages may not be properly identiﬁed [105]. Even if phylogenetic signal is retained, recov-ery of accurate phylogenies can be complicated. In particular, many gene families are patchily distributed in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and expla-nations of such patchiness can be controversial [106–108].
Interpretations of patchy distri-butions hinge on underlying assumptions [2]. For researchers who view vertical inheritance as the sole or dominant genetic paradigm, HGT rarely offers a satisfying explanation. In such cases, a patchy distribution is best explained by differential gene losses, misidentiﬁcation of genes, or simply phylogenetic artifacts. Although these factors can create patchy distributions, indiscriminately resorting to them as the chief explanation not only discounts the obvious existence of HGT in many eukaryotes, but also ignores the gene pool constraints from the common ancestor of eukaryotes and progenitors of organelles. Clearly, some reported cases of HGT turn out to be artifacts [4, 35], but the existence of some estab-lished artifacts does not discount the likelihood of HGT in many other cases.
On the other hand, patchy distribu-tions are easily explained based on current knowledge of HGT. For exam-ples, HGT from prokaryotes, sometimes involving the same genes independent-ly and recurrently [78, 109, 110], can spread prokaryotic genes among unre-lated eukaryotes. Further, the bacterial Figure 1. Illustration of the weak-link model of HGT. The unicellular or early developmental stages (spore, zygotes, embryos, etc.) are exposed to foreign genes. These weakly protected stages allow the entry and integration of foreign genes. A: In unicellular eukaryotes, foreign genes may be directly transmitted to offspring through mitosis. B: In multicellular eukaryotes with sexual reproduction, cell proliferation and differentiation spread the foreign genes to all cells including germ cells, which then give rise to male and female gametes. Subsequent fertilization allows foreign genes to be transmitted to offspring. C: In asexual multicellular eukaryotes, propagation of cells carrying foreign genes allows the foreign genes to be transmitted to offspring.

Think again ancestry of mitochondria and plastids, the widespread distribution of second-ary, tertiary, or transient plastids, and the presence of bacterial endosymbionts (e.g.
Wolbachia and Rickettsia in animals) in many eukaryotes, are all known to lead to gene transfer and, therefore, bacterial genes in eukaryotic genomes. In such cases, patchy distri-butions not only are expected, but also clearly reﬂect the very nature of HGT in eukaryotes [111].
Given the difﬁculties and complica-tions discussed above, it is important that putative cases of HGT in eukaryotes be investigated carefully. To do so, independent lines of evidence and alternative scenarios should be consid-ered. Many cases of patchy distribution probably reﬂect combined effects of duplication, gene loss, HGT and other processes [80, 112, 113]. Nevertheless, as long as vertical inheritance remains the null hypothesis, HGT in eukaryotes will likely be underestimated. Therefore, it is useful to bear in mind that HGT, although difﬁcult to “prove” in every individual case, offers a valid explana-tion for many of the atypical gene distributions in eukaryotes.
Conclusions and outlook A large percentage of eukaryotic genes are unquestionably of bacterial origin.
Because mitochondria and plastids represent ﬁxed gene pools, from which many genes have been lost completely during their evolution, OGT alone cannot adequately explain the large number of bacterial genes in eukaryotic genomes. The occurrence of recent HGT events in all major eukaryotic groups indicates that there are no insurmount-able barriers to HGT, even in complex multicellular forms. Additionally, the ﬁnding of many anciently acquired genes in eukaryotes suggests that HGT is a dynamic process that has operated continually throughout the history of eukaryotic evolution. The weak-link model of HGT hypothesizes that unicel-lular and early developmental stages are the most likely entry points for foreign genes into recipient cells. Given the universal existence of these weak-link entry points, HGT is expected to occur frequently, on an evolutionary time scale, in all groups of eukaryotes.
The weak-link hypothesis makes several explicit predictions that can be tested either by genome analyses or by experi-ments under controlled conditions.
Future work is critically needed to understand the overall scale of HGT, but also the contribution of HGT, compared to other genetic mechanisms such as de novo gene generation and duplication, to the expansion of gene pool in different eukaryotic lineages throughout evolutionary time.
Such work can be accomplished through careful evolutionary genomic analyses and will beneﬁt our understanding of the role of HGT in the innovation and evolution of eukaryotes.

args.summary:
This scientific review article by Jinling Huang (Bioessays, 2013) addresses the controversial significance of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in eukaryotic evolution. The author argues that while many eukaryotic genes are of bacterial origin, their presence cannot be adequately explained solely by derivation from mitochondria or plastids (organellar gene transfer, OGT). Key arguments include: (1) mitochondria and plastids represent fixed gene pools with extensive gene loss, creating a "closed system" that eventually reaches a dead end, whereas HGT represents an "open system" allowing genes from virtually unlimited sources; (2) no insurmountable barrier to HGT exists, even in complex multicellular eukaryotes, despite germ cell isolation; (3) recent and ancient HGT events have been documented in all major eukaryotic groups including cnidarians, mites, insects, nematodes, fish, and land plants.

The paper proposes the "weak-link model" of HGT, which suggests that unicellular and early developmental stages (spores, zygotes, embryos) serve as the most likely entry points for foreign genes into multicellular eukaryotes. In unicellular eukaryotes, all life stages are weak-link points and foreign genes transmit via mitosis. In multicellular eukaryotes with sexual reproduction, foreign genes introduced during early development spread through cell proliferation and differentiation into germ cells, then to offspring. In asexual multicellular eukaryotes, any cell carrying foreign genes can propagate them mitotically.

The model makes four specific predictions: (i) frequent HGT in unicellular eukaryotes; (ii) occurrence of foreign genes in multicellular eukaryotes with exposed early developmental stages; (iii) frequent HGT in asexual multicellular eukaryotes; (iv) existence of many anciently acquired genes in multicellular eukaryotes derived from their unicellular ancestors.

Quantitative data cited: acquired genes account for 4-5% of total genome in rumen ciliates and red alga Galdieria sulphuraria; over 3% of the nematode genome; 8-9% of gene content in bdelloid rotifers. A supertree analysis of 185 genomes showed strongest phylogenetic signals from cyanobacteria, alpha-proteobacteria, and archaebacteria, but also signals from other proteobacteria (16.7%) and various other bacteria (13.8%). The author concludes that HGT in eukaryotes is likely underestimated and recommends careful investigation of putative HGT cases with independent lines of evidence, since vertical inheritance as the null hypothesis leads to undercounting of HGT events.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Distinction between germ cell lineages producing gametes and somatic cells

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/Weismann%27s_Germ_Plasm.svg/500px-Weismann%27s_Germ_Plasm.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Weismann's_Germ_Plasm.svg)

Diagram of [August Weismann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Weismann "August Weismann")'s [germ plasm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germ_plasm "Germ plasm") theory. The hereditary material, the germ plasm, is confined to the [gonads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gonad "Gonad"). Somatic cells (of the body) [develop afresh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embryology "Embryology") in each generation from the germ plasm. Whatever may happen to those cells does not affect the next generation.

The **Weismann barrier**, proposed by [August Weismann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Weismann "August Weismann"), is the strict distinction between the "immortal" germ cell lineages producing gametes and "disposable" somatic cells in animals (but not plants), in contrast to [Charles Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin "Charles Darwin")'s proposed [pangenesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangenesis "Pangenesis") mechanism for inheritance.[[1]](#cite_note-Geison69-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)

In more precise terminology, hereditary information is copied only from [germline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germline "Germline") cells to [somatic cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somatic_cells "Somatic cells"). This means that new information from somatic mutation is not passed on to the germline. This *barrier* concept implies that somatic mutations are not inherited.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Weismann set out the concept in his 1892 book ″Das Keimplasma: eine Theorie der Vererbung″ (German for *The [Germ Plasm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germ_plasm "Germ plasm"): a theory of inheritance*).[[5]](#cite_note-5) The use of this theory, commonly in the context of the [germ plasm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germ_plasm "Germ plasm") theory of the late 19th century, before the development of better-based and more sophisticated concepts of genetics in the early 20th century, is sometimes referred to as **Weismannism**.[[6]](#cite_note-GJR-6) Some authors distinguish **Weismannist development** (either [preformistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preformationism "Preformationism") or [epigenetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epigenesis_(biology) "Epigenesis (biology)")) that in which there is a distinct germline, from [somatic embryogenesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somatic_embryogenesis "Somatic embryogenesis").[[7]](#cite_note-7) This type of development is correlated with the [evolution of death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolution_of_aging "Evolution of aging") of the somatic line.

The Weismann barrier was of great importance in its day and among other influences it effectively banished certain [Lamarckian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamarckism "Lamarckism") concepts: in particular, it would make Lamarckian inheritance from changes to the body (the soma) difficult or impossible.[[8]](#cite_note-Romanes_1893-8) It remains important, but has however required qualification in the light of modern understanding of [horizontal gene transfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horizontal_gene_transfer "Horizontal gene transfer") and some other genetic and histological developments.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

## Immortality of the germline

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Weismann_barrier&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Immortality of the germline")]

The Russian biologist and historian [Zhores A. Medvedev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhores_A._Medvedev "Zhores A. Medvedev"), reviewing Weismann's theory a century later, considered that the accuracy of [genome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genome "Genome") replicative and other synthetic systems alone could not explain the "immortal" [germ cell lineages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germline "Germline") proposed by Weismann. Rather Medvedev thought that known features of the biochemistry and genetics of [sexual reproduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_reproduction "Sexual reproduction") indicated the presence of unique information maintenance and restoration processes at the different stages of [gametogenesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gametogenesis "Gametogenesis"). In particular, Medvedev considered that the most important opportunities for information maintenance of [germ cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germ_cell "Germ cell") are created by [recombination during meiosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_recombination "Genetic recombination") and [DNA repair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_repair "DNA repair"); he saw these as processes within the germ cells that were capable of restoring the integrity of [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA "DNA") and [chromosomes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromosome "Chromosome") from the types of damage that caused irreversible ageing in [somatic cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somatic_cell "Somatic cell").[[10]](#cite_note-Medvedev1981-10)

## Basal animals

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Weismann_barrier&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Basal animals")]

[Basal animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basal_animals "Basal animals") such as sponges ([Porifera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porifera "Porifera")) and corals ([Anthozoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthozoa "Anthozoa")) contain multipotent stem cell lineages, that give rise to both somatic and reproductive cells. The Weismann barrier appears to be of a more recent evolutionary origin among animals.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

## Plants

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Weismann_barrier&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Plants")]

In plants, genetic changes in somatic lines can and do result in genetic changes in the germ lines, because the germ cells are produced by somatic cell lineages (vegetative [meristems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meristem "Meristem")), which may be old enough (many years) to have accumulated multiple mutations since seed germination, some of them subject to natural selection.[[12]](#cite_note-12) It is noteworthy in this context that, generally speaking, adult, reproducing plants tend to produce many more offspring in number than animal organisms.

This contrasts with Charles Darwin's proposed pangenesis mechanism for inheritance. In precise terms, hereditary information is copied only from germline cells to somatic cells, meaning somatic mutations are not passed on to the germline and are therefore not inherited. Weismann set out this concept in his 1892 book "Das Keimplasma: eine Theorie der Vererbung" (The Germ Plasm: a theory of inheritance). The theory's use in the context of germ plasm theory is sometimes called "Weismannism."

The barrier was historically important as it effectively eliminated certain Lamarckian concepts, making Lamarckian inheritance from changes to the body (soma) difficult or impossible. It required qualification in light of modern understanding of horizontal gene transfer and other genetic developments.

Key sections include:
- **Immortality of the germline**: Russian biologist Zhores A. Medvedev reviewed Weismann's theory a century later and considered that genome replication accuracy alone could not explain "immortal" germ cell lineages. He proposed that recombination during meiosis and DNA repair are key processes within germ cells capable of restoring DNA and chromosome integrity from damage that causes irreversible aging in somatic cells.
- **Basal animals**: Basal animals such as sponges (Porifera) and corals (Anthozoa) contain multipotent stem cell lineages that give rise to both somatic and reproductive cells, indicating the Weismann barrier is of more recent evolutionary origin among animals.

The Weismann barrier-the doctrine of germline segregation developed by the German biologist August Weismann in the late 19th century-has long been regarded as the decisive disproof of the Lamarckian idea. New discoveries in molecular genetics are showing the Weismann barrier to be just the opposite of what it has long been thought to be. Rather than isolating the germline cells, the Weismann barrier is the active manager of epigenetic inheritance between soma and germline.

args.summary:
This video essay (from ESFTV, posted April 9, 2012, ~4,199 views) reexamines the history and true nature of the Weismann barrier—the doctrine of germline segregation developed by German biologist August Weismann in the late 19th century. The author argues that the barrier has been misunderstood and misrepresented, and that modern discoveries in epigenetics are showing it to be the "active manager of epigenetic inheritance between soma and germline" rather than a barrier separating them.

The video corrects several historical myths: (1) Weismann's famous mouse-tail amputation experiment (over 20 generations showing no shortening of tails) was not weighted heavily by Weismann himself—it was elevated to legendary status by Thomas Hunt Morgan to support Morgan's own anti-Darwinian "mutationism" theory and to demolish Lamarckism; (2) Weismann's most important legacy was his particulate theory of inheritance (that heredity consists of discrete particles rather than a blending fluid), which rescued Darwinism from the "crisis of blending inheritance" and became the foundation for modern gene theory.

The narrative traces how Morgan, who was himself a staunch anti-Darwinist and harsh critic of Weismann, adopted only germline segregation from Weismann's thinking, elevating it to a general principle of evolution. Morgan's mutationism held that adaptation could only arise from random gene mutations, and the Weismann barrier served as an "impenetrable barrier between physiological adaptation and evolutionary change."

The video then presents modern epigenetic findings: DNA methylation patterns are heritable and constitute a second form of hereditary memory (epigenetic inheritance) beyond genetic sequence information. During embryonic development, different cell types silence different suites of genes via methylation. For gametes, sperm DNA becomes the most heavily methylated genome in the body (controlled by somatic cells in the testes), and while demethylation/reset occurs upon fertilization and during oocyte maturation, it is never complete—some methylation residue remains, imprinted by somatic cells. This suggests that germline segregation does NOT insulate the germline genome from somatic experience but instead "actively manages how the somatic genome imprints its adaptive experience onto the germline cells."

The author concludes that germline segregation was always a weak critique of Lamarckism: it applies only to sexually reproducing animals (plants, fungi, protists, and bacteria have no identifiable germline), and Weismann himself saw it as an evolved trait of a specific, limited set of animals—not a general principle as Morgan framed it. The video frames this as a potential resolution of the persistent "crisis of Darwinism," suggesting that subtle Lamarckism—that adaptation, not mutation alone, drives evolution—was present in classical Darwinian thinking.

# Weismann barrier

The **Weismann barrier** is the principle that hereditary information moves only from genes to body cells but never in reverse. In more precise terminology hereditary information moves only from [germline](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/Germline.html "Germline") cells to [somatic cells](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/Somatic_cells.html "Somatic cells") (or soma to germline feedback is impossible).
This is often confused with the [central dogma of molecular biology](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/Central_dogma_of_molecular_biology.html "Central dogma of molecular biology") which in its modern form states that information travels from [DNA](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/DNA.html "DNA") → [RNA](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/RNA.html "RNA") → [protein](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/Protein.html "Protein").

The theory is very important as it has implications for human [gene therapy](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/Gene_therapy.html "Gene therapy"). It also has implications in our understanding of [evolution](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/Evolution.html "Evolution") as it would imply that species aren't nearly as separable genetically as we once thought. Furthermore it opens the door to the existence of certain [Lamarckian](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/Jean-Baptiste_Lamarck.html "Jean-Baptiste Lamarck") concepts that previously had no supporting mechanism.

The use of this theory is sometimes referred to as **Weismannism**.

## History

The work of 19th century biologist [August Weismann](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/August_Weismann.html "August Weismann") was an early step in the founding of the science of [genetics](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/Genetics.html "Genetics"), and like any part of any science is subject to review in light of new data. Although the principle was seriously questioned at times in the 20th century, the research of Paul Kammerer and Trofim Lysenko failed to weaken the principle among the greater scientific community.

## Recent criticism

In the late 20th century there have been criticisms of an impermeable Weismann barrier. These criticisms are all centered around the activities of an enzyme called [reverse transcriptase](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/Reverse_transcriptase.html "Reverse transcriptase").

Evidence has begun to mount for [horizontal gene transfer](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/Horizontal_gene_transfer.html "Horizontal gene transfer"). Different species appear to be swapping genes through the activities of [retroviruses](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/Retrovirus.html "Retrovirus"). Retro-viruses are able to transfer genes between species because they reproduce by integrating their code into the genome of the host and they often move nearby code in the infected cell as well. Seeing as these viruses use RNA as their genetic information they need to use reverse transcriptase to convert their code into DNA first. If the cell they infect is a germline cell then that integrated DNA can become part of the gene pool of that species.

Other evidence against Weismann's barrier is found in the [immune system](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/Immune_system.html "Immune system"). A controversial theory of [Edward J. Steele](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/Edward_J._Steele.html "Edward J. Steele")'s suggests that [endogenous retroviruses](https://www.bionity.com/en/encyclopedia/Endogenous_retrovirus.html "Endogenous retrovirus") carry new versions of V genes from soma cells in the immune system to the germ line cells. This theory is expounded in his book *Lamarck's signature*. Edward J Steele observes that the immune system needs to be able to evolve fast to match the evolutionary pressure (as the infective agents evolve very fast). He also observes that there are plenty of endogenous retro-viruses in our genome and it seems likely that they have some purpose.

It should be noted that even if both of these possible exceptions turn out to be legitimate, the Weismann barrier just loses its absolute status. Without further examples, the penetration of the Weismann barrier is still very much an exception.

args.summary:
The Weismann barrier is a biological principle stating that hereditary information flows only from germline cells to somatic cells, and that reverse (soma-to-germline) feedback is impossible. This concept should not be confused with the central dogma of molecular biology (DNA → RNA → protein). The theory has important implications for human gene therapy: if the barrier is permeable, genetic treatments of somatic cells could result in inheritable genome changes, potentially leading to genetic engineering of the human species rather than just individuals. It also impacts understanding of evolution, suggesting species may not be as genetically separable as once thought, and opens the door to Lamarckian concepts lacking previously known supporting mechanisms. The application of the theory is sometimes called "Weismannism."

The theory traces to the work of 19th-century biologist August Weismann, an early contributor to genetics. Although seriously questioned during the 20th century, research by Paul Kammerer and Trofim Lysenko failed to weaken the principle among the scientific community. Late 20th-century criticisms of an impermeable barrier center on the enzyme reverse transcriptase. Evidence has mounted for horizontal gene transfer, where different species swap genes via retroviruses, which integrate their code into host genomes and can transfer nearby genetic material. If a germline cell is infected, the integrated DNA can enter the species' gene pool. Additional evidence against the barrier comes from the immune system; Edward J. Steele's controversial theory (expounded in his book "Lamarck's Signature") proposes that endogenous retroviruses carry new versions of V genes from somatic immune cells to germline cells, driven by the immune system's need to evolve rapidly against fast-evolving pathogens. Even if these exceptions prove legitimate, the Weismann barrier would only lose its absolute status—its penetration remains an exception without further examples. Related topics include epigenetic inheritance and pangenesis.

Research the comparative, historical, and methodological framing of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in multicellular eukaryotes (plants and animals) versus prokaryotes/microbes, and the history of discovery. Priorities: primary peer-reviewed literature (Nature, Science, PNAS, PLOS, Annual Reviews, Trends in Genetics) and landmark original papers. (b) TIMESCALES AND HISTORICAL CONTEXT: describe the history of HGT discovery in eukaryotes - from the earliest evidence (e.g., 1980s-1990s observations of bacterial-like genes, the 2001 Amborella mitochondrial genome finding by Adams et al., the 2011-2012 landmark genome-scale analyses by Yue et al. and the special issue on HGT in plants), the late 2000s bdelloid rotifer discoveries, and how advances in whole-genome sequencing, phylogenomics, and bioinformatics tools (e.g., detection methods based on compositional bias like GC content and codon usage, phylogenetic incongruence, and synteny with donor genomes) transformed the field; discuss the controversy and standards of evidence for detecting HGT (e.g., the tardigrade retraction debate about contamination and assembly artifacts). (c) OPEN QUESTIONS AND DEBATES: ongoing disputes about the extent and functional importance of HGT in plants and animals, the debate over neutral 'killer' acquisitions versus adaptive transfers, and whether some 'HGT' findings are artifacts of contamination or incomplete lineage sorting. --- SOURCE 1: Horizontal transfer of entire genomes via mitochondrial ... ---
URL: https://pure.psu.edu/en/publications/horizontal-transfer-of-entire-genomes-via-mitochondrial-fusion-in

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the Penn State PURE research database listing for the peer-reviewed article "Horizontal transfer of entire genomes via mitochondrial fusion in the angiosperm Amborella," published in the journal Science in 2013 (Volume 342, Issue 6165, pages 1468-1473). The article reports the complete mitochondrial genome sequence of the flowering plant Amborella trichopoda, an enormous 3.9-megabase genome containing six genome equivalents of foreign mitochondrial DNA acquired from green algae, mosses, and other angiosperms. Many of these horizontal transfers were large, including acquisition of entire mitochondrial genomes from three green algae and one moss. The authors propose a fusion-compatibility model to explain these findings, whereby Amborella captures whole mitochondria from diverse eukaryotes, followed by mitochondrial fusion (limited mechanistically to green plant mitochondria) and subsequent genome recombination. Factors contributing to the high level of foreign DNA include Amborella's epiphyte load, propensity to produce suckers from wounds, and its low rate of mitochondrial DNA loss. The article was authored by Danny W. Rice, Andrew J. Alverson, Aaron O. Richardson, Gregory J. Young, M. Virginia Sanchez-Puerta, Jérôme Munzinger, Kerrie Barry, Jeffrey L. Boore, Yan Zhang, Claude W. DePamphilis, Eric B. Knox, and Jeffrey D. Palmer, and has 353 Scopus citations. DOI: 10.1126/science.1246275.

--- SOURCE 2: Horizontal Transfer of Entire Genomes via Mitochondrial ... ---
URL: https://notablesdelaciencia.conicet.gov.ar/bitstream/handle/11336/2616/Rice2013.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper reports the complete mitochondrial genome sequence of Amborella trichopoda, a large shrub endemic to the rain forests of New Caledonia that is likely sister to all other angiosperms (diverging ~200 million years ago). The genome is enormous at 3.9 Mb (3,866,039 bp), assembled as five autonomously replicating circular chromosomes (3179, 244, 187, 137, and 119 kb). Remarkably, the genome contains approximately six genome equivalents of foreign mitochondrial DNA acquired from green algae, mosses, and other angiosperms, representing a striking example of horizontal gene transfer (HGT).

Key findings include:
- Four complete mitochondrial genomes were horizontally transferred: one from a moss (with architecture nearly identical to Physcomitrella and Anomodon) and three from green algae (donors A, B, C), plus a partial genome from a fourth green-algal donor (D). The green algal genomes likely came from the Coccomyxa subgroup of trebouxiophytes, possibly via lichens growing on Amborella.
- Approximately 753 kb of DNA was acquired from other angiosperms (about two genome equivalents), with donors identified including Santalales (parasitic plants, the major source), Fagales, Oxalidales, Ricinus communis, and Bambusa oldhamii. Some foreign tracts show evidence of serial angiosperm-to-angiosperm HGT.
- The genome also contains 138 kb of plastid DNA, mostly via intracellular gene transfer, with ~10 kb entering via foreign mitochondria.
- Of the 197 foreign mitochondrial protein genes, only 50 (25%) have full-length intact open reading frames, and most are pseudogenes; the majority of foreign genes are not functionally expressed. This makes Amborella mtDNA a striking example of neutral evolution and "junk DNA."

The authors propose a fusion-compatibility model: Amborella captured whole mitochondria from diverse green plants, followed by mitochondrial fusion (mechanistically limited to green plants) and genome recombination. They note that mitochondrial fusion in animals and fungi uses dynamin-related GTPases absent from green plants, suggesting a fundamentally different fusion mechanism in green plants. The ecological context—Amborella's heavy epiphyte load (mosses, lichens, other angiosperms), propensity to produce suckers from wounds (wounding may create new meristems that incorporate foreign mitochondria), and low rate of mitochondrial DNA loss—all contribute to the high level of foreign DNA. The transfers are likely millions of years old given extensive pseudogene decay but surprisingly intact retention of the whole-genome transfers.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We report the complete mitochondrial genome sequence of the flowering plant Amborella trichopoda. This enormous, 3.9 Mb genome contains six genome equivalents of foreign mitochondrial DNA, acquired from green algae, mosses, and other angiosperms. Many of these horizontal transfers were large, including acquisition of entire mitochondrial genomes from three green algae and one moss."

--- SOURCE 5: Gene transfer gone wild reveals driving force behind mitochondrial sex | EurekAlert! ---
URL: https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/695720

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a news release from Indiana University (via EurekAlert!) announcing groundbreaking research on horizontal gene transfer in the mitochondrial genome of Amborella trichopoda, a South Pacific shrub endemic to New Caledonia. The research, led by IU's Jeff Palmer and Danny Rice in collaboration with the U.S. Department of Energy, Penn State University, and the Institute of Research for Development in New Caledonia, uncovered the largest example of horizontal gene transfer (acquisition of foreign genes from other species) ever found in any organism. The study identified genes from multiple plant species in Amborella's mitochondrial genome, including the entire mitochondrial genomes of three green algae and one moss — marking the first time an organelle genome has captured entire foreign genomes (four total) and the first description of a land plant acquiring genes from green algae. The research demonstrates that mitochondrial fusion (merger of two mitochondria within a cell) drives mitochondrial gene transfer, and that incompatibility in fusion mechanisms between different phyla acts as a major barrier to unconstrained mitochondrial "sex" across the tree of life. Key findings include: (1) flowering plants and green algae, whose last common ancestor existed over a billion years ago, undergo mitochondrial fusion by the same mechanism, which differs from that of animals and fungi; and (2) Amborella retained the foreign DNA for tens of millions of years due to ecological exposure, developmental germline formation responses to wounding, and an exceptionally low rate of DNA loss. The study, "Horizontal Transfer of Entire Genomes via Mitochondrial Fusion in the Angiosperm Amborella," was published Dec. 20 in the journal Science, alongside two papers on Amborella's nuclear genomes. Funding came from the National Institutes of Health, National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy's Joint Genome Institute, and IU's METACyt Initiative (funded by the Lilly Endowment).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The research also shows, for the first time, that an organelle genome has captured an entire foreign genome, in this case, four of them. It is also the first description of a land plant acquiring genes from green algae., "The Amborella mitochondrial genome is like the old lady in the song who swallows a fly... the Amborella genome has swallowed whole mitochondrial genomes, of varying sizes, from a broad range of land plants and green algae. But instead of bursting from all this extra, mostly useless DNA, or purging the DNA, it's held on to it for tens of millions of years. So you can think of this genome as a constipated glutton... that has swallowed whole genomes from other plants and algae and also retained them in remarkably intact form for eons," said Jeff Palmer., "We found the first evidence that mitochondria of flowering plants and green algae, whose last common ancestor existed over a billion years ago, undergo fusion by the same mechanism. This mechanism appears to be different from that employed by animal and fungal mitochondria," said Danny Rice., Palmer said the new work provides "compelling evidence that mitochondrial fusion is the driving force for mitochondrial gene transfer and that incompatibility in the mechanism of mitochondrial fusion between different phyla – plants versus animals or fungi – provides the major barrier to unconstrained mitochondrial 'sex' across the evolutionary tree of life."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Mechanisms, detection, and impact of horizontal gene transfer in plant functional evolution ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12448838

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in The Plant Cell (2025) titled "Mechanisms, detection, and impact of horizontal gene transfer in plant functional evolution" by Lee Mariault, Camille Puginier, Jean Keller, Moaine El Baidouri, and Pierre-Marc Delaux (PMID: 40834228). The review explores the extent of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in the plant kingdom, focusing on mechanisms, detection methods, and evolutionary impact.

KEY FINDINGS ON PREVALENCE:
- HGT is significantly more common in plant genomes than previously assumed, involving transfers from bacteria, fungi, insects, and viruses
- Over 600 plant-to-plant HGT cases reported; more than 42% involve parasitic plants (Orobanchaceae and Convolvulaceae families) and their hosts, facilitated by haustorium contact
- More than 95% of plant-to-plant HGT events outside parasitic systems occurred within the Poaceae (grass) family
- Bacteria are the most frequent donors, with over 800 genes acquired from bacteria, particularly during origin of land plants and early divergence of seed plants
- Approximately 20 well-supported fungal-to-plant HGT events described, many involving endophytic Epichloë fungi
- Plant-to-insect HGT documented in whitefly Bemisia tabaci (25+ plant-derived genes, including a phenolic glucoside malonyltransferase gene)
- Viruses, particularly Caulimoviridae, found integrated in nuclear genomes of many plants

MECHANISMS OF HGT:
1. Genetic material exits donor nucleus via: transcription/mRNA export (mobile via plasmodesmata and phloem), double-strand breaks from genotoxic stress, apoptosis, or extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA, up to 400 kbp)
2. Transport to recipient via: haustoria (parasitic gateway), natural grafting (stock-scion contact), illegitimate pollination (heterospecific pollen in wind-pollinated grasses), or vectors (viruses, bacteria, nematodes, insects, fungi)
3. Integration requires nuclear import, with mRNA requiring reverse transcription (possibly via TE-associated reverse transcriptases or Caulimoviridae)

URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12862-022-02091-w

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access research article published on 30 November 2022 in BMC Ecology and Evolution (Volume 22, article 140) by C. T. Jones, E. Susko, and J. P. Bielawski. The paper, "Evolution of the connectivity and indispensability of a transferable gene: the simplicity hypothesis," presents a theoretical model testing the "simplicity hypothesis" proposed by Novick and Doolittle (2020).

Key concepts:
- Connectivity: the number of interactions between a transferable gene (or its protein product) and host genes/gene products; higher connectivity reduces the likelihood of successful horizontal gene transfer (HGT) into new microbial hosts (per the complexity hypothesis).
- Indispensability: the degree to which a microbial host's viability depends on the transferable gene during a neutral (non-selective) environmental state.
- The simplicity hypothesis posits that connectivity may increase over time within a single population via gene-host coevolution (toward a more "sessile" state), but that differential rates of HGT colonization across populations may counter this and reduce connectivity over time (toward a more "itinerant" state), constituting an evolutionary trade-off.

Model and methodology:
- The model treats copies of a transferable gene (T) within microbial host populations as populations of genes undergoing birth (via HGT into naïve populations, impacted by connectivity) and death (via gene loss, impacted by indispensability).
- The study uses both a deterministic model based on the Price equation and stochastic computer simulations.
- Three key assumptions: (1) coevolution independently changes both connectivity and indispensability; (2) a collective of spatially segregated microbial populations exists (some hosting the gene, some naïve); (3) environments have two states—selective (gene provides fitness advantage) and neutral (no advantage).
- Key model parameters: beta (β) = opportunity to colonize naïve microbial populations via HGT; delta (δ) = probability of neutral environmental state.

Key results:
- When β = 0.06 (low HGT opportunity), the transferable gene persisted in only 2 populations by evolving toward a more sessile state (higher indispensability and connectivity), despite the absence of coevolution causing extinction.
- When β = 0.08 (higher HGT opportunity), the gene evolved toward a more itinerant state (lower indispensability and connectivity), with the metapopulation expanding from ~800 to nearly 9,000 populations.
- The evolutionary outcome transitions from sessile to itinerant between β = 0.06 and β = 0.08.
- The opportunity to enter new microbial populations via HGT can drive connectivity toward lower values, especially in unstable environments; lack of such opportunity in stable environments drives connectivity toward higher values.

Predictions and potential tests:
- A gene might evolve more sessile when there is a stable selective environment (δ ≈ 0) but little opportunity for HGT (β ≈ 0), as might be found in oligotrophic environments (open ocean, deep subsurface, polar ice caps) for genes conferring nutrient metabolism.
- A gene might evolve more itinerant when HGT opportunity is high (β > 0) and environmental exposure to selective pressures is intermittent (δ > 0), as might be found in pathogens episodically exposed to antimicrobial substances.
- Predictions could be tested by comparing genes of these types or by comparing transferable genes in species with broad versus narrow niche breadth.

Conclusion: The model suggests connectivity can evolve toward higher values (sessile, less transferable) or lower values (itinerant, more transferable) depending on ecological conditions, consistent with the simplicity hypothesis. However, the authors note that better understanding of gene-host coevolutionary dynamics in natural microbial systems is required before further conclusions can be drawn about the hypothesis's veracity.
</summary>

**Background and Hypotheses:** The paper addresses horizontal gene transfer (HGT) among prokaryotes. Previous research showed that operational genes (housekeeping functions) are frequently horizontally transferred, while informational genes (transcription, translation, and related processes) are rarely transferred. Two competing hypotheses were tested: (1) the continual horizontal transfer hypothesis—operational genes have been transferred continuously since prokaryote divergence, and (2) the early massive horizontal transfer hypothesis—one or a few massive gene exchanges occurred early in prokaryotic evolution before diversification.

**Methodology:** The researchers analyzed six complete prokaryotic genomes: Aquifex aeolicus, Escherichia coli, Synechocystis 6803, Bacillus subtilis, Methanococcus jannaschii, and Archaeoglobus fulgidus. Analyses included star sequence alignments, paralog rooting, three phylogenetic methods (Jukes-Cantor distances, maximum parsimony, and paralinear/logdet distances), and tree distance metrics including peripheral branch-transfer and prune-and-regraft distances.

**Key Results:** Three tests consistently supported the continual horizontal transfer hypothesis: (1) Paralog rooting showed significantly different root distributions between operational and informational trees (P<0.0039, χ²=13.35); (2) Operational trees had mean peripheral branch-transfer distance of 2.3 steps vs. 1.2 for informational trees (P<0.0003, χ²=23.0); (3) Prune-and-regraft distance analysis showed >40% of operational trees require 2+ transfers vs. <10% for informational trees (P<0.00007, χ²=19.08). SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in the Reports of the National Center for Science Education (Volume 26, No. 3, May-June 2006) by Finn Pond of Whitworth College, argues that naturalistic/evolutionary models can plausibly explain the origin of biological complexity, countering claims by "Intelligent Design" (ID) advocates. ID proponents, following Michael Behe's "irreducible complexity" argument (from Darwin's Black Box, 1996), contend that only an "intelligent agent" can generate the information content and complexity in biological systems. Behe argued the bacterial flagellum is irreducibly complex—a system where removing any part causes it to cease functioning, which cannot be produced by slight, successive modifications of a precursor system.

The paper reviews four naturalistic models:
1) Incremental additions model: An initially beneficial association of components becomes essential over time (e.g., RNase P, where RNA has catalytic activity alone at very low activity, but functions better with its protein partner; hammerhead ribozymes showing 10-20 fold increased activity in the presence of RNA-binding proteins).
2) Scaffolding model: "Redundant complexity" and superfluous components are lost, leaving tightly-matched components (analogous to building an arch with scaffolding; gene duplications and variant isoforms serve as examples).
3) Co-option model: Existing structures are recruited for new functions (e.g., the Krebs/citric acid cycle, where intermediate stages had functions apart from their role in the cycle; V(D)J gene splicing in vertebrate immune systems; butterfly eyespots, vertebrate limbs, complex leaves, and feathers).
4) Emerging complexity/self-organization model: Schneider's "ev" program simulated evolution via mutation and selection, demonstrating that Darwinian processes can generate new information (measured in bits via Shannon information theory) and irreducibly complex systems from a random genome.

The paper critiques William Dembski's responses (in No Free Lunch, 2002), who demanded "causal specificity" and objected to the "ev" program (Schneider eliminated the disputed rule and found the same results; David Wolpert, co-developer of the No Free Lunch Theorems, said Dembski applied the theorems inappropriately). Howard Van Till noted that hypotheses falling short of full causal specificity may still be highly plausible applications of partially understood mechanisms, and complained that ID tends to denigrate them as "just-so stories."

The paper also critiques Dembski's "specified complexity" criterion (probability of 10^-150 for design) and his application to the bacterial flagellum. Dembski's probability calculation treated the flagellum as a discrete combinatorial object assembling by pure chance—a scenario no biologist has ever proposed. Dembski failed to account for all relevant ways an event might occur, despite stating this was necessary.

The conclusion presents Kwang Jeon's 1966 experiment where amoebae cultures dying from bacterial infection eventually recovered, establishing a mutually obligate endosymbiosis (essentially a new cell organelle) through undirected natural processes—demonstrating that natural causes can generate irreducibly linked systems. The paper concludes that demanding a detailed chain of causality is unrealistic, and that calculating the probability of the flagellum assembling by pure chance to detect design is simply wrong.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A news release from the Marine Biological Laboratory (MBL) reports on a study published in Science (2008) by researchers Irina Arkhipova (MBL's Josephine Bay Paul Center), Matthew Meselson (Harvard University), and Harvard graduate student Eugene Gladyshev. The study presents the first evidence of massive horizontal gene transfer in the animal kingdom—numerous chunks of foreign DNA from bacteria, fungi, and plants were discovered in the genome of the bdelloid rotifer Adineta vaga. --- SOURCE 1: Massive horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes from ... ---
URL: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0408336102

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PNAS research article (published December 14, 2004, in volume 101, issue 51, pages 17747-17752) by Ulfar Bergthorsson, Aaron O. Richardson, Gregory J. Young, Leslie R. Goertzen, and Jeffrey D. Palmer, titled "Massive horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes from diverse land plant donors to the basal angiosperm Amborella."

STUDY PURPOSE: The researchers investigated whether plants could acquire multiple foreign genes through horizontal gene transfer (HGT), moving beyond the previously known cases of single-gene acquisition. They focused on Amborella trichopoda, a basal angiosperm (a monotypic genus of shrubs endemic to New Caledonia) that was already known to possess one horizontally acquired gene and showed signs of containing more.

METHODOLOGY: The team used PCR amplification with conserved primers (~100 primer pairs) to comprehensively sequence the mitochondrial protein gene set of Amborella, plus variable numbers of mitochondrial genes from 28 other diverse land plants. They also conducted maximum-likelihood and parsimony phylogenetic analyses, using the Shimodaira-Hasegawa (SH) test to assess whether phylogenetically anomalous gene placements suggestive of HGT were statistically significant. To rule out contamination, HGT cases were confirmed from multiple independent DNA preparations from four different sources of Amborella material.

KEY RESULTS:
- Of the 40 protein genes present in the ancestral angiosperm mitochondrial genome, 31 were recovered from Amborella.
- Of these 31 genes, 20 showed evidence of one or more cases of HGT, for a total of 26 foreign genes acquired.
- Most transfers came from other angiosperms (especially eudicots), while others came from nonangiosperms, including six striking cases of transfer from at least three different moss donors.
- The five sequenced angiosperm mitochondrial genomes (rice, Arabidopsis, Brassica, Beta, and others) showed no evidence of HGT.
- Most transferred genes are intact (functional or recently transferred), while nine are pseudogenes.
- Evidence suggests the transferred genes reside in the mitochondrial genome (not chloroplast or nuclear), based on RNA editing patterns characteristic of mitochondria, nucleotide substitution rates, and PCR abundance.
- The 11 remaining singleton genes appear to be of vertical descent, placing Amborella as sister to all other angiosperms.

DISCUSSION AND SIGNIFICANCE: Amborella mtDNA has sustained proportionately more HGT than any other eukaryotic, or perhaps prokaryotic, genome yet examined. The study suggests HGT incidence varies markedly between plants. The authors speculate that Amborella's environment—mid-elevation montane tropical rain forests in New Caledonia where the plant's leaves and stems are often covered with diverse epiphytes including mosses—could promote direct plant-to-plant HGT (similar to mechanisms proposed for parasitic plants). The authors note limitations of their PCR approach, including missing rRNA/tRNA genes, chloroplast-derived sequences, and intergenic DNA, and emphasize that only sequencing the complete Amborella mitochondrial genome can comprehensively census its horizontally acquired DNA. They cite the SH test as supporting 14 of the transfers, with divergent duplicates in plant mtDNA representing xenologs (horizontal products) rather than paralogs.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Results indicate that Amborella has acquired one or more copies of 20 of its 31 known mitochondrial protein genes from other land plants, for a total of 26 foreign genes, whereas no evidence for HGT was found in the five sequenced genomes."; "Most of the Amborella transfers are from other angiosperms (especially eudicots), whereas others are from nonangiosperms, including six striking cases of transfer from (at least three different) moss donors."; "Amborella mtDNA has sustained proportionately more HGT than any other eukaryotic, or perhaps even prokaryotic, genome yet examined."; "Clearly, then, the incidence of HGT varies markedly from one plant to another. One wonders how many other Amborella-type situations exist among the ≈255,000 species of flowering plants."; "We are lucky that, of all angiosperms, Amborella happens to be so rich in HGT, because its distinctive position at the base of angiosperms makes it relatively easy to detect with reasonable confidence transfers from other angiosperms, even with the scanty taxon sampling of this study."
</key_excerpts>
