--- SOURCE 4: Gorgeous mosaic of mitochondrial genes created by horizontal transfer and gene conversion ---
URL: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1016295107

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research article published in PNAS (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) on November 29, 2010, by Weilong Hao, Aaron O. Richardson, Yihong Zheng, and Jeffrey D. Palmer (contributed by Palmer, received for review September 17, 2010). The paper reports the discovery of two lineages of plant mitochondrial genes exhibiting "gorgeous mosaicism" created through horizontal gene transfer (HGT) combined with repeated gene conversion between coresident native and foreign homologs.

Key findings:
- Two lineages of differentially mosaic mitochondrial genes were discovered: the atp1 gene in the genus Ternstroemia (Ericales) and the nad1/matR region in gingers (Hedychium and Boesenbergia of Zingiberaceae).
- The Ternstroemia atp1 genes are highly chimeric, with multiple (four or five) foreign regions interspersed with native regions across the three major clades, tracing back to a single initiating HGT event likely from Vaccinium (blueberry), inferred to have occurred 15-50 Myr ago between donor and recipient groups that diverged ~100 Myr ago.
- The ginger case involves HGT of the cd-4 intron region, occurring less than 26 Myr ago, with H-cis and H-trans copies in Hedychium both being chimeras of native ginger-derived and foreign eudicot-derived DNA.
- Gene conversion between native and foreign homologs was demonstrated for 5 of 17 cases of non-Amborella plant mitochondrial HGT examined.
- The paper proposes the duplicative HGT and differential gene conversion (DH-DC) model, which integrates HGT, ongoing gene conversion, and speciation to explain the diversification of mosaic genes.
- The mosaic genes also reflect prior conversions of two additional types: intramitochondrial retroprocessing (cDNA-mediated conversion) and interorganellar gene conversion between mitochondria and chloroplasts (across the ~2 billion year divergence between these organelles).
- Expression evidence (C-to-U RNA editing) confirms the mosaic genes are functional mitochondrial genes; only H-cis matR appears to be a pseudogene.
- Gene conversion introduced limited protein diversity (2-4 amino acid changes in Ternstroemia atp1; single changes in functional matR genes) but created substantial novel molecular variation, some potentially adaptive.

The article has 3,542 total views and 86 total citations (as of September 2026), with free access.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: Horizontal gene transfer is more frequent with increased heterotrophy and contributes to parasite adaptation ---
URL: https://www.pnas.org/doi/abs/10.1073/pnas.1608765113

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research article published in PNAS (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) titled "Horizontal gene transfer is more frequent with increased heterotrophy and contributes to parasite adaptation." The article was published October 24, 2016, in Vol. 113, No. 45, pages E7010-E7019 (DOI: 10.1073/pnas.1608765113). It is available with free access and has received 102 total citations.

AUTHORS: The study was conducted by Zhenzhen Yang, Yeting Zhang, Eric K. Wafula, and 13 other researchers including Loren A. Honaas, Paula E. Ralph, Sam Jones, Christopher R. Clarke, Siming Liu, Chun Su, Huiting Zhang, Naomi S. Altman, Stephan C. Schuster, Michael P. Timko, John I. Yoder, James H. Westwood, and corresponding author Claude W. dePamphilis (cwd3@psu.edu). It was edited by David M. Hillis of the University of Texas at Austin and approved September 20, 2016.

KEY FINDINGS: The paper tests the hypothesis that parasitic plants are especially prone to horizontal gene transfer (HGT) because of their intimate feeding contacts with host plant tissues. HGT is the nonsexual transfer and genomic integration of genetic materials between organisms. While HGT is common in prokaryotes, it appears rare in eukaryotes, but parasitic plants may be exceptions.

RESEARCH METHODS: The researchers examined transcriptomes of three parasitic members of Orobanchaceae (a plant family containing species spanning the full spectrum of parasitic capabilities) plus the free-living Lindenbergia. After initial phylogenetic detection and extensive validation, they identified 52 high-confidence horizontal transfer events, often from lineages of known host plants. The number of HGT events increased in species with the greatest parasitic dependence.

KEY RESULTS: 
- 52 high-confidence HGT events were detected, exceeding 50 expressed and likely functional HGT events in one family of parasitic plants
- HGT reflected parasite preferences for different host plants
- HGT was much more frequent in plants with increasing parasitic dependency
- Analyses of intron sequences provided evidence for integration of genomic fragments far more often than retro-processed RNA sequences
- Purifying selection predominates in functionally transferred sequences, with a small fraction of adaptively evolving sites
- HGT-acquired genes are preferentially expressed in the haustorium (the feeding organ of parasitic plants)
- HGT was strongly biased toward expression and protein types likely to contribute to haustorial function, suggesting functional HGT of host genes plays an important role in adaptive evolution of parasites

DATA AVAILABILITY: Sequence data archived at NCBI BioProject (ID codes SRP001053 and SRP083761) and at ppgp.huck.psu.edu. Scripts and alignments submitted to github user "dePamphilis" under directory "HGT_PNAS_2016."

FUNDING: Supported by NSF Plant Genome Research Program Awards DBI-0701748 and IOS-1238057 (to J.H.W., C.W.d., M.P.T., and J.I.Y.), with additional support from the Plant Biology graduate program and the Genetics graduate program at Penn State University, National Institute of Food and Agriculture Project 131997 (to J.H.W.), and NSF Grant IOS-1213059 (to M.P.T.).
</summary>

"Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is the nonsexual transfer and genomic integration of genetic materials between organisms. --- SOURCE 6: Widespread impact of horizontal gene transfer on plant colonization of land ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms2148

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Nature Communications on October 23, 2012, titled "Widespread impact of horizontal gene transfer on plant colonization of land" by Jipei Yue, Xiangyang Hu, Hang Sun, Yongping Yang, and Jinling Huang. The study challenges the conventional belief that horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is rare in complex multicellular eukaryotes like plants.

**Key findings:**
- Genome analyses of the moss Physcomitrella patens identified 128 genes across 57 families that were acquired from prokaryotes, fungi, or viruses through HGT
- Of these, 18 gene families are present in both green algae and land plants (acquired before land plant origin), while 39 families were acquired during or after land plant origin
- 19 gene families are found only in P. patens and their putative donors, suggesting recent transfer
- The majority of acquired genes derive from miscellaneous bacterial lineages; ten families from fungi, and one each from archaea and viruses
- 35 of the identified gene families are also present in seed plants, indicating retention of beneficial acquired genes
- Land plants emerged from charophycean green algae about 480-490 million years ago

**Biological functions of acquired genes:**
The horizontally acquired genes are involved in:
- Xylem formation, plant defence, nitrogen recycling
- Biosynthesis of starch, polyamines, hormones (including auxin), and glutathione
- Arginase genes (derived from bacterial agmatinase) involved in polyamine biosynthesis
- Subtilase gene family (derived from a single bacterial HGT event) involved in protein degradation, lateral root formation, xylem differentiation, cuticle development, and stomata pattern formation
- Auxin biosynthesis genes (AAE18 and YUC3)
- Glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCL) for glutathione formation (plant disease resistance, stress defence, heavy metal detoxification)
- Purine degradation and nitrogen recycling genes
- DNA replication and repair genes

**Proposed HGT mechanism model:**
The authors propose two entry points for foreign genes into the moss genome: (1) spore germination and early gametophyte development stage, and (2) fertilization and early embryo development stage. This model applies to nonvascular and seedless vascular plants with unprotected or weakly protected zygotes. Mosses are effective in DNA transformation, enabling uptake of foreign DNA, which likely facilitated their establishment in hostile terrestrial environments. Mycorrhizal associations with fungi also provided opportunities for gene transfer.

**Methodology:**
Using the AlienG computational tool, 910 genes were identified as potentially of prokaryotic, fungal, or viral origin from P. patens annotated protein sequences. After removing 394 genes (short scaffolds or high cyanobacterial identity suggesting plastid origin), 128 genes of 57 families were confirmed as HGT-derived through phylogenetic analyses with bootstrap support of 80% or higher, with cautious measures to reduce false positives including comprehensive database construction and balanced taxonomic sampling.

**Conclusions:**
The findings suggest HGT had a critical role in the transition of plants from aquatic to terrestrial environments, and demonstrate that HGT is a dynamic process with foreign genes gradually accumulating over time. The study suggests that anciently acquired genes are more frequent in plants than commonly expected, and that HGT had a widespread and profound impact on the evolution of multicellular eukaryotes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In complex multicellular eukaryotes such as animals and plants, horizontal gene transfer is commonly considered rare with very limited evolutionary significance. Here we show that horizontal gene transfer is a dynamic process occurring frequently in the early evolution of land plants. Our genome analyses of the moss Physcomitrella patens identified 57 families of nuclear genes that were acquired from prokaryotes, fungi or viruses."

--- SOURCE 7: Widespread horizontal gene transfer between plants and ... ---

<summary>
This is a bioRxiv preprint (DOI: 10.1101/2022.08.25.505314) titled "Widespread horizontal gene transfer between plants and their microbiota" by Shelly Haimlich, Yulia Fridman, Hitaishi Khandal, Sigal Savaldi-Goldstein, and Asaf Levy (from Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Technion-Israel Institute of Technology). - Identified 767 Arabidopsis proteins mapped to 60,850 bacterial proteins as potential molecular mimicry candidates.
- Detected 180 unique cross-kingdom HGT events: 84 genes likely transferred from plants to bacteria, and 96 genes from PA bacteria to plants.
- Additionally found 161 genes transferred between PA bacteria and the eukaryotic domain (source unclear), 65 genes with unclear inheritance patterns, and 361 genes with no HGT patterns.
- Rejected DNA contamination by confirming no homologous pairs exceeded 76% amino acid identity.

**Functional Enrichment:**
- Genes transferred from plants to bacteria are enriched in secreted proteins, carbohydrate catabolism enzymes (pectin esterase, glycosidase), and include chitinases (CHI, AT2G43570), endo beta mannanase (XCD1), and pectin lyases (PME5) — enabling bacteria to exploit plant-derived sugars.
- Genes transferred from bacteria to plants are enriched in redox homeostasis and cytoplasmic proteins, including many auxin biosynthesis YUCCA genes and nucleoside metabolic processes. 69/96 (72%) of such genes are found in all dicots and monocots, suggesting ancient HGT events.

**Taxonomic Patterns:**
- Bacteroidetes were enriched as gene acceptors from plants, while Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria were depleted as either acceptors or donors.
- Rhizobiales and Hyphomicrobiales (Proteobacteria) and Micrococcales (Actinobacteria) showed significantly fewer HGT events than expected.
- In most cases the donor/acceptor taxonomy remained "unknown" (multiple phyla involved).

**Recent HGT Examples:**
- The plant CHI (chitinase) gene is present in only 7 PA Streptomyces genomes (patchy distribution), with protein structures very similar (RMSD=0.791).
- The bacterial DET2 homologue (steroid-5-alpha-reductase, key in brassinosteroid biosynthesis) is nearly specific to plant-associated Leifsonia genus (Actinobacteria), located downstream of a tRNA gene; protein structures highly similar (RMSD=0.727) despite less than 50% sequence identity.

**Functional Validation (Proof-of-Concept):**
- The authors tested whether the Leifsonia DET2 homologue (lfDET2) could functionally replace the Arabidopsis DET2 gene. Arabidopsis DET2 is 46% identical to Leifsonia Det2 (similar to identity shared with rice and barley homologues).
- Expression of lfDET2 (driven by 35S or Arabidopsis DET2 promoters) in the Arabidopsis det2 mutant background rescued the dwarf phenotype and root meristem defects, restoring normal plant growth.
- lfDET2 localized to the endoplasmic reticulum, matching atDET2 localization.

**Conclusion:** The results suggest cross-kingdom HGT is relatively frequent and shaped the genomes of plants and their microbiota by adding adaptive traits. The transferred genes likely participate in molecular mimicry between hosts and their commensal microbiomes. Key author correspondence: alevy@mail.huji.ac.il.
</summary>

- HTTs are very frequent and widespread among monocots and dicots, contradicting the long-held view that LTR-RTs are inherited exclusively vertically

The study was conducted by Hongsheng Cai, Yingying Liu, and Changhong Guo at Harbin Normal University and the Harbin Academy of Agricultural Sciences in China.

BACKGROUND: HGT is a major driver of adaptive evolution in prokaryotes, but its occurrence in eukaryotes (particularly as recipients) has been debated. The study hypothesized that bacterial-plant associations, given their close contact, are a major source of HGT in plants.

METHODS: The researchers used a comparative genomic approach, downloading genome sequences from NCBI. They selected 43 angiosperm genomes and 151 plant-associated bacteria to construct ortholog groups using OrthoFinder (2987 groups after filtering). Phylogenetic trees were constructed using RAxML, and HGT events were detected following methods adapted from Yang et al. --- SOURCE 20: role of horizontal gene transfer ---
URL: https://www.ars.usda.gov/ARSUserFiles/50620500/Publications/HCK/horizon.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (Annu. Rev. Phytopathol. 2000, by U. Liane Rosewich and H. Corby Kistler) examines the role of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in fungal evolution. The authors define HGT as stable transfer of genetic material between individuals not attributable to vertical (meiotic or mitotic) processes. They note that although HGT evidence in eukaryotes remains largely anecdotal, fungi may have experienced more HGT than other eukaryotes, making them well-suited model systems because HGT can be tested experimentally.

The authors outline indirect evidence for HGT, including character-state discordance between element and organismal phylogenies, high similarity between elements in distantly related organisms, irregular distribution patterns, habitat-associated gene sharing, and genomic inconsistencies (G+C content, codon usage). Alternative explanations (erroneous phylogenies, paralog comparisons, ancestral retention, introgressive hybridization) must be considered. Phylogenetic tests include bootstrapping, maximum likelihood, T-PTP tests, and incongruence length differences.

The review organizes potential HGT cases by element type:
1. PLASMIDS: Fungal plasmids (usually 1-21 kb, linear, often mitochondrial) show discordant phylogenies, random global distribution patterns (e.g., 7 Neurospora plasmid groups among 225 isolates), and experimental transfer. Horizontal transfer was demonstrated experimentally by co-culturing unrelated strains (e.g., pAI2 from Ascobolus immersus to Podospora anserina; kalilo between Neurospora species).
2. MYCOVIRUSES: Lacking an extracellular phase, these transfer via cytoplasmic mixing. Some RdRp similarities between distant species suggest possible HGT.
3. INTRONS: Group I introns (nuclear, mitochondrial, and rRNA) and group II introns (organellar only) can move via homing and transposition. The best-substantiated case involves horizontal transfer of a group I intron from fungi to the angiosperm Peperomia. The cox1 intron i4 of Agrocybe aegerita showed 90.5% amino acid identity with the homologous intron in P. anserina, strongly supporting recent HGT. Intron phylogenies are often incongruent with species phylogenies.
4. TRANSPOSABLE ELEMENTS: Sporadic distribution patterns (e.g., grasshopper retrotransposon in Magnaporthe grisea, Fot1 in Fusarium oxysporum) suggest HGT, though stochastic loss is an alternative explanation. Vectors (symbionts/parasites) are proposed but unproven.

The authors conclude that HGT in fungi may be a more important evolutionary factor than in other eukaryotes, particularly for introns and plasmids, which may need periodic horizontal transfer for long-term persistence.
</summary>

In most cases, HGT is invoked after unusual features of genetic elements have become evident, including (a) an inconsistency between the phylogeny of the genetic element in question and the traditionally accepted phylogeny of the organisms...", "Horizontal transfer of the linear mitochondrial plasmid pAI2 from the discomycete A. immersus to mitochondria of a plasmid-free strain of the pyrenomycete Podospora anserina was achieved experimentally by merely co-culturing these unrelated strains.", "In summary, our compilation of potential intron horizontal transmissions in fungi indicates that horizontal transfer of introns among fungi may be quite common."

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution | Semantic Scholar ---
URL: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Horizontal-gene-transfer-in-eukaryotic-evolution-Keeling-Palmer/e752cd6145dc999140351f0334951a65465174b1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page describes a seminal 2008 review paper titled "Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution" by Patrick J. Keeling and Jeffrey D. Palmer, published in Nature Reviews Genetics (DOI: 10.1038/nrg2386). The paper has 1,313 citations and examines the growing number of well-supported cases of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) from both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, many with significant functional implications. Key trends highlighted include the important role of HGT in adaptation to specialized niches and the highly variable impact of HGT across different eukaryotic lineages.

The page also lists notable citing papers and references, including: the "weak-link model" of HGT in eukaryotes (Huang, 2013) proposing that unicellular and early developmental stages are entry points for foreign genes in multicellular eukaryotes; evidence from Bdelloid rotifers showing massive HGT with genes originating from bacteria, fungi, and plants (Gladyshev et al., 2008); massive HGT in Amborella trichopoda involving acquisition of hundreds of foreign mitochondrial genes (Richardson & Palmer, 2007); widespread horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes in flowering plants (Bergthorsson et al., 2003); and the "complexity hypothesis" (Jain et al., 1999) explaining why operational genes are more frequently transferred than informational genes. HGT is shown to play important roles in eukaryotic adaptation to parasitism, pathogenesis, anaerobiosis, and nitrogen/iron limitation in marine environments, and there is evidence of HGT in metazoans (sponges, cnidarians, rotifers, nematodes, molluscs, arthropods).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The number of well-supported cases of transfer from both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, many with significant functional implications, is now expanding rapidly and major recent trends include the important role of HGT in adaptation to certain specialized niches and the highly variable impact of HGT in different lineages."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution ---
URL: http://www.ask-force.org/web/HorizontalGT/Keeling-HGT-Eukaryotic-Evolution-2008.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (Keeling & Palmer, Nature Reviews Genetics, Aug 2008) examines horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in eukaryotic evolution, arguing that its importance is often overshadowed by more extensive study of HGT in prokaryotes. The authors note that eukaryotes arose via the grandest HGT events — endosymbiosis giving rise to mitochondria and plastids — but ongoing HGT in eukaryotes has been under-appreciated due to overshadowing by bacterial studies, evidence coming largely from protists rather than animals, and the erroneous 2001 claim of substantial HGT in the human genome that chilled the field.

Key methodological point: The gold standard for identifying HGT is phylogenetic incongruence (strong conflict between gene and organism phylogenies), though this requires adequate taxonomic sampling. Detecting and evaluating HGT requires formal phylogenetic analysis; the 2001 claim of ~100 human genes from bacteria was debunked by such analysis.

Major findings and trends:
- Massive endosymbiotic gene transfer (EGT): Organellar genomes encode only a small fraction of their proteins; most organelle proteins are encoded by nuclear genes. EGT tempo has been highly punctuated, with bursts of transfer interspersed with periods of stasis. In striking contrast to angiosperms (where 16 of 40 mitochondrial-protein genes show recent EGT), animals show profound stasis — not one functional EGT across 600 million years of metazoan evolution.
- Protein import constrains transfer: Hydrophobic organelle proteins are hardest to import and assemble, locking animal mitochondria into a small, irreducible set of core genes.
- Bacterial endosymbiont transfers: Large tracts of Wolbachia DNA have moved to insect/nematode nuclear genomes; in one case an entire Wolbachia genome was found in a fruitfly genome.
- Prokaryote–eukaryote transfers vary enormously: estimates range from zero to hundreds of bacterial genes per genome. Rumen-dwelling ciliates acquired ~4% of genes from bacteria, approaching bacterial levels. Only one of dozens of sequenced animal genomes (human) has been analyzed, with no credible cases of bacterial HGT found.
- Adaptive functions: Anaerobic parasites and rumen ciliates are rich in transferred genes related to anaerobic metabolism; HGT supports adaptation to specialized niches (parasitism, anaerobiosis, soil life).
- Frequency is a complex function of opportunity (phagotrophy/"you are what you eat"), germ-line segregation, and other factors, varying by lineage.
- Bacterial transfers dominate detected cases partly due to detection bias (easy to spot given large evolutionary distance) but also real opportunity — bacterial populations and gene pools are far larger.
- Eukaryote–eukaryote transfers are underestimated due to poor sampling, confounding gene duplication, and lack of systematic searches, but many cases exist, including fungal toxin gene transfer (~70 years ago) and plastid-targeted protein transfers between algal groups.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific perspective article by Jinling Huang (published in BioEssays in 2013) argues that horizontal gene transfer (HGT) has been a widespread and regular occurrence throughout eukaryotic evolution, and proposes the "weak-link model" to explain the mechanisms of HGT in eukaryotes.

**Key Arguments:**

1. **Barriers to HGT are not insurmountable:** Although protists are historically considered more likely to acquire genes than multicellular eukaryotes, recent HGT events have been documented in animals (cnidarians, mites, insects, nematodes, fish) and plants. While the physical isolation of germ cells from somatic cells may create barriers in complex multicellular organisms, these barriers are not insurmountable.

2. **Organellar gene transfer (OGT) cannot explain all bacterial genes:** While many bacterial genes in eukaryotes are attributed to mitochondrial (α-proteobacterial) or plastid (cyanobacterial) origins, OGT represents a "closed system" constrained by the fixed gene pool of organelles. Since organelles have lost many genes during evolution, their transferable gene pool is limited. The author argues that HGT—an "open system" allowing gene acquisition from virtually unlimited sources—better explains the many bacterial genes not clearly of organellar origin. Evidence includes strong phylogenetic signals for various proteobacterial groups (16.7%) and other bacteria (13.8%) beyond just cyanobacteria and α-proteobacteria.

3. **HGT occurs continually:** HGT has been documented in all major eukaryotic lineages, including recent acquisitions, convergent/recurrent gene transfers, entire metabolic pathways, and ancient events. Examples include: rumen ciliates and Galdieria sulphuraria (4-5% of genome from acquired genes), nematodes (over 3%), and bdelloid rotifers (8-9% of gene content).

**The Weak-Link Model:** For foreign genes to be stably inherited, they must (i) enter recipient cells, (ii) integrate into the recipient genome, and (iii) be transmitted to offspring. The author proposes that unicellular and early developmental stages (spores, zygotes, embryos) serve as "weak links" or entry points where nuclear DNA is relatively exposed to foreign DNA sources. 

**Predictions of the model:**
- (i) Frequent HGT in unicellular eukaryotes (all lifecycle stages are weak-link entry points)
- (ii) Occurrence of foreign genes in multicellular eukaryotes with fully exposed unicellular or early developmental stages
- (iii) Frequent HGT in asexual multicellular eukaryotes (no specific germ cells to serve as barriers)
- (iv) Existence of many anciently acquired genes in multicellular eukaryotes (derived from their unicellular ancestors)

**Why HGT may be underestimated:** The phylogenetic signal of acquired genes can be muted or erased by substitutions over time, HGT from uncultivated or extinct lineages may not be identified, and interpretations of patchy gene distributions often default to vertical inheritance explanations (differential gene loss, misidentification, phylogenetic artifacts) rather than HGT.

The article concludes that since mitochondria and plastids represent fixed gene pools with limited transferable genes, OGT alone cannot explain the abundance of bacterial genes in eukaryotic genomes. The weak-link model hypothesizes that HGT has operated continually throughout eukaryotic history and calls for future work using evolutionary genomic analyses to understand the scale of HGT and its contribution to gene pool expansion in different eukaryotic lineages.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article by Filip Husnik and John P. McCutcheon examining functional horizontal gene transfer (HGT) from bacteria to eukaryotes. The paper surveys the role of bacterial genes throughout the eukaryotic lineage, reviewing the steps HGTs take in becoming functional, which bacterial groups contribute these transfers, and what functions they bestow on eukaryotic recipients.

**Key findings:**
- HGTs are classified into two broad types: "maintenance transfers" (which maintain preexisting functions, particularly compensating for genome reduction in endosymbionts) and "innovative transfers" (which add new functionality to the recipient).
- Genes involved in host nutrition, protection, and adaptation to extreme environments are the most common HGTs from bacteria to eukaryotic genomes.

Large transfers (like the ~1.5 Mb Wolbachia fragment in pillbug Armadillidium vulgare that created a female sex chromosome) are exceptions to this pattern.
- The "weak-link model" explains HGT patterns: genes primarily enter cells at 'unprotected' lifecycle stages. Asexual multicellular eukaryotes like bdelloid rotifers (the most HGT-rich animals reported) have every cell as a weak link. Germ line infection by parasites/symbionts like Wolbachia also exposes hosts to HGT.

**Major functional categories of HGT:**
1. **Maintenance transfers**: Compensating for gene loss in obligate endosymbionts (e.g., in mealybugs, aphids, psyllids, whiteflies, Paulinella chromatophora, and trypanosomatids). Much of the HGT comes from bacteria other than the degenerating endosymbiont (e.g., reproductive manipulators like Wolbachia and Cardinium).
2. **Protection from bacteria**: Eukaryotes acquired bacterial weapons like tae proteins (Type IV secretion system amidase effectors, domesticated in at least three eukaryotic supergroups, some >800 million years old, verified to limit Borrelia burgdorferi in deer ticks), lysozymes, and pore-forming toxins (aerolysins) to fight both bacteria and eukaryotes.
3. **Nutrition**: Genes for carbohydrate degradation (in herbivorous insects, rumen ciliates, oomycetes, fungi, plant-parasitic nematodes, rotifers, choanoflagellates, tunicate cellulose synthase), amino acid/vitamin metabolism, and iron-binding proteins (in diatoms, Galdieria sulphuraria, Dictyostelium).
4. **Environmental adaptation**: Ice-binding proteins for cold environments (in diatoms, Phaeocystis antarctica, green algae), survival in hot/acidic/metal-rich environments (Galdieria sulphuraria), and protection from desiccation, oxidative, osmotic, and UV stress (rotifers, Antonospora locustae).

**Methodology caveats (Box 1):** HGT identification requires careful contamination control in sample preparation, sequence database searches (using Alien index or HGT index), phylogenetic evidence (with attention to long-branch attraction and taxon sampling), genomic evidence (co-assembly of HGT candidate with eukaryotic genes on a single scaffold), and population/microscopy/functional evidence (FISH localization, RNA-Seq expression data).

**Concluding remarks:** While HGT research has a history of misattributions (especially in animals like humans and tardigrades), many documented cases stand on solid ground. There is room for improvement in contamination screening and HGT verification methods. The authors argue for a focus on phylogenetically important but neglected groups such as protists, since the majority of eukaryotic diversity resides in these understudied organisms.

<summary>
This scientific review article, "Horizontal gene transfer: building the web of life" by Soucy, Huang, and Gogarten (published in Nature Reviews Genetics, August 2015, Volume 16), provides a comprehensive overview of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) — the sharing of genetic material between organisms not in a parent-offspring relationship — and its role in shaping evolution across all domains of life.

**Key mechanisms of HGT in prokaryotes:** The three most recognized mechanisms are conjugation (transfer via physical contact through a conjugation pilus), transformation (uptake of exogenous DNA from the environment), and transduction (gene delivery through phage predation, with generalized and specialized subtypes). More recently described mechanisms include gene transfer agents (GTAs) — phage-derived systems carrying random host DNA fragments — and cell fusion (bidirectional gene exchange, observed in archaea such as Haloferax and Sulfolobus).

**HGT in eukaryotes:** Gene exchange became more complicated with the evolution of the nucleus, but mechanisms include endosymbiotic gene transfer (EGT), introgression (gene flow from hybridization followed by backcrosses), the "you are what you eat" ratchet (gene acquisition through phagotrophy in protists), and the weak-link model (weakly protected unicellular or early developmental stages as entry points for foreign genes into multicellular eukaryotes).

**Detecting HGT:** Methods rely primarily on phylogenetic conflict (conflicting branching patterns between gene and species trees), gene composition analysis (codon usage and oligonucleotide composition), and pan-genome analysis. The pan-genome consists of the core genome (genes in all members) and accessory genome (genes in only some members). An analysis of 61 E. coli genomes revealed only 6% of gene families were present in all genomes.

**Evolutionary impact:** HGT is more frequent between closely related organisms — in haloarchaea, over 90% of HGTs were integrated through homologous recombination, and HGT frequency decreases exponentially with phylogenetic distance. HGT drives metabolic innovations (e.g., the methylaspartate cycle in haloarchaea, over 1,000 bacterial genes imported into haloarchaea enabling the move to aerobic environments) and shapes holobiont evolution. In human microbiomes, HGT is 25-fold more frequent between human-associated organisms than between organisms from different hosts or environments.

**Key examples of HGT effects:**

- The moss Physcomitrella patens acquired genes from fungi, bacteria, viruses, and aquatic animals
- The basal flowering plant Amborella trichopoda acquired at least four whole mitochondrial genomes from mosses and green algae
- Type II antifreeze protein genes were transferred among herring, smelt, and sea raven, aiding adaptation to icy water

- Genes from archaic to modern humans (brain development allele via introgression)
- Chlamydial genes found in photosynthetic eukaryotes, suggesting involvement in plastid establishment

**Conclusions:** While mechanisms of prokaryotic gene exchange are well understood, mechanisms in multicellular eukaryotes (weak-link model, sperm-mediated transfer, introgression) remain less clear. The Weismann barrier is a concept proposed by August Weismann that describes the strict distinction between "immortal" germ cell lineages (which produce gametes) and "disposable" somatic cells in animals, though not in plants. In precise terms, hereditary information is copied only from germline cells to somatic cells, meaning somatic mutations are not passed on to the germline and are therefore not inherited. SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Weismann barrier is a biological principle stating that hereditary information flows only from germline cells to somatic cells, and that reverse (soma-to-germline) feedback is impossible. This concept should not be confused with the central dogma of molecular biology (DNA → RNA → protein). The theory has important implications for human gene therapy: if the barrier is permeable, genetic treatments of somatic cells could result in inheritable genome changes, potentially leading to genetic engineering of the human species rather than just individuals. It also impacts understanding of evolution, suggesting species may not be as genetically separable as once thought, and opens the door to Lamarckian concepts lacking previously known supporting mechanisms. The application of the theory is sometimes called "Weismannism."

The theory traces to the work of 19th-century biologist August Weismann, an early contributor to genetics. Although seriously questioned during the 20th century, research by Paul Kammerer and Trofim Lysenko failed to weaken the principle among the scientific community. Late 20th-century criticisms of an impermeable barrier center on the enzyme reverse transcriptase. Evidence has mounted for horizontal gene transfer, where different species swap genes via retroviruses, which integrate their code into host genomes and can transfer nearby genetic material. If a germline cell is infected, the integrated DNA can enter the species' gene pool. Additional evidence against the barrier comes from the immune system; Edward J. Steele's controversial theory (expounded in his book "Lamarck's Signature") proposes that endogenous retroviruses carry new versions of V genes from somatic immune cells to germline cells, driven by the immune system's need to evolve rapidly against fast-evolving pathogens. Even if these exceptions prove legitimate, the Weismann barrier would only lose its absolute status—its penetration remains an exception without further examples. --- SOURCE 1: Horizontal gene transfer in bdelloid rotifers is ancient, ongoing and more frequent in species from desiccating habitats ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4632278

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article from BMC Biology (published November 4, 2015, doi:10.1186/s12915-015-0202-9) by Eyres et al., investigating horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in bdelloid rotifers. The authors hypothesized that bdelloids incorporate foreign DNA during chromosome repair following desiccation-induced double-strand breaks, which might contribute to species divergence and adaptation.

METHODS: The researchers sequenced transcriptomes of four congeneric Rotaria species from different habitats—two from permanent aquatic habitats (R. magnacalcarata and R. socialis, obligate epibionts on freshwater waterlice) and two from desiccating habitats (R. sordida from terrestrial moss and R. tardigrada from ephemeral pools). They identified putative foreign genes using the HGT index (h_U ≥30) and validated transcriptome results using a draft whole genome assembly of R. magnacalcarata.

RESULTS: All four species contained many genes matching non-metazoan genes more closely than metazoan genes. Transcript assemblies contained 60,542–121,350 contigs per species. The proportion of foreign genes (h_U ≥30) was 10.4% in R. magnacalcarata, 9.5% in R. socialis, 12.8% in R. sordida, and 14.1% in R. tardigrada—exceeding the 9.7% found in A. ricciae. Desiccation survival experiments confirmed habitat differences: none of the aquatic species survived desiccation, while 80.6% of R. sordida and 50% of R. tardigrada recovered after dehydration. There was a significant negative relationship between desiccation survival and proportion of HGT.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Nearly half of foreign genes were shared between all four species and the Adineta outgroup, indicating acquisition in a common ancestor predating the divergence of bdelloid families over 60 million years ago.
- Many hundreds of foreign genes were unique to particular species, indicating HGT is ongoing.
- Using a dated phylogeny (Rotaria's most recent common ancestor dated to 29 Mya), they estimated an average of 12.8 gains versus 2.0 losses of foreign genes per million years. The desiccating clade (R. sordida + R. tardigrada) had a threefold higher rate of gain and sixfold lower rate of loss than the aquatic clade.
- Differential loss of ancestral foreign genes associated with desiccation protection (glutathione and trypanothione metabolism enzymes) was found in the two non-desiccating species.
- Foreign genes came primarily from eubacteria (40.7% of transcripts), with fungal (19.2%), protist (28.7%), plant (10.0%), and archaeal (1.5%) origins. Most foreign genes were enzymes involved in catabolism of complex polysaccharides and stress responses.
- Genome validation showed 85% of R. magnacalcarata-unique foreign genes were present in its genome scaffolds, confirming transcriptome results and ruling out contamination (71% of unique foreign genes were on scaffolds also containing native metazoan genes).

CONCLUSIONS: Nearly half of foreign genes were acquired before bdelloid family divergence over 60 Mya, but HGT is ongoing and contributes to functional differences among species. The findings support the desiccation hypothesis: desiccating habitats promote HGT, though species from permanently aquatic habitats still possessed hundreds of foreign genes.
</summary>

This webpage from Biological Recording (biologicalrecording.co.uk) is a blog article titled "The Bizarre Biology of Bdelloid Rotifers" by Joss Carr, featuring a Q&A with Dr. Chris Wilson, a Lecturer in Biology at the University of Oxford. 

Key points covered:
- Bdelloid rotifers are tiny filter-feeding animals living in freshwater habitats worldwide (ponds, streams, lakes, moss, soil, puddles, ice sheets), among the most resilient of all animals.
- All bdelloid rotifers are females—no males have been observed in 300 years since discovery. Mothers lay eggs that hatch into genetic copies of themselves without sex, sperm, or fertilisation.
- They steal DNA from other organisms via horizontal gene transfer, with about 1 in 10 genes (approximately 10% of their genomes) copied from bacteria, fungi, and even plants.
- They have stolen dozens of antibiotic recipes from bacteria, which they use to fight off their own diseases—potentially leading to shortcuts in developing drugs against antibiotic-resistant infections in humans.

Q&A Highlights with Dr. Chris Wilson:
1. Species definition: Despite asexual reproduction, rotifers can be defined into discrete species based on morphology (consistent clustered forms), supplemented by DNA sequencing that corroborates distinct genetic clusters.
2. Gene stealing from animals: Very hard to determine; plant DNA is obvious in rotifer genomes but animal DNA would be less detectable. Dr. Wilson guesses they are almost certainly stealing genes from other animals.
3. Species identification difficulty: Very difficult because bdelloid rotifers are soft-bodied with diagnostic parts (wheel organs) tucked internally; must minimize time between field sampling and microscope viewing. The only identification key is in German and ~50 years old. Only a handful of people worldwide are skilled at identifying them to species level.
4. Horizontal gene transfer consistency: Generally consistent within species because most HGT occurred long ago—estimated at only once every ~100,000 years. Some genes are unique to particular species (more recent arrivals), and clusters appear consistent among individuals within species.
5. Mechanism of HGT: Unknown. No one has witnessed it; experiments to make rotifers "eat" DNA have failed. Hypotheses include DNA incorporation during desiccation-repair (though some non-desiccation-surviving rotifers still have horizontal genes) and "jumping DNA" (transposons). This remains an active research area.

**Methods:** The researchers analyzed carotenoid biosynthesis genes in 23 aphid genomes and 265 other insect species (288 total insects across 14 orders), using homologs from plants, fungi, and bacteria. A total of 26 carotenogenic genes were examined (11 from plants, 7 from bacteria, 8 from fungi), consolidated into 15 genes based on Pfam domains. Four aphid species with distinct colors were studied: Brevicoryne brassicae (greyish), Rhopalosiphum padi (black), Acyrthosiphon pisum, and Myzus persicae (with green-to-red color polymorphisms). RNAi knockdown experiments were performed on M. persicae.

**Key Results:**
1. **HGT origins:** Phylogenetic analysis revealed that GPS (Geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate synthase), PS (Phytoene synthase), and CD (Carotenoid desaturase) were acquired via HGT from fungi by ancestral insects, while CCO (Carotenoid cleavage oxygenase) is a native insect gene.
2. **Independent HGT events:** Most insect genomes contain two copies of GPS, likely resulting from independent HGT events based on distinct motif profiles and clustering patterns.
3. **Gene duplication:** Aphid genomes exhibit extensive duplication of PS and CD genes, a pattern uncommon in other insects. M. persicae had the highest number: 8 PS copies and 5 CD copies, while B. brassicae (6 PS, 3 CD), A. pisum (5 PS, 4 CD), and R. padi (4 PS, 2 CD) harbored fewer copies.
4. **Gene clustering:** PS and CD genes are tandemly arranged and clustered on chromosomes in aphids, mirroring fungal gene organization.
5. **Novel red-pigmentation gene:** PS-4390 was identified as a novel contributor to red pigmentation in M. persicae. In the green-reddish clone, PS-4390 and CD-4400 were expressed 3.84 and 9.87 times higher, respectively, in red forms than green forms (which are genetically identical). CD-4400 is a homolog of the tor gene in A. pisum.
6. **RNAi validation:** Knocking down PS-4390 or CD-4400 caused red aphids to fade to green—approximately 20% and 26.7% of RNAi-treated reddish-clone aphids lost red coloration for PS-4390 and CD-4400 knockdowns, respectively (11.7% for both in the green-reddish clone). Treatment occurred at the third instar stage with dsRNA feeding over 48 hours.

**Conclusions:** The study provides strong evidence that HGT can introduce multiple functionally related genes (GPS, PS, CD) into recipient genomes, allowing them to be co-opted into a functional biosynthetic pathway (carotenoid synthesis). SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page is an entry in the Nemaplex database (UC Davis) providing a comprehensive overview of the root-knot nematode genus Meloidogyne (Goeldi, 1892), the type species of which is Meloidogyne exigua. It covers taxonomy, morphology, distribution, economic importance, feeding/host-parasite interactions, symptoms, hosts, life cycle, damage, and management.

KEY POINTS:

Classification: Rhabditida → Tylenchina → Tylenchoidea → Meloidogynidae → Meloidogyninae. The name derives from Greek words meaning "apple-shaped" and "female."

History: The International Meloidogyne Project (J.N. Sasser, US-AID, ~1975-1985) advanced species separation using host range tests, chromosome counts (Triantaphyllou), juvenile head structure (Eisenback), protein gel electrophoresis, and DNA patterns. The North Carolina Differential Hosts Test distinguishes four common species (M. incognita races 1-4, M. arenaria races 1-2, M. javanica, M. hapla) using cotton, tobacco, pepper, watermelon, peanut, and tomato. There are about 100 described species (2021); 68 were listed in 1988 by Luc, Maggenti et al.

Morphology/Anatomy: Females have 2 prodelphic ovaries, are swollen, deposit eggs in a matrix secreted by six rectal glands (eggs not retained in the body), have an excretory pore usually anterior to the metacorpus, do not form cysts, and have fingerprint-like perineal cuticular striations. Males have 1-2 testes, no caudal alae, and a characteristic half-twist of the body. They are sedentary obligate root parasites that usually form galls; parthenogenesis predominates.

Distribution: Worldwide distribution; most widely recognized plant-parasitic nematode due to characteristic galling symptoms.

Economic Importance: In California's Nematode Pest Rating System, unencountered potentially hazardous species are A-rated; limited-distribution species like M. naasi and M. chitwoodi are B-rated; widespread species are C-rated. The "major" species (M. arenaria, M. hapla, M. incognita, M. javanica) were recognized since Chitwood's 1949 characterization. Emerging species (M. chitwoodi, M. fallax, M. minor, M. enterolobii, M. exigua, M. paranaensis) are increasingly recognized via biochemical/molecular methods; M. floridensis is a growing concern in California for overcoming Nemaguard rootstock resistance in Prunus.

Host-Parasite Interactions: J2 larvae are attracted to root tips (zone of elongation), lateral root emergence sites, and by CO2 (possibly via lowered pH from carbonic acid). They penetrate mechanically (stylet thrusts) and chemically (cellulase, pectinase), migrating between cortical cells toward the apex, then back to the vascular cylinder. Subventral glands (prominent in J2, atrophying in adults) are linked to giant cell initiation. The dorsal esophageal gland (DEG) secretions (packed in 800nm secretory granules) stimulate multinucleate giant cells; if the nematode is removed, giant cells atrophy. Giant cells form via acytokinetic mitosis (karyokinesis without cytokinesis / endoreduplication), while syncytia in Heterodera/Globodera form via repeated S-phase endoreduplication. Over 50 genes are upregulated in feeding cell development. Chorismate mutase from nematode esophageal glands suppresses pathogen-triggered immunity (salicylic acid pathway). The nematode also induces hyperplasia (galling), higher auxin and cytokinin levels in galled tissue, and systemically induces transcriptome/spliceome reprogramming (9064 splicing events in 2898 genes).

Symptoms: Yellowing, mid-day wilting, water/nutrient stress symptoms, gall formation, root branching, sometimes death with interacting organisms.

Hosts: Parasites of over 3,000 host plants as a genus; Jensen et al. (1977) listed 874 crop species for 7-8 species in the western U.S. M. incognita is extremely polyphagous (up to 3,000 plant species), while M. megatyla and M. pini are restricted to Pinus spp.

Life Cycle: J2 penetrate roots, migrate intercellularly to the vascular cylinder, induce feeding sites, become sedentary, molt through J3 and J4 (which pass within the J2 cuticle, do not feed), then molt to females which lay 400-500 eggs (up to 2,800) in a gelatinous matrix. Most growth occurs during the second stage. Cellulases in the egg-mass matrix (possibly acquired via horizontal gene transfer from bacteria) help digest a hole to the root surface. Sex reversal can occur under adverse conditions. Body weight increases ~250-fold (0.11 ug J2 to 300 ug female+egg mass); total energy demand = 1 calorie. Comparison table: Meloidogynidae have multinucleate giant cell feeding sites (vs. syncytium in Heteroderidae), wide host range, mainly parthenogenic reproduction, eggs in egg mass, no cyst, hatching from favorable environmental conditions, and acytokinetic mitosis + endoreduplication cell cycle.

Management (Host Plant Resistance): Resistance may be pre-infection (preventing entry) or post-infection (preventing egg-laying stage). The Mi gene (single dominant gene near centromere of chromosome 6) confers resistance to M. incognita, M. javanica, and M. arenaria, and also against potato aphid (Macrosiphum euphorbiae) and whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). It was transferred from wild Solanum peruvianum via embryo rescue techniques (Smith, 1944). The Aps-1 acid phosphatase isozyme marker (Rick and Fobes, 1974) aided breeding. The gene was cloned and sequenced in Dr. Valerie Williamson's lab at UC Davis and transferred to susceptible tomato via Agrobacterium. Resistance breaks down at soil temperatures >28°C and with repeated single-source resistance use in California, aggressive nematode strains are being selected (Kaloshian et al. 1996). A table shows vegetable cultivars with resistance: M. incognita has the most (109 total, including 43 tomato, 30 cowpea), with only 3 resistant cultivars for M. hapla.

- Identified 767 Arabidopsis proteins mapped to 60,850 bacterial proteins as potential molecular mimicry candidates.
- Detected 180 unique cross-kingdom HGT events: 84 genes likely transferred from plants to bacteria, and 96 genes from PA bacteria to plants.
- Additionally found 161 genes transferred between PA bacteria and the eukaryotic domain (source unclear), 65 genes with unclear inheritance patterns, and 361 genes with no HGT patterns.
- Rejected DNA contamination by confirming no homologous pairs exceeded 76% amino acid identity.

- Genes transferred from plants to bacteria are enriched in secreted proteins, carbohydrate catabolism enzymes (pectin esterase, glycosidase), and include chitinases (CHI, AT2G43570), endo beta mannanase (XCD1), and pectin lyases (PME5) — enabling bacteria to exploit plant-derived sugars.

- The plant CHI (chitinase) gene is present in only 7 PA Streptomyces genomes (patchy distribution), with protein structures very similar (RMSD=0.791).
- The bacterial DET2 homologue (steroid-5-alpha-reductase, key in brassinosteroid biosynthesis) is nearly specific to plant-associated Leifsonia genus (Actinobacteria), located downstream of a tRNA gene; protein structures highly similar (RMSD=0.727) despite less than 50% sequence identity.

--- SOURCE 22: Evidence for extensive horizontal gene transfer from the draft genome of a tardigrade - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4702960

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) on November 23, 2015 (doi: 10.1073/pnas.1510461112), reporting evidence for extensive horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in the genome of the tardigrade *Hypsibius dujardini*. The research was led by Thomas C. Boothby and Bob Goldstein at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, with collaborators from the University of Utah and Cofactor Genomics.

**Key Findings:**
- Approximately one-sixth (17.5%, or 6,663 genes) of the tardigrade genome was acquired through horizontal gene transfer—nearly double the proportion found in previous extreme cases of HGT in animals (the rotifer *Adineta ricciae* at 8-9%).
- The foreign genes originated from diverse sources: mostly bacteria (91.7%), plus Archaea, fungi, plants, and viruses (1,361 bacterial species, 40 archaeal species, 91 fungal species, 45 plant species, and 6 viruses).
- The genome was sequenced to 126-fold coverage using Illumina Moleculo long reads and short insert mate pair libraries, producing a 212.3 Mb assembly containing 38,145 predicted genes. The assembly contains 95.16% of core eukaryotic genes and 95.9% of publicly available H. dujardini EST sequences.
- Validation methods included HGT index calculations, phylogenetic analysis (gene trees for 107 genes using maximum likelihood and Bayesian analysis—101 of 103 trees supported HGT), PCR to confirm physical linkage of foreign genes to metazoan genes (98.3% success), and PacBio long-read sequencing (assemblies were 98.53% concordant per base).
- Horizontally transferred genes showed evidence of assimilation into the tardigrade genome: they acquired U2 spliceosomal introns (57.1% of bacterial-origin genes contained at least one intron), and codon usage evolved toward metazoan bias.
- 13.2% of unique protein domains are represented exclusively by genes of foreign origin, and 47.6% of H. dujardini protein families have been supplemented by at least one foreign member.
- Foreign genes expanded, supplemented, or replaced gene families involved in stress tolerance, including heat shock proteins (hsp70), catalases (antioxidant enzymes), DNA repair proteins (Ku proteins, umuC, recA/Rad51, Ada), and spermidine synthase enzymes.
- The tardigrade genome showed expansions in stress response genes: heat shock proteins (3.5-fold vs. D. melanogaster), chaperone proteins (4-fold vs. Dm), DNA damage repair enzymes (3.6-fold vs. Dm), and antioxidant pathway members (2.7-fold vs. Dm).
- *H. dujardini* and the bdelloid rotifer *A. ricciae* share 148 putative orthologs that were both horizontally transferred (3.5% overlap), mostly acquired through separate HGT events, including stress-related genes like superoxide dismutase, GST, Ku DNA repair protein, and hsp70.

**Proposed Mechanism:** The authors speculate that desiccation tolerance may predispose organisms to HGT: during rehydration, desiccated membranes become transiently leaky, allowing uptake of foreign DNA, and desiccation induces genomic double-strand breaks that are repaired by robust DNA repair mechanisms, potentially leading to accidental incorporation of foreign DNA.

**Controversy Note:** The article notes subsequent letters challenging the findings—see "Genome of a tardigrade: Horizontal gene transfer or bacterial contamination?" and "No evidence for extensive horizontal gene transfer from the draft genome of a tardigrade" (volume 113, pages E3054–E3057), with the authors' reply in "Reply to Bemm et al. and Arakawa: Identifying foreign genes in independent Hypsibius dujardini genome assemblies."

The genome sequence was deposited at DDBJ/EMBL/GenBank under accession LMYF00000000 (version LMYF01000000).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Smithsonian Magazine article (published around December 2015, authored by Maris Fessenden) reports on a scientific controversy regarding tardigrade genomes. Tardigrades (also called moss piglets or water bears) are microscopic aquatic invertebrates known for surviving extreme conditions like the vacuum of space, desiccation, and freezing.

The controversy began when a University of North Carolina (UNC) team, led by researchers including Thomas Boothby and Bob Goldstein, published research in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences reporting that the tardigrade species Hypsibius dujardini carries about 6,600 genes acquired through horizontal gene transfer from other organisms (mostly bacteria, but also fungi, plants, viruses, and archaea). They claimed this foreign DNA made up about 17.5 percent of the tardigrade's genome, and suggested these genes might explain the creatures' resilience to extreme conditions.

About a week later, a rival group from the University of Edinburgh, led by Mark Blaxter (including Sujai Kumar), challenged these findings. They had also sequenced the same species and found only between 36 and 500 horizontally transferred genes—a much smaller proportion. The Edinburgh group published their contradictory findings on the preprint server bioRxiv.org before formal peer review. They suspected the UNC group had mistakenly sequenced DNA from bacteria living alongside the tardigrades, confusing microbial genes with tardigrade genes. Blaxter noted that some DNA fragments were too rare to biologically belong to the same genome.

The UNC researchers acknowledged the possibility of contamination but defended their methodology, stating they were aware of the potential problem and would conduct additional analysis before further comment. They appreciated that their rivals published contradictory results quickly on bioRxiv.

The article highlights this back-and-forth as demonstrating how science can self-correct rapidly in the digital age—what took nine days in this case would have taken months in the past. Both teams praised the fast publication times and data sharing. As of publication, the jury was still out on how much of the tardigrade's genome comes from foreign sources.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"What is evident is the amazing new ability of science to self correct rapidly," Blaxter tells Yong.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 25: Water bears’ genetic borrowing questioned ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Science News article (published December 2015, by Tina Hesman Saey) reports on a scientific dispute over claims that tardigrades (water bears) are prolific gene borrowers through horizontal gene transfer. A previous study led by Bob Goldstein at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (published November 23, 2015, in PNAS) claimed that tardigrades (Hypsibius dujardini) obtained about 17 percent of their genes from bacteria and other organisms.

However, researchers in evolutionary biologist Mark Blaxter's lab at the University of Edinburgh conducted a new analysis (posted online December 1 on BioRxiv.org) concluding that the bacterial DNA in the reported tardigrade genome is mostly contamination, not genuine horizontal gene transfer. The Edinburgh team estimated that about 30 percent of the DNA in the North Carolina group's tardigrade genome may be contaminants, and that foreign genes may account for less than 1 percent of the tardigrade genome. Blaxter's team was able to confirm only 54 of the more than 6,600 proposed borrowed genes as genuinely embedded in the tardigrade genome.

Goldstein and coauthor Thomas Boothby acknowledged in a written comment that the new analysis "raises some reasonable concerns about contamination" in their paper, noting they had considered contamination as the most likely initial explanation.

Context for the discrepancy: Only 107 of the alleged foreign genes underwent close scrutiny in the original study, with results extrapolated to the rest. Salzberg (Johns Hopkins) noted the tardigrade genome's size of more than 212 million bases—more than twice what Goldstein's group previously reported—raised red flags. Tardigrades contain only about 1,000 cells, so scientists must pool many animals to get enough DNA, inevitably mixing in DNA from the microbiome and ingested algae. The assembled genome sits in thousands of small pieces.

University of Cambridge molecular cell biologist Chiara Boschetti cautioned that it's not yet established that the Edinburgh analysis is correct, noting they "may have over-cleaned their data." She framed the dispute as a positive example of scientific self-correction: "Such quick testing of extraordinary claims is how science should work... Let's find out where the truth is."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We said, 'This is so different from our assembly, something must be wrong,'" Blaxter recalls.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Multiple lateral gene transfers and duplications have promoted plant parasitism ability in nematodes - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2955110

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in PNAS (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) on October 12, 2010 (doi: 10.1073/pnas.1008486107, PMID: 20876108, PMCID: PMC2955110), authored by Etienne G.J. Danchin and colleagues from INRA Sophia-Antipolis (France) and CNRS Marseille (France). The article is titled "Multiple lateral gene transfers and duplications have promoted plant parasitism ability in nematodes."

MAIN TOPIC: The study investigates the evolutionary origins of plant cell wall-degrading/modifying enzymes found in plant-parasitic nematodes. These enzymes are generally absent from animals but show similarity to bacterial homologs, suggesting acquisition via lateral gene transfer (LGT).

KEY FINDINGS:
- The analysis demonstrates that multiple independent LGT events from different bacterial sources gave rise to six gene families involved in plant cell-wall modification in clade IV plant-parasitic nematodes (root-knot nematodes and cyst nematodes).
- The plant-parasitic nematode genome of Meloidogyne incognita contains more than 60 genes covering six different protein families for cell wall degradation—an unprecedented repertoire in animals, including cellulases, xylanases, polygalacturonases, pectate lyases, candidate arabinanases, and expansin-like proteins.
- The six gene families and their closest bacterial relatives include: GH28 polygalacturonases (closest to Ralstonia solanacearum), PL3 pectate lyases (closest to Actinomycetales like Clavibacter michiganensis), GH43 arabinanases (closest to Actinomycetales), GH5 cellulases (closest to Bacteroidetes and some insects), GH5 xylanases (closest to Clostridium acetobutylicum), and EXPN expansin-like proteins (closest to Actinomycetales).
- Multiple potential bacterial donors are plant pathogens or symbiotic soil bacteria that share plant hosts with nematodes, satisfying the criterion of sympatry for LGT to occur.
- Massive gene duplications following LGT acquisition account for the abundance and diversity of these multigenic families.
- Genes feature multiple introns (with at least one intron position shared across lineages), indicating early intron gain after LGT; GC content and codon usage of LGT-acquired genes are indistinguishable from other nematode genes, supporting ancient transfer.
- Four groups of bacteria may serve as potential donors; notably, Clavibacter michiganensis (which shares hosts with nematodes) possesses the PL3 most closely related to those of root-knot and cyst nematodes.

METHODOLOGY: Phylogenetic analyses were conducted using Bayesian methods (MrBayes) and bootstrapped maximum-likelihood approaches (RAxML); topology tests used CONSEL to reject monophyly of eukaryotes; GC content, codon use, and gene localization were analyzed using EMBOSS; immunolocalization studies were performed on tomato roots infected with M. incognita using antibodies against the CBM2 module of the ENG1 cellulase.

NOTABLE NOVEL FINDING: Protein immunolocalization revealed that CBM2-bearing proteins are secreted by root-knot nematodes during migratory stages AND at later sedentary parasitism stages—detected in eggs about to be extruded and at the vulva region of adult females. This suggests additional roles for these cell wall-degrading enzymes in the late stages of the parasite's life cycle, possibly in successful egg laying, critical for spreading offspring to surrounding roots.

CONCLUSIONS: LGT of bacterial origin, followed by gene duplications driven by selective advantage, was crucial for the emergence and proficiency of plant parasitism in nematodes. The authors suggest LGT in animals may be more frequent than generally considered, citing similar massive gene transfers in bdelloid rotifers. They note this phenomenon has "radically remolded evolutionary trends" and predict similar roles may be discovered in other animals.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Here we report that independent lateral gene transfers from different bacteria, followed by gene duplications and early gain of introns, have shaped this repertoire." , "Multiple functional acquisitions of exogenous genes that provide selective advantage were probably crucial for the emergence and proficiency of plant parasitism in nematodes." , "Our analysis shows that LGT events from several independent bacterial sources most likely gave rise to the six different gene families involved in plant cell-wall modification in clade IV plant-parasitic nematodes." , "Selective advantage associated with transfer of these genes probably has driven their duplications and facilitated fixation in the different populations and species of plant-parasitic nematodes." , "Far from being negligible, these LGT events certainly have radically remolded evolutionary trends in recipient organisms, and similar roles in other animals can be expected to be discovered."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: [PDF] Massive lateral transfer of genes encoding plant cell wall-degrading ... ---
URL: https://escholarship.org/content/qt2ww681pd/qt2ww681pd.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research article (published April 9, 2018, in PLOS Genetics) investigates the evolutionary origin of the nutritional versatility of Trichoderma fungi—molds that can parasitize other fungi, attack animals, and degrade plant biomass. 

**Methods:** The researchers conducted a phylogenomic analysis of 23 hypocrealean fungi (including nine Trichoderma spp. and the related Escovopsis weberi), using whole-genome sequences including five newly sequenced Trichoderma genomes. They analyzed 122 gene families encoding plant cell wall-degrading carbohydrate-active enzymes (pcwdCAZome) using gene tree/species tree reconciliation (NOTUNG analysis) to distinguish between gene duplication, gene loss, and lateral gene transfer (LGT).

**Key Findings:**
- Trichoderma evolved from an ancestor with limited cellulolytic capability that fed on fungi or arthropods, sharing a last common ancestor with entomoparasitic fungi (Cordycipitaceae, Ophiocordycipitaceae, Clavicipitaceae).
- Nearly half (41%, 50 of 122 phylogenetic groups) of the Trichoderma pcwdCAZome was obtained via LGT from plant-associated Ascomycota fungi, including Eurotiomycetes (16 cases), Leotiomycetes (7), Sordariomycetes (15), and Dothidiomycetes (2).
- No LGT was detected from Basidiomycota (despite these being common hosts of Trichoderma) or from prokaryotes.
- The only non-fungal LGT was for the auxiliary protein swollenin, putatively from green plants.
- Trichoderma is capable of endoparasitism and adelphoparasitism (parasitism on closely related fungi, even within the same genus/family), which may have facilitated LGT from phylogenetically related Ascomycota donors.
- Escovopsis weberi, a close relative that parasitizes Basidiomycota, showed no such nutritional versatility or LGT events, challenging the host-habitat hypothesis.
- Four GH families (GH6, GH26, GH51, GH62) appear entirely derived from LGT events.
- The study suggests LGT from plant-associated fungi allowed primarily mycotrophic Trichoderma to evolve into decomposers of plant biomass—an unprecedented degree of lateral gene transfer for fungal pcwdCAZyme genes.

**Conclusion:** The authors propose that LGT is linked to Trichoderma's unique ability to parasitize taxonomically related fungi (Ascomycota), and that lateral transfer of genes resulted in profound nutritional expansion, contributing to the emergence of a generalist capable of feeding on organic matter of any origin.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Nearly one-half of the genes in Trichoderma pcwdCAZome (41%) were obtained via LGT from plant-associated filamentous fungi belonging to different classes of Ascomycota, while no LGT was observed from other potential donors."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This ScienceDirect topic page provides an AI-generated overview of Meloidogyne incognita, a species of root-knot nematode (RKN) harmful to chili plants and other crops. The page compiles chapters and articles on resistance research, particularly focusing on RNA interference (RNAi) strategies to engineer nematode-resistant plants.

Key findings from the articles include:

**RNAi-Based Resistance (2007, 2022):** The parasitism gene 16D10 of M. incognita encodes a conserved RKN peptide secreted from subventral glands that stimulates root growth and functions as a ligand for plant transcription factors during feeding-site formation. Transgenic Arabidopsis plants expressing dsRNA against 16D10 showed 69-93% reduction in RKN eggs across the four major RKN species (M. incognita, M. javanica, M. arenaria, M. hapla) — a resistance range unattainable with natural RKN resistance genes. A 2022 review documents host-delivered RNAi (HD-RNAi) targeting multiple effector genes with significant reductions in galls and egg masses, including: 16D10 (63-90% gall reduction), Mi-CRT calreticulin, 8D05 (up to 90% gall reduction), Misp12 (65% reduction in J3/J4s, 69% in mature females), Mimsp40 (up to 50% gall reduction), msp-18 and msp-20 (47% reduction), Mi-msp-1, Mi-msp2 (52-54% galls, 60-66% females, 84-95% egg masses), and Mi-msp3 (89%), Mi-msp5 (78%), Mi-msp18 (86%), Mi-msp24 (89%).

**Horizontal Gene Transfer (2011):** Sixty genes across six protein families in the M. incognita genome resulted from HGT from bacterial sources, including cellulases, pectate lyases, and expansin-like proteins involved in degrading plant cell walls — facilitating the nematode's exploitation of plants as a new ecological niche.

**Endophytic Interactions (2020):** M. incognita infection shifts bacterial root endophytic community composition in tomatoes, enriching Sphingobacteriales, Flavobacteriales, Rhodocyclales, and Enterobacteriales.

**Nematode Secretions (2008):** Describes how nematode esophageal gland cell secretions, including cell-wall modifying proteins, chorismate mutase, CLE peptides, and ubiquitin-pathway proteins, are released through the stylet to form specialized feeding cells.
</summary>

This range of resistance is unique and cannot be obtained by any natural RKN resistance gene."

--- SOURCE 7: Interactions between Plant Parasitic Nematodes and Bacteria ---
URL: https://agriarticles.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/E-05-03-80-258-261.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article from Agri Articles (e-Magazine for Agricultural Articles, Volume 05, Issue 03, May-June 2025, ISSN: 2582-9882) by Banajit Baishya examines interactions between plant-parasitic nematodes (PPNs) and bacteria, focusing on the evolutionary role of bacterial gene acquisition and current biocontrol applications.

Key topics covered:
1. **Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT)**: Genome-to-genome analyses of root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.) suggest certain genes were derived from bacteria through horizontal gene transfer, with rhizobacteria (Rhizobium, Pseudomonas, Bacillus) identified as the predominant 'gene donor' group. These acquired genes (encoding cellulases, pectate lyases, and Nod factor-like proteins) are directly related to the parasitic lifestyle, aiding host plant invasion. The author proposes that HGT from soil bacteria may have facilitated the origin of parasitism in Meloidogyne and represented key steps in speciation of plant-parasitic nematodes.

2. **Pasteuria penetrans**: A bacterial hyperparasite of plant-parasitic nematodes, closely related to Bacillus spp. (with considerable genome synteny to Bacillus subtilis). Its mode of action includes: attachment of endospores to the nematode cuticle; germination and penetration after the nematode infects a plant root; colonization of the nematode body (particularly reproductive tissues, preventing egg production); and sporulation inside the nematode, killing it and releasing new endospores into the soil. Its species-specificity and spore durability make it a promising biological control agent.

3. **Types of nematode-bacteria interactions**: The article categorizes interactions as neutral, obligate mutualistic (e.g., entomopathogenic nematodes with symbiotic bacteria), protocooperation (disease complexes), commensalism (uncommon), competition (both injured), natural enemy attack (nematodes suffer), and obligate parasitic.

4. **Nematode-induced physiological changes**: Sedentary endoparasites form galls (giant cells) or syncytia—nutrient-rich cells that act as substrates for bacterial colonization.

5. **Wolbachia and animal parasitic nematodes**: Wolbachia is an obligate, Rickettsia-like, maternally inherited, intracellular α-proteobacteria (0.5μm diameter, enclosed in double trilaminate membrane). It forms a tripartite symbiotic relationship involving the host reservoir (humans and mammals), the parasite (filarial nematodes causing onchocerciasis/river blindness, lymphatic filariasis/elephantiasis, and dirofilariasis/heartworm), and the endosymbiont.

6. **Endosymbionts and PPNs**: Four major endosymbionts associated with PPNs—Cardinium, Wolbachia, Xiphinematobacter, and Burkholderia—arise from divergent phyla (Bacteroidetes, Verrucomicrobia, Alphaproteobacteria, Betaproteobacteria). Endosymbionts help nematodes digest plant cells or synthesize essential nutrients (e.g., Xiphinematobacter synthesizes essential amino acids to supplement Xiphinema americanum's diet of root phloem). Nematodes achieve cell wall degrading capacity (cellulases, glucanases, pectinases) by acquiring additional endosymbionts like Wolbachia-like Rickettsiales ancestors, and evolve with symbionts until HGT occurs.

**Conclusion**: Interactions between PPNs and bacteria are complex and significantly influence plant health and disease progression. PPNs can create entry points for pathogenic bacteria promoting co-infections, while certain bacteria can inhibit nematode activity antagonistically or via plant defense mechanisms. Plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) have emerged as promising biocontrol agents offering an environmentally friendly alternative to chemical treatments. Molecular and genomic tools are essential for unraveling these mechanisms, and a holistic, integrated approach combining biological, ecological, and technological insights will be key to managing these pests effectively.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Based on genome-to-genome analyses of gene sequences obtained from plant-parasitic, root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.), it seems likely that certain genes have been derived from bacteria by horizontal gene transfer. Strikingly, a common theme underpinning the function of these genes is their apparent direct relationship to the nematodes' parasitic lifestyle."

SUMMARY:
<summary>

The study was conducted by researchers at North Carolina State University, Washington University School of Medicine, and Divergence Inc., including Elizabeth H Scholl, Jeffrey L Thorne, James P McCarter, and David Mck Bird. METHODOLOGY: The researchers developed a two-step phylogenetic filter based on genome-to-genome comparisons. First, Meloidogyne EST sequences (from M. incognita, M. javanica, and M. hapla) were translated and compared against C. elegans and Drosophila melanogaster genomes, as well as bacterial sequences. The study hypothesizes that acquisition of genetic material from soil bacteria through horizontal transfer may have represented key steps in the evolution of plant parasitism in Meloidogyne and possibly facilitated speciation of plant-parasitic nematodes.
