SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an Academia.edu webpage for the 2004 paper "From the Cover: Massive horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes from diverse land plant donors to the basal angiosperm Amborella" by Ulfar Bergthorsson, published in Proceedings of The National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).

Key findings of the paper (from the abstract):
- The study focused on Amborella trichopoda, a basal angiosperm, because it was already known to possess one horizontally acquired gene and preliminary analyses suggested it contained several more.
- Researchers comprehensively sequenced the mitochondrial protein gene set of Amborella, sequenced a variable number of mitochondrial genes from 28 other diverse land plants, and conducted phylogenetic analyses including the five sequenced mitochondrial genomes of angiosperms.
- Results showed that Amborella has acquired one or more copies of 20 of its 31 known mitochondrial protein genes from other land plants, for a total of 26 foreign genes, while no evidence for HGT was found in the five sequenced genomes.
- Most Amborella transfers came from other angiosperms (especially eudicots), while others came from nonangiosperms, including six striking cases of transfer from at least three different moss donors.
- Most transferred genes are intact, consistent with functionality and/or recency of transfer.
- Conclusion: Amborella mtDNA has sustained proportionately more HGT than any other eukaryotic, or perhaps even prokaryotic, genome yet examined.

The page also includes related papers, most notably:
- "Widespread horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes in flowering plants" (Bergthorsson, Nature, 2003) showing HGT is evolutionarily frequent between distantly related flowering plants, occurring with gene duplication, recapture of genes lost through nuclear transfer, and chimaeric half-monocot/half-dicot genes.
- "Horizontal Transfer of Entire Genomes via Mitochondrial Fusion in the Angiosperm Amborella" (Science, 2013) reporting the complete 3.9 Mb Amborella mitochondrial genome containing six genome equivalents of foreign mitochondrial DNA from green algae, mosses, and other angiosperms, proposing a fusion-compatibility model.
- Other related papers cover mitochondrial genome evolution in Magnolia, mosses (Physcomitrella), Geranium, early land plants, Silene latifolia, Vitis vinifera, and parasitic plants.

The page contains 34 references, author information (Ulfar Bergthorsson, University of New Mexico), and related topics including Plant Genome Project and Molecular Sequence Data.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper reports the complete mitochondrial genome sequence of Amborella trichopoda, a large shrub endemic to the rain forests of New Caledonia that is likely sister to all other angiosperms (diverging ~200 million years ago). The genome is enormous at 3.9 Mb (3,866,039 bp), assembled as five autonomously replicating circular chromosomes (3179, 244, 187, 137, and 119 kb). Remarkably, the genome contains approximately six genome equivalents of foreign mitochondrial DNA acquired from green algae, mosses, and other angiosperms, representing a striking example of horizontal gene transfer (HGT).

Key findings include:
- Four complete mitochondrial genomes were horizontally transferred: one from a moss (with architecture nearly identical to Physcomitrella and Anomodon) and three from green algae (donors A, B, C), plus a partial genome from a fourth green-algal donor (D). The green algal genomes likely came from the Coccomyxa subgroup of trebouxiophytes, possibly via lichens growing on Amborella.
- Approximately 753 kb of DNA was acquired from other angiosperms (about two genome equivalents), with donors identified including Santalales (parasitic plants, the major source), Fagales, Oxalidales, Ricinus communis, and Bambusa oldhamii. Some foreign tracts show evidence of serial angiosperm-to-angiosperm HGT.
- The genome also contains 138 kb of plastid DNA, mostly via intracellular gene transfer, with ~10 kb entering via foreign mitochondria.
- Of the 197 foreign mitochondrial protein genes, only 50 (25%) have full-length intact open reading frames, and most are pseudogenes; the majority of foreign genes are not functionally expressed. This makes Amborella mtDNA a striking example of neutral evolution and "junk DNA."

The authors propose a fusion-compatibility model: Amborella captured whole mitochondria from diverse green plants, followed by mitochondrial fusion (mechanistically limited to green plants) and genome recombination. They note that mitochondrial fusion in animals and fungi uses dynamin-related GTPases absent from green plants, suggesting a fundamentally different fusion mechanism in green plants. The ecological context—Amborella's heavy epiphyte load (mosses, lichens, other angiosperms), propensity to produce suckers from wounds (wounding may create new meristems that incorporate foreign mitochondria), and low rate of mitochondrial DNA loss—all contribute to the high level of foreign DNA. The transfers are likely millions of years old given extensive pseudogene decay but surprisingly intact retention of the whole-genome transfers.
</summary>

This enormous, 3.9 Mb genome contains six genome equivalents of foreign mitochondrial DNA, acquired from green algae, mosses, and other angiosperms. Many of these horizontal transfers were large, including acquisition of entire mitochondrial genomes from three green algae and one moss."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PNAS research article (published December 14, 2004, in volume 101, issue 51, pages 17747-17752) by Ulfar Bergthorsson, Aaron O. Richardson, Gregory J. Young, Leslie R. Goertzen, and Jeffrey D. Palmer, titled "Massive horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes from diverse land plant donors to the basal angiosperm Amborella."

STUDY PURPOSE: The researchers investigated whether plants could acquire multiple foreign genes through horizontal gene transfer (HGT), moving beyond the previously known cases of single-gene acquisition. They focused on Amborella trichopoda, a basal angiosperm (a monotypic genus of shrubs endemic to New Caledonia) that was already known to possess one horizontally acquired gene and showed signs of containing more.

METHODOLOGY: The team used PCR amplification with conserved primers (~100 primer pairs) to comprehensively sequence the mitochondrial protein gene set of Amborella, plus variable numbers of mitochondrial genes from 28 other diverse land plants. They also conducted maximum-likelihood and parsimony phylogenetic analyses, using the Shimodaira-Hasegawa (SH) test to assess whether phylogenetically anomalous gene placements suggestive of HGT were statistically significant. To rule out contamination, HGT cases were confirmed from multiple independent DNA preparations from four different sources of Amborella material.

KEY RESULTS:
- Of the 40 protein genes present in the ancestral angiosperm mitochondrial genome, 31 were recovered from Amborella.
- Of these 31 genes, 20 showed evidence of one or more cases of HGT, for a total of 26 foreign genes acquired.
- Most transfers came from other angiosperms (especially eudicots), while others came from nonangiosperms, including six striking cases of transfer from at least three different moss donors.
- The five sequenced angiosperm mitochondrial genomes (rice, Arabidopsis, Brassica, Beta, and others) showed no evidence of HGT.
- Most transferred genes are intact (functional or recently transferred), while nine are pseudogenes.
- Evidence suggests the transferred genes reside in the mitochondrial genome (not chloroplast or nuclear), based on RNA editing patterns characteristic of mitochondria, nucleotide substitution rates, and PCR abundance.
- The 11 remaining singleton genes appear to be of vertical descent, placing Amborella as sister to all other angiosperms.

DISCUSSION AND SIGNIFICANCE: Amborella mtDNA has sustained proportionately more HGT than any other eukaryotic, or perhaps prokaryotic, genome yet examined. The study suggests HGT incidence varies markedly between plants. The authors speculate that Amborella's environment—mid-elevation montane tropical rain forests in New Caledonia where the plant's leaves and stems are often covered with diverse epiphytes including mosses—could promote direct plant-to-plant HGT (similar to mechanisms proposed for parasitic plants). The authors note limitations of their PCR approach, including missing rRNA/tRNA genes, chloroplast-derived sequences, and intergenic DNA, and emphasize that only sequencing the complete Amborella mitochondrial genome can comprehensively census its horizontally acquired DNA. They cite the SH test as supporting 14 of the transfers, with divergent duplicates in plant mtDNA representing xenologs (horizontal products) rather than paralogs.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Results indicate that Amborella has acquired one or more copies of 20 of its 31 known mitochondrial protein genes from other land plants, for a total of 26 foreign genes, whereas no evidence for HGT was found in the five sequenced genomes."; "Most of the Amborella transfers are from other angiosperms (especially eudicots), whereas others are from nonangiosperms, including six striking cases of transfer from (at least three different) moss donors."; "Amborella mtDNA has sustained proportionately more HGT than any other eukaryotic, or perhaps even prokaryotic, genome yet examined."; "Clearly, then, the incidence of HGT varies markedly from one plant to another. One wonders how many other Amborella-type situations exist among the ≈255,000 species of flowering plants."; "We are lucky that, of all angiosperms, Amborella happens to be so rich in HGT, because its distinctive position at the base of angiosperms makes it relatively easy to detect with reasonable confidence transfers from other angiosperms, even with the scanty taxon sampling of this study."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Parasitic plants steal genes from their hosts | ScienceDaily ---
URL: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/06/120608100846.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A study published June 8, 2012, in BioMed Central's open access journal BMC Genomics reveals that the Malaysian parasitic plant Rafflesia cantleyi — which produces 50cm diameter flowers — has 'stolen' genes from its host, Tetrastigma rafflesiae, a member of the grape family. This represents horizontal gene transfer (movement of genes between two different organisms), as opposed to vertical gene transfer (between parents and offspring). While bacteria are known to use horizontal gene transfer (e.g., for antibiotic resistance), recent studies show plants, especially parasitic plants and their hosts, can also use it due to their intimate physical connections.

Researchers from Singapore, Malaysia, and the USA collaborated to systematically investigate horizontal gene transfer between these two plants. By examining the transcriptome (transcribed products of switched-on genes), they found 49 genes transcribed by the parasite — accounting for 2% of its total transcriptome — that originally belonged to the host. Three quarters of these transcripts appear to have replaced the parasite's own versions. Most of these genes had been integrated into the parasite's nucleus. Analysis of genetic drift between the parasite and host genes indicated the genes were acquired gradually over time.

Prof Charles Davis (Harvard University Herbaria) co-led the project with Prof Joshua Rest (Stony Brook University). Davis noted the elevated rate of horizontal gene transfer raises the possibility of a 'fitness' benefit to the parasite, such as improving nutrient extraction from the host or helping it evade the host's defenses. He also noted that about one third of the parasite's own genes have evolved to resemble those of T. rafflesia, and understanding how T. rafflesia manages its 'genomic deception' could provide insights into the slow war between plant parasites and their hosts.

Rafflesia cantleyi is an obligate holoparasite — fully dependent on its host for sustenance. The study's journal reference is: Zhenxiang Xi, Robert K Bradley, Kenneth J Wurdack, K.M. Wong, M. Sugumaran, Kirsten Bomblies, Joshua S Rest and Charles C Davis. "Horizontal transfer of expressed genes in a parasitic flowering plant." BMC Genomics, 13:227; 2012. DOI: 10.1186/1471-2164-13-227.
</summary>

"The elevated rate of horizontal gene transfer between T. rafflesiae and its parasite R. cantleyi raises the possibility that there is a 'fitness' benefit to the parasite. --- SOURCE 13: Ferns Borrowed Genes to Thrive in Low Light | Duke Today ---
URL: https://today.duke.edu/2014/04/hornwort

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A Duke University-led team has determined that ferns acquired the neochrome gene through horizontal gene transfer from hornworts (moss-related plants), which helped ferns adapt to low-light environments and diversify during the age of dinosaurs when flowering plants created shaded canopies. The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on April 14, 2014.

Neochrome is a "chimeric" gene—a hybrid of two other genes coding for photoreceptor proteins that sense blue and red light. This gives ferns a unique advantage in forests shaded by flowering plants, as filtered canopy light has more red than blue light, helping ferns "see" better.

Lead author Fay-Wei Li, a PhD student in Duke's biology department, investigated the gene's origin by combing through plant genomes from the Duke Herbarium and the 1000 Plants Initiative. Neochrome was found in hornwort genomes. Three possible explanations were tested: a shared common ancestor, independent evolution, or horizontal gene transfer. Ferns and hornworts diverged 400 million years ago. The analysis ruled out a common ancestor (since no seed plants retain the gene) and independent evolution. By constructing a family tree of light-sensitive genes, researchers found fern neochrome nested neatly within the hornwort lineage, with the gene versions separating about 179 million years ago—strong evidence of horizontal gene transfer.

Researchers are still exploring how horizontal gene transfer occurs in plants. In microbes, bacteria, fungi, and viruses mediate such transfers. Ferns' unique life cycle may facilitate this: gametophytes (the fern form producing sex cells) lack protective cuticles, are compact structures with exposed sex organs, and have extensive contact with competing plants—making foreign genetic material like neochrome easily passed to subsequent generations. The transfer appears to have occurred at just the right moment in fern evolutionary history, enabling their expansion in the shade of flowering plants. The work was supported by grants from the National Science Foundation, Duke University, and others.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Horizontal Transfer of a Plant Transposon | PLOS Biology ---
URL: https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.0040005

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed open-access research article published in PLOS Biology (December 20, 2005) by Diao X, Freeling M, and Lisch D, reporting the first well-documented evidence of horizontal transfer of a nuclear-encoded gene between higher plants.

**Key finding:** A subset of Mu-like elements (MULEs) in the genus Setaria (millets) is remarkably similar to a small family of MULEs in rice (Oryza sativa). The authors sequenced MULEs from eight species of Setaria and compared them to rice sequences, finding approximately 90% identity over 585 bp between Setaria faberi elements and a rice element (Os493) on Chromosome 5. A nearly complete Setaria element (Sf4) showed 88% overall nucleotide identity over 3.8 kb with the rice element.

**Evidence for horizontal transfer:** The Setaria and rice lineages diverged roughly 50 million years ago (Panicoid and Bambusoid grass subfamilies). The degree of similarity in noncoding regions (introns) and synonymous sites far exceeds what would be expected from vertical transmission. Key evidence:
- The MULE introns are 89% identical (227 bp total) between Setaria and rice, whereas introns of host genes (like waxy) are only ~52% identical between these species.
- The dS/dN ratio between the Setaria and rice MULEs is only 1.82 (weak selection), compared to 7.2-9.8 for host genes like waxy, acc1, and oxidoreductase.
- In contrast, comparisons of rice MULEs with homologous maize (Zm890) and sorghum (Sb632) elements show high exon similarity but dramatically reduced intron similarity (58% and 46% respectively), consistent with normal vertical transmission and selection on exons only.
- Synonymous substitution rates (dS) of 0.41-1.17 in host genes, with only 76% average identity in coding sequences and 40% in untranslated sequences between Setaria and rice.
- The region surrounding the Os493 insertion in rice does not exhibit reduced mutation frequency (flanking genes show typical divergence - exons 85% identical, introns only 50% identical with maize orthologs).
- Codon bias was ruled out (Nc value of 48 for both sequences, indicating moderate bias).

**Additional findings:** Southern blot hybridization revealed a discontinuous distribution of this MULE class. The elements were detected in rice, some Setaria species, and three species of East Asian bamboo (Shibataea kumasaca, Fargesia nitida, Phyllostachys vivax) but not in Central American bamboos (Chusquea montana, Chusquea quila, Otatea acuminata) or other grass subfamilies (Chloridoideae, Pooideae). The transfer is estimated to have occurred before the divergence of indica and japonica rice (~1 million years ago) and possibly before the rice-bamboo divergence. The authors speculate the transfer may have involved a vector, and note the possible physical proximity of the species' ancestors (southeast Asia).

**Context:** The paper notes that while horizontal transfer has been well-documented among animal transposons (P elements, mariner elements) and plant mitochondrial genes, this represents the first demonstrated case for nuclear-encoded plant genes. The elements appear to be inactive, likely due to epigenetic inactivation of foreign DNA. The authors suggest a comprehensive search for horizontally transferred plant genes is now warranted given the availability of sequence data.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This is the first well-documented example of horizontal transfer of any nuclear-encoded genes between higher plants."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Multiple horizontal transfers of nuclear ribosomal genes between phylogenetically distinct grass lineages ---
URL: https://www.pnas.org/doi/pdf/10.1073/pnas.1613375114

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper (published in PNAS, February 14, 2017, vol. 114, no. 7) investigates horizontal gene transfer (HGT) of nuclear ribosomal DNA (rDNA) between phylogenetically distinct grass lineages. The study identified nonnative rRNA gene copies in 16 diploid barley (Hordeum) species, traced via internal transcribed spacer (ITS) sequences to five distinct Panicoideae genera (Arundinella, Euclasta, Paspalum, Panicum, and Setaria) - a lineage that split from the Pooideae approximately 60 million years ago. Between one and five panicoid ITS types were found in various Hordeum and Pseudoroegneria individuals, with South American taxa accumulating multiple copies. The transfers were estimated to have occurred 1-5 Mya based on phylogenetic analysis, with at least nine independent transfer events inferred. The likely most ancient transfer (Panicum 1) occurred in the common ancestor of section Stenostachys in Central Asia, dating to 1.7-5.0 Mya.

Methodology included PCR-based screening of Triticeae species, phylogenetic analyses (Bayesian inference and maximum parsimony), construction and sequencing of a BAC library from H. bogdanii (revealing a ~70-kbp region of Panicum-derived DNA interrupted by two Hordeum-specific Copia-like transposable elements, with transposition events dated to 0.25-0.29 Mya), FISH cytogenetic analysis to locate insertion sites, and RT-PCR transcription assays. Key findings include complete absence of panicoid rDNA transcription, indications of silencing via pseudogenization (base substitutions in conserved 5.8S and ITS2 motifs), and retention of selectively neutral DNA over significant evolutionary time periods.

The authors conclude that HGT between vascular plants is not a rare event, is not restricted to one or a few genes, and can be selectively neutral. They propose aphids and endophytic fungi (particularly Epichloë) as potential vectors, given the historical geographic overlap of species due to climate changes over the past 5 million years. The paper suggests the supposed rarity of nuclear HGT in plant genomes likely reflects technical limitations in detection rather than a genuine biological phenomenon.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The movement of nuclear DNA from one vascular plant species to another in the absence of fertilization is thought to be rare. Here, nonnative rRNA gene [ribosomal DNA (rDNA)] copies were identified in a set of 16 diploid barley (Hordeum) species; their origin was traceable via their internal transcribed spacer (ITS) sequence to five distinct Panicoideae genera, a lineage that split from the Pooideae about 60 Mya."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: The Curious Case of Horizontal Gene Transfer – SCIENCE NEXT DOOR ---
URL: https://sciencenextdoorcom.wordpress.com/2021/04/29/the-curious-case-of-horizontal-gene-transfer

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, "The Curious Case of Horizontal Gene Transfer" by Suhani Sharma (published April 29, 2021, on the Science Next Door blog), explores how plants, not just bacteria, engage in Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT), which is the transmission of genes between organisms without reproduction via transformation, transduction, and conjugation. The article highlights two key cases:

**Grasses:** Research led by the University of Sheffield (Dr. Luke Dunning, senior author, and Samuel Hibdige, PhD researcher) found over 100 examples in grasses—including wheat, maize, rice, and barley—where genes had significantly different histories from the species they were found in. In some cases, HGT levels exceeded 40% of the genome, making these plants "naturally genetically modified." The study detected a statistical increase in species with modified stems called 'rhizomes.'

**Cuscata/Rafflesiaceae (Parasitic Plants):** The article discusses the Rafflesia arnoldii (giant corpse flower, with flowers weighing ~10 kg) and Sapria. A 2014 paper by Jeanmaire Molina found these plants had ditched their entire chloroplast genome. Follow-up research by Charles Davis and Liming Cai at Harvard University found that nearly half (44%) of genes conserved across plant lineages had disappeared from Sapria—more than twice the gene losses in dodders (Cuscuta) and four times the losses in witchweeds (Striga). Despite gene loss, Sapria's genome remains as large as a human's because it is loaded with borrowed genes from hosts (described as "a huge graveyard of DNA"), and 90% of its genome consists of DNA transposons ("jumping genes"). Researchers hypothesize that transposons may be the engines driving HGT, helping the parasites carry and insert gene fragments, and potentially contributing to unique features like the large flowers. The article notes these critically endangered plants face conservation challenges.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We found over 100 examples where the gene had a significantly different history to the species it was found in." - Dr. Luke Dunning; "If we can determine how this process is happening it may allow us to naturally modify crops and make them more resistant to climate change." - Dr. Luke Dunning; "We still don't know how this is happening or what the full implications are. But, we know it is widespread in grasses, a family of plants that provide a majority of the food we eat." - Samuel Hibdige; "We knew that there would be loss, but we didn't think it would be on the order of 44% of its genes." - Charles Davis; "Because these parasites have been stealing (or borrowing) genes for millennia, their genome is like a huge graveyard of DNA." - Liming Cai
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Grasses pass genes from one species to another but we don’t know how | New Scientist ---
URL: https://www.newscientist.com/article/2275559-grasses-pass-genes-from-one-species-to-another-but-we-dont-know-how

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This New Scientist article reports on research led by Luke Dunning at the University of Sheffield demonstrating that lateral (horizontal) gene transfer is widespread among grass species. This review article (Acta Biologica Cracoviensia Series Botanica 63/2: 17–28, 2021) by Góraalski et al. from Jagiellonian University summarizes the current state of knowledge on horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in parasitic plants. HGT allows genetic material to flow between distantly related organisms, was first discovered in plants in the early 21st century, and is especially prevalent in parasitic plants due to their intimate physical contact with hosts.

Key findings and topics covered:

1. **Factors facilitating HGT**: Close physical contact between organisms is the most important factor. This includes parasitism (via haustoria), epiphytism, grafting, and root-to-root inosculation. Holoparasites are better HGT subjects than hemiparasites due to their complete dependence on hosts for organic substances.

2. **HGT frequency correlates with parasitic dependence**: A study of Orobanchaceae (Yang et al., 2016) found 32 HGTs in the holoparasite Phelipanche aegyptiaca, 10 in the obligate hemiparasite Striga hermonthica, 2 in the facultative hemiparasite Triphysaria versicolor, and only 1 in free-living Lindenbergia. Kado and Innan (2018) found 106 transferred genes in holoparasites (22 in Orobanche minor, 84 in Aeginetia indica) but none in facultative parasites. Cuscuta shows higher rates than Orobanchaceae, possibly because its haustorial stem connections to flowers/gametes are permanently shorter distance (Yang et al., 2019).

3. **DNA vs. RNA as carriers**: Evidence supports both mechanisms. The ShContig9484 gene in Striga hermonthica (transferred from sorghum) shows traces of mRNA origin (poly-A tail). However, later studies on Cuscuta (108 functional genes) and other species indicate most functional genes were transferred via DNA, based on presence of introns.

4. **Adaptive role of HGT**: Transfers may serve adaptive functions. Rafflesia cantleyi likely acquired dozens of transcribed genes from its host (Xi et al., 2012), possibly for "genomic deception" to evade host defenses. In Cuscuta campestris, many HGT-acquired genes are expressed in haustoria and involved in defense and amino acid metabolism (Yang et al., 2019). Eighteen functional genes in Cuscuta belong to the same families as independently transferred genes in Orobanchaceae, supporting adaptive roles. In Sapria himalayana, at least 1.2% of the genome was acquired via HGT from the host (Cai et al., 2021).

5. **Source and target genomes**: Plant cells have nuclear, mitochondrial, and plastid genomes involved in HGT and intracellular gene transfer (IGT). Mitochondria are the most frequent recipients of alien DNA due to their frequent fusion/fission and higher noncoding DNA content (72-89% vs. 40-45% in plastids). Examples include massive HGT in Amborella trichopoda (3.9-Mb mitochondrial genome with many transfers), parasite-to-host transfers (atp1, atp6, matR from Cuscuta to Plantago; atp6 in Orobanche coerulescens from Asteraceae), Cynomorium coccineum (10 transfers of 5 mitochondrial genes), and Lophophytum mirabile (over 80% alien DNA in 9 of 60 chromosomal molecules from legumes). Plastid genome HGT is rarer but exists.

6. **Mycoheterotrophs**: Despite sharing heterotrophic features with parasites, mycoheterotrophs show almost no HGT because they lack haustorium-like connections; plant-to-plant transfer would require two steps through fungi.

7. **Future questions**: The review proposes examining whether population sizes and genetic drift play roles in HGT fixation, both at organismal and subcellular (organelle population) levels.

Notable citing papers indicate HGT is more frequent with increased heterotrophy and contributes to parasite adaptation (Yang et al., 2016, PNAS); convergent HGT and cross-talk of mobile nucleic acids in parasitic plants (Yang et al., 2019, Nature Plants); and studies of holoparasitic plants like Lophophytum mirabile where 80% of protein-coding mitochondrial gene content was host-derived (Sanchez-Puerta et al., 2017, New Phytologist). Key references establish foundational work including HGT in Striga hermonthica (witchweed, Yoshida et al., 2010, Science), widespread horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes in flowering plants (Bergthorsson et al., 2003, Nature), and massive mitochondrial gene transfer in parasitic flowering plant clades (Xi et al., 2013, PLoS Genetics).

--- SOURCE 20: Massive Mitochondrial Gene Transfer in a Parasitic Flowering Plant Clade | PLOS Genetics ---
URL: https://journals.plos.org/plosgenetics/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pgen.1003265

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in PLOS Genetics (February 14, 2013) documenting the first comprehensive assessment of rampant horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in plants involving the mitochondrial genome. The study, led by Zhenxiang Xi and Yuguo Wang at Harvard University, focused on Rafflesiaceae—a clade of endophytic holoparasitic flowering plants (including Rafflesia, Rhizanthes, and Sapria) known for possessing the world's largest flowers, which parasitize members of the grapevine family (Tetrastigma spp., Vitaceae).

METHODOLOGY: The researchers used next-generation sequencing (Illumina Genome Analyzer II with 100 bp paired-end reads) to sequence 38 mitochondrial protein-coding and ribosomal RNA genes common to angiosperms from Rafflesia cantleyi, Rafflesia tuan-mudae, Sapria himalayana (three Rafflesiaceae species), and three Vitaceae species (Tetrastigma cruciatum, Tetrastigma rafflesiae, and Leea guineensis). Sequences were assembled de novo using ABySS v1.2.1 and analyzed via maximum likelihood phylogenetics with RAxML v7.2.8. Gene sequences were categorized as vertically transferred (VGT), horizontally transferred (HGT), or unassigned based on phylogenetic position and bootstrap percentage (BP) support, using both conservative (70 BP) and less conservative (50 BP) thresholds.

KEY FINDINGS:
1. Extraordinarily high HGT rates in the mitochondrial genome: Conservatively, 24% of gene sequences in R. cantleyi (5 of 21), 26% in R. tuan-mudae (5 of 19), and 41% in S. himalayana (11 of 27) showed evidence of HGT using the 70 BP threshold. Under the 50 BP threshold, rates were 29%, 32%, and 47%, respectively. This contrasts with only ~2.1% of nuclear gene transcripts previously shown to be acquired via HGT in R. cantleyi.
2. Eleven mitochondrial genes showed evidence of HGT under the conservative threshold: cob, cox3, rpl5, rps4 (maintaining both horizontally and vertically transferred homologs), and atp4, cox1, cox2, rps1, rps7, rps13, sdh3 (containing only transgenic sequences). Five additional genes (atp9, atp1, rpl2, rps14, sdh4) showed HGT under the less conservative threshold.
3. In S. himalayana, evidence of HGT was found in 14 genes potentially of plastid origin, with 13 supporting host-to-parasite HGT (placed sister to or nested within Vitaceae with ≥70 BP).
4. Transgenes are likely functional: Six of seven transgene sequences in R. cantleyi and R. tuan-mudae, and 13 of 16 in S. himalayana maintain intact reading frames. All transgenes in R. cantleyi showed evidence of expression (transcription), with expression levels not significantly different from native genes (p-value=0.19, Welch's t test).
5. Evidence of homologous recombination displacement: Seven assembled contigs contained both transgenes and native genes, and some transgenes maintained synteny with donor and recipient lineages, suggesting native genes were displaced via homologous recombination (e.g., the nad5 exon A/rps7 region matching Vitis synteny).
6. Timing of HGT: The study identified both ancient HGT events (five genes: atp1, atp4, cox1, rps7, atpA, likely occurring after the origin of stem group Rafflesiaceae ~83.1-109.5 Ma and before crown group Rafflesiaceae ~69.5-95.9 Ma) and recent events (28 instances found exclusively in either Rafflesia or Sapria, or in both but not forming a clade). Ancient transgenes did not group with current Tetrastigma hosts, suggesting historical parasitism of different host lineages ("ghost of HGT's past").
7. Rigorous contamination controls: Sample preparation of Rafflesiaceae was performed separately from Tetrastigma work; transgenes showed significant sequence divergence from current hosts compared to the divergence between the two Tetrastigma species (mean distance 0.042189 for Rafflesia, 0.020265 for Sapria versus 0.001984 between Tetrastigma species, p<0.01); and assembled contigs contained both transgenes and native genes.

CONCLUSION: This study establishes for the first time that although HGT involving nuclear genes is appreciable (~2.1% in R. cantleyi), HGT involving mitochondrial genes in these parasitic plants is "an order of magnitude higher" (24-41%), a pattern that may be general for other parasitic plant clades and perhaps more broadly for angiosperms.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Strikingly, our phylogenetic analyses conservatively indicate that 24%–41% of these gene sequences show evidence of HGT in Rafflesiaceae, depending on the species."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 21: Ophioglossaceae — In Defense of Plants ---
URL: https://www.indefenseofplants.com/blog/tag/Ophioglossaceae

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from "In Defense of Plants" covers two blog posts about fascinating members of the Ophioglossaceae family (adder's tongue ferns).

**First Post: An Awesome Ophioglossum (May 2016)**
- Describes the southern adder's tongue fern (Ophioglossum pychnostichum), a small, ancient member of the fern lineage commonly found alongside trails in grasslands.
- For much of its life, it exists as a gametophyte followed by an underground fleshy rhizome, nourished solely by an obligate association with mycorrhizal fungi. After years of storing nutrients, mature individuals produce a single sterile leaf and eventually a spore-bearing structure called a "sporophyll."
- Distributed throughout the Northern Hemisphere (North America, Europe, temperate Asia), it is of conservation concern in several states because its unpredictable lifecycle makes population estimates difficult.
- The Ophioglossaceae family is notable for staggeringly large chromosome counts; one species, Ophioglossum reticulatum, has 1,260 chromosomes (compared to humans' 46).

**Second Post: A Fern With Flower Genes (December 2015)**
- Harvard researchers studying the rattlesnake fern (Botrypus virginianum) genome found that one set of genes placed it in Ophioglossaceae, but two other genes placed it in Loranthaceae, a completely unrelated family of flowering plants.
- This represents the first documented case of horizontal gene transfer (transfer of genes without reproduction) between an angiosperm and a fern. Previous plant examples involved ferns and hornworts, or parasitic plants and their hosts.
- The rattlesnake fern, believed to have evolved in Asia and radiated via ancient land bridges, picked up foreign genes before this radiation.
- Two hypotheses for the transfer: (1) root parasitism by an ancient mistletoe species (Loranthaceae includes mistletoes; though most are stem parasites, at least three genera use root parasitism) - considered less likely since root-parasitic mistletoes don't currently exist in Asia; (2) indirect transfer via a shared mycorrhizal network, since rattlesnake ferns are obligate mycotrophs - a hypothesis that could explain many other unexplained examples of horizontal gene transfer.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
One species in particular - Ophioglossum reticulatum - boasts a whopping set of 1260 chromosomes. To put that into perspective, we humans only have 46.

--- SOURCE 23: Ferns Are Super Weird – And Their Genomes Are Even More Chaotic Than We Thought : ScienceAlert ---
URL: https://www.sciencealert.com/ferns-are-super-weird-and-their-genomes-are-even-more-chaotic-than-we-thought

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Scientists have finally sequenced the genomes of three homosporous ferns—the flying spider-monkey tree fern (Alsophila spinulosa, published May 2022 in Nature Plants), the maidenhair fern (Adiantum capillus-veneris), and the C-fern (Ceratopteris richardii, published this week in Nature Plants)—revealing that ferns are DNA hoarders and "kleptomaniacs." The C-fern work, contributed to by Doug Soltis of the Florida Museum of Natural History and a team from 28 institutions, took over eight years and resulted in a genome of 7.46 gigabases spread across 39 chromosome pairs—more than twice the size of the human genome. Previously, scientists attributed ferns' immense genomes and high chromosome counts to repeated whole-genome duplication, but the new research contradicts this prevailing view. Instead, 85% of the C. richardii genome (and a similar proportion in A. capillus-veneris) consists of transposons (jumping genes) and repetitive "scrappy" DNA debris, suggesting ferns are simply inefficient at shedding junk DNA, like hoarders. Notably, the study also found evidence that C. richardii acquired defense genes against a membrane-puncturing toxin from bacteria via horizontal gene transfer, which occurred multiple times. This is significant because ferns are the closest living relatives of all seed plants and produce chemical deterrents to herbivores that may be useful in agricultural research. A related record holder, Ophioglossum reticulatum (adder's tongue fern), holds the record for the most chromosomes in a multicellular organism, with around 720 chromosome pairs per cell.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 25: [PDF] Fern Genomics: Unfurling the Mystery of Plant Chromosome Numbers ---
URL: https://www.scientia.global/wp-content/uploads/Paul_Wolf.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article discusses Dr. Paul G. Wolf's research at the University of Alabama in Huntsville (Department of Biological Sciences) investigating plant chromosome numbers through fern genomics, specifically focusing on genome downsizing mechanisms following polyploidy. 

Key scientific context: Seed plants and some ferns are "heterosporous" (producing two spore types), while most ferns are "homosporous" (producing one spore type). Homosporous plants possess significantly more chromosomes than heterosporous plants—the fern Ophioglossum reticulatum has over 1,400 chromosomes (the highest for any plant, animal, or fungus, compared to humans' 46). Genome doubling during reproduction leads to "polyploidy" (e.g., tetraploids with four sets of chromosomes). While whole genome duplications are common in plant evolution and beneficial for crop breeding (wheat, cotton, potatoes are polyploid), they can cause genetic instability and infertility. Heterosporous plants lose excess genetic content through "genome downsizing" mechanisms, while homosporous ferns appear to have different or absent downsizing mechanisms—evidenced by their positively correlated chromosome number and genome size.

Dr. Wolf's methodology: His early work sequenced chloroplast DNA to establish evolutionary relationships among fern species. He sequenced the first complex fern-like genome in 2011, published first genetic sequences for two heterosporous fern species in 2018, and is currently assembling the first full genome sequence for the homosporous fern Ceratopteris richardii. With PhD student Sylvia Kinosian, he is investigating genetic and chromosome variation across the Ceratopteris genus, including a natural tetraploid (C. thalictroides) and lab-generated hybrid tetraploid crosses between C. richardii and C. pteridoides. Ceratopteris ferns are advantageous as a model genus due to their rapid lifecycle (145 days for a full cycle), allowing multiple experiments including chromosome behavior observation during spore-producing cell division.

The research also examines whether other life history traits (like the photosynthetic gametophyte stage in homosporous plants) correlate with spore type, since the spore type-chromosome correlation may not be causal. Some homosporous plants "silence" extra genes rather than removing them, potentially negating polyploidy's negative effects.

Implications: This synthesis approach could address broader biological concepts and deepen understanding of crop improvement methods, since exploiting natural or artificial polyploidy is effective for introducing beneficial traits into crops but can cause genetic instability.

Dr. Wolf earned his PhD in Botany from Washington State University, did postdoctoral research at UC Irvine, was a professor at Utah State University, and is now Professor and Chair at the University of Alabama in Huntsville. The research is funded by the US National Science Foundation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This series of experiments will begin to address the question of whether ferns are unable to downsize genomes as rapidly as flowering plants," says Dr Wolf.
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a 2019 scientific paper titled "Lateral transfers of large DNA fragments spread functional genes among grasses," published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Volume 116, no. 10, pages 4416-4425. The authors include Dunning, L.T., Olofsson, J.K., Parisod, C., Choudhury, R.R., Moreno-Villena, J.J., Yang, Y., Dionora, J., Quick, W.P., Park, M., Bennetzen, J.L., Besnard, G., Nosil, P., Osborne, C.P., and Christin, P.-A.

The study addresses whether lateral gene transfer (LGT) plays an important role in multicellular eukaryotes like plants, challenging the traditional view that vertical inheritance is paramount. The researchers assembled a chromosome-level genome for the grass Alloteropsis semialata, a species previously suspected of exhibiting two LGTs, and screened it against genomic data from 146 other grass species.

Key findings:
- Discovered 57 additional LGTs in the A. semialata nuclear genome, involving at least nine different donor species.
- These LGTs are clustered in 23 laterally acquired genomic fragments up to 170 kb long, accumulated during the diversification of Alloteropsis.
- The majority of the 59 total LGTs in A. semialata are expressed and added functions to the recipient genome.
- Functional LGTs were also detected in the genomes of five other grass species, showing the process is likely widespread in this globally important plant group.

Conclusion: LGT appears to represent a potent evolutionary force capable of spreading functional genes among distantly related grass species. The paper is open access under a CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0 license and available on the CGIAR (CGSpace) repository.

--- SOURCE 6: Footprints of parasitism in the genome of the parasitic flowering plant Cuscuta campestris | Nature Communications ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-04344-z

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in Nature Communications (volume 9, article 2515, 2018), describes the first reported genome sequence of a parasitic plant: the field dodder (Cuscuta campestris), a member of the Convolvulaceae family (Solanales). The parasitic plant infects a broad range of host species across the plant kingdom through specialized haustoria that penetrate host tissue and connect vascular systems.

Key findings include:
- Genome characteristics: C. campestris has 2n=56 small chromosomes with a 1C value of 581 Mbp. The assembled draft genome was ~477 Mbp (about 86% of the k-mer-based estimate), containing 44,303 predicted high-confidence gene loci across 6,907 scaffolds with an N50 of 1.38 Mbp. BUSCO analysis showed 82.1% of 1,440 conserved plant genes were present, with 59% present in duplicated form.
- Transposons: 46.2% (221 Mbp) of the genome is transposon-derived, dominated by LTR retrotransposons (96% of mobile elements), with a recent amplification wave around 1.5 million years ago.
- Whole-genome duplication: Evidence indicates a recent genome duplication event (~1.5 mya), with a peak synonymous substitution rate (dS) of 0.05 between paralogs. 59% of genes had syntenic paralogs (vs. 23% in Arabidopsis thaliana).
- Gene loss: The parasite lost genes needed for high photosynthetic activity, including genes for the NDH-dependent cyclic electron transport pathway and chlorophyll turnover enzymes, explaining its low photosynthesis rates. Genes for soil nutrient uptake (iron transporters, root nitrate uptake system NRT2/NAR2, mycorrhizal symbiosis proteins) were also lost due to the absence of a root system. However, core photosynthesis, amino acid, fatty acid, and vitamin synthesis pathways were retained, likely to re-fix CO2 for carbon efficiency.
- Horizontal gene transfer (HGT): Beyond two previously known HGT cases, 64 novel high-confidence HGT candidates from at least 32 donor sequences were identified, mostly tracing to preferred host orders Fabales and Caryophyllales. A notable example shows two adjacent C. campestris genes with high homology to neighboring carrot (Daucus carota) genes, including conserved intron positions and post-transfer duplication, providing evidence of integration of larger stretches of genomic DNA from hosts.

The study concludes that the parasitic lifestyle has left characteristic footprints in the C. campestris genome, and will enable genome-guided studies of host-parasite interactions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The genome contains signatures of a fairly recent whole-genome duplication and lacks genes for pathways superfluous to a parasitic lifestyle. Specifically, genes needed for high photosynthetic activity are lost, explaining the low photosynthesis rates displayed by the parasite."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a bioRxiv preprint (DOI: 10.1101/2022.08.25.505314) titled "Widespread horizontal gene transfer between plants and their microbiota" by Shelly Haimlich, Yulia Fridman, Hitaishi Khandal, Sigal Savaldi-Goldstein, and Asaf Levy (from Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Technion-Israel Institute of Technology). It has since been published in ISME Communications (doi: 10.1093/ismeco/ycae073).

**Objective & Hypothesis:** The authors hypothesized that the spatial proximity and long-term relationships between plants and their microbiota promote cross-kingdom horizontal gene transfer (HGT). They tested this using Arabidopsis thaliana and its extensively sequenced microbiome.

**Methodology:**
- Compared A. thaliana genes against 582 fully sequenced commensal bacteria isolated from Arabidopsis (plant-associated, PA), covering 1,051 genomes total (including 441 non-plant-associated bacteria, plants, fungi, archaea, and other eukaryotes).
- Used BLASTP with threshold of at least 35% amino acid identity across at least 80% of both proteins.
- Filtered out 'trivial hits' shared with organelles (mitochondria and chloroplast, which originate in bacteria).
- Constructed gene trees from multiple sequence alignments to detect phylogenetic evidence of HGT (where gene trees and genome trees were inconsistent).

**Key Results:**
- Identified 767 Arabidopsis proteins mapped to 60,850 bacterial proteins as potential molecular mimicry candidates.
- Detected 180 unique cross-kingdom HGT events: 84 genes likely transferred from plants to bacteria, and 96 genes from PA bacteria to plants.
- Additionally found 161 genes transferred between PA bacteria and the eukaryotic domain (source unclear), 65 genes with unclear inheritance patterns, and 361 genes with no HGT patterns.
- Rejected DNA contamination by confirming no homologous pairs exceeded 76% amino acid identity.

**Functional Enrichment:**
- Genes transferred from plants to bacteria are enriched in secreted proteins, carbohydrate catabolism enzymes (pectin esterase, glycosidase), and include chitinases (CHI, AT2G43570), endo beta mannanase (XCD1), and pectin lyases (PME5) — enabling bacteria to exploit plant-derived sugars.
- Genes transferred from bacteria to plants are enriched in redox homeostasis and cytoplasmic proteins, including many auxin biosynthesis YUCCA genes and nucleoside metabolic processes. 69/96 (72%) of such genes are found in all dicots and monocots, suggesting ancient HGT events.

**Taxonomic Patterns:**
- Bacteroidetes were enriched as gene acceptors from plants, while Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria were depleted as either acceptors or donors.
- Rhizobiales and Hyphomicrobiales (Proteobacteria) and Micrococcales (Actinobacteria) showed significantly fewer HGT events than expected.
- In most cases the donor/acceptor taxonomy remained "unknown" (multiple phyla involved).

**Recent HGT Examples:**
- The plant CHI (chitinase) gene is present in only 7 PA Streptomyces genomes (patchy distribution), with protein structures very similar (RMSD=0.791).
- The bacterial DET2 homologue (steroid-5-alpha-reductase, key in brassinosteroid biosynthesis) is nearly specific to plant-associated Leifsonia genus (Actinobacteria), located downstream of a tRNA gene; protein structures highly similar (RMSD=0.727) despite less than 50% sequence identity.

**Functional Validation (Proof-of-Concept):**
- The authors tested whether the Leifsonia DET2 homologue (lfDET2) could functionally replace the Arabidopsis DET2 gene. Arabidopsis DET2 is 46% identical to Leifsonia Det2 (similar to identity shared with rice and barley homologues).
- Expression of lfDET2 (driven by 35S or Arabidopsis DET2 promoters) in the Arabidopsis det2 mutant background rescued the dwarf phenotype and root meristem defects, restoring normal plant growth.
- lfDET2 localized to the endoplasmic reticulum, matching atDET2 localization.

**Conclusion:** The results suggest cross-kingdom HGT is relatively frequent and shaped the genomes of plants and their microbiota by adding adaptive traits. The transferred genes likely participate in molecular mimicry between hosts and their commensal microbiomes. Key author correspondence: alevy@mail.huji.ac.il.

* , Rohan Bythell-Douglas

## Abstract

Obligate parasitic plants in the Orobanchaceae germinate after sensing plant hormones, strigolactones, exuded from host roots. In Arabidopsis thaliana, the a/b-hydrolase D14 acts as a strigolactone receptor that controls shoot branching, whereas its ancestral paralog, KAI2, mediates karrikin-specific germination responses.We observed that KAI2, but not D14, is present at higher copy numbers in parasitic species than in nonparasitic relatives. KAI2 paralogs in parasites are distributed into three phylogenetic clades.The fastest-evolving clade, KAI2d, contains the majority of KAI2 paralogs. Homology models predict that the ligandbinding pockets of KAI2d resemble D14. KAI2d transgenes confer strigolactone-specific germination responses to Arabidopsis thaliana. Thus, the KAI2 paralogs D14 and KAI2d underwent convergent evolution of strigolactone recognition, respectively enabling developmental responses to strigolactones in angiosperms and host detection in parasites.

This webpage presents a peer-reviewed research article published in the journal Science on July 31, 2015, titled "Convergent evolution of strigolactone perception enabled host detection in parasitic plants" by Conn et al. (authors include Caitlin E. Conn, Rohan Bythell-Douglas, Drexel Neumann, Satoko Yoshida, Bryan Whittington, James H. Westwood, Ken Shirasu, Charles S. Bond, Kelly A. Dyer, and David C. Nelson).

The study investigates how obligate parasitic plants in the Orobanchaceae family germinate upon sensing strigolactones (plant hormones) exuded from host roots. In Arabidopsis thaliana, the α/β-hydrolase D14 acts as a strigolactone receptor controlling shoot branching, while its ancestral paralog KAI2 mediates karrikin-specific germination responses.

- KAI2 (but not D14) is present at higher copy numbers in parasitic species than in nonparasitic relatives

# Evolution and function of strigolactone / karrikin receptors

by [Mary Williams](https://blog.aspb.org/author/mwilliams/ "View all posts by Mary Williams")

***Karrikins*** are small molecules found in smoke that promote seed germination and have been [![Picture1](https://blog.aspb.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/Picture14-262x300.jpg)](https://blog.aspb.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/Picture14.jpg)associated with the activation of seeds following fire ([Nelson et al., 2012](http://www.annualreviews.org/doi/abs/10.1146/annurev-arplant-042811-105545)). ***Strigolactones*** are structurally similar small molecules that act as endogenous hormones and as secreted signals that promote the germination of parasitic plants and branching responses in mycrorrhizal fungi ([Brewer et al., 2013](http://www.cell.com/molecular-plant/abstract/S1674-2052(14)60877-7); [de Saint Germain et al, 2013](http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1369526613000903); [Waldie et al., 2014](http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/tpj.12488/abstract)). Studies in Arabidopsis showed that these two families of molecules share some aspects of their recognition pathways. Specifically, the related proteins D14 and KAI2 are components of receptor complexes for strigolactones and karrikins respectively ([Waters et al., 2012](http://dev.biologists.org/content/139/7/1285.abstract); [Smith and Li, 2014](http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1369526614000880)).

Phylogenetic studies indi[![Picture2](https://blog.aspb.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/Picture22.jpg)](https://blog.aspb.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/Picture22.jpg)cate that the KAI2/D14 protein family has resulted from two or more gene duplication events. The KAI2 clade is thought to be ancestral, with a duplication event (D1) leading to the D14 clade and a second event (D2) occurring in angiosperms. Using a functional approach, [Waters et al.,](http://www.plantcell.org/content/27/7/1925) (2015) showed that the *KAI2*-like genes in liverworts (*Marchantia polymorpha*) and lycophytes (*Selaginella* *moellendorffii*) could not substitute for D14 activity in Arabidopsis, but that one of the *KAI2*-like genes from *Selaginella* was able to partially substitute for KAI2 activity. These results support the model that KAI2 function is ancestral to D14 function, and that strigolactone perception by D14 proteins is derived.

Additional studies have demonstrated another gene amplification event specifically occurring in parasitic plants of the Orobanchaceae family. Interestingly, this event, which is correlated with a germination response to strigolactones, occurred in the KAI2 [![Picture3](https://blog.aspb.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/Picture3.png)](https://blog.aspb.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/Picture3.png)lineage, not the D14 lineage as might have been expected ([Conn et al., 2015](http://www.sciencemag.org/content/349/6247/540.short); [Tsuchiya et al., 2015](http://www.sciencemag.org/content/349/6250/864.abstract)). These observations suggest that ***strigolactone perception arose twice independently*** within the KAI2/D14 protein family. The identity of preferred ligands for other members of the KAI2 protein family, including those expressed in green algae and basal land plants, remains obscure.

Open questions include the nature of the ancestral functions of the KAI2/D14 pathway in plants and green algae (see [Delaux et al., 2012](http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1469-8137.2012.04209.x/abstract)), the role of protein degradation (see [Jiang et al., 2013](http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v504/n7480/full/nature12870.html); [Zhou et al., 2013](http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v504/n7480/full/nature12878.html)) and substrate hydrolysis in downstream signaling (see [Tsuchiya et al., 2015](http://www.sciencemag.org/content/349/6250/864.abstract)), how endogenous strigolactones exert their diverse roles in plant development, and how fungi perceive strigolactones (see [Ruyter-Spira, C. and Bouwmeester, H., 2012](http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1469-8137.2012.04261.x/abstract)).

args.summary:
This article from Plant Science Today (ASPB blog) by Mary Williams reviews the evolution and function of strigolactone and karrikin receptors, published around August 2015.

**Key background:**
- Karrikins are small molecules found in smoke that promote seed germination, associated with plant activation after fires.
- Strigolactones are structurally similar small molecules that act as endogenous hormones and secreted signals promoting germination of parasitic plants and branching responses in mycorrhizal fungi.
- In Arabidopsis, related proteins D14 and KAI2 are receptor complex components for strigolactones and karrikins respectively.

**Evolutionary findings:**
- Phylogenetic studies indicate the KAI2/D14 protein family arose from two or more gene duplication events. The KAI2 clade is ancestral, with duplication D1 leading to the D14 clade and a second event (D2) occurring in angiosperms.
- Functional studies (Waters et al., 2015) showed KAI2-like genes in liverworts (Marchantia polymorpha) and lycophytes (Selaginella moellendorffii) could not substitute for D14 activity in Arabidopsis, but one Selaginella KAI2-like gene partially substituted for KAI2 activity. This supports KAI2 function being ancestral to D14, with strigolactone perception by D14 being derived.
- A gene amplification event in parasitic plants of the Orobanchaceae family occurred in the KAI2 lineage (not D14), correlated with germination response to strigolactones.
- These observations suggest strigolactone perception arose twice independently within the KAI2/D14 family.
- The preferred ligands for other KAI2 family members (including from green algae and basal land plants) remain unknown.

**Open questions:**
- Ancestral functions of the KAI2/D14 pathway in plants and green algae
- The role of protein degradation and substrate hydrolysis in downstream signaling
- How endogenous strigolactones exert diverse roles in plant development
- How fungi perceive strigolactones

The article includes an extensive reference list covering key studies by Brewer et al. (2013), Conn et al. (2015), Nelson et al. (2012), Tsuchiya et al. (2015), Waters et al. (2012, 2015), and others on strigolactone/karrikin biology.

# New strigolactone receptor advances knowledge of how germination is induced in parasitic plants

July 31, 2015

RIKEN CSRS and the University of Georgia researchers have found genes for strigolactone receptors that induce germination of parasitic plants. The joint research group compared the genomic sequences of parasitic plants and non-parasitic plants, discovering an increase in the number of genes that code for the KAI2 proteins. Upon analyzing the structure of the KAI2 proteins, researchers determined that part of the KAI2 proteins in parasitic plants are similar to the Arabidopsis thaliana D14 protein, which is a known strigolactone receptor.

This finding suggested that parasitic plants use KAI2 proteins as strigolactone receptors. Upon introducing the a KAI2 protein from a parasitic plant into an Arabidopsis kai2 mutant, the researchers successfully created a plant that germinated in response to strigolactone. It is believed that the KAI2 genes from the parasitic plant evolved independently of the D14 gene in Arabidopsis and acquired strigolactone receptor functionality.

Parasitic plants such as Striga and Orobanche are plant pests that cause agricultural damage worldwide. Understanding the mechanisms of seed germination of parasitic plants should lead to prevention of agricultural damage.

Original article

:   C. E. Conn, R. Bythell-Douglas, D. Neumann, S. Yoshida, B. Whittington, J. H. Westwood, K. Shirasu, C. S. Bond, K. A. Dyer, D. C. Nelson,
:   "Convergent evolution of strigolactone perception enabled host detection in parasitic plants".

:   Plant Immunity Research Group

The joint research group compared genomic sequences of parasitic and non-parasitic plants, finding an increased number of genes coding for KAI2 proteins in parasitic plants. Since parasitic plants such as Striga and Orobanche cause significant agricultural damage worldwide, understanding their seed germination mechanisms could lead to prevention of agricultural losses. The findings were published in Science (doi: 10.1126/science.aab1140) in the article "Convergent evolution of strigolactone perception enabled host detection in parasitic plants" by Conn, Bythell-Douglas, Neumann, Yoshida, Whittington, Westwood, Shirasu, Bond, Dyer, and Nelson. The article was published by Oxford University Press (OUP) with DOI 10.1093/pcp/pcad026. The authors are Saori Takei, Yuta Uchiyama, Marco Bürger, Taiki Suzuki, Shoma Okabe, Joanne Chory, and Yoshiya Seto. The page lists the article as open access and includes a bibliography and abstract sections. The page also lists several related publications citing this work, including papers on strigolactone biosynthetic pathway conservation in root parasitic plants, strigolactone perception in Phtheirospermum japonicum, divergent receptors shaping strigolactone perception, dominant-negative KAI2d paralogs in root parasitic plants, in vitro monitoring of strigolactone signaling complexes, strigolactone research updates, strigolactone biosynthesis and perception knowledge, structural diversity of strigolactones, and radicle growth regulation of root parasitic plants by auxin-related compounds.

## Significance

Eukaryotes normally receive their genetic material from their parents but may occasionally, like prokaryotes do, acquire DNA from unrelated organisms through horizontal transfer (HT). In animals and plants, HT mostly concerns transposable elements (TEs), probably because these pieces of DNA can move within genomes. Assessing the impact of HTs on eukaryote evolution and the factors shaping the dynamics of these HTs requires large-scale systematic studies. We have analyzed the genomes from 195 insect species and found that no fewer than 2,248 events of HT of TEs occurred during the last 10 My, particularly between insects that were closely related and geographically close. These results suggest that HT of TEs plays a major role in insect genome evolution.

## Abstract

Horizontal transfer (HT) of genetic material is central to the architecture and evolution of prokaryote genomes. Within eukaryotes, the majority of HTs reported so far are transfers of transposable elements (TEs). These reports essentially come from studies focusing on specific lineages or types of TEs. Because of the lack of large-scale survey, the amount and impact of HT of TEs (HTT) in eukaryote evolution, as well as the trends and factors shaping these transfers, are poorly known. Here, we report a comprehensive analysis of HTT in 195 insect genomes, representing 123 genera and 13 of the 28 insect orders. We found that these insects were involved in at least 2,248 HTT events that essentially occurred during the last 10 My. We show that DNA transposons transfer horizontally more often than retrotransposons, and unveil phylogenetic relatedness and geographical proximity as major factors facilitating HTT in insects. Even though our study is restricted to a small fraction of insect biodiversity and to a recent evolutionary timeframe, the TEs we found to be horizontally transferred generated up to 24% (2.08% on average) of all nucleotides of insect genomes. Together, our results establish HTT as a major force shaping insect genome evolution.

Horizontal transfer (HT) is the transmission of genetic material between organisms through a mechanism other than reproduction. In prokaryotes, HT is pervasive, its mechanisms are well understood, and it is now viewed as one of the main forces shaping genome architecture and evolution ([1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r1), [2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r2)). In contrast, the study of HT in eukaryotes is less documented, but has been increasingly investigated. The majority of genes horizontally acquired by eukaryotes come from bacteria, but the extent to which these transfers have contributed to eukaryote evolution is still unclear ([3](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r3), [4](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r4)). Gene transfers from eukaryote to eukaryote appear to be largely limited to filamentous organisms, such as oomycetes and fungi ([5](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r5), [6](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r6)).

In animals and plants, very few cases of such horizontal gene transfers (HGTs) have been reported so far ([7](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r7), [8](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r8)). In fact, most of the genetic material that is horizontally transferred in animals and plants consists of transposable elements (TEs) ([9](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r9)–[11](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r11)), which are pieces of DNA able to move from a chromosomal locus to another ([12](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r12)). The greater ability of TEs to move between organisms certainly relates to their intrinsic ability to transpose within genomes, which genes cannot do. HT of TEs (HTT) may allow these elements to enter naive genomes, which they invade by making copies of themselves, and then escape before they become fully silenced by anti-TE defenses ([13](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r13)). A growing number of studies have identified such HTT ([11](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r11), [14](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r14)–[16](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r16)). However, a common drawback of these studies has been the inclusion of a limited set of TEs ([11](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r11)) or organisms ([16](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r16)), which hampers our understanding of the breadth of HTT, its contribution to genome evolution, and of the factors and barriers shaping these transfers in eukaryotes ([13](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r13)). In this study, we overcame these limitations by performing a large-scale, comprehensive analysis of HTT in insects. We focused on insects because a large number of whole-genome sequences are publicly available for this group and because insect genomes are known to harbor diverse and highly dynamic TE landscapes ([17](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r17)).

## Results and Discussion

To detect HTT in insects, we de novo characterized TEs in all reference genome assemblies available in GenBank as of May 2016 (_n_ = 195 species; [Dataset S1](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#supplementary-materials) and [Fig. S1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#sfig01)) which represent 123 genera and 13 of the 28 insect orders. To minimize detection biases, we did not rely on established genome annotations that are available for only a subset of the species included in our study, and instead treated every species’ genome equally. This automatic characterization was performed with the RepeatModeler pipeline ([18](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r18)) and led to the identification of 53,452 TE families assigned to 98 superfamilies ([Dataset S2](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#supplementary-materials)). These exclude 3,417 families whose consensus sequences were found to include genes that may not belong to TEs ([_SI Materials and Methods_](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#sec-3)), as well as all short interspersed element (SINE) consensus sequences, which might correspond to RNA pseudogenes ([19](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r19)). For each species, the consensus sequences of TE families were used to locate TE copies in genomic contigs. TE copies >100 base pairs were compared by pairwise reciprocal homology searches between every two species. After filtering out short and low-score alignments, and alignments between TEs from different superfamilies, we retained a total of ∼5.9 million hits, each of which indicated TE homology between two genomes.

TEs inherited from a recent common ancestor by descendent species, rather than horizontally transferred between these species, may present homology passing our filters. We identified clades of related insect species for which this situation may happen, by relying on the common assumption that inherited TEs evolve neutrally and similarly to synonymous sites of protein coding genes ([20](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r20)). This assumption implies that TEs showing higher interspecific homology than the synonymous sites of orthologous genes should share a more recent ancestor than the host species, and hence be the result of HT ([16](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r16), [21](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r21)). Conversely, TEs whose divergence is similar to the synonymous divergence of orthologous genes may be vertically inherited. We thus collapsed a clade of insect species into a lineage if (_i_) a fraction (>0.3%) of its core orthologous genes showed lower synonymous divergence than the highest nucleotide divergence of TEs or (_ii_) these species diverged in the last 40 My ([_Materials and Methods_](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#sec-5) and [Fig. S2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#sfig02)). This collapsing resulted in the delineation of 81 lineages. We ignored all homologies within these lineages and considered the ∼1.46 million hits between species from distinct lineages to essentially result from HT.

To translate these hits into a minimum number of HTT events, it must be considered that many hits may result from a single TE that transferred between two lineages and transposed into multiple similar copies. The resulting hits have a distinct feature: The copies they involve diverged within the recipient lineage after the transfer; hence, they should be more similar to each other than to copies from the other lineage. We applied a heuristic approach based on this principle ([_Materials and Methods_](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#sec-5)) to cluster hits within each pair of lineages and TE superfamily into candidate HTT events. We also considered that a transferred TE might have degraded into nonoverlapping parts that share no sequence homology. To avoid counting these parts as several independently transferred elements, we further clustered hits on the basis of insufficient nucleotide or protein homology between copies. These two rounds of clustering yielded 4,499 HTT events for all pairs of insect lineages ([Fig. 1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#fig01)), after discarding transfers that involved fewer than five TE copies per lineage. Taking pairs of lineages separately, each of these transfers represents an independent HTT event.

To infer the minimum number of HTT events across all 81 insect lineages, we considered that any HTT inferred in a pair of lineages might not reflect a direct transfer from one to the other, but separate acquisitions of TEs from other sources, which may already be counted as HTTs in other lineage pairs. There is no method that can discriminate between direct transfer and such “indirect” transfers. However, it is possible to avoid counting indirect HTTs, by constructing networks of insect species sharing similar TEs, in which the minimum number of HTT events is the number of lineages minus one. This parsimonious count resulted in 2,248 HTT events among the 81 insect lineages considered in our study ([Fig. 2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#fig02) and [Dataset S2](https://www.pnas.org/lookup/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#supplementary-materials)). This unprecedented figure is more than four times higher than the total number of HTT events reported so far in metazoans, plants, and fungi combined ([10](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r10)). Such a high number is still not unexpected, given that studies focusing on one or a few TEs often found one or more HTT events between multiple, distantly related taxa ([11](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r11), [14](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r14)–[16](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r16), [22](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r22)).

Nonetheless, the actual number of HTT events that occurred in insects must largely exceed our inference, for at least four reasons. First, the inherent difficulty in resolving highly similar TE copies as distinct loci during genome assembly may have made some TE families undetectable or unable to pass our selection filters. Second, homology can only be found between recently diverged TEs, putting a maximum date on the HTT events that initiated the divergences. We estimate that the HTT events we uncovered mainly occurred in the last 10 My (assuming that TEs evolve similarly to synonymous sites for which we inferred an overall mutation rate; [Fig. S2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#sfig02)). Third, we conservatively collapsed many species into lineages within which HTT events have been characterized in previous studies ([9](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r9)). Fourth, the available insect genome sequences represent a very small fraction of the known diversity of insects. However, we found that 72 of the 81 lineages and 176 of the 195 species were involved in at least one HTT event. Therefore, HTT is not only widespread in insects, but the true number of HTT events is likely to be several orders of magnitude larger than the number we report.

The tremendous amount of HTT events we uncovered in insects enabled us to statistically assess the impact of two main factors on this process: phylogenetic and geographic distance. For the former, we relied on recently estimated divergence times ([23](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r23)), and the latter involved assigning as many insect species as possible (_n_ = 179) to the six main biogeographic realms. The effects of the two factors may not be confounded, because there is no positive correlation (_R_ = −0.01) between species relatedness and geographic cooccurrence (originating from the same realm) among the 81 lineages we defined. We first tested whether HTT events were more likely to occur between less divergent lineages, as observed in bacteria ([24](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r24), [25](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r25)). Our analysis revealed a significant negative correlation between the number of HTT events and the divergence times of the lineages ([Fig. 3](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#fig03)). This pattern could, in theory, reflect vertical inheritance mistakenly inferred as HTT. Indeed, the number of vertically inherited TEs for which we can detect sequence similarities between lineages decreases with their divergence time. If that was the cause for the pattern shown in [Fig. 3](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#fig03), the fraction of species per lineage that are found to share TEs with another lineage, due to an apparent HTT, should also decrease with the divergence of these lineages ([_SI Discussion_](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#sec-4)). We did not observe such a decrease ([Table S1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#st01)), and therefore saw no evidence that homology between vertically inherited TEs was frequently counted as HTT. The phylogenetic effect we observed is also unlikely to be explained by reduced opportunities of HTT between phylogenetically distant species, because these are not more geographically distant on average. Instead, as proposed for HGT and HTT in bacteria ([1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r1), [25](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r25), [26](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r26)), compatibility between TEs and recipient host cells may decrease as genetic distance from source lineages increases. Transposition is known to involve a number of interactions between TEs and host cellular factors (e.g., transcription factors and chromatin), which, depending on the type of TE, may be limited or very intricate ([27](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r27)–[30](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r30)). For example, some DNA transposons from the Tc1-Mariner superfamily only require their transposase to transpose in vitro ([27](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r27)). Weak dependence on host factors may explain why Tc1-Mariner TEs were found to be transferred between more or less distantly related taxa ([31](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r31)). Our systematic search supports this hypothesis as the highest number of HTT in insects was found for members of the Tc1-Mariner superfamily ([Fig. 2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#fig02)). Interestingly, retrotransposons show lower transfer rates between distantly related lineages than DNA transposons ([Fig. 3](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#fig03)). Compared with DNA transposons, retrotransposons may require host factors that: (_i_) are more numerous and diverse, and/or (_ii_) tend to be less conserved between taxa. Such differences may explain the overall higher numbers of HTT events of DNA transposons than retrotransposons reported in our study (1,813 vs. 435 transfers; [Fig. 2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#fig02)) and others ([13](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r13), [32](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114#core-collateral-r32)).
