--- SOURCE 3: The Curious Case of Horizontal Gene Transfer – SCIENCE NEXT DOOR ---
URL: https://sciencenextdoorcom.wordpress.com/2021/04/29/the-curious-case-of-horizontal-gene-transfer

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, "The Curious Case of Horizontal Gene Transfer" by Suhani Sharma (published April 29, 2021, on the Science Next Door blog), explores how plants, not just bacteria, engage in Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT), which is the transmission of genes between organisms without reproduction via transformation, transduction, and conjugation. The article highlights two key cases:

**Grasses:** Research led by the University of Sheffield (Dr. Luke Dunning, senior author, and Samuel Hibdige, PhD researcher) found over 100 examples in grasses—including wheat, maize, rice, and barley—where genes had significantly different histories from the species they were found in. In some cases, HGT levels exceeded 40% of the genome, making these plants "naturally genetically modified." The study detected a statistical increase in species with modified stems called 'rhizomes.'

**Cuscata/Rafflesiaceae (Parasitic Plants):** The article discusses the Rafflesia arnoldii (giant corpse flower, with flowers weighing ~10 kg) and Sapria. A 2014 paper by Jeanmaire Molina found these plants had ditched their entire chloroplast genome. Follow-up research by Charles Davis and Liming Cai at Harvard University found that nearly half (44%) of genes conserved across plant lineages had disappeared from Sapria—more than twice the gene losses in dodders (Cuscuta) and four times the losses in witchweeds (Striga). Despite gene loss, Sapria's genome remains as large as a human's because it is loaded with borrowed genes from hosts (described as "a huge graveyard of DNA"), and 90% of its genome consists of DNA transposons ("jumping genes"). Researchers hypothesize that transposons may be the engines driving HGT, helping the parasites carry and insert gene fragments, and potentially contributing to unique features like the large flowers. The article notes these critically endangered plants face conservation challenges.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We found over 100 examples where the gene had a significantly different history to the species it was found in." - Dr. Luke Dunning; "If we can determine how this process is happening it may allow us to naturally modify crops and make them more resistant to climate change." - Dr. Luke Dunning; "We still don't know how this is happening or what the full implications are. But, we know it is widespread in grasses, a family of plants that provide a majority of the food we eat." - Samuel Hibdige; "We knew that there would be loss, but we didn't think it would be on the order of 44% of its genes." - Charles Davis; "Because these parasites have been stealing (or borrowing) genes for millennia, their genome is like a huge graveyard of DNA." - Liming Cai
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Grasses pass genes from one species to another but we don’t know how | New Scientist ---
URL: https://www.newscientist.com/article/2275559-grasses-pass-genes-from-one-species-to-another-but-we-dont-know-how

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This New Scientist article reports on research led by Luke Dunning at the University of Sheffield demonstrating that lateral (horizontal) gene transfer is widespread among grass species. The study examined the genomes of 17 grass species, some evolving independently for 50 million years (including rice, wheat, and foxtail millet), and found that 13 of the 17 species carried laterally transferred genes, with 170 genes transferred in total. The team estimates 3.72 out of every 10,000 grass genes are detectably laterally transferred, though lead author Dunning calls this "a massive underestimate" since only some transferred genes are fixed by natural selection.

Key findings include that lateral transfer is more common among closely related species but still occurs in distantly related ones, and transfers are more frequent in grasses with rhizomes (underground stems that allow asexual reproduction), as foreign DNA in rhizomes can become incorporated into the germline through every cell of the clone. The mechanism remains unknown ("the million-dollar question"), with wind-borne "illegitimate pollination" suggested as a possible vector rather than hybridization.

The article provides context that lateral gene transfer was previously thought restricted to bacteria, but increasing eukaryotic genome sequencing has revealed many examples. Julia Van Etten of Rutgers University notes that laterally transferred genes, while a small percentage of genomes, can have major evolutionary impacts—citing red algae that acquired genes for arsenic and mercury detoxification. The research was published in New Phytologist (DOI: 10.1111/nph.17328), and Dunning speculates that lateral gene transfer may underpin some traits in domesticated crop grasses like wheat.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We've shown that lateral gene transfer is a widespread process in grasses," says Luke Dunning at the University of Sheffield in the UK., "People thought it was completely restricted to bacteria and didn't happen in eukaryotes," says Dunning. "It's probably only been 10 to 15 years that that's really shifted.", "But that is a massive underestimate," says Dunning, because only some transferred genes will be favoured by natural selection and become common in a population. "It's probably an ongoing process happening all the time, and then you're only going to fix one or two.", "The million-dollar question is to find out how it's happening," says Dunning., "They're thriving because they've horizontally acquired genes for arsenic detoxification and mercury detoxification, and they're able to take up sugars so they don't have to photosynthesise all the time. They've changed their entire lifestyle," says Julia Van Etten at Rutgers University.

--- SOURCE 16: Achievements in Horizontal Gene Transfer Studies in Parasitic Plants ---
URL: https://abcbot.pl/pdf/63_2/2021-02-abcbot-02.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (Acta Biologica Cracoviensia Series Botanica 63/2: 17–28, 2021) by Góraalski et al. from Jagiellonian University summarizes the current state of knowledge on horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in parasitic plants. HGT allows genetic material to flow between distantly related organisms, was first discovered in plants in the early 21st century, and is especially prevalent in parasitic plants due to their intimate physical contact with hosts.

Key findings and topics covered:

1. **Factors facilitating HGT**: Close physical contact between organisms is the most important factor. This includes parasitism (via haustoria), epiphytism, grafting, and root-to-root inosculation. Holoparasites are better HGT subjects than hemiparasites due to their complete dependence on hosts for organic substances.

2. **HGT frequency correlates with parasitic dependence**: A study of Orobanchaceae (Yang et al., 2016) found 32 HGTs in the holoparasite Phelipanche aegyptiaca, 10 in the obligate hemiparasite Striga hermonthica, 2 in the facultative hemiparasite Triphysaria versicolor, and only 1 in free-living Lindenbergia. Kado and Innan (2018) found 106 transferred genes in holoparasites (22 in Orobanche minor, 84 in Aeginetia indica) but none in facultative parasites. Cuscuta shows higher rates than Orobanchaceae, possibly because its haustorial stem connections to flowers/gametes are permanently shorter distance (Yang et al., 2019).

3. **DNA vs. RNA as carriers**: Evidence supports both mechanisms. The ShContig9484 gene in Striga hermonthica (transferred from sorghum) shows traces of mRNA origin (poly-A tail). However, later studies on Cuscuta (108 functional genes) and other species indicate most functional genes were transferred via DNA, based on presence of introns.

4. **Adaptive role of HGT**: Transfers may serve adaptive functions. Rafflesia cantleyi likely acquired dozens of transcribed genes from its host (Xi et al., 2012), possibly for "genomic deception" to evade host defenses. In Cuscuta campestris, many HGT-acquired genes are expressed in haustoria and involved in defense and amino acid metabolism (Yang et al., 2019). Eighteen functional genes in Cuscuta belong to the same families as independently transferred genes in Orobanchaceae, supporting adaptive roles. In Sapria himalayana, at least 1.2% of the genome was acquired via HGT from the host (Cai et al., 2021).

5. **Source and target genomes**: Plant cells have nuclear, mitochondrial, and plastid genomes involved in HGT and intracellular gene transfer (IGT). Mitochondria are the most frequent recipients of alien DNA due to their frequent fusion/fission and higher noncoding DNA content (72-89% vs. 40-45% in plastids). Examples include massive HGT in Amborella trichopoda (3.9-Mb mitochondrial genome with many transfers), parasite-to-host transfers (atp1, atp6, matR from Cuscuta to Plantago; atp6 in Orobanche coerulescens from Asteraceae), Cynomorium coccineum (10 transfers of 5 mitochondrial genes), and Lophophytum mirabile (over 80% alien DNA in 9 of 60 chromosomal molecules from legumes). Plastid genome HGT is rarer but exists.

6. **Mycoheterotrophs**: Despite sharing heterotrophic features with parasites, mycoheterotrophs show almost no HGT because they lack haustorium-like connections; plant-to-plant transfer would require two steps through fungi.

7. **Future questions**: The review proposes examining whether population sizes and genetic drift play roles in HGT fixation, both at organismal and subcellular (organelle population) levels.

Sequences were assembled de novo using ABySS v1.2.1 and analyzed via maximum likelihood phylogenetics with RAxML v7.2.8. Gene sequences were categorized as vertically transferred (VGT), horizontally transferred (HGT), or unassigned based on phylogenetic position and bootstrap percentage (BP) support, using both conservative (70 BP) and less conservative (50 BP) thresholds.

KEY FINDINGS:
1. Extraordinarily high HGT rates in the mitochondrial genome: Conservatively, 24% of gene sequences in R. cantleyi (5 of 21), 26% in R. tuan-mudae (5 of 19), and 41% in S. himalayana (11 of 27) showed evidence of HGT using the 70 BP threshold. Under the 50 BP threshold, rates were 29%, 32%, and 47%, respectively. This contrasts with only ~2.1% of nuclear gene transcripts previously shown to be acquired via HGT in R. cantleyi.
2. Eleven mitochondrial genes showed evidence of HGT under the conservative threshold: cob, cox3, rpl5, rps4 (maintaining both horizontally and vertically transferred homologs), and atp4, cox1, cox2, rps1, rps7, rps13, sdh3 (containing only transgenic sequences). Five additional genes (atp9, atp1, rpl2, rps14, sdh4) showed HGT under the less conservative threshold.
3. In S. himalayana, evidence of HGT was found in 14 genes potentially of plastid origin, with 13 supporting host-to-parasite HGT (placed sister to or nested within Vitaceae with ≥70 BP).
4. Transgenes are likely functional: Six of seven transgene sequences in R. cantleyi and R. tuan-mudae, and 13 of 16 in S. himalayana maintain intact reading frames. All transgenes in R. cantleyi showed evidence of expression (transcription), with expression levels not significantly different from native genes (p-value=0.19, Welch's t test).
5. Evidence of homologous recombination displacement: Seven assembled contigs contained both transgenes and native genes, and some transgenes maintained synteny with donor and recipient lineages, suggesting native genes were displaced via homologous recombination (e.g., the nad5 exon A/rps7 region matching Vitis synteny).
6. Timing of HGT: The study identified both ancient HGT events (five genes: atp1, atp4, cox1, rps7, atpA, likely occurring after the origin of stem group Rafflesiaceae ~83.1-109.5 Ma and before crown group Rafflesiaceae ~69.5-95.9 Ma) and recent events (28 instances found exclusively in either Rafflesia or Sapria, or in both but not forming a clade). Ancient transgenes did not group with current Tetrastigma hosts, suggesting historical parasitism of different host lineages ("ghost of HGT's past").
7. Rigorous contamination controls: Sample preparation of Rafflesiaceae was performed separately from Tetrastigma work; transgenes showed significant sequence divergence from current hosts compared to the divergence between the two Tetrastigma species (mean distance 0.042189 for Rafflesia, 0.020265 for Sapria versus 0.001984 between Tetrastigma species, p<0.01); and assembled contigs contained both transgenes and native genes.

CONCLUSION: This study establishes for the first time that although HGT involving nuclear genes is appreciable (~2.1% in R. cantleyi), HGT involving mitochondrial genes in these parasitic plants is "an order of magnitude higher" (24-41%), a pattern that may be general for other parasitic plant clades and perhaps more broadly for angiosperms.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Strikingly, our phylogenetic analyses conservatively indicate that 24%–41% of these gene sequences show evidence of HGT in Rafflesiaceae, depending on the species."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://www.indefenseofplants.com/blog/tag/Ophioglossaceae

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from "In Defense of Plants" covers two blog posts about fascinating members of the Ophioglossaceae family (adder's tongue ferns).

**First Post: An Awesome Ophioglossum (May 2016)**
- Describes the southern adder's tongue fern (Ophioglossum pychnostichum), a small, ancient member of the fern lineage commonly found alongside trails in grasslands.
- For much of its life, it exists as a gametophyte followed by an underground fleshy rhizome, nourished solely by an obligate association with mycorrhizal fungi. After years of storing nutrients, mature individuals produce a single sterile leaf and eventually a spore-bearing structure called a "sporophyll."
- Distributed throughout the Northern Hemisphere (North America, Europe, temperate Asia), it is of conservation concern in several states because its unpredictable lifecycle makes population estimates difficult.
- The Ophioglossaceae family is notable for staggeringly large chromosome counts; one species, Ophioglossum reticulatum, has 1,260 chromosomes (compared to humans' 46).

**Second Post: A Fern With Flower Genes (December 2015)**
- Harvard researchers studying the rattlesnake fern (Botrypus virginianum) genome found that one set of genes placed it in Ophioglossaceae, but two other genes placed it in Loranthaceae, a completely unrelated family of flowering plants.
- This represents the first documented case of horizontal gene transfer (transfer of genes without reproduction) between an angiosperm and a fern. Previous plant examples involved ferns and hornworts, or parasitic plants and their hosts.
- The rattlesnake fern, believed to have evolved in Asia and radiated via ancient land bridges, picked up foreign genes before this radiation.
- Two hypotheses for the transfer: (1) root parasitism by an ancient mistletoe species (Loranthaceae includes mistletoes; though most are stem parasites, at least three genera use root parasitism) - considered less likely since root-parasitic mistletoes don't currently exist in Asia; (2) indirect transfer via a shared mycorrhizal network, since rattlesnake ferns are obligate mycotrophs - a hypothesis that could explain many other unexplained examples of horizontal gene transfer.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
One species in particular - Ophioglossum reticulatum - boasts a whopping set of 1260 chromosomes. To put that into perspective, we humans only have 46.

URL: https://www.sciencealert.com/ferns-are-super-weird-and-their-genomes-are-even-more-chaotic-than-we-thought

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Scientists have finally sequenced the genomes of three homosporous ferns—the flying spider-monkey tree fern (Alsophila spinulosa, published May 2022 in Nature Plants), the maidenhair fern (Adiantum capillus-veneris), and the C-fern (Ceratopteris richardii, published this week in Nature Plants)—revealing that ferns are DNA hoarders and "kleptomaniacs." The C-fern work, contributed to by Doug Soltis of the Florida Museum of Natural History and a team from 28 institutions, took over eight years and resulted in a genome of 7.46 gigabases spread across 39 chromosome pairs—more than twice the size of the human genome. Previously, scientists attributed ferns' immense genomes and high chromosome counts to repeated whole-genome duplication, but the new research contradicts this prevailing view. Instead, 85% of the C. richardii genome (and a similar proportion in A. capillus-veneris) consists of transposons (jumping genes) and repetitive "scrappy" DNA debris, suggesting ferns are simply inefficient at shedding junk DNA, like hoarders. Notably, the study also found evidence that C. richardii acquired defense genes against a membrane-puncturing toxin from bacteria via horizontal gene transfer, which occurred multiple times. This is significant because ferns are the closest living relatives of all seed plants and produce chemical deterrents to herbivores that may be useful in agricultural research. A related record holder, Ophioglossum reticulatum (adder's tongue fern), holds the record for the most chromosomes in a multicellular organism, with around 720 chromosome pairs per cell.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 25: [PDF] Fern Genomics: Unfurling the Mystery of Plant Chromosome Numbers ---
URL: https://www.scientia.global/wp-content/uploads/Paul_Wolf.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article discusses Dr. Paul G. Wolf's research at the University of Alabama in Huntsville (Department of Biological Sciences) investigating plant chromosome numbers through fern genomics, specifically focusing on genome downsizing mechanisms following polyploidy. 

Key scientific context: Seed plants and some ferns are "heterosporous" (producing two spore types), while most ferns are "homosporous" (producing one spore type). Homosporous plants possess significantly more chromosomes than heterosporous plants—the fern Ophioglossum reticulatum has over 1,400 chromosomes (the highest for any plant, animal, or fungus, compared to humans' 46). Genome doubling during reproduction leads to "polyploidy" (e.g., tetraploids with four sets of chromosomes). While whole genome duplications are common in plant evolution and beneficial for crop breeding (wheat, cotton, potatoes are polyploid), they can cause genetic instability and infertility. Heterosporous plants lose excess genetic content through "genome downsizing" mechanisms, while homosporous ferns appear to have different or absent downsizing mechanisms—evidenced by their positively correlated chromosome number and genome size.

Dr. Wolf's methodology: His early work sequenced chloroplast DNA to establish evolutionary relationships among fern species. He sequenced the first complex fern-like genome in 2011, published first genetic sequences for two heterosporous fern species in 2018, and is currently assembling the first full genome sequence for the homosporous fern Ceratopteris richardii. With PhD student Sylvia Kinosian, he is investigating genetic and chromosome variation across the Ceratopteris genus, including a natural tetraploid (C. thalictroides) and lab-generated hybrid tetraploid crosses between C. richardii and C. pteridoides. Ceratopteris ferns are advantageous as a model genus due to their rapid lifecycle (145 days for a full cycle), allowing multiple experiments including chromosome behavior observation during spore-producing cell division.

The research also examines whether other life history traits (like the photosynthetic gametophyte stage in homosporous plants) correlate with spore type, since the spore type-chromosome correlation may not be causal. Some homosporous plants "silence" extra genes rather than removing them, potentially negating polyploidy's negative effects.

Implications: This synthesis approach could address broader biological concepts and deepen understanding of crop improvement methods, since exploiting natural or artificial polyploidy is effective for introducing beneficial traits into crops but can cause genetic instability.

Dr. Wolf earned his PhD in Botany from Washington State University, did postdoctoral research at UC Irvine, was a professor at Utah State University, and is now Professor and Chair at the University of Alabama in Huntsville. The research is funded by the US National Science Foundation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This series of experiments will begin to address the question of whether ferns are unable to downsize genomes as rapidly as flowering plants," says Dr Wolf.
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a 2019 scientific paper titled "Lateral transfers of large DNA fragments spread functional genes among grasses," published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Volume 116, no. 10, pages 4416-4425. The authors include Dunning, L.T., Olofsson, J.K., Parisod, C., Choudhury, R.R., Moreno-Villena, J.J., Yang, Y., Dionora, J., Quick, W.P., Park, M., Bennetzen, J.L., Besnard, G., Nosil, P., Osborne, C.P., and Christin, P.-A.

The study addresses whether lateral gene transfer (LGT) plays an important role in multicellular eukaryotes like plants, challenging the traditional view that vertical inheritance is paramount. The researchers assembled a chromosome-level genome for the grass Alloteropsis semialata, a species previously suspected of exhibiting two LGTs, and screened it against genomic data from 146 other grass species.

Key findings:
- Discovered 57 additional LGTs in the A. semialata nuclear genome, involving at least nine different donor species.
- These LGTs are clustered in 23 laterally acquired genomic fragments up to 170 kb long, accumulated during the diversification of Alloteropsis.
- The majority of the 59 total LGTs in A. semialata are expressed and added functions to the recipient genome.
- Functional LGTs were also detected in the genomes of five other grass species, showing the process is likely widespread in this globally important plant group.

Conclusion: LGT appears to represent a potent evolutionary force capable of spreading functional genes among distantly related grass species. The paper is open access under a CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0 license and available on the CGIAR (CGSpace) repository.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Footprints of parasitism in the genome of the parasitic flowering plant Cuscuta campestris | Nature Communications ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-04344-z

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in Nature Communications (volume 9, article 2515, 2018), describes the first reported genome sequence of a parasitic plant: the field dodder (Cuscuta campestris), a member of the Convolvulaceae family (Solanales). The parasitic plant infects a broad range of host species across the plant kingdom through specialized haustoria that penetrate host tissue and connect vascular systems.

Key findings include:
- Genome characteristics: C. campestris has 2n=56 small chromosomes with a 1C value of 581 Mbp. The assembled draft genome was ~477 Mbp (about 86% of the k-mer-based estimate), containing 44,303 predicted high-confidence gene loci across 6,907 scaffolds with an N50 of 1.38 Mbp. BUSCO analysis showed 82.1% of 1,440 conserved plant genes were present, with 59% present in duplicated form.
- Transposons: 46.2% (221 Mbp) of the genome is transposon-derived, dominated by LTR retrotransposons (96% of mobile elements), with a recent amplification wave around 1.5 million years ago.
- Whole-genome duplication: Evidence indicates a recent genome duplication event (~1.5 mya), with a peak synonymous substitution rate (dS) of 0.05 between paralogs. 59% of genes had syntenic paralogs (vs. 23% in Arabidopsis thaliana).
- Gene loss: The parasite lost genes needed for high photosynthetic activity, including genes for the NDH-dependent cyclic electron transport pathway and chlorophyll turnover enzymes, explaining its low photosynthesis rates. Genes for soil nutrient uptake (iron transporters, root nitrate uptake system NRT2/NAR2, mycorrhizal symbiosis proteins) were also lost due to the absence of a root system. However, core photosynthesis, amino acid, fatty acid, and vitamin synthesis pathways were retained, likely to re-fix CO2 for carbon efficiency.
- Horizontal gene transfer (HGT): Beyond two previously known HGT cases, 64 novel high-confidence HGT candidates from at least 32 donor sequences were identified, mostly tracing to preferred host orders Fabales and Caryophyllales. A notable example shows two adjacent C. campestris genes with high homology to neighboring carrot (Daucus carota) genes, including conserved intron positions and post-transfer duplication, providing evidence of integration of larger stretches of genomic DNA from hosts.

The study concludes that the parasitic lifestyle has left characteristic footprints in the C. campestris genome, and will enable genome-guided studies of host-parasite interactions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The genome contains signatures of a fairly recent whole-genome duplication and lacks genes for pathways superfluous to a parasitic lifestyle. Specifically, genes needed for high photosynthetic activity are lost, explaining the low photosynthesis rates displayed by the parasite."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This original research article, published in Frontiers in Plant Science (22 August 2022, Volume 13, DOI: 10.3389/fpls.2022.980033), investigates bidirectional mRNA transfer between the parasitic dodder plant (Cuscuta australis) and its hosts: sweet orange (Citrus sinensis "Newhall") and periwinkle (Catharanthus roseus). The study was conducted by researchers from South China Agricultural University (Guangzhou, China). The holoparasitic dodder transfers mRNA and plant pathogens like "Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus" (CLas), the causative agent of citrus Huanglongbing, between hosts. The researchers sequenced transcriptomes of dodder and host tissues from three regions (interface/haustoria region, host stem, and dodder stem) to characterize mRNA transfer.

Key findings:
- mRNA transfer was bidirectional in both host systems, with most transfer events occurring in the interface (haustoria) tissue
- The periwinkle–dodder system showed more frequent mRNA transfer than the citrus–dodder system (611 vs. 512 dodder mobile transcripts in host stems; 1,717 vs. 63 host mobile transcripts in interface tissue)
- A higher number of reads was identified in the periwinkle system (51,959 dodder reads in periwinkle stem, 58,990 periwinkle reads in interface) compared to citrus (21,788 dodder reads in citrus stem, 8,220 citrus reads in interface)
- Host cell wall composition differences (higher mannan and xylan in woody citrus) and phylogenetic relatedness may explain differences in transfer efficiency between systems

Functional analysis revealed that:
- A large number of transferred mRNAs were involved in secondary metabolism and stress response
- Dodder transcripts encoding proteins associated with microtubule-based processes and cell wall biogenesis were transferred to host tissues (potentially contributing to haustoria formation)
- Transcripts involved in translational elongation, plasmodesmata, and auxin-activated signaling were transmitted between species
- Transcripts involved in shoot system development and flower development (including FT/FLOWERING LOCUS T) were transferred bidirectionally, with host FT proteins potentially activating dodder flowering
- Host transcripts involved in seed germination (encoding glycosyltransferase) and flower development were transferred to dodder, potentially benefiting dodder reproduction

Notable highly abundant dodder-origin transcripts in hosts: MIP aquaporin protein (DM860_000198) and S-adenosylmethionine synthetase 1 (DM860_002589), which may play important biological roles in dodder–host interactions. The study used RNA-seq (Illumina NovaSeq 6000, 150bp paired-end reads, 36-44 million reads per library), with reads mapped to reference genomes of the three species using CLC Genomic Workbench. Mobile transcripts were defined as those with ≥4 mapped reads. Verification was performed via in silico mapping and PCR for four transcripts (NsLTP from citrus, Mito_carr from periwinkle, S-AdoMet_synt_C and HSP90 from dodder). Data are publicly available at NCBI under accession PRJNA847378. The research was funded by the National Key Research and Development Program of China and the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

This is a bioRxiv preprint (DOI: 10.1101/2022.08.25.505314) titled "Widespread horizontal gene transfer between plants and their microbiota" by Shelly Haimlich, Yulia Fridman, Hitaishi Khandal, Sigal Savaldi-Goldstein, and Asaf Levy (from Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Technion-Israel Institute of Technology). It has since been published in ISME Communications (doi: 10.1093/ismeco/ycae073).

**Objective & Hypothesis:** The authors hypothesized that the spatial proximity and long-term relationships between plants and their microbiota promote cross-kingdom horizontal gene transfer (HGT). They tested this using Arabidopsis thaliana and its extensively sequenced microbiome.

**Methodology:**
- Compared A. thaliana genes against 582 fully sequenced commensal bacteria isolated from Arabidopsis (plant-associated, PA), covering 1,051 genomes total (including 441 non-plant-associated bacteria, plants, fungi, archaea, and other eukaryotes).
- Used BLASTP with threshold of at least 35% amino acid identity across at least 80% of both proteins.
- Filtered out 'trivial hits' shared with organelles (mitochondria and chloroplast, which originate in bacteria).
- Constructed gene trees from multiple sequence alignments to detect phylogenetic evidence of HGT (where gene trees and genome trees were inconsistent).

**Key Results:**
- Identified 767 Arabidopsis proteins mapped to 60,850 bacterial proteins as potential molecular mimicry candidates.
- Detected 180 unique cross-kingdom HGT events: 84 genes likely transferred from plants to bacteria, and 96 genes from PA bacteria to plants.
- Additionally found 161 genes transferred between PA bacteria and the eukaryotic domain (source unclear), 65 genes with unclear inheritance patterns, and 361 genes with no HGT patterns.
- Rejected DNA contamination by confirming no homologous pairs exceeded 76% amino acid identity.

**Functional Enrichment:**
- Genes transferred from plants to bacteria are enriched in secreted proteins, carbohydrate catabolism enzymes (pectin esterase, glycosidase), and include chitinases (CHI, AT2G43570), endo beta mannanase (XCD1), and pectin lyases (PME5) — enabling bacteria to exploit plant-derived sugars.
- Genes transferred from bacteria to plants are enriched in redox homeostasis and cytoplasmic proteins, including many auxin biosynthesis YUCCA genes and nucleoside metabolic processes. 69/96 (72%) of such genes are found in all dicots and monocots, suggesting ancient HGT events.

**Taxonomic Patterns:**
- Bacteroidetes were enriched as gene acceptors from plants, while Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria were depleted as either acceptors or donors.
- Rhizobiales and Hyphomicrobiales (Proteobacteria) and Micrococcales (Actinobacteria) showed significantly fewer HGT events than expected.
- In most cases the donor/acceptor taxonomy remained "unknown" (multiple phyla involved).

**Recent HGT Examples:**
- The plant CHI (chitinase) gene is present in only 7 PA Streptomyces genomes (patchy distribution), with protein structures very similar (RMSD=0.791).
- The bacterial DET2 homologue (steroid-5-alpha-reductase, key in brassinosteroid biosynthesis) is nearly specific to plant-associated Leifsonia genus (Actinobacteria), located downstream of a tRNA gene; protein structures highly similar (RMSD=0.727) despite less than 50% sequence identity.

**Functional Validation (Proof-of-Concept):**
- The authors tested whether the Leifsonia DET2 homologue (lfDET2) could functionally replace the Arabidopsis DET2 gene. Arabidopsis DET2 is 46% identical to Leifsonia Det2 (similar to identity shared with rice and barley homologues).
- Expression of lfDET2 (driven by 35S or Arabidopsis DET2 promoters) in the Arabidopsis det2 mutant background rescued the dwarf phenotype and root meristem defects, restoring normal plant growth.
- lfDET2 localized to the endoplasmic reticulum, matching atDET2 localization.

**Conclusion:** The results suggest cross-kingdom HGT is relatively frequent and shaped the genomes of plants and their microbiota by adding adaptive traits. The transferred genes likely participate in molecular mimicry between hosts and their commensal microbiomes. Key author correspondence: alevy@mail.huji.ac.il.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We detected 180 unique genes that were horizontally transferred between plants and their microbiota. Genes transferred from plants to their microbiota are enriched in secreted proteins that metabolize carbohydrates, whereas microbes transferred to plants genes that are enriched in redox homeostasis functions."
</key_excerpts>

messages.content: Search results: --- SOURCE 1: Convergent evolution of strigolactone perception enabled host detection in parasitic plants - the UWA Profiles and Research Repository --- URL: https://research-repository.uwa.edu.au/en/publications/convergent-evolution-of-strigolactone-perception-enabled-host-det-2 SUMMARY: This webpage presents a peer-reviewed research article published in the journal Science on July 31, 2015, titled "Convergent evolution of strigolactone perception enabled host detection in parasitic plants" by Conn et al. (authors include Caitlin E. Conn, Rohan Bythell-Douglas, Drexel Neumann, Satoko Yoshida, Bryan Whittington, James H. Westwood, Ken Shirasu, Charles S. Bond, Kelly A. Dyer, and David C. Nelson). The study investigates how obligate parasitic plants in the Orobanchaceae family germinate upon sensing strigolactones (plant hormones) exuded from host roots. In Arabidopsis thaliana, the α/β-hydrolase D14 acts as a strigolactone receptor controlling shoot branching, while its ancestral paralog KAI2 mediates karrikin-specific germination responses. Key findings: - KAI2 (but not D14) is present at higher copy numbers in parasitic species than in nonparasitic relatives - KAI2 paralogs in parasites are distributed into three phylogenetic clades - The fastest-evolving clade, KAI2d, contains the majority of KAI2 paralogs - Homology models predict that the ligand-binding pockets of KAI2d resemble D14 - KAI2d transgenes confer strigolactone-specific germination responses to Arabidopsis thaliana The study concludes that the KAI2 paralogs D14 and KAI2d underwent convergent evolution of strigolactone recognition, respectively enabling developmental responses to strigolactones in angiosperms and host detection in parasites. Publication details: Science, Volume 349, Issue 6247, pages 540-543 (4 pages), DOI: 10.1126/science.aab1140, PMID 26228149, ISSN 0036-8075. It has 265 citations in Scopus. The paper is affiliated with the School of Molecular Sciences at University of Western Australia (Charles S. Bond). "Obligate parasitic plants in the Orobanchaceae germinate after sensing plant hormones, strigolactones, exuded from host roots.", "In Arabidopsis thaliana, the a/b-hydrolase D14 acts as a strigolactone receptor that controls shoot branching, whereas its ancestral paralog, KAI2, mediates karrikin-specific germination responses.", "We observed that KAI2, but not D14, is present at higher copy numbers in parasitic species than in nonparasitic relatives.", "Homology models predict that the ligandbinding pockets of KAI2d resemble D14. KAI2d transgenes confer strigolactone-specific germination responses to Arabidopsis thaliana.", "Thus, the KAI2 paralogs D14 and KAI2d underwent convergent evolution of strigolactone recognition, respectively enabling developmental responses to strigolactones in angiosperms and host detection in parasites." -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --- SOURCE 2: Evolution and function of strigolactone / karrikin receptors | Plant Science Today --- URL: https://blog.aspb.org/research-in-focus-evolution-and-function-of-strigolactone-karrikin-receptors SUMMARY: This article from Plant Science Today (ASPB blog) by Mary Williams reviews the evolution and function of strigolactone and karrikin receptors, published around August 2015. **Key background:** - Karrikins are small molecules found in smoke that promote seed germination, associated with plant activation after fires. - Strigolactones are structurally similar small molecules that act as endogenous hormones and secreted signals promoting germination of parasitic plants and branching responses in mycorrhizal fungi. - In Arabidopsis, related proteins D14 and KAI2 are receptor complex components for strigolactones and karrikins respectively. **Evolutionary findings:** - Phylogenetic studies indicate the KAI2/D14 protein family arose from two or more gene duplication events. The KAI2 clade is ancestral, with duplication D1 leading to the D14 clade and a second event (D2) occurring in angiosperms. - Functional studies (Waters et al., 2015) showed KAI2-like genes in liverworts (Marchantia polymorpha) and lycophytes (Selaginella moellendorffii) could not substitute for D14 activity in Arabidopsis, but one Selaginella KAI2-like gene partially substituted for KAI2 activity. This supports KAI2 function being ancestral to D14, with strigolactone perception by D14 being derived. - A gene amplification event in parasitic plants of the Orobanchaceae family occurred in the KAI2 lineage (not D14), correlated with germination response to strigolactones. - These observations suggest strigolactone perception arose twice independently within the KAI2/D14 family. - The preferred ligands for other KAI2 family members (including from green algae and basal land plants) remain unknown. **Open questions:** - Ancestral functions of the KAI2/D14 pathway in plants and green algae - The role of protein degradation and substrate hydrolysis in downstream signaling - How endogenous strigolactones exert diverse roles in plant development - How fungi perceive strigolactones The article includes an extensive reference list covering key studies by Brewer et al. (2013), Conn et al. (2015), Nelson et al. (2012), Tsuchiya et al. (2015), Waters et al. (2012, 2015), and others on strigolactone/karrikin biology. "Karrikins are small molecules found in smoke that promote seed germination and have been associated with the activation of seeds following fire."; "Strigolactones are structurally similar small molecules that act as endogenous hormones and as secreted signals that promote the germination of parasitic plants and branching responses in mycrorrhizal fungi."; "These observations suggest that strigolactone perception arose twice independently within the KAI2/D14 protein family."; "The KAI2 clade is thought to be ancestral, with a duplication event (D1) leading to the D14 clade and a second event (D2) occurring in angiosperms."; "These results support the model that KAI2 function is ancestral to D14 function, and that strigolactone perception by D14 proteins is derived." -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --- SOURCE 3: New strigolactone receptor advances knowledge of how germination is induced in parasitic plants | RIKEN Center for Sustainable Resource Science --- URL: https://csrs.riken.jp/en/topics/press/press20150731.html SUMMARY: On July 31, 2015, researchers from RIKEN CSRS and the University of Georgia reported a significant discovery related to strigolactone receptors in parasitic plants. The joint research group compared genomic sequences of parasitic and non-parasitic plants, finding an increased number of genes coding for KAI2 proteins in parasitic plants. Structural analysis revealed that part of the KAI2 proteins in parasitic plants resemble the Arabidopsis thaliana D14 protein, a known strigolactone receptor, suggesting parasitic plants use KAI2 proteins as strigolactone receptors. The researchers confirmed this by introducing a KAI2 protein from a parasitic plant into an Arabidopsis kai2 mutant, successfully creating a plant that germinated in response to strigolactone. The KAI2 genes appear to have evolved independently of the D14 gene in Arabidopsis, acquiring strigolactone receptor functionality through convergent evolution. Since parasitic plants such as Striga and Orobanche cause significant agricultural damage worldwide, understanding their seed germination mechanisms could lead to prevention of agricultural losses. The findings were published in Science (doi: 10.1126/science.aab1140) in the article "Convergent evolution of strigolactone perception enabled host detection in parasitic plants" by Conn, Bythell-Douglas, Neumann, Yoshida, Whittington, Westwood, Shirasu, Bond, Dyer, and Nelson. Contacts for the study were Ken Shirasu (Group Director) and Satoko Yoshida (Senior Research Scientist) of the Plant Immunity Research Group at RIKEN. The joint research group compared the genomic sequences of parasitic plants and non-parasitic plants, discovering an increase in the number of genes that code for the KAI2 proteins. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --- SOURCE 4: PLANT EVOLUTION. The article was published by Oxford University Press (OUP) with DOI 10.1093/pcp/pcad026. The authors are Saori Takei, Yuta Uchiyama, Marco Bürger, Taiki Suzuki, Shoma Okabe, Joanne Chory, and Yoshiya Seto. The page lists the article as open access and includes a bibliography and abstract sections. The page also lists several related publications citing this work, including papers on strigolactone biosynthetic pathway conservation in root parasitic plants, strigolactone perception in Phtheirospermum japonicum, divergent receptors shaping strigolactone perception, dominant-negative KAI2d paralogs in root parasitic plants, in vitro monitoring of strigolactone signaling complexes, strigolactone research updates, strigolactone biosynthesis and perception knowledge, structural diversity of strigolactones, and radicle growth regulation of root parasitic plants by auxin-related compounds. A Divergent Clade KAI2 Protein in the Root Parasitic Plant Orobanche minor Is a Highly Sensitive Strigolactone Receptor and Is Involved in the Perception of Sesquiterpene Lactones, DOI: 10.1093/pcp/pcad026, Published by Oxford University Press (OUP), Authors: Saori Takei, Yuta Uchiyama, Marco Bürger, Taiki Suzuki, Shoma Okabe, Joanne Chory, Yoshiya Seto, Functional conservation of the strigolactone biosynthetic pathway in root parasitic plants, Highly Sensitive Strigolactone Perception by a Divergent Clade KAI2 Receptor in a Facultative Root Parasitic Plant, Phtheirospermum japonicum, Divergent Receptors Shape Strigolactone Perception in a Facultative Parasitic Plant, Dominant-Negative KAI2d Paralogs Putatively Attenuate Strigolactone Responses in Root Parasitic Plants -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --- SOURCE 6: Massive horizontal transfer of transposable elements in insects --- URL: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1621178114 SUMMARY: This is a PNAS research article (DOI: 10.1073/pnas.1621178114) published April 17, 2017, in volume 114, issue 18, pages 4721-4726, authored by Jean Peccoud, Vincent Loiseau, Richard Cordaux, and Clément Gilbert. It was edited by Nancy L. Craig (Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine) and approved March 20, 2017 (received December 22, 2016). TITLE AND FOCUS: The article, "Massive horizontal transfer of transposable elements in insects," reports a comprehensive large-scale analysis of horizontal transfer (HT) of transposable elements (TEs) in insects. METHODOLOGY: The researchers conducted a de novo characterization of TEs in 195 insect genomes from GenBank (as of May 2016), representing 123 genera and 13 of the 28 insect orders. Using the RepeatModeler pipeline, they identified 53,452 TE families assigned to 98 superfamilies. They compared TE copies >100 base pairs across species via pairwise reciprocal homology searches, retaining ~5.9 million hits. They collapsed related species into 81 lineages to distinguish vertically inherited TEs from horizontally transferred ones. Hits were clustered into HTT (horizontal transfer of TEs) events. KEY RESULTS: - At least 2,248 HTT events occurred among the 81 insect lineages, mostly within the last 10 million years (My) - This number is "more than four times higher than the total number of HTT events reported so far in metazoans, plants, and fungi combined" - 72 of the 81 lineages and 176 of the 195 species were involved in at least one HTT event - DNA transposons (class II) transfer horizontally more often than retrotransposons (class I): 1,813 vs. 435 transfers - The Tc1-Mariner superfamily had the highest number of HTT events - Horizontally transferred TEs generated up to 24.6% (2.08% on average) of all nucleotides of insect genomes - Phylogenetic relatedness and geographical proximity were identified as major factors facilitating HTT in insects - There was a significant negative correlation between number of HTT events and lineage divergence times (likely due to compatibility between TEs and host cellular factors decreasing with genetic distance) - Geographic proximity favors HTT, with recent transfers preferentially involving species from the same biogeographic realm CONCLUSION: The results establish HTT as a major force shaping insect genome evolution and call for further assessments of HTT's influence on other taxonomic groups and the ecological factors affecting HTT dynamics. "We have analyzed the genomes from 195 insect species and found that no fewer than 2,248 events of HT of TEs occurred during the last 10 My, particularly between insects that were closely related and geographically close. These results suggest that HT of TEs plays a major role in insect genome evolution." -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --- SOURCE 7: Horizontal Gene Transfers in Plants --- URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2075-1729/11/8/857 SUMMARY: This is a scientific review article titled "Horizontal Gene Transfers in Plants" published in the journal Life (2021, 11(8), 857; DOI: 10.3390/life11080857), authored by Emilie Aubin, Moaine El Baidouri, and Olivier Panaud from the Laboratoire Génome et Développement des Plantes, Université de Perpignan Via Domitia, France. The review was submitted on 9 July 2021, revised 10 August 2021, accepted 16 August 2021, and published 21 August 2021. It was designated as an Editor's Choice and Open Access review article. The article provides an up-to-date view of horizontal gene transfers (HGTs)—the interspecific transmission of genetic information across reproductive barriers—in plants. Historically considered rare in eukaryotes, HGTs have been shown through next-generation sequencing (NGS) and comparative genomics to be common in nature, affecting all living organisms including plants. Key topics covered: - **HGT Detection Criteria**: Three criteria are used for detection via comparative genomics: high similarity (HS), phylogenetic incongruence (PI), and patchy distribution in phylogenies (PD). HS is most commonly used with large genomic datasets. - **Parasitism**: Many HGT cases involve host/parasite interactions. Examples include: mitochondrial gene (atp1) transfer between parasitic plants (Cuscuta, Bartsia) and Plantago species; 0.1–0.2% of genes in obligate parasitic plants originating from HGT (with large regions over 100 kbp transferred at once); the Fhb7 wheat Fusarium head blight resistance gene originating from a fungus-to-plant transfer; Agrobacterium T-DNA integrating into plant genomes (including in Nicotiana glauca, Linaria vulgaris, and sweet potato); and virus-to-plant transfers including endogenous pararetroviral-like sequences in rice. - **Grafting**: Grafting experiments between Nicotiana species demonstrated genetic material exchange, complete chloroplast transfer ("plastid capture"), and the de novo generation of allopolyploid plants from graft sites, suggesting grafting could be a mechanism of natural HGT. - **Food Chain**: The "you are what you eat" hypothesis; example of the sea slug Elysia chlorotica acquiring chloroplasts from algae Vaucheria litorea, though this is not transgenerational. - **Other Routes**: Notable transfers include: the entire genomes of algae and a moss mitochondria into the angiosperm Amborella (3.9 Mbp total, ~6 genome equivalents); neochrome gene HGT to ferns at 179 Mya enabling low-light adaptation; PPC gene transfers enabling C4 photosynthesis; 59 HGTs in the grass Alloteropsis semialata from at least nine donors; transfer of Transferrin genes from insects to Theobroma cacao; and plant-to-animal transfers (DTAFP genes, trehalose-6-phosphate synthase genes in rotifers, and the BtPMaT1 gene enabling whiteflies to neutralize plant toxins). - **Horizontal Transfers of Transposable Elements (HTTs)**: TEs are particularly prone to horizontal transfer because they exist in extrachromosomal forms during transposition. HTTs may allow TEs to escape host silencing/degradation. Examples include MULE transposons between rice and millet, the LTR-retrotransposon Route66 among grasses, Copia25 across angiosperms, and 32 HTTs detected among 42 plant genomes, leading to an estimate of hundreds of thousands of HTTs occurring among flowering plants within the last two million years. **Conclusions**: HGTs are widespread in eukaryotes; most involve species in biological promiscuity (parasitism, grafting, viral/bacterial/fungal vectors). Future challenges include developing methods to detect recent, biologically relevant HGTs using combined omics approaches, and understanding how HGTs occur between unrelated species, potentially with parasites acting as "genetic bridges" for adaptive gene spread within ecosystems. The authors declare no conflict of interest. Funding was provided by a BQR grant of the University of Perpignan and the Institut Universitaire de France (Panaud), and a PhD grant from région Occitanie (Aubin). "In plants, as in all eukaryotes, the vertical transmission of genetic information through reproduction ensures the maintenance of the integrity of species. However, many reports over the past few years have clearly shown that horizontal gene transfers, referred to as HGTs (the interspecific transmission of genetic information across reproductive barriers) are very common in nature and concern all living organisms including plants." -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --- SOURCE 8: Horizontal transfer and evolution of transposable elements in vertebrates | Nature Communications --- URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-15149-4 SUMMARY: This is a scientific research article published in Nature Communications (Volume 11, Article 1362, 2020) by Hua-Hao Zhang, Jean Peccoud, Clément Gilbert and colleagues, investigating horizontal transfer of transposable elements (HTT) in vertebrates. **Methods:** The researchers screened 307 vertebrate genomes publicly available on GenBank. They de novo characterized transposable elements (TEs) using RepeatModeler and RepeatMasker pipelines, extracting more than 133 million TE copies ≥300 bp. Reciprocal nucleotide BLAST searches (87,818 searches) were conducted comparing TE copies between species pairs that diverged more than 40 million years ago. To ensure detected hits reflected horizontal transfer rather than vertical inheritance, they required hits involving copies whose synonymous divergence (Ks) was lower than 99.5% of Ks values of core orthologous genes, and excluded any hits involving species that diverged within the last 120 million years (which removed most mammals and birds from analysis). Hits were clustered into "hit groups" representing separate transfer events. **Key Results:** - A minimum of 975 independent HTT events were inferred between lineages diverged more than 120 million years ago—more than ten times the previously identified HTTs involving vertebrates - 93.7% of these transfers involved ray-finned fishes (Actinopterygii), despite fishes representing only 64 of the 307 genomes analyzed - Less than 3% of transfers involved mammals and birds (only 24 events detected), despite these representing 218 species - Statistical permutation tests showed ray-finned fish HTT numbers exceeded null expectations for all TE classes and superfamilies, while mammal and bird transfers were 16-100 times less than random expectations - Tc1/Mariner DNA transposons were the most common TE type involved in horizontal transfer, followed by the Rex-Babar non-LTR retrotransposon superfamily (87.6% of whose transfers were among teleost fishes) - LINE 1 retrotransposons generated the most annotated copies overall but rarely relied on horizontal transfer - Endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) showed few host switches between vertebrate classes **Selection Findings:** Analysis of Ka/Ks ratios revealed that HTT incurs purifying selection (conserved protein evolution) on all TE types, confirming that functional transposition proteins are required for a TE to invade new genomes. In the absence of HTT, DNA transposons evolve neutrally within genomes, unlike most retrotransposons which evolve under purifying selection due to cis-preference (proteins processing their own encoding RNA). This cis-preference helps retrotransposons persist within host lineages over long time periods. DNA transposons and Jockey retrotransposons evolved under relaxed selection within genomes (Ka/Ks not significantly below 1), consistent with trans-complementation replication mechanisms, while LTR retrotransposons showed the lowest Ka/Ks ratios. **Conclusion:** The study provides the first large-scale quantification of HTT in vertebrates and of the selective constraints acting on TEs during vertical versus horizontal transmission, establishing that different TE classes experience distinct selection regimes depending on their transmission mode. "Here we screen 307 vertebrate genomes and infer a minimum of 975 independent HTT events between lineages that diverged more than 120 million years ago. HTT distribution greatly differs from null expectations, with 93.7% of these transfers involving ray-finned fishes and less than 3% involving mammals and birds.", "HTT incurs purifying selection (conserved protein evolution) on all TEs, confirming that producing functional transposition proteins is required for a TE to invade new genomes. In the absence of HTT, DNA transposons appear to evolve neutrally within genomes, unlike most retrotransposons, which evolve under purifying selection.", "The high interspecific mobility of DNA transposons is consistent with the 'blurry' promoters and low reliance on host factors enabling these TEs to easily transpose in a large panel of hosts.", "Ray-finned fishes (Actinopterygii) contribute the vast majority (~94%) of transfer events despite representing just 64 of the 307 studied genomes. By comparison, only 24 detected HTT events involve mammals and birds, even though they represent 218 species among the 307 we analyzed.", "While trans-complementation allows the replication of non-functional TEs within hosts, only those encoding functional proteins may successfully move between genetically divergent species if the recipient genomes lack the proteins that could transpose these TEs." -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --- SOURCE 9: Widespread and frequent horizontal transfers of transposable elements in plants --- URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4009612 SUMMARY: A scientific article published in Genome Research (May 2014) by El Baidouri et al. reporting on widespread horizontal transfers of transposable elements (TEs) in plants. About 58% (103/177) of genes from episode 1 and 71% (76/107) from episode 2 have been retained in seed plants, demonstrating significant cumulative effects. 6. Bacteria were the majority source of acquired genes, with fungi contributing about 48% and 36% of acquired genes in bryophytes and lycophytes respectively. Viral and animal sources were also identified. 7. Acquired genes affected numerous plant activities including stress responses (drought, aluminum resistance, pathogen defense), metabolite and ion transport (at least 10 transporter families), growth and development (phytohormone signaling, vascular development, cell wall metabolism), and specialized metabolism (about 27.8% of acquired genes). NOTABLE EXAMPLES: The ALS3/NAP3 ABC transporter complex (co-transferred from bacteria, involved in aluminum resistance), DIT1 gene (from fungi to lycophytes, involved in spore wall maturation), fungal FB lectin in liverworts (experimentally shown to cause 80% mortality in diamondback moth larvae vs. 8.8% control), LEA2 proteins (desiccation resistance), ricin/abrin toxin gene family (from bacteria to seed plants), and chalcone synthase and stilbene synthase (from bacteria for phenylpropanoid metabolism). CONCLUSIONS: The authors argue that HGT must be considered a major force in plant evolution alongside gene duplication, mutation, and new gene origination. They explain the decline in recent HGT in seed plants may reflect stabilized physical environments or developmental shifts rather than barriers to HGT. Seed-plant-specific acquired genes are disproportionately related to biotic stress responses, reflecting adaptation to increasing pathogen/herbivore diversity. "We found that two major episodes of HGT events occurred in land plant evolution, corresponding to the early evolution of streptophytes and the origin of land plants, respectively. Importantly, a vast majority of the genes acquired in the two episodes have been retained in descendant groups, affecting numerous activities and processes of land plants." -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --- SOURCE 22: Major episodes of horizontal gene transfer drove the ... --- URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35235827 SUMMARY: by J Ma · 2022 · Cited by 147 — Two major episodes of HGT events occurred in land plant evolution, corresponding to the early evolution of streptophytes and the origin of land -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --- SOURCE 23: [PDF] Regulatory features determine the evolutionary fate of laterally ... --- URL: https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/231722/1/2025.08.22.671697v1.full.pdf SUMMARY: This is a preprint (bioRxiv, submitted 2025) titled "Regulatory features determine the evolutionary fate of laterally acquired genes in plants," by Collins et al. from the University of Sheffield and collaborators. The study investigates lateral gene transfer (LGT) in the grass genus Alloteropsis, focusing on what factors influence the integration and long-term retention of transferred genes. **Key Findings:** - Most laterally acquired genes are degenerating: ~68-73% show reduced expression, higher truncation rates (33.3% vs 16.2% for vertical homologs), and significantly higher DNA methylation in gene bodies. These genes are lost at a rate 500x higher than vertically inherited genes. - Putatively functional laterally acquired genes had expression levels significantly more similar to their donor xenolog than to their vertically inherited homolog, suggesting co-transfer of cis-regulatory elements (promoters) on the transferred DNA fragments is key to retention. - Functional transfers are associated with greater expression divergence between donor and recipient orthologs, but NOT greater coding sequence (dN, dS, dN/dS) divergence. - Laterally acquired genes show increased relaxed selection compared to vertical homologs. - Time since acquisition does not correlate with degeneration status overall. - Example: laterally acquired PCK gene in C4 Alloteropsis enabled subfunctionalization, with the acquired copy specialized for C4 photosynthesis and the vertical copy retained for housekeeping gluconeogenesis. **Methods:** 55 RNA-Seq datasets from five Alloteropsis accessions across four tissues (leaf base, leaf tip, leaf sheath, root), bisulfite sequencing for methylation analysis, reference-based transcript quantification with Salmon, statistical analyses using LMMs, Wilcoxon tests, binomial tests, and CodeML selection models. 282 laterally acquired genes analyzed (168 unique in the pangenome). **Conclusion:** Most LGT events in plants are transient and non-adaptive, but genes carrying their own cis-regulatory elements that can be expressed in the recipient, and that provide regulatory novelty, are more likely to persist and contribute to long-term evolutionary innovation. Overall, laterally acquired genes are expressed at significantly lower levels compared to vertically inherited homologs (p = 1.87 × 10-14)... laterally acquired genes are generally expressed at significantly lower levels (LMM; p < 2 x 10-16) than their xenolog in the donor. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --- SOURCE 24: Multiple independent acquisitions of a metallophore ... --- URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-61162-w SUMMARY: This is a scientific research article published in Nature Communications (volume 16, article 8339, 2025) titled "Multiple independent acquisitions of a metallophore-synthesis gene by plants through horizontal microbial gene transfer." The study investigates the evolutionary history of the nicotianamine synthase (NAS) gene, which produces the metallophore nicotianamine (NA) that chelates transition metals (Fe, Cu, Zn, Ni, Mn) for transport in plants. Key findings: - Contrary to prior assumptions of a single ancient horizontal gene transfer (HGT), the NAS gene was acquired independently from distinct microbial donors by at least five plant lineages. - The NAS gene is absent from streptophyte algae, lycophytes, hornworts, and most liverworts (except Blasia pusilla), confirming it was not present in ancestral land plants. - Within mosses, three distinct NAS gene lineages exist: FunNAS (from a Pezizomycete fungus, acquired ~275 mya), HypNAS (from an Agaromycete fungus, replacing FunNAS ~210 mya), and TetNAS (from bacteria). A fourth PolNAS gene was transferred moss-to-moss between Polytrichales and the lineage sister to Bartramiales. - The EupNAS gene was acquired by euphyllophytes (ferns and seed plants) between 437-400 mya. - The NAS gene was also transferred from plants back to a fungus (marine sordariomycete Lindra) and to an insect (the whitefly Bemisia tabaci) - the only known metazoan to carry the gene. - Knockout experiments in Physcomitrium patens showed that removing the FunNAS gene slowed growth, decreased photosystem II efficiency (Fv/Fm), and prevented sexual organogenesis, demonstrating the gene's critical physiological function. - Mosses are the only land plant lineage universally lacking mycorrhizal associations, and NAS may partially compensate for absence of fungal symbionts by enhancing internal metal distribution. Methods included screening 133 bryophyte genomes, phylogenetic analyses of 330 NAS protein sequences using maximum likelihood (IQTREE2), MEME motif analysis, and mass spectrometry (HILIC/ICP-MS and ESI-MS) to detect the metallophore. The study challenges assumptions of deep homology for microbial genes in plants and suggests highly dynamic, recurrent HGT events during plant diversification on land. "Analyses of the gene space of land plant model organisms suggest that such transfers are unique and ancient. However here, using genomic data spanning the diversity of mosses, we demonstrate that a metallophore-synthesis gene was acquired independently from distinct microbial donors by at least five plant lineages." -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --- SOURCE 25: Major episodes of horizontal gene transfer drove the evolution of land plants --- URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1674205222000491 SUMMARY: This is a Research Article published in Molecular Plant (Volume 15, Issue 5, 2 May 2022, pages 857-871), titled "Major episodes of horizontal gene transfer drove the evolution of land plants." The article is open access under a Creative Commons license (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0). DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molp.2022.02.001. Authors: Jianchao Ma, Shuanghua Wang, Xiaojing Zhu, Guiling Sun, Guanxiao Chang, Linhong Li, Xiangyang Hu, Shouzhou Zhang, Yun Zhou, Chun-Peng Song, and Jinling Huang (first two authors contributed equally). Key findings from the abstract: - The study performed systematic analyses of genes acquired through horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in different plant groups and throughout land plant evolution, addressing how HGT contributed to the evolution of animals and plants. - Relatively recent HGT events occurred in charophytes and all major land plant groups, but their frequency declined rapidly in seed plants. - Two major episodes of HGT events occurred in land plant evolution: one corresponding to the early evolution of streptophytes and the other to the origin of land plants. - A vast majority of the genes acquired during these two episodes have been retained in descendant groups, affecting numerous activities and processes of land plants. - The researchers analyzed acquired genes involved in stress responses, ion and metabolite transport, growth and development, and specialized metabolism, and assessed the cumulative effects of HGT in land plants. The article contains 4 figures, including: (1) summary of HGT event numbers in 12 representative species of charophytes; (2) analyses of dityrosine biosynthesis protein 1 (DIT1) from lycophytes and fungi; (3) horizontal transfer of the ALS3/NAP3 ABC transporter complex genes; and (4) additional examples of horizontally acquired genes in plants. Key words: plant evolution, adaptation, streptophytes, cumulative effect, stress response, growth and development. Article metrics: 116-117 citations, 147 Mendeley readers, 1 blog mention, 7 news mentions, and 149 social media shares/likes/comments. The article has been cited by 117 works, including a notable example: the Fhb7 gene horizontally transferred from Fusarium to Thinopyrum elongatum for head blight resistance in wheat (discussed in a citing article on plant pan-genomics). "We found that relatively recent HGT events occurred in charophytes and all major land plant groups, but their frequency declined rapidly in seed plants. Two major episodes of HGT events occurred in land plant evolution, corresponding to the early evolution of streptophytes and the origin of land plants, respectively." --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We have read the article “Evidence for extensive horizontal gene transfer from the draft genome of a tardigrade” ([1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1525116113#core-collateral-r1)) with interest and were astonished by the high number of genes horizontally transferred into the tardigrade genome. Still, we were surprised by the reported genome size of >200 Mbp, which is in stark contrast to a previously published size of ∼78 Mbp determined by the same group ([2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1525116113#core-collateral-r2)).

To investigate this difference, we reestimated the genome size based on the Illumina read datasets _k_-mer spectra. Averaged, the estimated genome size was (109 No alternative text available 18) Mbp and thereby in close agreement with the experimental estimates. Close examination of the _k_-mer spectra revealed a substantial number of _k_-mers with a coverage much lower than the true genome peak(s), pointing to a substantial amount of contamination. Because contaminations can impede the assembly process dramatically, we set out to reduce them upfront. First, we identified those _k_-mers that are present in all Illumina read datasets (trusted _k_-mers). Next, we extracted all Moleculo reads covered by at least 95% with trusted _k_-mers. Indeed, only 9.6% of the _k_-mers were supported by all read datasets. Still, these recovered 90% of the Moleculo dataset, providing an expected genome coverage of 60-fold.

We then assembled the trusted and the untrusted Moleculo reads separately. The trusted dataset assembled into 126 Mbp (N50 17 Kbp), an assembly size that fits with our previous estimates and is in agreement with results of an independent genome project ([3](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1525116113#core-collateral-r3)). The untrusted dataset resulted in an assembly of 39 Mbp (N50 110 Mbp), showing a suspiciously high number of large contigs (1.1 Mbp to 4.7 Mbp). In total, the untrusted assembly encoded 38,305 genes, of which 5,576 were almost identical (identity ≥99%, expected value ≤1 No alternative text available No alternative text available) to 3,641 genes predicted by ref. [1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1525116113#core-collateral-r1). Of those, 2,200 had reciprocal best hits in 1,501 genes that were flagged horizontal gene transfer (HGT)-derived by ref. [1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1525116113#core-collateral-r1). Comparing structural features revealed that both assemblies are dramatically different in their GC spectra, their per-site coverage, and their per-site variability, as well as their gene spacing ([Fig. 1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1525116113#fig01)).

(_A_) Per-site coverage of trusted and untrusted assembly based on mappings of Moleculo reads. Contigs from the untrusted assembly generally don’t share the coverage of the trusted, most likely nuclear, genome. (_B_) GC content of trusted and untrusted assembly estimated using sliding window approach. The untrusted assembly contains multiple peaks pointing toward contig subpopulations with different GC content. (_C_) Per-site variability of trusted and untrusted assembly, which can serve as ploidy proxy. The untrusted variability spectrum seems distorted and contains a multitude of different peaks, whereas the trusted assembly shows a typical diploid spectrum. (_D_) Length distribution of intergenetic regions. Intragenetic regions are significantly larger in the trusted assembly than in the untrusted.

Closer inspection of the largest contigs revealed that they strongly resemble complete bacterial genomes ([Fig. 2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1525116113#fig02)), with up to 4,783 genes on a single contig. For us, it seems highly unlikely that the genome of _Hypsibius dujardini_ contains continuous parts of bacterial sequences in the size of up to 4.7 Mbp, coding for several thousand genes, with different structural properties than the rest of the eukaryotic genome. Rather, we see this as strong evidence for a dramatic bacterial contamination in the assembly.

Fig. 2.

Open in Viewer![Image 7](https://www.pnas.org/cms/10.1073/pnas.1525116113/asset/39770347-aa42-4013-9993-9639a7b92413/assets/graphic/pnas.1525116113fig02.jpeg)

Circular map of an unknown bacterial genome probably belonging to the _Chitinophagaceae_ drawn with CGView. Tracks 1 and 2 (blue) indicate GeneMark-S annotated genes on forward and reverse strand. Track 3 (red) visualizes regions of homology to a set of 30,844 _Chitinophagaceae_ proteins downloaded from UniProtKB. Track 4 (green) shows homology between GeneMark-S predicted proteins and the published protein set of ref. [1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1525116113#core-collateral-r1).

Admittedly, bacterial contamination can hardly be avoided when sequencing complete animals. Still, finding noneukaryotic genes in a eukaryotic background does not necessarily point to HGT, especially without a proper quality control of input data and further experimental evidence. We thus suggest that the published high rate of HGT in the genome of _H. dujardini_ is an artifact of sample preparation rather than a biological signal.

args.summary:
This is a PNAS Letter (published online May 12, 2016, in issue Vol. 113, No. 22, pages E3054-E3056) titled "Genome of a tardigrade: Horizontal gene transfer or bacterial contamination?" by Felix Bemm, Clemens Leonard Weiß, Jörg Schultz, and Frank Förster.

CONTEXT: The letter responds to a November 2015 research article by Boothby et al. that claimed "extensive horizontal gene transfer (HGT)" in the draft genome of the tardigrade Hypsibius dujardini. The authors were astonished by the reported >200 Mbp genome size, contrasting with the same group's earlier estimate of ~78 Mbp.

METHODOLOGY AND FINDINGS: The authors reestimated the genome size using k-mer spectra from Illumina read datasets, finding an averaged size of ~109 ± 18 Mbp. They discovered substantial contamination (k-mers with coverage much lower than genome peaks). They identified "trusted" k-mers present in all read datasets (only 9.6% of k-mers) that still recovered 90% of the Moleculo dataset at ~60-fold coverage. The trusted dataset assembled into 126 Mbp (N50 17 Kbp), fitting prior estimates; the untrusted dataset assembled into 39 Mbp with suspiciously large contigs (1.1-4.7 Mbp), encoding 38,305 genes, of which 5,576 were nearly identical to Boothby et al.'s predicted genes (with 2,200 reciprocal best hits in 1,501 genes flagged as HGT-derived).

KEY EVIDENCE OF CONTAMINATION: The largest contigs resembled complete bacterial genomes (up to 4,783 genes on a single contig), likely from the Chitinophagaceae family (visualized in a circular CGView map). The trusted and untrusted assemblies differed dramatically in GC spectra, per-site coverage, per-site variability (ploidy proxy), and gene spacing.

CONCLUSION: The authors argue it is "highly unlikely" that H. dujardini's genome contains continuous bacterial sequences up to 4.7 Mbp with thousands of genes; they view this as strong evidence of bacterial contamination. They conclude that "the published high rate of HGT in the genome of H. dujardini is an artifact of sample preparation rather than a biological signal," noting that finding noneukaryotic genes in a eukaryotic background doesn't necessarily indicate HGT without proper quality control and experimental evidence.

RELATED ARTICLES: This letter is accompanied by another letter from Kazuharu Arakawa ("No evidence for extensive horizontal gene transfer from the draft genome of a tardigrade," DOI 10.1073/pnas.1602711113) and a reply by Boothby and Goldstein ("Reply to Bemm et al. and Arakawa," DOI 10.1073/pnas.1601149113). It references Koutsovoulos et al. (2016, "No evidence for extensive horizontal gene transfer in the genome of the tardigrade Hypsibius dujardini").

DATA AVAILABILITY: All scripts, settings, and methodological details are available at https://github.com/greatfireball/hypsibius_genome_revised.

METRICS: The article has 8,402 total views, 41 total citations, and an Altmetric score of 54 (picked up by 1 news outlet, 5 blogs, 20 X users, 3 Wikipedia pages, 3 Reddit posts, 1 Bluesky user).

# No evidence for extensive horizontal gene transfer in the genome of the tardigrade *Hypsibius dujardini*

* Georgios Koutsovoulos
* , Sujai Kumar
* , Dominik R Laetsch
* , Lewis Stevens
* , [Jennifer Daub](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/persons/jennifer-daub/)
* , [Claire Conlon](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/persons/claire-conlon/)
* , Habib Maroon
* , Fran Thomas
* , Aziz A Aboobaker
* , Mark Blaxter

* [School of Biological Sciences](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/organisations/school-of-biological-sciences/)

Research output: Contribution to journal › Article › peer-review

## Abstract

Tardigrades are meiofaunal ecdysozoans that are key to understanding the origins of Arthropoda. Many species of Tardigrada can survive extreme conditions through cryptobiosis. In a recent paper [Boothby TC, et al. (2015) *Proc Natl Acad Sci USA* 112(52):15976-15981], the authors concluded that the tardigrade *Hypsibius dujardini* had an unprecedented proportion (17%) of genes originating through functional horizontal gene transfer (fHGT) and speculated that fHGT was likely formative in the evolution of cryptobiosis. We independently sequenced the genome of *H. dujardini.* As expected from whole-organism DNA sampling, our raw data contained reads from nontarget genomes. Filtering using metagenomics approaches generated a draft *H. dujardini* genome assembly of 135 Mb with superior assembly metrics to the previously published assembly. Additional microbial contamination likely remains. We found no support for extensive fHGT. Among 23,021 gene predictions we identified 0.2% strong candidates for fHGT from bacteria and 0.2% strong candidates for fHGT from nonmetazoan eukaryotes. Cross-comparison of assemblies showed that the overwhelming majority of HGT candidates in the Boothby et al. genome derived from contaminants. We conclude that fHGT into *H. dujardini* accounts for at most 1-2% of genes and that the proposal that one-sixth of tardigrade genes originate from functional HGT events is an artifact of undetected contamination.
