In addition to the native copies of _atp1, atp6_, and _matR_, a second copy of each of these genes was amplified from _P. coronopus_ and _P. macrorhiza_. A second copy of _atp1_ and _matR_ was also amplified from _P. subspathulata_. These additional copies all group in an anomalous position, together with or within Convolvulaceae (Solanales), with high bootstrap support (Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F1)). Moreover, in each case, they are nested within the parasitic genus _Cuscuta_, a position that is weakly supported for two genes and strongly supported (90%) for _atp6_(Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F1)). Taken together, the strongly supported placement of these sequences within Convolulaceae, their close affinity with _Cuscuta_ and their strongly supported exclusion from the _Plantago_ clades of native homologs indicate that all three genes were probably transferred horizontally from a species of _Cuscuta_ into the common ancestor of _P. coronopus_, _P. macrorhiza_ and _P. subspathulata_. [Note that none of the three genes was recovered from either _P. crassifolia_ or _P. maritima_, the two successively sister lineages of the _P. coronopus_ clade.]

Errors in phylogenetic reconstruction can lead to erroneous claims of HGT. However, this is unlikely to be the case here. For each gene, the phylogenetic position of the putative foreign copies is robust; their placement was unaffected by choice of phylogenetic method (maximum likelihood, parsimony or neighbour-joining), by elimination of predicted sites of RNA editing from the data, by removing the native _Plantago_ genes from the data or by broadening the taxon sampling to representatives from across core eudicots (Additional File [4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#S4)). Furthermore, for all three genes, the Shimodaira-Hasegawa test [[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B61)], which is a likelihood-based statistical test of alternative tree topologies, strongly rejected (_P_< 0.05) the placement of the foreign clade within Plantaginaceae in the position expected if the clade arose by gene duplication rather than by HGT (Additional File [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#S5)). More generally, with the exception of the anomalous placement of the foreign clade of _Plantago_ sequences, the strongly supported relationships throughout the rest of the three gene trees are consistent with the currently accepted organismal phylogeny [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B62)], arguing against any pervasive phylogenetic issues.

It has been argued that nuclear-encoded fragments of mitochondrial DNA (numts) may sometimes be mistaken for horizontally transferred DNA [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B45),[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B46)], perhaps due to phylogenetic artifacts arising from the very different mutation rates in the two genomes. In general, however, numts should behave like gene duplications in phylogenetic analyses and group with their mitochondrial progenitor sequences. As described above, this is clearly not the case for the _Plantago_ sequences. Indeed, the strongly supported placement of the putatively foreign _Plantago_ copy of all three mitochondrial genes with Convolvulaceae (Solanales), convincingly apart from the native _Plantago_ homologs - which are well embedded within multiple strongly supported lineages of Lamiales (Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F1)) - makes the numt phylogenetic artifact hypothesis untenable in the case of _Plantago_.

Misidentification or contamination of DNA is another problem that can lead to incorrect inferences of HGT. However, wholesale misidentification can be clearly ruled out by the fact that intact sequences grouping within Plantaginaceae have been obtained for multiple loci (including 10 mitochondrial, six plastid and two nuclear loci from _P. coronopus_) from all _Plantago_ samples used in this study (Additional File [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#S3)) and during our previous investigations of substitution rates [[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B56)]. Contamination of DNA stocks with some unknown secondary source can also be discounted. All horizontally acquired copies were amplified and sequenced at least twice from each DNA sample. Furthermore, at least two independent DNA samples were prepared from each plant grown at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln (Additional File [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#S3)). Finally, of all sequenced loci, only _atp1, atp6_ and _matR_ gave any indication that more than one gene copy was present, and all of these additional copies are clearly pseudogenes (see the next section). By contrast, contamination with DNA from a different plant would be expected to produce multiple gene copies from more than just three of the 38 surveyed mitochondrial genes, and all of the additional copies should look functional.

### Horizontally transferred genes are unexpressed pseudogenes

An unusual characteristic of _Plantago_ mitochondrial genes is that their nucleotide sequences are highly divergent due to the unusually high mutation rates [[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B55)-[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B58)]. This is evident here for the native copies of _atp1_, _atp6_ and _matR_(Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F1)). Despite this divergence, all of the native _Plantago_ sequences are intact with no frameshifting indels or internal stop codons (Additional File [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#S1)). In addition, all four native mitochondrial and plastid genes from _P. coronopus_ line C examined by reverse transcription (RT)-PCR - including the native _atp1_ and _matR_ genes - were found to be transcribed (Figure [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F2)), as were the native _atp1_ and _matR_ genes from _P. macrorhiza_ line B (data not shown). The smaller size and the presence of three C-to-U changes in the _P. coronopus cox1_ cDNA relative to genomic DNA (Figure [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F2), lane 3) indicate that the transcript had undergone intron splicing and RNA editing, which verifies that the cDNA sample was indeed derived from RNA. Thus, the native _atp1_, _atp6_ and _matR_ genes are likely to be _bona fide_ genes encoding functional _Plantago_ mitochondrial proteins.

### Phylogenetic incongruence within clades of horizontally acquired genes

We amplified and sequenced native copies of three mitochondrial genes (_atp1, atp6_ and _matR_), two plastid regions (_rbcL_ and intergenic _trnL/trnF_) and the internal transcribed spacer (ITS) of the nuclear ribosomal repeat from 4-6 species of _Plantago_, including multiple _P. coronopus_ and _P. macrorhiza_ lines for most genes, and at least two other members of Plantaginaceae (Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F1)). Phylogenetic relationships for all native loci are consistent with previous phylogenies [[59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B59),[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B60),[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B63)], although it should be noted that the particular relationship among _P. coronopus, P. macrorhiza_ and _P. subspathulata_ is not resolved here or elsewhere ([[59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B59),[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B60)]; JPM and JDP, unpublished data).

We also sequenced foreign copies of all three mitochondrial genes from the six different _P. coronopus_ and _P. macrorhiza_ lines. Surprisingly, the sequences from the different _P. coronopus_ lines were never monophyletic and the _P. macrorhiza_ lines were not monophyletic for the _atp6_ and _matR_ genes (Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F1)). Furthermore, the phylogenetic relationship among the foreign _atp1_ sequences varies dramatically compared to the topology for _matR_ and _atp6_. For example, _P. coronopus_ line A groups with lines B and C for _atp1_ but with line D for _atp6_ and _matR_. The inconsistent and reproducible phylogenetic pattern for various lines rules out seed misidentification as the source of taxonomic conflict and indicates a complicated evolutionary history for these pseudogenes.

### Complex patterns of sequence divergence in horizontally transferred genes

An unexpectedly complex history of the foreign genes following their arrival in _Plantago_ is also indicated by patterns of sequence divergence (Figure [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F1), Additional File [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#S1)). There are very few if any nucleotide differences among the native mitochondrial copies of _atp1, atp6_ and _matR_ within the _P. coronopus_ clade of three species. In fact, the most divergent sequences within the _P. coronopus_ clade for native mitochondrial genes are >99% identical to one another, which is comparable to divergence levels of plastid sequences sampled from the same plants. In stark contrast, the foreign genes are much more divergent. The most divergent sequences for the foreign genes are only 90%, 92% and 84% identical for _atp1_, _atp6_ and _matR_, respectively, and these extremes of divergence actually reside among the multiple lines of _P. coronopus_ sampled.

In order to explore this rate variation further, we used a codon-based model of sequence evolution to evaluate synonymous (dS) and non-synonymous (dN) divergence for native and foreign homologs from particular species pairs (Table [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#T1)). These analyses corroborate patterns observed by simple comparison of sequence identities: the native mitochondrial genes are essentially identical to one another, whereas the foreign homologs are much more divergent. Levels of synonymous divergence are 15-25 times higher between the foreign pseudogenes from _P. coronopus_ and _P. macrorhiza_ compared to native genes from the same species. Results from individual gene dS analyses are generally consistent with the combined analysis (Table [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#T1)). Non-synonymous values are more variable, which is probably the result of differential selection pressures acting on the genes, even the pseudogenes to some extent because ω < 1 in all cases.

The differences in the substitution rate between the native and foreign homologs suggest that either: (1) they do not reside in the same genome; (2) they are in the same genome but there is intra-genomic variability in the rate of synonymous substitution; or (3) not all of the foreign copies isolated for a particular gene are orthologous to one another. These are the subclades comprising _P. coronopus_ B and C and _P. subspathulata_ for _atp1_ and _P. coronopus_ A and D and _P. macrorhiza_ A for _atp6_.

### Multiple gene conversions of foreign _atp1_ by native _atp1_

The presence, owing to HGT, of two different copies of each of these three genes in the same plant prompted us to search systematically for evidence of any history of gene conversion between xenologs. The OrgConv program [[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B64)] failed to find evidence of gene conversion in _atp6_ and _matR_ but detected three significant (_P_< 0.001) candidate cases of gene conversion in _atp1_(Figure [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F3)). The first conversion event was identified in the foreign genes from _P. coronopus_ lines A-C and _P. subspathulata_. With the exception of a single autapomorphy in _P. coronopus_ B and C, all four foreign genes are identical over a 40 nt region (positions 150-189) to the native _atp1_ genes of _P. coronopus_ and _P. macrorhiza_ but differ from the _Cuscuta_ sequence (representing the donor group) at six or seven sites (Figure [3a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F3)). We therefore infer a native-to-foreign gene conversion event in the common ancestor of these four foreign _atp1_ sequences. The second example of gene conversion was found in the foreign _atp1_ genes from _P. macrorhiza_ lines A and B. In these two lines, a 15 nucleotide (nt) region (positions 298-312) is identical to the native _atp1_ copy from both _P. macrorhiza_ and _P. coronopus_ but differs from _Cuscuta atp1_ at five sites and from the other foreign _Plantago atp1_ genes at six sites (Figure [3a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F3)). The third conversion also involves the foreign _atp1_ gene from _P. macrorhiza_ line B and is found only in this sequence. However, unlike the previous example, the converting sequence does not appear to be the native _P. macrorhiza atp1_ gene. Instead, the 157-nt, putative conversion region (positions 582-738) is most similar to _P. sericea_(Figure [3a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F3)), a distantly related species of _Plantago_ in a different subgenus. Phylogenetic analysis places this converted region strongly with native _atp1_ genes from _P. lanceolata_ and _P. sericea_(89% bootstrap support), specifically as sister to _P. sericea_, whereas the unconverted sections of this sequence group in the originally identified position with the foreign _atp1_ copy of _P. macrorhiza_ line A (Figure [3b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F3)).

### Mitochondrial location of horizontally transferred genes

In previous studies [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B23),[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B25),[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B30),[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B31)], a mitochondrial location for horizontally acquired genes was inferred by finding sites of RNA editing in their transcripts. However, expression was not detected for any of the foreign copies identified here (Figure [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F2)), so we took advantage of the fact that the mitochondrial, plastid and nuclear genomes differ widely in copy number in plant cells to determine the compartmental location of these unexpressed pseudogenes. The plastid genome is generally present in hundreds to thousands of copies per leaf cell, the mitochondrial genome in tens to hundreds of copies per cell and the nuclear genome usually only in two copies per cell [[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B65),[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B66)]. As a precedent, we point out that the differential copy number between nuclear and mitochondrial genomes has enabled an accurate estimation of genome location by Southern blot hybridization (for example, [[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B54),[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B55)]). Here we use quantitative (q) PCR instead of blots for two reasons: the intrinsically quantitative nature of qPCR and the opportunity to factor out sequence divergence (by using primers that perfectly match all sequences; Southern blot studies can be confounded by differential substitution rates, both between mitochondrion and nucleus, and among plant lineages).

QPCR was performed with primers designed to known loci in the nuclear (_phyA_), mitochondrial (native _atp1_ and _cox1_) and plastid (_rbcL_ and intergenic spacer _trnL_/_trnF_) genomes, as well as to the horizontally acquired pseudogenes (_atp1, atp6_ and _matR_). All eight of these regions were amplified from _P. coronopus_ line C using total genomic DNA, mitochondrial-enriched DNA and plastid-enriched DNA and the relative intensities were compared (Figure [4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F4)). The known mitochondrial, plastid and nuclear genes display patterns generally consistent with expectation, although mitochondrial DNA copy number in _P. coronopus_ may be relatively low compared to other plants. In the total DNA preparation (Figure [4a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F4)), the plastid genes are in the highest copy (lowest cycle number), the nuclear gene is in the lowest copy and the mitochondrial genes are at an intermediate level. In the mitochondrial-enriched preparation (Figure [4b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F4)), the plastid DNA is still in the highest copy and the nuclear DNA remains the lowest but the mitochondrial DNA is shifted substantially to the left relative to the other two genomes, indicating that considerable enrichment for mitochondrial DNA was indeed achieved. In the plastid-enriched preparation (Figure [4c](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F4)), all three genomes are well-separated and, importantly, this preparation appears to be substantially enriched in both plastid _and_ mitochondrial sequences relative to nuclear ones.

Figure 4
[![Image 18: Figure 4](https://pmc-oa-opendata.s3.amazonaws.com/PMC3022774.1/1741-7007-8-150-4.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=3022774_1741-7007-8-150-4.jpg)

[Open in a new tab](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/figure/F4/)

**Genomic location of foreign genes**. Quantitative polymerase chain reaction was used to amplify five loci of known genomic origin [plastid _rbcL_(light green) and _trnL_/_trnF_(dark green), mitochondrial _atp1_(light pink) and _matR_(dark pink) and nuclear _phyA_(maroon)] and three foreign genes of uncertain provenance [_atp1_(light blue), _atp6_(medium blue) and _matR_(dark blue)]. All eight reactions were run in duplicate using as templates, either total genomic DNA (A), mitochondrial-enriched DNA (B) or plastid-enriched DNA (C) isolated from _Plantago coronopus_ line C.

For all three preparations of plant DNA, the three foreign genes amplify at rates comparable to the two native mitochondrial genes examined. This is most evident in the plastid-enriched DNA which provides the greatest separation among mitochondrial, plastid and nuclear genes, but it is also consistent in the other two DNA preparations. The clear and consistent association of the three foreign _atp1_ genes with mtDNA in terms of copy number indicates that, in _P. coronopus_ line C at least, they are located in the mitochondrion, most likely integrated into the mitochondrial genome.

### Gene transfer was DNA mediated

There are a number of possible mechanisms of horizontal transfer, some of which include a stage involving RNA. In order to test whether transfer occurred through an RNA intermediate, we looked for evidence of C-to-U RNA editing that occurs at multiple positions in nearly all mitochondrial protein-gene transcripts from flowering plants [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B47)-[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B53)]. If an RNA intermediate is involved, there must be a point at which the transcript is reverse transcribed back into cDNA. Assuming that reverse transcription occurs after RNA editing of the transcript, the edited positions containing U in the RNA will be reverse transcribed to T residues in the cDNA. Thus, an RNA-mediated gene transfer event should contain T residues at most, or all, sites of RNA editing in the original donor gene [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B34),[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B35)], whereas a transfer of genomic DNA should retain C residues at the edit sites.

A comparison of editing positions in _Cuscuta_ to homologous positions in the _Plantago_ HGT copies shows that there is no evidence for a massive C to T conversion in _Plantago_ that would be expected if the transfer(s) was RNA mediated (Figure [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#F5)). Known edit sites in six species were used to predict edit sites in _C. europaea_ using the RNA-editing prediction tool PREP-Aln [[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3022774#B67)]. In total, 26 edit sites are predicted for _C. europaea_: 1 in _atp1_, 15 in _atp6_ and 10 in _matR_. Of these, 22 are in regions also sequenced for the HGT copies from _P. coronopus_ and _P. macrorhiza_. _P. macrorhiza_ has a cytidine at all 22 positions and _P. coronopus_ has 20

args.summary:
This scientific article, published in BMC Biology (Dec 22, 2010), investigates the horizontal gene transfer (HGT) of mitochondrial genes between parasitic plants of the genus Cuscuta (dodders) and species of Plantago. The study was conducted by Jeffrey P. Mower and colleagues from Indiana University Bloomington, University of Nebraska-Lincoln, and University of Toronto institutions.

Key findings:
- A PCR-based survey of 38 mitochondrial genes revealed that at least three genes (atp1, atp6, and matR) were recently transferred from Cuscuta to a small clade of three closely-related Plantago species (P. coronopus, P. macrorhiza, and P. subspathulata).
- The identical phylogenetic distribution of the three foreign genes indicates they were likely acquired via a single, DNA-mediated HGT event - the best evidence to date that multiple mitochondrial genes can be transferred through a single HGT event.
- Quantitative PCR assays demonstrated that the three transferred genes have a mitochondrial location in Plantago coronopus line C.
- All transferred genes degraded into pseudogenes shortly after transfer (containing indels disrupting reading frames and introducing premature stop codons), and RT-PCR analyses showed none are detectably transcribed.
- Three cases of gene conversion were detected between native and foreign copies of the atp1 gene, detected via the OrgConv program (P < 0.001), suggesting transferred genes may generate mitochondrial genetic diversity.
- Evidence for DNA-mediated transfer came from retention of cytidines at ancestral RNA editing sites - of 22 predicted edit sites, P. macrorhiza retained cytidines at all 22 positions and P. coronopus at 20, ruling out an RNA intermediate.
- Sampling of multiple individuals from recipient Plantago revealed complex phylogenetic discrepancies and patterns of sequence divergence, implying a complicated post-transfer history likely involving additional transfers, gene duplication, differential loss, and mutation-rate variation (synonymous divergence was 15-25 times higher in foreign genes than native genes).

The study's conclusions suggest that direct haustorial contact between parasitic plants and their hosts facilitates genetic transfer, and that further research will require sequencing multiple mitochondrial and nuclear genomes from Plantago to fully unravel this history.

Research the comparative, historical, and methodological framing of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in multicellular eukaryotes (plants and animals) versus prokaryotes/microbes, and the history of discovery. Priorities: primary peer-reviewed literature (Nature, Science, PNAS, PLOS, Annual Reviews, Trends in Genetics) and landmark original papers. (b) TIMESCALES AND HISTORICAL CONTEXT: describe the history of HGT discovery in eukaryotes - from the earliest evidence (e.g., 1980s-1990s observations of bacterial-like genes, the 2001 Amborella mitochondrial genome finding by Adams et al., the 2011-2012 landmark genome-scale analyses by Yue et al. and the special issue on HGT in plants), the late 2000s bdelloid rotifer discoveries, and how advances in whole-genome sequencing, phylogenomics, and bioinformatics tools (e.g., detection methods based on compositional bias like GC content and codon usage, phylogenetic incongruence, and synteny with donor genomes) transformed the field; discuss the controversy and standards of evidence for detecting HGT (e.g., the tardigrade retraction debate about contamination and assembly artifacts). (c) OPEN QUESTIONS AND DEBATES: ongoing disputes about the extent and functional importance of HGT in plants and animals, the debate over neutral 'killer' acquisitions versus adaptive transfers, and whether some 'HGT' findings are artifacts of contamination or incomplete lineage sorting. --- SOURCE 1: Horizontal transfer of entire genomes via mitochondrial ... ---
URL: https://pure.psu.edu/en/publications/horizontal-transfer-of-entire-genomes-via-mitochondrial-fusion-in

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the Penn State PURE research database listing for the peer-reviewed article "Horizontal transfer of entire genomes via mitochondrial fusion in the angiosperm Amborella," published in the journal Science in 2013 (Volume 342, Issue 6165, pages 1468-1473). The article reports the complete mitochondrial genome sequence of the flowering plant Amborella trichopoda, an enormous 3.9-megabase genome containing six genome equivalents of foreign mitochondrial DNA acquired from green algae, mosses, and other angiosperms. Many of these horizontal transfers were large, including acquisition of entire mitochondrial genomes from three green algae and one moss. The authors propose a fusion-compatibility model to explain these findings, whereby Amborella captures whole mitochondria from diverse eukaryotes, followed by mitochondrial fusion (limited mechanistically to green plant mitochondria) and subsequent genome recombination. Factors contributing to the high level of foreign DNA include Amborella's epiphyte load, propensity to produce suckers from wounds, and its low rate of mitochondrial DNA loss. The article was authored by Danny W. Rice, Andrew J. Alverson, Aaron O. Richardson, Gregory J. Young, M. Virginia Sanchez-Puerta, Jérôme Munzinger, Kerrie Barry, Jeffrey L. Boore, Yan Zhang, Claude W. DePamphilis, Eric B. Knox, and Jeffrey D. Palmer, and has 353 Scopus citations. DOI: 10.1126/science.1246275.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This enormous, 3.9-megabase genome contains six genome equivalents of foreign mitochondrial DNA, acquired from green algae, mosses, and other angiosperms."; "Many of these horizontal transfers were large, including acquisition of entire mitochondrial genomes from three green algae and one moss."; "We propose a fusion-compatibility model to explain these findings, with Amborella capturing whole mitochondria from diverse eukaryotes, followed by mitochondrial fusion (limited mechanistically to green plant mitochondria) and then genome recombination."; "Amborella's epiphyte load, propensity to produce suckers from wounds, and low rate of mitochondrial DNA loss probably all contribute to the high level of foreign DNA in its mitochondrial genome."

SUMMARY:
<summary>

They note that mitochondrial fusion in animals and fungi uses dynamin-related GTPases absent from green plants, suggesting a fundamentally different fusion mechanism in green plants. KEY FINDINGS ON PREVALENCE:
- HGT is significantly more common in plant genomes than previously assumed, involving transfers from bacteria, fungi, insects, and viruses
- Over 600 plant-to-plant HGT cases reported; more than 42% involve parasitic plants (Orobanchaceae and Convolvulaceae families) and their hosts, facilitated by haustorium contact

- Plant-to-insect HGT documented in whitefly Bemisia tabaci (25+ plant-derived genes, including a phenolic glucoside malonyltransferase gene)
- Viruses, particularly Caulimoviridae, found integrated in nuclear genomes of many plants

MECHANISMS OF HGT:
1. Genetic material exits donor nucleus via: transcription/mRNA export (mobile via plasmodesmata and phloem), double-strand breaks from genotoxic stress, apoptosis, or extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA, up to 400 kbp)
2. Transport to recipient via: haustoria (parasitic gateway), natural grafting (stock-scion contact), illegitimate pollination (heterospecific pollen in wind-pollinated grasses), or vectors (viruses, bacteria, nematodes, insects, fungi)
3. Integration requires nuclear import, with mRNA requiring reverse transcription (possibly via TE-associated reverse transcriptases or Caulimoviridae)

TRANSGENERATIONAL CONSIDERATIONS:
- HGT in vegetative tissues may be an evolutionary dead end unless germ cells arise from somatic cells (unlike animals)
- Vegetative/asexual reproduction (rhizomes, tubers, bulbs, runners, stolons, suckers, bulbils, epiphyllous buds) provides a plausible route for transgenerational inheritance of horizontally transferred genes
- Underground vegetative buds contact the rhizosphere, increasing exposure to foreign DNA

DETECTION METHODS:
- High sequence similarity between donor and recipient (higher than vertical orthologs)
- Phylogenetic incongruence with species phylogeny
- Patchy taxonomic distributions
- Detection constrained by a "window of HGT observation" defined by genetic divergence, transfer age, and gene fate
- Requires integration of multiple lines of evidence plus experimental validation to rule out contamination

CONCLUSION: Expanding phylogenomic scrutiny of the plant kingdom should reveal the full extent of HGT. In situ sequencing and combinations of synthetic biology and experimental evolution may allow catching ongoing HGT and testing functional relevance of such events.

- The study uses both a deterministic model based on the Price equation and stochastic computer simulations.
- Three key assumptions: (1) coevolution independently changes both connectivity and indispensability; (2) a collective of spatially segregated microbial populations exists (some hosting the gene, some naïve); (3) environments have two states—selective (gene provides fitness advantage) and neutral (no advantage).

- When β = 0.06 (low HGT opportunity), the transferable gene persisted in only 2 populations by evolving toward a more sessile state (higher indispensability and connectivity), despite the absence of coevolution causing extinction.
- When β = 0.08 (higher HGT opportunity), the gene evolved toward a more itinerant state (lower indispensability and connectivity), with the metapopulation expanding from ~800 to nearly 9,000 populations.
- The evolutionary outcome transitions from sessile to itinerant between β = 0.06 and β = 0.08.
- The opportunity to enter new microbial populations via HGT can drive connectivity toward lower values, especially in unstable environments; lack of such opportunity in stable environments drives connectivity toward higher values.

Predictions and potential tests:
- A gene might evolve more sessile when there is a stable selective environment (δ ≈ 0) but little opportunity for HGT (β ≈ 0), as might be found in oligotrophic environments (open ocean, deep subsurface, polar ice caps) for genes conferring nutrient metabolism.
- A gene might evolve more itinerant when HGT opportunity is high (β > 0) and environmental exposure to selective pressures is intermittent (δ > 0), as might be found in pathogens episodically exposed to antimicrobial substances.
- Predictions could be tested by comparing genes of these types or by comparing transferable genes in species with broad versus narrow niche breadth.

Conclusion: The model suggests connectivity can evolve toward higher values (sessile, less transferable) or lower values (itinerant, more transferable) depending on ecological conditions, consistent with the simplicity hypothesis. However, the authors note that better understanding of gene-host coevolutionary dynamics in natural microbial systems is required before further conclusions can be drawn about the hypothesis's veracity.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PNAS research article titled "Horizontal gene transfer among genomes: The complexity hypothesis" by Ravi Jain, Maria C. Rivera, and James A. Lake, published March 30, 1999 (Vol. 96, No. 7, pp. 3801-3806, DOI: 10.1073/pnas.96.7.3801). The article has been cited 871 times with 22,353 total views.

**Background and Hypotheses:** The paper addresses horizontal gene transfer (HGT) among prokaryotes. Previous research showed that operational genes (housekeeping functions) are frequently horizontally transferred, while informational genes (transcription, translation, and related processes) are rarely transferred. Two competing hypotheses were tested: (1) the continual horizontal transfer hypothesis—operational genes have been transferred continuously since prokaryote divergence, and (2) the early massive horizontal transfer hypothesis—one or a few massive gene exchanges occurred early in prokaryotic evolution before diversification.

**Methodology:** The researchers analyzed six complete prokaryotic genomes: Aquifex aeolicus, Escherichia coli, Synechocystis 6803, Bacillus subtilis, Methanococcus jannaschii, and Archaeoglobus fulgidus. They identified 312 orthologous gene sets (203 operational and 109 informational), with 144 reliable orthologs (88 operational, 56 informational) used for testing. Analyses included star sequence alignments, paralog rooting, three phylogenetic methods (Jukes-Cantor distances, maximum parsimony, and paralinear/logdet distances), and tree distance metrics including peripheral branch-transfer and prune-and-regraft distances.

**Key Results:** Three tests consistently supported the continual horizontal transfer hypothesis: (1) Paralog rooting showed significantly different root distributions between operational and informational trees (P<0.0039, χ²=13.35); (2) Operational trees had mean peripheral branch-transfer distance of 2.3 steps vs. 1.2 for informational trees (P<0.0003, χ²=23.0); (3) Prune-and-regraft distance analysis showed >40% of operational trees require 2+ transfers vs. <10% for informational trees (P<0.00007, χ²=19.08). Branch length analysis showed mean central branch lengths were significantly shorter for operational trees (0.071 ± 0.05) than informational trees (0.237 ± 0.05 substitutions per position), consistent with extensive horizontal transfer in operational genes, while peripheral branch lengths showed minimal rate differences.

**The Complexity Hypothesis:** The authors propose that informational genes are members of large, complex systems (e.g., translation requires ~100 coordinated gene products in E. coli), whereas operational genes typically interact with few products (e.g., thioredoxin-thioredoxin reductase complex). Using a simplified model where each required interaction has a 0.25 probability, a transferred ribosomal protein S5 would have success probability of 0.25⁶ (=0.00024), about 1,000 times less than a thioredoxin protein requiring one interaction. The authors suggest the operational gene component of prokaryotes can be viewed functionally as "a single global organism" due to the vast extent of horizontal transfer.

**Funding/Acknowledgments:** Research supported by NSF grants to J.A.L. and an NIH predoctoral training grant to R.J. Data available at http://www.lifesci.ucla.edu/medbio/faculty/Lake/Research/Complexity/.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 15: The Evolution of Biological Complexity | National Center for Science Education ---
URL: https://ncse.ngo/evolution-biological-complexity

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in the Reports of the National Center for Science Education (Volume 26, No. 3, May-June 2006) by Finn Pond of Whitworth College, argues that naturalistic/evolutionary models can plausibly explain the origin of biological complexity, countering claims by "Intelligent Design" (ID) advocates. ID proponents, following Michael Behe's "irreducible complexity" argument (from Darwin's Black Box, 1996), contend that only an "intelligent agent" can generate the information content and complexity in biological systems. Behe argued the bacterial flagellum is irreducibly complex—a system where removing any part causes it to cease functioning, which cannot be produced by slight, successive modifications of a precursor system.

The paper reviews four naturalistic models:
1) Incremental additions model: An initially beneficial association of components becomes essential over time (e.g., RNase P, where RNA has catalytic activity alone at very low activity, but functions better with its protein partner; hammerhead ribozymes showing 10-20 fold increased activity in the presence of RNA-binding proteins).
2) Scaffolding model: "Redundant complexity" and superfluous components are lost, leaving tightly-matched components (analogous to building an arch with scaffolding; gene duplications and variant isoforms serve as examples).
3) Co-option model: Existing structures are recruited for new functions (e.g., the Krebs/citric acid cycle, where intermediate stages had functions apart from their role in the cycle; V(D)J gene splicing in vertebrate immune systems; butterfly eyespots, vertebrate limbs, complex leaves, and feathers).
4) Emerging complexity/self-organization model: Schneider's "ev" program simulated evolution via mutation and selection, demonstrating that Darwinian processes can generate new information (measured in bits via Shannon information theory) and irreducibly complex systems from a random genome.

The paper critiques William Dembski's responses (in No Free Lunch, 2002), who demanded "causal specificity" and objected to the "ev" program (Schneider eliminated the disputed rule and found the same results; David Wolpert, co-developer of the No Free Lunch Theorems, said Dembski applied the theorems inappropriately). Howard Van Till noted that hypotheses falling short of full causal specificity may still be highly plausible applications of partially understood mechanisms, and complained that ID tends to denigrate them as "just-so stories."

The paper also critiques Dembski's "specified complexity" criterion (probability of 10^-150 for design) and his application to the bacterial flagellum. Dembski's probability calculation treated the flagellum as a discrete combinatorial object assembling by pure chance—a scenario no biologist has ever proposed. Dembski failed to account for all relevant ways an event might occur, despite stating this was necessary.

The conclusion presents Kwang Jeon's 1966 experiment where amoebae cultures dying from bacterial infection eventually recovered, establishing a mutually obligate endosymbiosis (essentially a new cell organelle) through undirected natural processes—demonstrating that natural causes can generate irreducibly linked systems. The paper concludes that demanding a detailed chain of causality is unrealistic, and that calculating the probability of the flagellum assembling by pure chance to detect design is simply wrong.
</summary>

"By irreducibly complex I mean a single system composed of several well-matched, interacting parts that contribute to the basic function, wherein the removal of any one of the parts causes the system to effectively cease functioning." (Behe 1996: 39)

URL: https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/882418

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A news release from the Marine Biological Laboratory (MBL) reports on a study published in Science (2008) by researchers Irina Arkhipova (MBL's Josephine Bay Paul Center), Matthew Meselson (Harvard University), and Harvard graduate student Eugene Gladyshev. The study presents the first evidence of massive horizontal gene transfer in the animal kingdom—numerous chunks of foreign DNA from bacteria, fungi, and plants were discovered in the genome of the bdelloid rotifer Adineta vaga. While horizontal gene transfer is common in bacteria, it was previously unheard of on such a large scale in animals.

This finding may help explain how bdelloid rotifers, which are exclusively asexual, have diversified into more than 360 species over 40 million years of evolution—a phenomenon sometimes called an "evolutionary scandal" because it contradicts the notion that sexual reproduction confers evolutionary advantage. The study suggests that if bdelloids can incorporate foreign DNA from their environment, they could also pick up DNA from other bdelloids, which evolutionarily is almost as good as having sex.

The researchers propose a mechanism: bdelloids can survive total desiccation by entering a dehydrated suspended state, and during this phase both the rotifer and its food break down, potentially allowing foreign DNA to enter the germ line. During rehydration, DNA breakage is repaired and foreign DNA may become incorporated. This idea was inspired by earlier work (Gladyshev and Meselson, 2008) showing bdelloids are exceptionally good at recovering from ionizing radiation that shatters DNA. Most foreign genes were clustered near chromosome tips (telomeres). The work was supported by the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health. Citation: Gladyshev, E.A., M. Meselson, and I.R. Arkhipova. 2008. Massive Horizontal Gene Transfer in Bdelloid Rotifers. Science 320: 1210-1213.

--- SOURCE 1: Massive horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes from ... ---
URL: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0408336102

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PNAS research article (published December 14, 2004, in volume 101, issue 51, pages 17747-17752) by Ulfar Bergthorsson, Aaron O. Richardson, Gregory J. Young, Leslie R. Goertzen, and Jeffrey D. Palmer, titled "Massive horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes from diverse land plant donors to the basal angiosperm Amborella."

STUDY PURPOSE: The researchers investigated whether plants could acquire multiple foreign genes through horizontal gene transfer (HGT), moving beyond the previously known cases of single-gene acquisition. They focused on Amborella trichopoda, a basal angiosperm (a monotypic genus of shrubs endemic to New Caledonia) that was already known to possess one horizontally acquired gene and showed signs of containing more.

METHODOLOGY: The team used PCR amplification with conserved primers (~100 primer pairs) to comprehensively sequence the mitochondrial protein gene set of Amborella, plus variable numbers of mitochondrial genes from 28 other diverse land plants. They also conducted maximum-likelihood and parsimony phylogenetic analyses, using the Shimodaira-Hasegawa (SH) test to assess whether phylogenetically anomalous gene placements suggestive of HGT were statistically significant. To rule out contamination, HGT cases were confirmed from multiple independent DNA preparations from four different sources of Amborella material.

KEY RESULTS:
- Of the 40 protein genes present in the ancestral angiosperm mitochondrial genome, 31 were recovered from Amborella.
- Of these 31 genes, 20 showed evidence of one or more cases of HGT, for a total of 26 foreign genes acquired.
- Most transfers came from other angiosperms (especially eudicots), while others came from nonangiosperms, including six striking cases of transfer from at least three different moss donors.
- The five sequenced angiosperm mitochondrial genomes (rice, Arabidopsis, Brassica, Beta, and others) showed no evidence of HGT.
- Most transferred genes are intact (functional or recently transferred), while nine are pseudogenes.
- Evidence suggests the transferred genes reside in the mitochondrial genome (not chloroplast or nuclear), based on RNA editing patterns characteristic of mitochondria, nucleotide substitution rates, and PCR abundance.
- The 11 remaining singleton genes appear to be of vertical descent, placing Amborella as sister to all other angiosperms.

DISCUSSION AND SIGNIFICANCE: Amborella mtDNA has sustained proportionately more HGT than any other eukaryotic, or perhaps prokaryotic, genome yet examined. The study suggests HGT incidence varies markedly between plants. The authors speculate that Amborella's environment—mid-elevation montane tropical rain forests in New Caledonia where the plant's leaves and stems are often covered with diverse epiphytes including mosses—could promote direct plant-to-plant HGT (similar to mechanisms proposed for parasitic plants). The authors note limitations of their PCR approach, including missing rRNA/tRNA genes, chloroplast-derived sequences, and intergenic DNA, and emphasize that only sequencing the complete Amborella mitochondrial genome can comprehensively census its horizontally acquired DNA. They cite the SH test as supporting 14 of the transfers, with divergent duplicates in plant mtDNA representing xenologs (horizontal products) rather than paralogs.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Results indicate that Amborella has acquired one or more copies of 20 of its 31 known mitochondrial protein genes from other land plants, for a total of 26 foreign genes, whereas no evidence for HGT was found in the five sequenced genomes."; "Most of the Amborella transfers are from other angiosperms (especially eudicots), whereas others are from nonangiosperms, including six striking cases of transfer from (at least three different) moss donors."; "Amborella mtDNA has sustained proportionately more HGT than any other eukaryotic, or perhaps even prokaryotic, genome yet examined."; "Clearly, then, the incidence of HGT varies markedly from one plant to another. One wonders how many other Amborella-type situations exist among the ≈255,000 species of flowering plants."; "We are lucky that, of all angiosperms, Amborella happens to be so rich in HGT, because its distinctive position at the base of angiosperms makes it relatively easy to detect with reasonable confidence transfers from other angiosperms, even with the scanty taxon sampling of this study."

They selected 43 angiosperm genomes and 151 plant-associated bacteria to construct ortholog groups using OrthoFinder (2987 groups after filtering). Phylogenetic trees were constructed using RAxML, and HGT events were detected following methods adapted from Yang et al. Validation involved adding more taxa, BLAST searches against refseq databases, hidden Markov models, protein domain checks, and statistical analysis. HGTs were functionally annotated using the KEGG pathway database, and gene expression was analyzed in GENEVESTIGATOR.

RESULTS:
- 373 potential HGT events were identified (present in more than 2 species), with 90 confirmed as true events (27.27%-86.5% sequence similarity).
- Donor bacterial genera from Alpha-protobacteria, Beta-protobacteria, and Firmicutes (which include numerous plant-associated genera) were significantly enriched for HGT (p < 0.01), supporting the role of plant-bacterial interactions.
- The most enriched functional categories were metabolism of amino acids, cofactors/vitamins, and carbohydrates, plus genetic information processing. Nearly 83% of transferred genes coded for enzymes (oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases), with others including transporters, inhibitors, DNA-repair, and signaling proteins.
- A case example: Glyoxalase I (GlyI) transfer from bacteria to plants, confirmed by maximum likelihood and Bayesian phylogenetic analyses, leading to Ni/Co-dependent GlyI enzyme activity in plants.
- No clade- or species-specific HGTs were detected; all occurred anciently during the origin of angiosperm plants. Two transferred genes had >70% sequence similarity, likely representing relatively recent specific transfers (e.g., Agrobacteria).
- 309 "one-species" HGT events were identified and all were confirmed to be artifacts of sequencing error or inaccurate annotation (despite 40-100% sequence similarity).

CONCLUSIONS: The study confirmed that bacterial-plant interactions contribute to HGT from bacteria to plants. Both ancient transfer (during angiosperm origin) and recent specific transfer (e.g., Agrobacteria) occurred during plant evolution. The results can explain the discontinuity of HGT from prokaryotes to eukaryotes and suggest the "70% rule" (a key argument against eukaryotic HGT) should be re-evaluated.

FUNDING: Supported by The National Key Research and Development Program of China (2017YFD0101303), Heilongjiang Postdoctoral Fund (LBH-Z20160), and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (31770575, 31972507). No conflicts of interest were reported. The article is open access.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is recognized as a major driver of adaptive evolution in prokaryotes. However, HGT seems impossible in eukaryotes, particularly as recipients; therefore, debate rages regarding whether HGT takes place in eukaryotes, in addition to its potential mechanism or frequency., In total, 373 HGT events were identified based on a pipeline procedure, and 90 HGTs were confirmed as true events, with 27.27%–86.5% sequence similarities., The most enriched functional categories of the HGTs were metabolism processes of amino acids, cofactors and vitamins, and carbohydrates, and genetic information processing., No clade- or species-specific HGTs were detected, and all occurred anciently during the origin of angiosperm plants. In addition, we identified 309 'one-species' HGT events, and as expected, all the events could be accounted for as sequence errors or inaccurate annotations., We propose that both ancient transfer and recent specific transfer (e.g. Agrobacteria) occurred in the course of plant evolution.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 20: role of horizontal gene transfer ---
URL: https://www.ars.usda.gov/ARSUserFiles/50620500/Publications/HCK/horizon.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (Annu. Rev. Phytopathol. 2000, by U. Liane Rosewich and H. Corby Kistler) examines the role of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in fungal evolution. The authors define HGT as stable transfer of genetic material between individuals not attributable to vertical (meiotic or mitotic) processes. They note that although HGT evidence in eukaryotes remains largely anecdotal, fungi may have experienced more HGT than other eukaryotes, making them well-suited model systems because HGT can be tested experimentally.

The authors outline indirect evidence for HGT, including character-state discordance between element and organismal phylogenies, high similarity between elements in distantly related organisms, irregular distribution patterns, habitat-associated gene sharing, and genomic inconsistencies (G+C content, codon usage). Alternative explanations (erroneous phylogenies, paralog comparisons, ancestral retention, introgressive hybridization) must be considered. Phylogenetic tests include bootstrapping, maximum likelihood, T-PTP tests, and incongruence length differences.

The review organizes potential HGT cases by element type:
1. PLASMIDS: Fungal plasmids (usually 1-21 kb, linear, often mitochondrial) show discordant phylogenies, random global distribution patterns (e.g., 7 Neurospora plasmid groups among 225 isolates), and experimental transfer. Horizontal transfer was demonstrated experimentally by co-culturing unrelated strains (e.g., pAI2 from Ascobolus immersus to Podospora anserina; kalilo between Neurospora species).
2. MYCOVIRUSES: Lacking an extracellular phase, these transfer via cytoplasmic mixing. Some RdRp similarities between distant species suggest possible HGT.
3. INTRONS: Group I introns (nuclear, mitochondrial, and rRNA) and group II introns (organellar only) can move via homing and transposition. The best-substantiated case involves horizontal transfer of a group I intron from fungi to the angiosperm Peperomia. The cox1 intron i4 of Agrocybe aegerita showed 90.5% amino acid identity with the homologous intron in P. anserina, strongly supporting recent HGT. Intron phylogenies are often incongruent with species phylogenies.
4. TRANSPOSABLE ELEMENTS: Sporadic distribution patterns (e.g., grasshopper retrotransposon in Magnaporthe grisea, Fot1 in Fusarium oxysporum) suggest HGT, though stochastic loss is an alternative explanation. Vectors (symbionts/parasites) are proposed but unproven.

The authors conclude that HGT in fungi may be a more important evolutionary factor than in other eukaryotes, particularly for introns and plasmids, which may need periodic horizontal transfer for long-term persistence.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In this review article we summarize reports of genetic exchanges between fungal populations and between fungi and other organisms that have been attributed to horizontal transfer mechanisms.", "We define HGT as the stable transfer of genetic material between individuals, not directly attributable to vertical, i.e. meiotic or mitotic, processes...", "Evidence for HGT in fungi and other eukaryotes is indirect. In most cases, HGT is invoked after unusual features of genetic elements have become evident, including (a) an inconsistency between the phylogeny of the genetic element in question and the traditionally accepted phylogeny of the organisms...", "Horizontal transfer of the linear mitochondrial plasmid pAI2 from the discomycete A. immersus to mitochondria of a plasmid-free strain of the pyrenomycete Podospora anserina was achieved experimentally by merely co-culturing these unrelated strains.", "In summary, our compilation of potential intron horizontal transmissions in fungi indicates that horizontal transfer of introns among fungi may be quite common."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution | Semantic Scholar ---
URL: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Horizontal-gene-transfer-in-eukaryotic-evolution-Keeling-Palmer/e752cd6145dc999140351f0334951a65465174b1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page describes a seminal 2008 review paper titled "Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution" by Patrick J. Keeling and Jeffrey D. Palmer, published in Nature Reviews Genetics (DOI: 10.1038/nrg2386). The paper has 1,313 citations and examines the growing number of well-supported cases of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) from both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, many with significant functional implications. Key trends highlighted include the important role of HGT in adaptation to specialized niches and the highly variable impact of HGT across different eukaryotic lineages.

The page also lists notable citing papers and references, including: the "weak-link model" of HGT in eukaryotes (Huang, 2013) proposing that unicellular and early developmental stages are entry points for foreign genes in multicellular eukaryotes; evidence from Bdelloid rotifers showing massive HGT with genes originating from bacteria, fungi, and plants (Gladyshev et al., 2008); massive HGT in Amborella trichopoda involving acquisition of hundreds of foreign mitochondrial genes (Richardson & Palmer, 2007); widespread horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes in flowering plants (Bergthorsson et al., 2003); and the "complexity hypothesis" (Jain et al., 1999) explaining why operational genes are more frequently transferred than informational genes. HGT is shown to play important roles in eukaryotic adaptation to parasitism, pathogenesis, anaerobiosis, and nitrogen/iron limitation in marine environments, and there is evidence of HGT in metazoans (sponges, cnidarians, rotifers, nematodes, molluscs, arthropods).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The number of well-supported cases of transfer from both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, many with significant functional implications, is now expanding rapidly and major recent trends include the important role of HGT in adaptation to certain specialized niches and the highly variable impact of HGT in different lineages."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution ---
URL: http://www.ask-force.org/web/HorizontalGT/Keeling-HGT-Eukaryotic-Evolution-2008.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (Keeling & Palmer, Nature Reviews Genetics, Aug 2008) examines horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in eukaryotic evolution, arguing that its importance is often overshadowed by more extensive study of HGT in prokaryotes. The authors note that eukaryotes arose via the grandest HGT events — endosymbiosis giving rise to mitochondria and plastids — but ongoing HGT in eukaryotes has been under-appreciated due to overshadowing by bacterial studies, evidence coming largely from protists rather than animals, and the erroneous 2001 claim of substantial HGT in the human genome that chilled the field.

Key methodological point: The gold standard for identifying HGT is phylogenetic incongruence (strong conflict between gene and organism phylogenies), though this requires adequate taxonomic sampling. Detecting and evaluating HGT requires formal phylogenetic analysis; the 2001 claim of ~100 human genes from bacteria was debunked by such analysis.

Major findings and trends:
- Massive endosymbiotic gene transfer (EGT): Organellar genomes encode only a small fraction of their proteins; most organelle proteins are encoded by nuclear genes. EGT tempo has been highly punctuated, with bursts of transfer interspersed with periods of stasis. In striking contrast to angiosperms (where 16 of 40 mitochondrial-protein genes show recent EGT), animals show profound stasis — not one functional EGT across 600 million years of metazoan evolution.
- Protein import constrains transfer: Hydrophobic organelle proteins are hardest to import and assemble, locking animal mitochondria into a small, irreducible set of core genes.
- Bacterial endosymbiont transfers: Large tracts of Wolbachia DNA have moved to insect/nematode nuclear genomes; in one case an entire Wolbachia genome was found in a fruitfly genome.
- Prokaryote–eukaryote transfers vary enormously: estimates range from zero to hundreds of bacterial genes per genome. Rumen-dwelling ciliates acquired ~4% of genes from bacteria, approaching bacterial levels. Only one of dozens of sequenced animal genomes (human) has been analyzed, with no credible cases of bacterial HGT found.
- Adaptive functions: Anaerobic parasites and rumen ciliates are rich in transferred genes related to anaerobic metabolism; HGT supports adaptation to specialized niches (parasitism, anaerobiosis, soil life).
- Frequency is a complex function of opportunity (phagotrophy/"you are what you eat"), germ-line segregation, and other factors, varying by lineage.
- Bacterial transfers dominate detected cases partly due to detection bias (easy to spot given large evolutionary distance) but also real opportunity — bacterial populations and gene pools are far larger.
- Eukaryote–eukaryote transfers are underestimated due to poor sampling, confounding gene duplication, and lack of systematic searches, but many cases exist, including fungal toxin gene transfer (~70 years ago) and plastid-targeted protein transfers between algal groups.
- Organelle–organelle HGT: One extraordinary case of recent cytochrome b transfers among sympatric Mexican beetles; plant mitochondrial DNA is unexpectedly active in HGT while plastid and animal mitochondrial DNAs show none.
- Eukaryote–prokaryote transfers are rare but include tubulin genes in the bacterium Prosthecobacter, actin/profilin in Microcystis, and a eukaryotic FBA in Prochlorococcus/Synechococcus, presumably due to opportunity and intron barriers.

The article emphasizes that HGT in eukaryotes is now emerging at an increasing rate, accounts for many adaptively important traits, and has altered concepts of the genome, species, and the tree (or web) of life.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Extant eukaryotes arose by HGT on the grandest scale possible — the endosymbiosis and subsequent genetic integration of entire organisms that gave rise to the mitochondrion and the plastid."; "The gold standard for identifying HGT with confidence is phylogenetic incongruence — this occurs if there is strong conflict between the phylogenies of the gene and of the organism."; "By contrast, animals exhibit profound stasis in mitochondrial gene content: not one case of functional EGT has been reported across the 600 million years of metazoan evolution, despite sequencing of thousands of animal mitochondrial genomes."; "This has led to the 'you are what you eat' theory of HGT."; "Although we can safely generalize that overall levels of bacterial genes in nuclear genomes vary substantially among eukaryotes, too few 'whole' genomes have been examined to allow much insight into patterns, much less rates, of both horizontal transfer and loss of transferred genes."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution | Nature Reviews Genetics ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/nrg2386

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article titled "Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution" by Patrick J. Keeling (University of British Columbia) and Jeffrey D. Palmer (Indiana University), published in Nature Reviews Genetics, Volume 9, pages 605–618 (2008). The article has over 35,000 accesses, 1,239 citations, and 182 Altmetric mentions.

MAIN TOPIC: The article examines horizontal gene transfer (HGT, also known as lateral gene transfer) — the non-sexual movement of genetic information between genomes — and its role in eukaryotic genome evolution. While HGT is more prevalent and better understood in prokaryotes, this review documents its significant impact on eukaryotic evolution.

KEY FINDINGS AND POINTS:
1. Definition: HGT is the non-sexual movement of genetic information between genomes, where incoming DNA/RNA can replace existing genes or introduce new genes.
2. HGT in eukaryotes has been overshadowed by its prevalence in bacterial genomes, but many cases involving eukaryotes have been documented. Its impact varies by lineage, and lineages most affected (like protists) are often the least studied at the genomic level.
3. Endosymbiosis has been extensive in eukaryotic evolution. Mitochondria and plastids (derived from endosymbiosis) contributed many genes to the nucleus, and subsequent endosymbioses allowed genes to move between eukaryotes. Persistent endosymbionts like Wolbachia are now recognized as major sources of DNA in host nuclei.
4. HGT without symbiosis is also common; most documented cases involve bacterial genes in eukaryotic nuclei. Bacteria may be the major source of new genes due to their abundance.
5. Eukaryote-to-eukaryote transfers may be more common than appreciated. Extensive gene exchange between mitochondrial genomes of plants provides the highest known levels of eukaryote–eukaryote transfer.
6. Transferred genes often have clear functional or ecological implications. For example, several highly derived anaerobes acquired metabolic genes from bacteria that contributed to their adaptation to anaerobic environments.
7. Ancient HGT events can serve as clues to organismal relationships, with several shared by major eukaryotic lineages (e.g., animals and fungi, or chromalveolates).
8. Recent transfers are more commonly observed than ancient ones, possibly indicating that transferred genes provide transient advantages but are frequently not retained long-term.
9. Major outstanding questions include: the fate of transferred genes over time, mechanisms of HGT, and what determines HGT's differential impact across lineages.

The article includes figures on eukaryotic evolution bifurcations/reticulations, sources of transferred genes ("you are what you eat, what you live on, what lives on you, and what lives in you"), and different kinds of transfer effects on gene phylogeny. The full content is behind a subscription paywall, though the abstract and key points are accessible.

Related articles referenced include "Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes: aligning theory with data" (2024), "A global survey of prokaryotic genomes reveals the eco-evolutionary pressures driving horizontal gene transfer" (2024), and "A compendium of horizontal gene transfers in Metazoa" (2026).

The reference list (over 57 references) covers foundational work on HGT including Doolittle's phylogenetic classification work, studies on endosymbiotic gene transfer from organelles to nuclei, Wolbachia genome integration in insects, HGT in parasitic protozoa and rumen ciliates, and large-scale genomic analyses of gene transfer in plants and animals.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Horizontal gene transfer (HGT; also known as lateral gene transfer) is the non-sexual movement of genetic information between genomes. Incoming DNA or RNA can replace existing genes, or can introduce new genes into a genome."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: [PDF] Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes: The weak‐link model - UTH e-Class ---
URL: https://eclass.uth.gr/modules/document/index.php?course=BIO_U_130&download=%2F5e4e356bU0rN%2F5e4e3a64rbc6.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific perspective article by Jinling Huang (published in BioEssays in 2013) argues that horizontal gene transfer (HGT) has been a widespread and regular occurrence throughout eukaryotic evolution, and proposes the "weak-link model" to explain the mechanisms of HGT in eukaryotes.

**Key Arguments:**

1. **Barriers to HGT are not insurmountable:** Although protists are historically considered more likely to acquire genes than multicellular eukaryotes, recent HGT events have been documented in animals (cnidarians, mites, insects, nematodes, fish) and plants. While the physical isolation of germ cells from somatic cells may create barriers in complex multicellular organisms, these barriers are not insurmountable.

2. **Organellar gene transfer (OGT) cannot explain all bacterial genes:** While many bacterial genes in eukaryotes are attributed to mitochondrial (α-proteobacterial) or plastid (cyanobacterial) origins, OGT represents a "closed system" constrained by the fixed gene pool of organelles. Since organelles have lost many genes during evolution, their transferable gene pool is limited. The author argues that HGT—an "open system" allowing gene acquisition from virtually unlimited sources—better explains the many bacterial genes not clearly of organellar origin. Evidence includes strong phylogenetic signals for various proteobacterial groups (16.7%) and other bacteria (13.8%) beyond just cyanobacteria and α-proteobacteria.

3. **HGT occurs continually:** HGT has been documented in all major eukaryotic lineages, including recent acquisitions, convergent/recurrent gene transfers, entire metabolic pathways, and ancient events. Examples include: rumen ciliates and Galdieria sulphuraria (4-5% of genome from acquired genes), nematodes (over 3%), and bdelloid rotifers (8-9% of gene content).

**The Weak-Link Model:** For foreign genes to be stably inherited, they must (i) enter recipient cells, (ii) integrate into the recipient genome, and (iii) be transmitted to offspring. The author proposes that unicellular and early developmental stages (spores, zygotes, embryos) serve as "weak links" or entry points where nuclear DNA is relatively exposed to foreign DNA sources. 

**Predictions of the model:**
- (i) Frequent HGT in unicellular eukaryotes (all lifecycle stages are weak-link entry points)
- (ii) Occurrence of foreign genes in multicellular eukaryotes with fully exposed unicellular or early developmental stages
- (iii) Frequent HGT in asexual multicellular eukaryotes (no specific germ cells to serve as barriers)
- (iv) Existence of many anciently acquired genes in multicellular eukaryotes (derived from their unicellular ancestors)

**Why HGT may be underestimated:** The phylogenetic signal of acquired genes can be muted or erased by substitutions over time, HGT from uncultivated or extinct lineages may not be identified, and interpretations of patchy gene distributions often default to vertical inheritance explanations (differential gene loss, misidentification, phylogenetic artifacts) rather than HGT.

The article concludes that since mitochondria and plastids represent fixed gene pools with limited transferable genes, OGT alone cannot explain the abundance of bacterial genes in eukaryotic genomes. The weak-link model hypothesizes that HGT has operated continually throughout eukaryotic history and calls for future work using evolutionary genomic analyses to understand the scale of HGT and its contribution to gene pool expansion in different eukaryotic lineages.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Because mitochondria and plastids alone cannot adequately explain the presence of all, or even the majority, of bacterial genes in eukaryotes. Available data indicate that no insurmountable barrier to HGT exists, even in complex multicellular eukaryotes."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes: aligning theory with data | Nature Reviews Genetics ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-023-00688-5

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article by Patrick J. Keeling (University of British Columbia) published in Nature Reviews Genetics (volume 25, pages 416–430, 2024), titled "Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes: aligning theory with data." The article addresses the curious discrepancy in horizontal gene transfer (HGT) between prokaryotes and eukaryotes. While HGT has played a pronounced role in bacterial and archaeal evolution, its role in eukaryotes is less clear. Behaviors unique to eukaryotic cells — phagocytosis and endosymbiosis — have been proposed to increase HGT frequency, yet nuclear genomes encode fewer HGTs than bacteria and archaea.

The article's central thesis is that any increased chance of acquiring new genes through phagocytosis and endosymbiosis is offset by a reduced need for these genes in eukaryotes, because selection in most eukaryotes operates on variation not readily generated by HGT. The paper reviews existing theory in the context of growing data on HGT in eukaryotes, including three figures covering differences between eukaryotic, bacterial, and archaeal cells; ecological strategies that promote or suppress HGT; and endosymbiotic gene transfer in early organelle evolution.

Key discussion points from the references include a long-standing debate (epitomized by Martin 2017 vs. Leger et al. 2018) about whether HGT took place in nuclear genomes, with subsequent work (Van Etten & Bhattacharya 2020) shifting the question from "whether" HGT affected eukaryotes to "how much." The article discusses documented HGT cases including massive mitochondrial gene transfer in the plant Amborella, plastid gene replacement, bacterial-to-eukaryotic transfers in mealybugs and tardigrades, and phytoplankton pangenome analysis showing varying degrees of HGT impact on ecologically important algae. Important distinctions are made between functional transfers that persist in evolutionary time versus simple non-functional uptake of DNA. The article notes that systematic analyses show ancient transfers are rare compared to recent ones (with the exception of endosymbiotic gene transfers), mirroring observations in bacteria. The article had 13k accesses and 126 citations at the time of publication.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Behaviours unique to eukaryotic cells — phagocytosis and endosymbiosis — have been proposed to increase the frequency of HGT, but nuclear genomes encode fewer HGTs than bacteria and archaea.", "any increased chance of acquiring new genes through phagocytosis and endosymbiosis is offset by a reduced need for these genes in eukaryotes, because selection in most eukaryotes operates on variation not readily generated by HGT.", "This Review aims to turn the page on the debate from whether HGT affected eukaryotes to focusing on how it changed their ecology and evolution." (Van Etten & Bhattacharya, 2020), "This paper provides a thorough review of bacterial-to-eukaryotic HGT, placing a much needed emphasis on functional transfers that will persist in evolutionary time, as distinguished from the simple non-functional uptake of DNA." (Husnik & McCutcheon, 2018), "This paper describes a systematic analysis of HGT across the tree of eukaryotes showing ancient transfers are rare in comparison with recent ones, mirroring earlier observations on bacteria." (Katz, 2015)
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Uneven distribution of prokaryote-derived horizontal gene transfer in fungi: a lifestyle-dependent phenomenon ---
URL: https://journals.asm.org/doi/abs/10.1128/mbio.02855-24

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in mBio (Vol. 16, No. 1, 8 January 2025) titled "Uneven distribution of prokaryote-derived horizontal gene transfer in fungi: a lifestyle-dependent phenomenon," authored by Fei Liu, Shi-Hui Wang, Ratchadawan Cheewangkoon, and Rui-Lin Zhao of the ASM Journals. The article is open access, an Evolution research article published 29 November 2024, with 20 total citations and 5,551 downloads. DOI: 10.1128/mbio.02855-24.

Methodology: The researchers systematically searched for HGT events across 829 representative fungal genomes (primarily Dikarya), including 563 Ascomycota and 257 Basidiomycota genomes representing 11 classes (Agaricomycetes 188, Sordariomycetes 151, Dothideomycetes 139, Saccharomycetes 82, Leotiomycetes 57, Lecanoromycetes 52, Eurotiomycetes 48, Tremellomycetes 27, Pezizomycetes 12, Exobasidiomycetes 12, Ustilaginomycetes 10). Out of 7,091,363 genes on contigs longer than 100 kb, they used sequence similarity and phylogeny-based approaches, initially identifying 29,796 candidate HGT genes, with 9,703 failing phylogenetic validation, yielding a final set of 20,093 putative HGT genes.

Key results:
- 20,093 genes across 750 fungal genomes were likely acquired from prokaryotes and viruses: 19,973 (99.4%) from bacteria, 78 (0.4%) from archaea, and 42 (0.2%) from viruses, stemming from 8,815 distinct HGT events (6,953 species-specific, 1,862 involving two or more species). These constitute 0.21% of total genes analyzed.
- No correlation was found between HGT number and total genome size (P-value = 0.18).
- Validation: genes recovered at 90.0%–95.8% (average 94.0%) via PacBio/Illumina sequencing. Overlap of 80%–91% with previously identified HGT genes in budding yeast. HGT genes had average 46% identity with closest non-fungal homologs, significantly different from non-HGT genes (P < 0.05).
- Eight lifestyle-related traits significantly influence HGT diversity (P < 0.05): primary lifestyle, decay type, decay substrate, animal biotrophic capacity, growth form, hymenium type, fruitbody type, and endophytic interaction capability, confirmed via RDA and PGLS analyses.
- Parasites exhibited the highest estimated number of HGT-acquired genes, followed by saprotrophs, with symbionts showing the lowest.
- Ascomycota had higher median HGT genes (16/genome) than Basidiomycota (14/genome). Tremellomycetes (47) and Exobasidiomycetes (38) had the highest median HGT genes, while Agaricomycetes had the lowest (10).
- Notable examples: yeast Vanrija pseudolonga harbored the highest number of HGT genes (223); mycoparasite Xylogone sp. was among top 10 genomes; plant pathogen Calonectria ilicicola harbored 130 HGTs.
- Donor bacteria: Proteobacteria (45%), Actinobacteria (36%), Firmicutes (7%), Bacteroidetes (6%).
- HGT genes were significantly closer to transposable elements (P = 2.03e-07). Top functions: SDR family oxidoreductase, alpha/beta hydrolase, and GNAT family N-acetyltransferase. GO analysis showed associations with metabolism- and cellular-related terms.
- 1,938 genes had N-terminal secretion motifs and 286 had virulence factor annotations, suggesting roles in pathogenicity. HGT genes were associated with carbohydrate metabolism, amino acid metabolism, and xenobiotics biodegradation.
- Majority of HGT genes show Ka/Ks values below 0.5 (purifying/negative selection); four genes (alpha/beta fold hydrolase, GNAT N-acetyltransferase, serine/threonine protein kinase, HNH endonuclease) showed Ka/Ks > 1 (positive selection).
- 44% of HGT genes acquired introns (25,467 introns total, all gained after insertion); 23% of gained introns had BLAST hits to native fungal genomes (average 86% identity), suggesting intron origin from native genomes.
- Horizontally transferred genes with introns have significantly higher expression levels compared to intron-lacking genes, suggesting a role for intron gains in adaptation of HGT-acquired genes.

Conclusion: The study highlights the influence of lifestyle on HGT diversity in fungi and underscores the substantial contribution of HGT to fungal adaptation, metabolic diversity, and ecological success.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Using a combination of sequence similarity and phylogeny-based approaches, we detected 20,093 prokaryotic-derived transferred genes across 750 fungal genomes, via 8,815 distinct HGT events."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Beyond Agrobacterium-Mediated Transformation: Horizontal Gene Transfer from Bacteria to Eukaryotes ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9473684

SUMMARY:

**Key mechanisms of HGT in prokaryotes:** The three most recognized mechanisms are conjugation (transfer via physical contact through a conjugation pilus), transformation (uptake of exogenous DNA from the environment), and transduction (gene delivery through phage predation, with generalized and specialized subtypes). More recently described mechanisms include gene transfer agents (GTAs) — phage-derived systems carrying random host DNA fragments — and cell fusion (bidirectional gene exchange, observed in archaea such as Haloferax and Sulfolobus).

**HGT in eukaryotes:** Gene exchange became more complicated with the evolution of the nucleus, but mechanisms include endosymbiotic gene transfer (EGT), introgression (gene flow from hybridization followed by backcrosses), the "you are what you eat" ratchet (gene acquisition through phagotrophy in protists), and the weak-link model (weakly protected unicellular or early developmental stages as entry points for foreign genes into multicellular eukaryotes).

**Detecting HGT:** Methods rely primarily on phylogenetic conflict (conflicting branching patterns between gene and species trees), gene composition analysis (codon usage and oligonucleotide composition), and pan-genome analysis. The pan-genome consists of the core genome (genes in all members) and accessory genome (genes in only some members). An analysis of 61 E. coli genomes revealed only 6% of gene families were present in all genomes.

**Evolutionary impact:** HGT is more frequent between closely related organisms — in haloarchaea, over 90% of HGTs were integrated through homologous recombination, and HGT frequency decreases exponentially with phylogenetic distance. HGT drives metabolic innovations (e.g., the methylaspartate cycle in haloarchaea, over 1,000 bacterial genes imported into haloarchaea enabling the move to aerobic environments) and shapes holobiont evolution. In human microbiomes, HGT is 25-fold more frequent between human-associated organisms than between organisms from different hosts or environments.

- The moss Physcomitrella patens acquired genes from fungi, bacteria, viruses, and aquatic animals

- Genes from archaic to modern humans (brain development allele via introgression)

<summary>
The Weismann barrier is a concept proposed by August Weismann that describes the strict distinction between "immortal" germ cell lineages (which produce gametes) and "disposable" somatic cells in animals, though not in plants. This contrasts with Charles Darwin's proposed pangenesis mechanism for inheritance. In precise terms, hereditary information is copied only from germline cells to somatic cells, meaning somatic mutations are not passed on to the germline and are therefore not inherited. Weismann set out this concept in his 1892 book "Das Keimplasma: eine Theorie der Vererbung" (The Germ Plasm: a theory of inheritance). The theory's use in the context of germ plasm theory is sometimes called "Weismannism."

The barrier was historically important as it effectively eliminated certain Lamarckian concepts, making Lamarckian inheritance from changes to the body (soma) difficult or impossible. It required qualification in light of modern understanding of horizontal gene transfer and other genetic developments.
