The Weismann barrier is a biological principle stating that hereditary information flows only from germline cells to somatic cells, and that reverse (soma-to-germline) feedback is impossible. This concept should not be confused with the central dogma of molecular biology (DNA → RNA → protein). The theory has important implications for human gene therapy: if the barrier is permeable, genetic treatments of somatic cells could result in inheritable genome changes, potentially leading to genetic engineering of the human species rather than just individuals. It also impacts understanding of evolution, suggesting species may not be as genetically separable as once thought, and opens the door to Lamarckian concepts lacking previously known supporting mechanisms. The application of the theory is sometimes called "Weismannism."

The theory traces to the work of 19th-century biologist August Weismann, an early contributor to genetics. Although seriously questioned during the 20th century, research by Paul Kammerer and Trofim Lysenko failed to weaken the principle among the scientific community. Late 20th-century criticisms of an impermeable barrier center on the enzyme reverse transcriptase. Evidence has mounted for horizontal gene transfer, where different species swap genes via retroviruses, which integrate their code into host genomes and can transfer nearby genetic material. If a germline cell is infected, the integrated DNA can enter the species' gene pool. Additional evidence against the barrier comes from the immune system; Edward J. Steele's controversial theory (expounded in his book "Lamarck's Signature") proposes that endogenous retroviruses carry new versions of V genes from somatic immune cells to germline cells, driven by the immune system's need to evolve rapidly against fast-evolving pathogens. Even if these exceptions prove legitimate, the Weismann barrier would only lose its absolute status—its penetration remains an exception without further examples. Related topics include epigenetic inheritance and pangenesis.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Weismann barrier is the principle that hereditary information moves only from genes to body cells but never in reverse. In more precise terminology hereditary information moves only from germline cells to somatic cells (or soma to germline feedback is impossible)." "This is often confused with the central dogma of molecular biology which in its modern form states that information travels from DNA → RNA → protein." "If the Weismann barrier is permeable then genetic treatments of somatic cells may actually result in an inheritable change to the genome, possibly resulting in the genetic engineering of the human species rather than just individuals." "A controversial theory of Edward J. Steele's suggests that endogenous retroviruses carry new versions of V genes from soma cells in the immune system to the germ line cells." "It should be noted that even if both of these possible exceptions turn out to be legitimate, the Weismann barrier just loses its absolute status. Without further examples, the penetration of the Weismann barrier is still very much an exception."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution | Semantic Scholar ---
URL: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Horizontal-gene-transfer-in-eukaryotic-evolution-Keeling-Palmer/e752cd6145dc999140351f0334951a65465174b1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page describes a seminal 2008 review paper titled "Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution" by Patrick J. Keeling and Jeffrey D. Palmer, published in Nature Reviews Genetics (DOI: 10.1038/nrg2386). The paper has 1,313 citations and examines the growing number of well-supported cases of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) from both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, many with significant functional implications. Key trends highlighted include the important role of HGT in adaptation to specialized niches and the highly variable impact of HGT across different eukaryotic lineages.

The page also lists notable citing papers and references, including: the "weak-link model" of HGT in eukaryotes (Huang, 2013) proposing that unicellular and early developmental stages are entry points for foreign genes in multicellular eukaryotes; evidence from Bdelloid rotifers showing massive HGT with genes originating from bacteria, fungi, and plants (Gladyshev et al., 2008); massive HGT in Amborella trichopoda involving acquisition of hundreds of foreign mitochondrial genes (Richardson & Palmer, 2007); widespread horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes in flowering plants (Bergthorsson et al., 2003); and the "complexity hypothesis" (Jain et al., 1999) explaining why operational genes are more frequently transferred than informational genes. HGT is shown to play important roles in eukaryotic adaptation to parasitism, pathogenesis, anaerobiosis, and nitrogen/iron limitation in marine environments, and there is evidence of HGT in metazoans (sponges, cnidarians, rotifers, nematodes, molluscs, arthropods).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The number of well-supported cases of transfer from both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, many with significant functional implications, is now expanding rapidly and major recent trends include the important role of HGT in adaptation to certain specialized niches and the highly variable impact of HGT in different lineages."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution ---
URL: http://www.ask-force.org/web/HorizontalGT/Keeling-HGT-Eukaryotic-Evolution-2008.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (Keeling & Palmer, Nature Reviews Genetics, Aug 2008) examines horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in eukaryotic evolution, arguing that its importance is often overshadowed by more extensive study of HGT in prokaryotes. The authors note that eukaryotes arose via the grandest HGT events — endosymbiosis giving rise to mitochondria and plastids — but ongoing HGT in eukaryotes has been under-appreciated due to overshadowing by bacterial studies, evidence coming largely from protists rather than animals, and the erroneous 2001 claim of substantial HGT in the human genome that chilled the field.

Key methodological point: The gold standard for identifying HGT is phylogenetic incongruence (strong conflict between gene and organism phylogenies), though this requires adequate taxonomic sampling. Detecting and evaluating HGT requires formal phylogenetic analysis; the 2001 claim of ~100 human genes from bacteria was debunked by such analysis.

Major findings and trends:
- Massive endosymbiotic gene transfer (EGT): Organellar genomes encode only a small fraction of their proteins; most organelle proteins are encoded by nuclear genes. EGT tempo has been highly punctuated, with bursts of transfer interspersed with periods of stasis. In striking contrast to angiosperms (where 16 of 40 mitochondrial-protein genes show recent EGT), animals show profound stasis — not one functional EGT across 600 million years of metazoan evolution.
- Protein import constrains transfer: Hydrophobic organelle proteins are hardest to import and assemble, locking animal mitochondria into a small, irreducible set of core genes.
- Bacterial endosymbiont transfers: Large tracts of Wolbachia DNA have moved to insect/nematode nuclear genomes; in one case an entire Wolbachia genome was found in a fruitfly genome.
- Prokaryote–eukaryote transfers vary enormously: estimates range from zero to hundreds of bacterial genes per genome. Rumen-dwelling ciliates acquired ~4% of genes from bacteria, approaching bacterial levels. Only one of dozens of sequenced animal genomes (human) has been analyzed, with no credible cases of bacterial HGT found.
- Adaptive functions: Anaerobic parasites and rumen ciliates are rich in transferred genes related to anaerobic metabolism; HGT supports adaptation to specialized niches (parasitism, anaerobiosis, soil life).
- Frequency is a complex function of opportunity (phagotrophy/"you are what you eat"), germ-line segregation, and other factors, varying by lineage.
- Bacterial transfers dominate detected cases partly due to detection bias (easy to spot given large evolutionary distance) but also real opportunity — bacterial populations and gene pools are far larger.
- Eukaryote–eukaryote transfers are underestimated due to poor sampling, confounding gene duplication, and lack of systematic searches, but many cases exist, including fungal toxin gene transfer (~70 years ago) and plastid-targeted protein transfers between algal groups.
- Organelle–organelle HGT: One extraordinary case of recent cytochrome b transfers among sympatric Mexican beetles; plant mitochondrial DNA is unexpectedly active in HGT while plastid and animal mitochondrial DNAs show none.
- Eukaryote–prokaryote transfers are rare but include tubulin genes in the bacterium Prosthecobacter, actin/profilin in Microcystis, and a eukaryotic FBA in Prochlorococcus/Synechococcus, presumably due to opportunity and intron barriers.

The article emphasizes that HGT in eukaryotes is now emerging at an increasing rate, accounts for many adaptively important traits, and has altered concepts of the genome, species, and the tree (or web) of life.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Extant eukaryotes arose by HGT on the grandest scale possible — the endosymbiosis and subsequent genetic integration of entire organisms that gave rise to the mitochondrion and the plastid."; "The gold standard for identifying HGT with confidence is phylogenetic incongruence — this occurs if there is strong conflict between the phylogenies of the gene and of the organism."; "By contrast, animals exhibit profound stasis in mitochondrial gene content: not one case of functional EGT has been reported across the 600 million years of metazoan evolution, despite sequencing of thousands of animal mitochondrial genomes."; "This has led to the 'you are what you eat' theory of HGT."; "Although we can safely generalize that overall levels of bacterial genes in nuclear genomes vary substantially among eukaryotes, too few 'whole' genomes have been examined to allow much insight into patterns, much less rates, of both horizontal transfer and loss of transferred genes."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution | Nature Reviews Genetics ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/nrg2386

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article titled "Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution" by Patrick J. Keeling (University of British Columbia) and Jeffrey D. Palmer (Indiana University), published in Nature Reviews Genetics, Volume 9, pages 605–618 (2008). The article has over 35,000 accesses, 1,239 citations, and 182 Altmetric mentions.

MAIN TOPIC: The article examines horizontal gene transfer (HGT, also known as lateral gene transfer) — the non-sexual movement of genetic information between genomes — and its role in eukaryotic genome evolution. While HGT is more prevalent and better understood in prokaryotes, this review documents its significant impact on eukaryotic evolution.

KEY FINDINGS AND POINTS:
1. Definition: HGT is the non-sexual movement of genetic information between genomes, where incoming DNA/RNA can replace existing genes or introduce new genes.
2. HGT in eukaryotes has been overshadowed by its prevalence in bacterial genomes, but many cases involving eukaryotes have been documented. Its impact varies by lineage, and lineages most affected (like protists) are often the least studied at the genomic level.
3. Endosymbiosis has been extensive in eukaryotic evolution. Mitochondria and plastids (derived from endosymbiosis) contributed many genes to the nucleus, and subsequent endosymbioses allowed genes to move between eukaryotes. Persistent endosymbionts like Wolbachia are now recognized as major sources of DNA in host nuclei.
4. HGT without symbiosis is also common; most documented cases involve bacterial genes in eukaryotic nuclei. Bacteria may be the major source of new genes due to their abundance.
5. Eukaryote-to-eukaryote transfers may be more common than appreciated. Extensive gene exchange between mitochondrial genomes of plants provides the highest known levels of eukaryote–eukaryote transfer.
6. Transferred genes often have clear functional or ecological implications. For example, several highly derived anaerobes acquired metabolic genes from bacteria that contributed to their adaptation to anaerobic environments.
7. Ancient HGT events can serve as clues to organismal relationships, with several shared by major eukaryotic lineages (e.g., animals and fungi, or chromalveolates).
8. Recent transfers are more commonly observed than ancient ones, possibly indicating that transferred genes provide transient advantages but are frequently not retained long-term.
9. Major outstanding questions include: the fate of transferred genes over time, mechanisms of HGT, and what determines HGT's differential impact across lineages.

The article includes figures on eukaryotic evolution bifurcations/reticulations, sources of transferred genes ("you are what you eat, what you live on, what lives on you, and what lives in you"), and different kinds of transfer effects on gene phylogeny. The full content is behind a subscription paywall, though the abstract and key points are accessible.

Related articles referenced include "Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes: aligning theory with data" (2024), "A global survey of prokaryotic genomes reveals the eco-evolutionary pressures driving horizontal gene transfer" (2024), and "A compendium of horizontal gene transfers in Metazoa" (2026).

The reference list (over 57 references) covers foundational work on HGT including Doolittle's phylogenetic classification work, studies on endosymbiotic gene transfer from organelles to nuclei, Wolbachia genome integration in insects, HGT in parasitic protozoa and rumen ciliates, and large-scale genomic analyses of gene transfer in plants and animals.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Horizontal gene transfer (HGT; also known as lateral gene transfer) is the non-sexual movement of genetic information between genomes. Incoming DNA or RNA can replace existing genes, or can introduce new genes into a genome."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: [PDF] Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes: The weak‐link model - UTH e-Class ---
URL: https://eclass.uth.gr/modules/document/index.php?course=BIO_U_130&download=%2F5e4e356bU0rN%2F5e4e3a64rbc6.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific perspective article by Jinling Huang (published in BioEssays in 2013) argues that horizontal gene transfer (HGT) has been a widespread and regular occurrence throughout eukaryotic evolution, and proposes the "weak-link model" to explain the mechanisms of HGT in eukaryotes.

**Key Arguments:**

1. **Barriers to HGT are not insurmountable:** Although protists are historically considered more likely to acquire genes than multicellular eukaryotes, recent HGT events have been documented in animals (cnidarians, mites, insects, nematodes, fish) and plants. While the physical isolation of germ cells from somatic cells may create barriers in complex multicellular organisms, these barriers are not insurmountable.

2. **Organellar gene transfer (OGT) cannot explain all bacterial genes:** While many bacterial genes in eukaryotes are attributed to mitochondrial (α-proteobacterial) or plastid (cyanobacterial) origins, OGT represents a "closed system" constrained by the fixed gene pool of organelles. Since organelles have lost many genes during evolution, their transferable gene pool is limited. The author argues that HGT—an "open system" allowing gene acquisition from virtually unlimited sources—better explains the many bacterial genes not clearly of organellar origin. Evidence includes strong phylogenetic signals for various proteobacterial groups (16.7%) and other bacteria (13.8%) beyond just cyanobacteria and α-proteobacteria.

3. **HGT occurs continually:** HGT has been documented in all major eukaryotic lineages, including recent acquisitions, convergent/recurrent gene transfers, entire metabolic pathways, and ancient events. Examples include: rumen ciliates and Galdieria sulphuraria (4-5% of genome from acquired genes), nematodes (over 3%), and bdelloid rotifers (8-9% of gene content).

**The Weak-Link Model:** For foreign genes to be stably inherited, they must (i) enter recipient cells, (ii) integrate into the recipient genome, and (iii) be transmitted to offspring. The author proposes that unicellular and early developmental stages (spores, zygotes, embryos) serve as "weak links" or entry points where nuclear DNA is relatively exposed to foreign DNA sources. 

**Predictions of the model:**
- (i) Frequent HGT in unicellular eukaryotes (all lifecycle stages are weak-link entry points)
- (ii) Occurrence of foreign genes in multicellular eukaryotes with fully exposed unicellular or early developmental stages
- (iii) Frequent HGT in asexual multicellular eukaryotes (no specific germ cells to serve as barriers)
- (iv) Existence of many anciently acquired genes in multicellular eukaryotes (derived from their unicellular ancestors)

**Why HGT may be underestimated:** The phylogenetic signal of acquired genes can be muted or erased by substitutions over time, HGT from uncultivated or extinct lineages may not be identified, and interpretations of patchy gene distributions often default to vertical inheritance explanations (differential gene loss, misidentification, phylogenetic artifacts) rather than HGT.

The article concludes that since mitochondria and plastids represent fixed gene pools with limited transferable genes, OGT alone cannot explain the abundance of bacterial genes in eukaryotic genomes. The weak-link model hypothesizes that HGT has operated continually throughout eukaryotic history and calls for future work using evolutionary genomic analyses to understand the scale of HGT and its contribution to gene pool expansion in different eukaryotic lineages.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Because mitochondria and plastids alone cannot adequately explain the presence of all, or even the majority, of bacterial genes in eukaryotes. Available data indicate that no insurmountable barrier to HGT exists, even in complex multicellular eukaryotes."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes: aligning theory with data | Nature Reviews Genetics ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-023-00688-5

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article by Patrick J. Keeling (University of British Columbia) published in Nature Reviews Genetics (volume 25, pages 416–430, 2024), titled "Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes: aligning theory with data." The article addresses the curious discrepancy in horizontal gene transfer (HGT) between prokaryotes and eukaryotes. While HGT has played a pronounced role in bacterial and archaeal evolution, its role in eukaryotes is less clear. Behaviors unique to eukaryotic cells — phagocytosis and endosymbiosis — have been proposed to increase HGT frequency, yet nuclear genomes encode fewer HGTs than bacteria and archaea.

The article's central thesis is that any increased chance of acquiring new genes through phagocytosis and endosymbiosis is offset by a reduced need for these genes in eukaryotes, because selection in most eukaryotes operates on variation not readily generated by HGT. The paper reviews existing theory in the context of growing data on HGT in eukaryotes, including three figures covering differences between eukaryotic, bacterial, and archaeal cells; ecological strategies that promote or suppress HGT; and endosymbiotic gene transfer in early organelle evolution.

Key discussion points from the references include a long-standing debate (epitomized by Martin 2017 vs. Leger et al. 2018) about whether HGT took place in nuclear genomes, with subsequent work (Van Etten & Bhattacharya 2020) shifting the question from "whether" HGT affected eukaryotes to "how much." The article discusses documented HGT cases including massive mitochondrial gene transfer in the plant Amborella, plastid gene replacement, bacterial-to-eukaryotic transfers in mealybugs and tardigrades, and phytoplankton pangenome analysis showing varying degrees of HGT impact on ecologically important algae. Important distinctions are made between functional transfers that persist in evolutionary time versus simple non-functional uptake of DNA. The article notes that systematic analyses show ancient transfers are rare compared to recent ones (with the exception of endosymbiotic gene transfers), mirroring observations in bacteria. The article had 13k accesses and 126 citations at the time of publication.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Behaviours unique to eukaryotic cells — phagocytosis and endosymbiosis — have been proposed to increase the frequency of HGT, but nuclear genomes encode fewer HGTs than bacteria and archaea.", "any increased chance of acquiring new genes through phagocytosis and endosymbiosis is offset by a reduced need for these genes in eukaryotes, because selection in most eukaryotes operates on variation not readily generated by HGT.", "This Review aims to turn the page on the debate from whether HGT affected eukaryotes to focusing on how it changed their ecology and evolution." (Van Etten & Bhattacharya, 2020), "This paper provides a thorough review of bacterial-to-eukaryotic HGT, placing a much needed emphasis on functional transfers that will persist in evolutionary time, as distinguished from the simple non-functional uptake of DNA." (Husnik & McCutcheon, 2018), "This paper describes a systematic analysis of HGT across the tree of eukaryotes showing ancient transfers are rare in comparison with recent ones, mirroring earlier observations on bacteria." (Katz, 2015)
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Uneven distribution of prokaryote-derived horizontal gene transfer in fungi: a lifestyle-dependent phenomenon ---
URL: https://journals.asm.org/doi/abs/10.1128/mbio.02855-24

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in mBio (Vol. 16, No. 1, 8 January 2025) titled "Uneven distribution of prokaryote-derived horizontal gene transfer in fungi: a lifestyle-dependent phenomenon," authored by Fei Liu, Shi-Hui Wang, Ratchadawan Cheewangkoon, and Rui-Lin Zhao of the ASM Journals. The article is open access, an Evolution research article published 29 November 2024, with 20 total citations and 5,551 downloads. DOI: 10.1128/mbio.02855-24.

Methodology: The researchers systematically searched for HGT events across 829 representative fungal genomes (primarily Dikarya), including 563 Ascomycota and 257 Basidiomycota genomes representing 11 classes (Agaricomycetes 188, Sordariomycetes 151, Dothideomycetes 139, Saccharomycetes 82, Leotiomycetes 57, Lecanoromycetes 52, Eurotiomycetes 48, Tremellomycetes 27, Pezizomycetes 12, Exobasidiomycetes 12, Ustilaginomycetes 10). Out of 7,091,363 genes on contigs longer than 100 kb, they used sequence similarity and phylogeny-based approaches, initially identifying 29,796 candidate HGT genes, with 9,703 failing phylogenetic validation, yielding a final set of 20,093 putative HGT genes.

Key results:
- 20,093 genes across 750 fungal genomes were likely acquired from prokaryotes and viruses: 19,973 (99.4%) from bacteria, 78 (0.4%) from archaea, and 42 (0.2%) from viruses, stemming from 8,815 distinct HGT events (6,953 species-specific, 1,862 involving two or more species). These constitute 0.21% of total genes analyzed.
- No correlation was found between HGT number and total genome size (P-value = 0.18).
- Validation: genes recovered at 90.0%–95.8% (average 94.0%) via PacBio/Illumina sequencing. Overlap of 80%–91% with previously identified HGT genes in budding yeast. HGT genes had average 46% identity with closest non-fungal homologs, significantly different from non-HGT genes (P < 0.05).
- Eight lifestyle-related traits significantly influence HGT diversity (P < 0.05): primary lifestyle, decay type, decay substrate, animal biotrophic capacity, growth form, hymenium type, fruitbody type, and endophytic interaction capability, confirmed via RDA and PGLS analyses.
- Parasites exhibited the highest estimated number of HGT-acquired genes, followed by saprotrophs, with symbionts showing the lowest.
- Ascomycota had higher median HGT genes (16/genome) than Basidiomycota (14/genome). Tremellomycetes (47) and Exobasidiomycetes (38) had the highest median HGT genes, while Agaricomycetes had the lowest (10).
- Notable examples: yeast Vanrija pseudolonga harbored the highest number of HGT genes (223); mycoparasite Xylogone sp. was among top 10 genomes; plant pathogen Calonectria ilicicola harbored 130 HGTs.
- Donor bacteria: Proteobacteria (45%), Actinobacteria (36%), Firmicutes (7%), Bacteroidetes (6%).
- HGT genes were significantly closer to transposable elements (P = 2.03e-07). Top functions: SDR family oxidoreductase, alpha/beta hydrolase, and GNAT family N-acetyltransferase. GO analysis showed associations with metabolism- and cellular-related terms.
- 1,938 genes had N-terminal secretion motifs and 286 had virulence factor annotations, suggesting roles in pathogenicity. HGT genes were associated with carbohydrate metabolism, amino acid metabolism, and xenobiotics biodegradation.
- Majority of HGT genes show Ka/Ks values below 0.5 (purifying/negative selection); four genes (alpha/beta fold hydrolase, GNAT N-acetyltransferase, serine/threonine protein kinase, HNH endonuclease) showed Ka/Ks > 1 (positive selection).
- 44% of HGT genes acquired introns (25,467 introns total, all gained after insertion); 23% of gained introns had BLAST hits to native fungal genomes (average 86% identity), suggesting intron origin from native genomes.
- Horizontally transferred genes with introns have significantly higher expression levels compared to intron-lacking genes, suggesting a role for intron gains in adaptation of HGT-acquired genes.

Conclusion: The study highlights the influence of lifestyle on HGT diversity in fungi and underscores the substantial contribution of HGT to fungal adaptation, metabolic diversity, and ecological success.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Beyond Agrobacterium-Mediated Transformation: Horizontal Gene Transfer from Bacteria to Eukaryotes ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9473684

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article by Benoît Lacroix and Vitaly Citovsky (Department of Biochemistry and Cell Biology, State University of New York, Stony Brook) published in Current Topics in Microbiology and Immunology (2018;418:443, doi:10.1007/82_2018_82, PMID: 29500561, PMCID: PMC9473684). The paper reviews horizontal gene transfer (HGT) from bacteria to eukaryotes, moving beyond the traditionally studied Agrobacterium-mediated transformation.

Key content:
- The importance of bacterium-to-eukaryote HGT in evolution remains debated, but increasing genomic data reveals many cases likely representing a significant force in adaptive evolution. Beyond massive organelle-to-nucleus gene transfer (endosymbiotic gene transfer/EGT), HGT from non-organelle bacteria is gaining recognition.
- Three pathways for DNA exchange exist: transformation (uptake of free DNA), transduction (bacteriophage-mediated), and conjugation (T4SS/plasmid-mediated requiring cell-to-cell contact). Trans-kingdom conjugation via Type IV secretion systems (T4SS) is the only demonstrated natural pathway of DNA transfer from bacteria to eukaryotic cells.
- Donor species now known to transfer DNA to eukaryotes include: Agrobacterium spp. (the classical example, transferring T-DNA and causing tumors/opines in dicotyledonous plants); Rhizobium etli (possesses its own complete vir system on plasmid p42a); Rhizobium trifolii, R. leguminosarum, Phyllobacterium myrsinacearum, Sinorhizobium meliloti, NGR234, Mesorhizobium loti, and Ensifer adhaerens (after acquiring Agrobacterium vir/T-DNA plasmids); Escherichia coli (transfer to yeast, human cells, diatoms via T4SS); Bartonella henselae (transfer to human endothelial cells, requiring host cell division for nuclear entry); and Helicobacter pylori (may translocate DNA recognized by TLR9 receptor).
- Recipient hosts span virtually all eukaryotic clades: plants, yeast, fungi, sea urchins, cultured animal cells, and humans.
- Stable vs. transient HGT: transferred DNA may be expressed without integration (transient expression); integration requires additional steps including genome conservation through cell divisions, regeneration into functional organisms, germline transmission, and evolutionary conservation.
- HGT signatures in eukaryotic genomes detected via unexpected phyletic distribution, base composition, codon usage, intron analysis, synteny; caution needed against contamination and insufficient criteria (e.g., contested claims about human genome HGT and tardigrade Hypsibius dujardini contamination).
- Documented examples: fungi (Colletotrichum with 11 HGT events, Verticillum glucan glycosyltransferase), red alga Galdieria sulphuraria (up to 5% of protein-encoding genes from bacteria, including arsenic pump), Dictyostelium discoideum (18 genes), Blastocystis (up to 2.5% of genes, 80% bacterial), plants (T-DNA in Nicotiana glauca and many Nicotiana species, Linaria vulgaris/dalmatica, sweet potato Ipomoea batatas from A. rhizogenes; genes for auxin biosynthesis, transaldolase from Actinobacteria, gamma-glutamylcysteine ligase), and animals (Hydra, bdelloid rotifers, Wolbachia endosymbionts in arthropods/nematodes possibly up to 30% of recipient genome, plant-parasitic nematodes, coffee berry borer Hypothenemus hampei mannanase HhMAN1 from Bacillus).
- Biotechnology applications: Agrobacterium is the major vector for plant transformation, insertional mutagenesis (Arabidopsis collections), CRISPR/Cas9 delivery, and fungal transformation; potential future tools include R. etli for recalcitrant plants, E. coli for yeast/fungi, and B. henselae or engineered H. pylori as vectors for human gene therapy avoiding viral vectors.
- Conclusions: bacterium-to-eukaryote HGT likely occurs across a wide range of donor-recipient combinations, with close ecological/physical association between donor and recipient being a key requirement, and proteobacteria and cyanobacteria being overrepresented as donors.
</summary>

</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: 1 1 Functional horizontal gene transfer from bacteria to eukaryotes 2 ---
URL: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20230001188/downloads/20230001188.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article by Filip Husnik and John P. McCutcheon examining functional horizontal gene transfer (HGT) from bacteria to eukaryotes. The paper surveys the role of bacterial genes throughout the eukaryotic lineage, reviewing the steps HGTs take in becoming functional, which bacterial groups contribute these transfers, and what functions they bestow on eukaryotic recipients.

**Key findings:**
- HGTs are classified into two broad types: "maintenance transfers" (which maintain preexisting functions, particularly compensating for genome reduction in endosymbionts) and "innovative transfers" (which add new functionality to the recipient).
- Genes involved in host nutrition, protection, and adaptation to extreme environments are the most common HGTs from bacteria to eukaryotic genomes.
- Functional transfers more likely involve: relatively short foreign DNA fragments, landing in gene-poor dynamic genome regions, undergoing duplication, and gaining introns to become more eukaryotic in nature. Large transfers (like the ~1.5 Mb Wolbachia fragment in pillbug Armadillidium vulgare that created a female sex chromosome) are exceptions to this pattern.
- The "weak-link model" explains HGT patterns: genes primarily enter cells at 'unprotected' lifecycle stages. Asexual multicellular eukaryotes like bdelloid rotifers (the most HGT-rich animals reported) have every cell as a weak link. Germ line infection by parasites/symbionts like Wolbachia also exposes hosts to HGT.

**Major functional categories of HGT:**
1. **Maintenance transfers**: Compensating for gene loss in obligate endosymbionts (e.g., in mealybugs, aphids, psyllids, whiteflies, Paulinella chromatophora, and trypanosomatids). Much of the HGT comes from bacteria other than the degenerating endosymbiont (e.g., reproductive manipulators like Wolbachia and Cardinium).
2. **Protection from bacteria**: Eukaryotes acquired bacterial weapons like tae proteins (Type IV secretion system amidase effectors, domesticated in at least three eukaryotic supergroups, some >800 million years old, verified to limit Borrelia burgdorferi in deer ticks), lysozymes, and pore-forming toxins (aerolysins) to fight both bacteria and eukaryotes.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Wikipedia article on Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT) or Lateral Gene Transfer (LGT), defined as the movement of genetic material between organisms other than by vertical transmission (parent to offspring). HGT is the primary mechanism for the spread of antibiotic resistance in bacteria and plays an important role in bacterial evolution, including the degradation of novel compounds like human-created pesticides and the evolution, maintenance, and transmission of virulence. It involves temperate bacteriophages and plasmids, with mechanisms including transformation, transduction, and conjugation.

HISTORY: Griffith's experiment (1928) first suggested bacterial transformation. Horizontal genetic transfer was described in 1951 in Seattle, showing transfer of a viral gene into Corynebacterium diphtheriae created a virulent strain. Inter-bacterial gene transfer was first described in a 1959 Japanese publication demonstrating transfer of antibiotic resistance between different bacterial species. Syvanen (mid-1980s) postulated lateral gene transfer has existed since the beginning of life. Molecular biologists such as Peter Gogarten have described HGT as "A New Paradigm for Biology."

MECHANISMS include: (1) Transformation – uptake/expression of foreign DNA; (2) Transduction – bacterial DNA moved by bacteriophages; (3) Bacterial conjugation – transfer via plasmid during cell-to-cell contact using Type IV Secretion Systems; (4) Gene transfer agents – virus-like elements encoded by the host found in alphaproteobacteria.

HORIZONTAL TRANSPOSON TRANSFER (HTT): Transposable elements (jumping genes) can carry resistance genes between genomes. HTT is increasingly recognized as common in eukaryotes as well as prokaryotes. DNA transposons and LTR retroelements are more likely to undergo HTT due to stable double-stranded DNA intermediates. In plants, LTR retrotransposons of the Copia superfamilies (specifically Ale and Ivana lineages with low copy numbers) are more likely to transfer horizontally. Proposed vectors include arthropods, viruses, freshwater snails, and endosymbiotic bacteria. Spatial and taxonomic proximity favor HTT.

DETECTION: HGT is typically inferred using bioinformatics (parametric methods identifying atypical sequence signatures, or identifying discrepancies in evolutionary history). Shotgun metagenomics can identify phylogenetic mismatches indicating HGT. Transferred genes are called "xenologs."

VIRUSES: The Sputnik satellite virus can perform horizontal gene transfer between viruses, as some of its genes are closely related to mimivirus and mamavirus genes, paralleling how bacteriophages ferry genes between bacteria.

PROKARYOTES: HGT is common among bacteria and between bacteria and archaea. It is a significant cause of increased drug resistance and spread of virulence factors like exotoxins and exoenzymes. Examples include multi-drug resistant S. aureus, Shiga toxins in E. coli via transduction with Shigella. Restriction-modification systems provide immunity against HGT. Horizontally transferred elements play roles in virulence of E. coli, Salmonella, Streptococcus, and Clostridium perfringens. HGT is active around secondary/specialized metabolite production. The integrated conjugative element (ICE) Bs1 plays a role in the SOS response of Bacillus subtilis.

BACTERIAL TRANSFORMATION: A complex, energy-requiring developmental process requiring about 40 genes in Bacillus subtilis. Competence is induced by high cell density or nutritional limitation and appears to be an adaptation for DNA repair. It occurs in at least 67 prokaryotic species. It can be viewed as a primitive sexual process.

BACTERIAL CONJUGATION: Uses Type IV Secretion Systems (T4SS). Single-strand DNA binding proteins (SSBs) encoded in conjugative plasmids may aid conjugation though some (like PrgE in pCF10 of Enterococcus faecalis) are not essential. Conjugation is important in microbiomes, contributing to genetic diversity and evolution, including antibiotic resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Mycobacterial conjugation (in M. smegmatis) differs from E. coli: it is chromosome rather than plasmid based.

ARCHAEAL DNA TRANSFER: Haloarchaea derived 126 composite gene families from bacterial genomes, allowing adaptation to salty environments. Sulfolobus solfataricus and S. acidocaldarius undergo UV-induced pili formation, cellular aggregation, and high-frequency DNA exchange/recombination for DNA repair via homologous recombination. The ups operon (five genes) is highly induced by UV and employed in these processes, increasing fitness after UV exposure.

EUKARYOTES: HGT has occurred within eukaryotes from chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes to the nuclear genome (per endosymbiotic theory). Horizontal transfer occurs from bacteria to fungi like Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Agrobacterium can transfer genes to plants (causing crown galls). Monarch butterflies and silkworms have been genetically modified by HGT from wasp bracovirus. This mini-review by David A. **In silico detection methods:** The review describes several approaches for locating HGT in fungal genomes, including: (a) patchy phyletic distribution of genes, (b) locating shared introns in unrelated species or intronless genes in intron-rich species, (c) finding shared genes among unrelated species sharing a niche/geographical location, (d) conserved synteny blocks, (e) codon usage variation, and (f) atypical GC content. However, phylogenetic inference is identified as the most convincing method, using topological incongruence between gene trees and species phylogenies. Surrogate methods (similarity searches, GC composition, codon usage) are faster but less accurate; notable failures include the unsupported claim of 223 genes transferred from bacterial pathogens to humans and 19 eukaryotic genes in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The author emphasizes that surrogate methods should never be used in isolation and recommends a total evidence approach with cross-corroboration from multiple independent methods, ideally validated by phylogenetic inference.

**Mechanisms facilitating fungal HGT:** Several mechanisms are described: bacterium-to-Saccharomyces cerevisiae conjugation via bacterial conjugative plasmids, Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated transformation (ATMT), plasmid transfer between Candida glabrata and S. cerevisiae via cell lysis or cytoduction, ecological proximity (a wine yeast strain gained 65 KB from Zygosaccharomyces bailii), whole chromosomal transfer (Mycosphaerella graminicola has eight dispensable chromosomes from an unknown fungal source), and anastomosis (conidial anastomosis tubes allowing genetic exchange). This scientific paper reports the complete mitochondrial genome sequence of Amborella trichopoda, a large shrub endemic to the rain forests of New Caledonia that is likely sister to all other angiosperms (diverging ~200 million years ago). The genome is enormous at 3.9 Mb (3,866,039 bp), assembled as five autonomously replicating circular chromosomes (3179, 244, 187, 137, and 119 kb). - Four complete mitochondrial genomes were horizontally transferred: one from a moss (with architecture nearly identical to Physcomitrella and Anomodon) and three from green algae (donors A, B, C), plus a partial genome from a fourth green-algal donor (D). - Of the 197 foreign mitochondrial protein genes, only 50 (25%) have full-length intact open reading frames, and most are pseudogenes; the majority of foreign genes are not functionally expressed. This makes Amborella mtDNA a striking example of neutral evolution and "junk DNA."

The authors propose a fusion-compatibility model: Amborella captured whole mitochondria from diverse green plants, followed by mitochondrial fusion (mechanistically limited to green plants) and genome recombination. They note that mitochondrial fusion in animals and fungi uses dynamin-related GTPases absent from green plants, suggesting a fundamentally different fusion mechanism in green plants. The ecological context—Amborella's heavy epiphyte load (mosses, lichens, other angiosperms), propensity to produce suckers from wounds (wounding may create new meristems that incorporate foreign mitochondria), and low rate of mitochondrial DNA loss—all contribute to the high level of foreign DNA. The transfers are likely millions of years old given extensive pseudogene decay but surprisingly intact retention of the whole-genome transfers.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PNAS research article (published December 14, 2004, in volume 101, issue 51, pages 17747-17752) by Ulfar Bergthorsson, Aaron O. Richardson, Gregory J. Young, Leslie R. Goertzen, and Jeffrey D. Palmer, titled "Massive horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes from diverse land plant donors to the basal angiosperm Amborella."

STUDY PURPOSE: The researchers investigated whether plants could acquire multiple foreign genes through horizontal gene transfer (HGT), moving beyond the previously known cases of single-gene acquisition. They focused on Amborella trichopoda, a basal angiosperm (a monotypic genus of shrubs endemic to New Caledonia) that was already known to possess one horizontally acquired gene and showed signs of containing more.

METHODOLOGY: The team used PCR amplification with conserved primers (~100 primer pairs) to comprehensively sequence the mitochondrial protein gene set of Amborella, plus variable numbers of mitochondrial genes from 28 other diverse land plants. They also conducted maximum-likelihood and parsimony phylogenetic analyses, using the Shimodaira-Hasegawa (SH) test to assess whether phylogenetically anomalous gene placements suggestive of HGT were statistically significant. To rule out contamination, HGT cases were confirmed from multiple independent DNA preparations from four different sources of Amborella material.

KEY RESULTS:
- Of the 40 protein genes present in the ancestral angiosperm mitochondrial genome, 31 were recovered from Amborella.
- Of these 31 genes, 20 showed evidence of one or more cases of HGT, for a total of 26 foreign genes acquired.
- Most transfers came from other angiosperms (especially eudicots), while others came from nonangiosperms, including six striking cases of transfer from at least three different moss donors.
- The five sequenced angiosperm mitochondrial genomes (rice, Arabidopsis, Brassica, Beta, and others) showed no evidence of HGT.
- Most transferred genes are intact (functional or recently transferred), while nine are pseudogenes.
- Evidence suggests the transferred genes reside in the mitochondrial genome (not chloroplast or nuclear), based on RNA editing patterns characteristic of mitochondria, nucleotide substitution rates, and PCR abundance.
- The 11 remaining singleton genes appear to be of vertical descent, placing Amborella as sister to all other angiosperms.

DISCUSSION AND SIGNIFICANCE: Amborella mtDNA has sustained proportionately more HGT than any other eukaryotic, or perhaps prokaryotic, genome yet examined. The study suggests HGT incidence varies markedly between plants. The authors speculate that Amborella's environment—mid-elevation montane tropical rain forests in New Caledonia where the plant's leaves and stems are often covered with diverse epiphytes including mosses—could promote direct plant-to-plant HGT (similar to mechanisms proposed for parasitic plants). The authors note limitations of their PCR approach, including missing rRNA/tRNA genes, chloroplast-derived sequences, and intergenic DNA, and emphasize that only sequencing the complete Amborella mitochondrial genome can comprehensively census its horizontally acquired DNA. They cite the SH test as supporting 14 of the transfers, with divergent duplicates in plant mtDNA representing xenologs (horizontal products) rather than paralogs.

--- SOURCE 6: Parasitic plants steal genes from their hosts | ScienceDaily ---
URL: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/06/120608100846.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A study published June 8, 2012, in BioMed Central's open access journal BMC Genomics reveals that the Malaysian parasitic plant Rafflesia cantleyi — which produces 50cm diameter flowers — has 'stolen' genes from its host, Tetrastigma rafflesiae, a member of the grape family. This represents horizontal gene transfer (movement of genes between two different organisms), as opposed to vertical gene transfer (between parents and offspring). While bacteria are known to use horizontal gene transfer (e.g., for antibiotic resistance), recent studies show plants, especially parasitic plants and their hosts, can also use it due to their intimate physical connections.

Researchers from Singapore, Malaysia, and the USA collaborated to systematically investigate horizontal gene transfer between these two plants. By examining the transcriptome (transcribed products of switched-on genes), they found 49 genes transcribed by the parasite — accounting for 2% of its total transcriptome — that originally belonged to the host. Three quarters of these transcripts appear to have replaced the parasite's own versions. Most of these genes had been integrated into the parasite's nucleus. Analysis of genetic drift between the parasite and host genes indicated the genes were acquired gradually over time.

Prof Charles Davis (Harvard University Herbaria) co-led the project with Prof Joshua Rest (Stony Brook University). Davis noted the elevated rate of horizontal gene transfer raises the possibility of a 'fitness' benefit to the parasite, such as improving nutrient extraction from the host or helping it evade the host's defenses. He also noted that about one third of the parasite's own genes have evolved to resemble those of T. rafflesia, and understanding how T. rafflesia manages its 'genomic deception' could provide insights into the slow war between plant parasites and their hosts.

Rafflesia cantleyi is an obligate holoparasite — fully dependent on its host for sustenance. The study's journal reference is: Zhenxiang Xi, Robert K Bradley, Kenneth J Wurdack, K.M. Wong, M. Sugumaran, Kirsten Bomblies, Joshua S Rest and Charles C Davis. "Horizontal transfer of expressed genes in a parasitic flowering plant." BMC Genomics, 13:227; 2012. DOI: 10.1186/1471-2164-13-227.

--- SOURCE 13: Ferns Borrowed Genes to Thrive in Low Light | Duke Today ---
URL: https://today.duke.edu/2014/04/hornwort

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A Duke University-led team has determined that ferns acquired the neochrome gene through horizontal gene transfer from hornworts (moss-related plants), which helped ferns adapt to low-light environments and diversify during the age of dinosaurs when flowering plants created shaded canopies. The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on April 14, 2014.

Neochrome is a "chimeric" gene—a hybrid of two other genes coding for photoreceptor proteins that sense blue and red light. This gives ferns a unique advantage in forests shaded by flowering plants, as filtered canopy light has more red than blue light, helping ferns "see" better.

Lead author Fay-Wei Li, a PhD student in Duke's biology department, investigated the gene's origin by combing through plant genomes from the Duke Herbarium and the 1000 Plants Initiative. Neochrome was found in hornwort genomes. Three possible explanations were tested: a shared common ancestor, independent evolution, or horizontal gene transfer. Ferns and hornworts diverged 400 million years ago. The analysis ruled out a common ancestor (since no seed plants retain the gene) and independent evolution. By constructing a family tree of light-sensitive genes, researchers found fern neochrome nested neatly within the hornwort lineage, with the gene versions separating about 179 million years ago—strong evidence of horizontal gene transfer.

Researchers are still exploring how horizontal gene transfer occurs in plants. In microbes, bacteria, fungi, and viruses mediate such transfers. Ferns' unique life cycle may facilitate this: gametophytes (the fern form producing sex cells) lack protective cuticles, are compact structures with exposed sex organs, and have extensive contact with competing plants—making foreign genetic material like neochrome easily passed to subsequent generations. The transfer appears to have occurred at just the right moment in fern evolutionary history, enabling their expansion in the shade of flowering plants. The work was supported by grants from the National Science Foundation, Duke University, and others.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Horizontal Transfer of a Plant Transposon | PLOS Biology ---
URL: https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.0040005

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed open-access research article published in PLOS Biology (December 20, 2005) by Diao X, Freeling M, and Lisch D, reporting the first well-documented evidence of horizontal transfer of a nuclear-encoded gene between higher plants.

**Key finding:** A subset of Mu-like elements (MULEs) in the genus Setaria (millets) is remarkably similar to a small family of MULEs in rice (Oryza sativa). The authors sequenced MULEs from eight species of Setaria and compared them to rice sequences, finding approximately 90% identity over 585 bp between Setaria faberi elements and a rice element (Os493) on Chromosome 5. A nearly complete Setaria element (Sf4) showed 88% overall nucleotide identity over 3.8 kb with the rice element.

**Evidence for horizontal transfer:** The Setaria and rice lineages diverged roughly 50 million years ago (Panicoid and Bambusoid grass subfamilies). The degree of similarity in noncoding regions (introns) and synonymous sites far exceeds what would be expected from vertical transmission. Key evidence:
- The MULE introns are 89% identical (227 bp total) between Setaria and rice, whereas introns of host genes (like waxy) are only ~52% identical between these species.
- The dS/dN ratio between the Setaria and rice MULEs is only 1.82 (weak selection), compared to 7.2-9.8 for host genes like waxy, acc1, and oxidoreductase.
- In contrast, comparisons of rice MULEs with homologous maize (Zm890) and sorghum (Sb632) elements show high exon similarity but dramatically reduced intron similarity (58% and 46% respectively), consistent with normal vertical transmission and selection on exons only.
- Synonymous substitution rates (dS) of 0.41-1.17 in host genes, with only 76% average identity in coding sequences and 40% in untranslated sequences between Setaria and rice.
- The region surrounding the Os493 insertion in rice does not exhibit reduced mutation frequency (flanking genes show typical divergence - exons 85% identical, introns only 50% identical with maize orthologs).
- Codon bias was ruled out (Nc value of 48 for both sequences, indicating moderate bias).

**Additional findings:** Southern blot hybridization revealed a discontinuous distribution of this MULE class. The elements were detected in rice, some Setaria species, and three species of East Asian bamboo (Shibataea kumasaca, Fargesia nitida, Phyllostachys vivax) but not in Central American bamboos (Chusquea montana, Chusquea quila, Otatea acuminata) or other grass subfamilies (Chloridoideae, Pooideae). The transfer is estimated to have occurred before the divergence of indica and japonica rice (~1 million years ago) and possibly before the rice-bamboo divergence. The authors speculate the transfer may have involved a vector, and note the possible physical proximity of the species' ancestors (southeast Asia).

**Context:** The paper notes that while horizontal transfer has been well-documented among animal transposons (P elements, mariner elements) and plant mitochondrial genes, this represents the first demonstrated case for nuclear-encoded plant genes. The elements appear to be inactive, likely due to epigenetic inactivation of foreign DNA. The authors suggest a comprehensive search for horizontally transferred plant genes is now warranted given the availability of sequence data.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This is the first well-documented example of horizontal transfer of any nuclear-encoded genes between higher plants."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Multiple horizontal transfers of nuclear ribosomal genes between phylogenetically distinct grass lineages ---
URL: https://www.pnas.org/doi/pdf/10.1073/pnas.1613375114

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper (published in PNAS, February 14, 2017, vol. 114, no. 7) investigates horizontal gene transfer (HGT) of nuclear ribosomal DNA (rDNA) between phylogenetically distinct grass lineages. The study identified nonnative rRNA gene copies in 16 diploid barley (Hordeum) species, traced via internal transcribed spacer (ITS) sequences to five distinct Panicoideae genera (Arundinella, Euclasta, Paspalum, Panicum, and Setaria) - a lineage that split from the Pooideae approximately 60 million years ago. Between one and five panicoid ITS types were found in various Hordeum and Pseudoroegneria individuals, with South American taxa accumulating multiple copies. The transfers were estimated to have occurred 1-5 Mya based on phylogenetic analysis, with at least nine independent transfer events inferred. The likely most ancient transfer (Panicum 1) occurred in the common ancestor of section Stenostachys in Central Asia, dating to 1.7-5.0 Mya.

Methodology included PCR-based screening of Triticeae species, phylogenetic analyses (Bayesian inference and maximum parsimony), construction and sequencing of a BAC library from H. bogdanii (revealing a ~70-kbp region of Panicum-derived DNA interrupted by two Hordeum-specific Copia-like transposable elements, with transposition events dated to 0.25-0.29 Mya), FISH cytogenetic analysis to locate insertion sites, and RT-PCR transcription assays. Key findings include complete absence of panicoid rDNA transcription, indications of silencing via pseudogenization (base substitutions in conserved 5.8S and ITS2 motifs), and retention of selectively neutral DNA over significant evolutionary time periods.

The authors conclude that HGT between vascular plants is not a rare event, is not restricted to one or a few genes, and can be selectively neutral. They propose aphids and endophytic fungi (particularly Epichloë) as potential vectors, given the historical geographic overlap of species due to climate changes over the past 5 million years. The paper suggests the supposed rarity of nuclear HGT in plant genomes likely reflects technical limitations in detection rather than a genuine biological phenomenon.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The movement of nuclear DNA from one vascular plant species to another in the absence of fertilization is thought to be rare. Here, nonnative rRNA gene [ribosomal DNA (rDNA)] copies were identified in a set of 16 diploid barley (Hordeum) species; their origin was traceable via their internal transcribed spacer (ITS) sequence to five distinct Panicoideae genera, a lineage that split from the Pooideae about 60 Mya."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: The Curious Case of Horizontal Gene Transfer – SCIENCE NEXT DOOR ---
URL: https://sciencenextdoorcom.wordpress.com/2021/04/29/the-curious-case-of-horizontal-gene-transfer

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, "The Curious Case of Horizontal Gene Transfer" by Suhani Sharma (published April 29, 2021, on the Science Next Door blog), explores how plants, not just bacteria, engage in Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT), which is the transmission of genes between organisms without reproduction via transformation, transduction, and conjugation. The article highlights two key cases:

**Grasses:** Research led by the University of Sheffield (Dr. Luke Dunning, senior author, and Samuel Hibdige, PhD researcher) found over 100 examples in grasses—including wheat, maize, rice, and barley—where genes had significantly different histories from the species they were found in. In some cases, HGT levels exceeded 40% of the genome, making these plants "naturally genetically modified." The study detected a statistical increase in species with modified stems called 'rhizomes.'

**Cuscata/Rafflesiaceae (Parasitic Plants):** The article discusses the Rafflesia arnoldii (giant corpse flower, with flowers weighing ~10 kg) and Sapria. A 2014 paper by Jeanmaire Molina found these plants had ditched their entire chloroplast genome. Follow-up research by Charles Davis and Liming Cai at Harvard University found that nearly half (44%) of genes conserved across plant lineages had disappeared from Sapria—more than twice the gene losses in dodders (Cuscuta) and four times the losses in witchweeds (Striga). Despite gene loss, Sapria's genome remains as large as a human's because it is loaded with borrowed genes from hosts (described as "a huge graveyard of DNA"), and 90% of its genome consists of DNA transposons ("jumping genes"). Researchers hypothesize that transposons may be the engines driving HGT, helping the parasites carry and insert gene fragments, and potentially contributing to unique features like the large flowers. The article notes these critically endangered plants face conservation challenges.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We found over 100 examples where the gene had a significantly different history to the species it was found in." - Dr. Luke Dunning; "If we can determine how this process is happening it may allow us to naturally modify crops and make them more resistant to climate change." - Dr. Luke Dunning; "We still don't know how this is happening or what the full implications are. But, we know it is widespread in grasses, a family of plants that provide a majority of the food we eat." - Samuel Hibdige; "We knew that there would be loss, but we didn't think it would be on the order of 44% of its genes." - Charles Davis; "Because these parasites have been stealing (or borrowing) genes for millennia, their genome is like a huge graveyard of DNA." - Liming Cai
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Grasses pass genes from one species to another but we don’t know how | New Scientist ---
URL: https://www.newscientist.com/article/2275559-grasses-pass-genes-from-one-species-to-another-but-we-dont-know-how

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This New Scientist article reports on research led by Luke Dunning at the University of Sheffield demonstrating that lateral (horizontal) gene transfer is widespread among grass species. The study examined the genomes of 17 grass species, some evolving independently for 50 million years (including rice, wheat, and foxtail millet), and found that 13 of the 17 species carried laterally transferred genes, with 170 genes transferred in total. The team estimates 3.72 out of every 10,000 grass genes are detectably laterally transferred, though lead author Dunning calls this "a massive underestimate" since only some transferred genes are fixed by natural selection.

Key findings include that lateral transfer is more common among closely related species but still occurs in distantly related ones, and transfers are more frequent in grasses with rhizomes (underground stems that allow asexual reproduction), as foreign DNA in rhizomes can become incorporated into the germline through every cell of the clone. The mechanism remains unknown ("the million-dollar question"), with wind-borne "illegitimate pollination" suggested as a possible vector rather than hybridization.

The article provides context that lateral gene transfer was previously thought restricted to bacteria, but increasing eukaryotic genome sequencing has revealed many examples. Julia Van Etten of Rutgers University notes that laterally transferred genes, while a small percentage of genomes, can have major evolutionary impacts—citing red algae that acquired genes for arsenic and mercury detoxification. The research was published in New Phytologist (DOI: 10.1111/nph.17328), and Dunning speculates that lateral gene transfer may underpin some traits in domesticated crop grasses like wheat.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We've shown that lateral gene transfer is a widespread process in grasses," says Luke Dunning at the University of Sheffield in the UK., "People thought it was completely restricted to bacteria and didn't happen in eukaryotes," says Dunning. "It's probably only been 10 to 15 years that that's really shifted.", "But that is a massive underestimate," says Dunning, because only some transferred genes will be favoured by natural selection and become common in a population. "It's probably an ongoing process happening all the time, and then you're only going to fix one or two.", "The million-dollar question is to find out how it's happening," says Dunning., "They're thriving because they've horizontally acquired genes for arsenic detoxification and mercury detoxification, and they're able to take up sugars so they don't have to photosynthesise all the time. They've changed their entire lifestyle," says Julia Van Etten at Rutgers University.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: [PDF] Identification of universal grass genes and es- timates of their monocot ---
URL: https://repository.rothamsted.ac.uk/id/eprint/32896/1/vbaf079.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research paper by Rowan A. C. Mitchell from Rothamsted Research (UK) describing the development of a bioinformatics pipeline that identifies "universal grass genes" - highly conserved protein-coding genes present in all grasses (Poaceae) - and estimates whether they have monocot-, commelinid-, or grass-specific functions.

**Background/Context:** Grasses are crucial for agriculture, providing ~70% of human caloric intake and 30% of protein. Key grass adaptations (morphology with protected meristems, silica-rich tissues, fast stomatal responses, ferulate-containing cell walls, unique inflorescences) arose between 230-110 million years ago.

**Methodology:** 
- Used Ensembl Plants release 56 data from 16 grass full genomes (8 each from BOP and PACMAD clades, including rice, wheat, barley, maize, sorghum, millet, sugar cane, rye, Lolium, and models Brachypodium and Setaria) plus 58 non-grass species
- Used rice and maize as reference species (representing BOP and PACMAD clades respectively)
- Built Hidden Markov Model (HMM) profiles from group alignments (MUSCLE alignment + hmmbuild from HMMER v3.3.2)
- Used genBlastG to search genome sequences for missing gene models (splice-canonical search); this step more than doubled universal groups from 6,352 to 13,312
- Pipeline ran for 11 days on Rothamsted Linux High Performance Cluster (912 CPU cores, 16TiB memory)
- Scripts available at https://github.com/Rowan-ACM/universal_grass_peps

**Key Results:**
- Identified 13,312 highly conserved, universal groups of grass protein-coding genes (all ≥12 Ensembl gene models each, minimum relative HMM score R>0.65)
- genBlastG generated 14,921 new gene models; 76% of 1,932 rice genBlastG gene models were validated against the IC4R rice annotation with >90% coverage and average 93% peptide identity
- 98.8% of groups had matches in newly sequenced Bambusoideae and Arundinoideae genomes (99.2% and 99.6% respectively; all but 1.2% matched both)
- 91% of groups had all members in the same OrthoFinder orthogroup
- HMM-based specificity metric S performed better than simple percentage identity in discriminating between known specific (31 genes from 25 publications) and non-specific (215 ribosomal/metabolic peptides) test sets: at 3% false negative rate, S>0.25 gave 8% false positives vs 15% for pairwise identity
- 4,609 groups classified as monocot-/commelinid-/grass-specific (394 monocot-specific, 1,411 commelinid-specific, 2,804 grass-specific)
- 920 supergroups of closely related function identified
- Specific genes enriched for regulatory functions (transcription and protein activity control) and hydroxycinnamoyl transferase activity; trait associations include grain size (70 groups), flowering time (50 groups), plus defence and abiotic stress traits

**Limitations:** The R cut-off of 0.65 is inclusive (90% of expected universal non-specific genes passed) but may include groups with similar-but-not-identical functions; groups can contain outliers due to erroneous gene models; universality depends on genome assembly/annotation quality.

**Availability:** The universal_grass_peps database is downloadable at https://data.rothamsted.ac.uk/dataset/universal_grass_peps. It can be used by researchers to assess whether experimentally identified grass genes (from QTLs, transcriptomes, proteomics) are involved in monocot-/commelinid-/grass-specific traits. Funded by UK BBSRC (grant BB/K007599/1 and "Designing Future Wheat" strategic grant).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: The genome and transcriptome of the parasitic plant Striga sequenced ---
URL: https://phys.org/news/2019-12-genome-transcriptome-parasitic-striga-sequenced.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On December 6, 2019, RIKEN announced the first sequencing of the genome of the parasitic plant Striga (commonly known as witchweed), a major agricultural pest causing billions of dollars in crop losses annually by tapping into host plant roots and depriving them of water and nutrients. Ken Shirasu's team at the RIKEN Center for Sustainable Resource Science sequenced the genome of a Striga species that invaded the US in the 1950s, along with the transcriptome of the most devastating Striga species.

Key findings from the analysis:
- The genome contains roughly 35,000 protein-coding genes
- Evidence of two whole-genome duplication events in its evolution
- The Striga genome evolved in three phases as theorized for parasitic plants:
  1. Acquired genes to form infectious roots by repurposing genes involved in lateral root regulation
  2. Lost certain functions to rely on hosts for resources (e.g., photosynthesis-related gene families shrank since it relies on host carbon; lost genes for hormonal response to environmental stimuli like water loss)
  3. Became specialized on specific hosts, with dramatic expansion of the strigolactone-sensing gene family enabling seedlings to recognize and colonize a wide range of hosts
- Comparison with other plant genomes revealed transfers of large genomic fragments between species, suggesting Striga can acquire genetic material from its hosts

The findings enable monitoring of Striga spreading at the genome level in fields, potentially helping select cultivars and chemicals. The research was published in Current Biology (DOI: 10.1016/j.cub.2019.07.086).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"With this genomic data, we can also currently monitor Striga spreading in field at the genome level," says Shirasu. --- SOURCE 16: Achievements in Horizontal Gene Transfer Studies in Parasitic Plants ---
URL: https://abcbot.pl/pdf/63_2/2021-02-abcbot-02.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (Acta Biologica Cracoviensia Series Botanica 63/2: 17–28, 2021) by Góraalski et al. from Jagiellonian University summarizes the current state of knowledge on horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in parasitic plants. HGT allows genetic material to flow between distantly related organisms, was first discovered in plants in the early 21st century, and is especially prevalent in parasitic plants due to their intimate physical contact with hosts.

Key findings and topics covered:

1. **Factors facilitating HGT**: Close physical contact between organisms is the most important factor. This includes parasitism (via haustoria), epiphytism, grafting, and root-to-root inosculation. Holoparasites are better HGT subjects than hemiparasites due to their complete dependence on hosts for organic substances.

2. **HGT frequency correlates with parasitic dependence**: A study of Orobanchaceae (Yang et al., 2016) found 32 HGTs in the holoparasite Phelipanche aegyptiaca, 10 in the obligate hemiparasite Striga hermonthica, 2 in the facultative hemiparasite Triphysaria versicolor, and only 1 in free-living Lindenbergia. Kado and Innan (2018) found 106 transferred genes in holoparasites (22 in Orobanche minor, 84 in Aeginetia indica) but none in facultative parasites. Cuscuta shows higher rates than Orobanchaceae, possibly because its haustorial stem connections to flowers/gametes are permanently shorter distance (Yang et al., 2019).

3. **DNA vs. RNA as carriers**: Evidence supports both mechanisms. The ShContig9484 gene in Striga hermonthica (transferred from sorghum) shows traces of mRNA origin (poly-A tail). However, later studies on Cuscuta (108 functional genes) and other species indicate most functional genes were transferred via DNA, based on presence of introns.

4. **Adaptive role of HGT**: Transfers may serve adaptive functions. Rafflesia cantleyi likely acquired dozens of transcribed genes from its host (Xi et al., 2012), possibly for "genomic deception" to evade host defenses. In Cuscuta campestris, many HGT-acquired genes are expressed in haustoria and involved in defense and amino acid metabolism (Yang et al., 2019). Eighteen functional genes in Cuscuta belong to the same families as independently transferred genes in Orobanchaceae, supporting adaptive roles. In Sapria himalayana, at least 1.2% of the genome was acquired via HGT from the host (Cai et al., 2021).

5. **Source and target genomes**: Plant cells have nuclear, mitochondrial, and plastid genomes involved in HGT and intracellular gene transfer (IGT). Mitochondria are the most frequent recipients of alien DNA due to their frequent fusion/fission and higher noncoding DNA content (72-89% vs. 40-45% in plastids). Examples include massive HGT in Amborella trichopoda (3.9-Mb mitochondrial genome with many transfers), parasite-to-host transfers (atp1, atp6, matR from Cuscuta to Plantago; atp6 in Orobanche coerulescens from Asteraceae), Cynomorium coccineum (10 transfers of 5 mitochondrial genes), and Lophophytum mirabile (over 80% alien DNA in 9 of 60 chromosomal molecules from legumes). Plastid genome HGT is rarer but exists.

6. **Mycoheterotrophs**: Despite sharing heterotrophic features with parasites, mycoheterotrophs show almost no HGT because they lack haustorium-like connections; plant-to-plant transfer would require two steps through fungi.

7. **Future questions**: The review proposes examining whether population sizes and genetic drift play roles in HGT fixation, both at organismal and subcellular (organelle population) levels.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Scientists have finally sequenced the genomes of three homosporous ferns—the flying spider-monkey tree fern (Alsophila spinulosa, published May 2022 in Nature Plants), the maidenhair fern (Adiantum capillus-veneris), and the C-fern (Ceratopteris richardii, published this week in Nature Plants)—revealing that ferns are DNA hoarders and "kleptomaniacs." The C-fern work, contributed to by Doug Soltis of the Florida Museum of Natural History and a team from 28 institutions, took over eight years and resulted in a genome of 7.46 gigabases spread across 39 chromosome pairs—more than twice the size of the human genome. Previously, scientists attributed ferns' immense genomes and high chromosome counts to repeated whole-genome duplication, but the new research contradicts this prevailing view. Instead, 85% of the C. richardii genome (and a similar proportion in A. capillus-veneris) consists of transposons (jumping genes) and repetitive "scrappy" DNA debris, suggesting ferns are simply inefficient at shedding junk DNA, like hoarders. Notably, the study also found evidence that C. richardii acquired defense genes against a membrane-puncturing toxin from bacteria via horizontal gene transfer, which occurred multiple times. This is significant because ferns are the closest living relatives of all seed plants and produce chemical deterrents to herbivores that may be useful in agricultural research. A related record holder, Ophioglossum reticulatum (adder's tongue fern), holds the record for the most chromosomes in a multicellular organism, with around 720 chromosome pairs per cell.

--- SOURCE 25: [PDF] Fern Genomics: Unfurling the Mystery of Plant Chromosome Numbers ---
URL: https://www.scientia.global/wp-content/uploads/Paul_Wolf.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article discusses Dr. Paul G. Wolf's research at the University of Alabama in Huntsville (Department of Biological Sciences) investigating plant chromosome numbers through fern genomics, specifically focusing on genome downsizing mechanisms following polyploidy. 

Key scientific context: Seed plants and some ferns are "heterosporous" (producing two spore types), while most ferns are "homosporous" (producing one spore type). Homosporous plants possess significantly more chromosomes than heterosporous plants—the fern Ophioglossum reticulatum has over 1,400 chromosomes (the highest for any plant, animal, or fungus, compared to humans' 46). Genome doubling during reproduction leads to "polyploidy" (e.g., tetraploids with four sets of chromosomes). While whole genome duplications are common in plant evolution and beneficial for crop breeding (wheat, cotton, potatoes are polyploid), they can cause genetic instability and infertility. Heterosporous plants lose excess genetic content through "genome downsizing" mechanisms, while homosporous ferns appear to have different or absent downsizing mechanisms—evidenced by their positively correlated chromosome number and genome size.

Dr. Wolf's methodology: His early work sequenced chloroplast DNA to establish evolutionary relationships among fern species. He sequenced the first complex fern-like genome in 2011, published first genetic sequences for two heterosporous fern species in 2018, and is currently assembling the first full genome sequence for the homosporous fern Ceratopteris richardii. With PhD student Sylvia Kinosian, he is investigating genetic and chromosome variation across the Ceratopteris genus, including a natural tetraploid (C. thalictroides) and lab-generated hybrid tetraploid crosses between C. richardii and C. pteridoides. Ceratopteris ferns are advantageous as a model genus due to their rapid lifecycle (145 days for a full cycle), allowing multiple experiments including chromosome behavior observation during spore-producing cell division.

The research also examines whether other life history traits (like the photosynthetic gametophyte stage in homosporous plants) correlate with spore type, since the spore type-chromosome correlation may not be causal. Some homosporous plants "silence" extra genes rather than removing them, potentially negating polyploidy's negative effects.

Implications: This synthesis approach could address broader biological concepts and deepen understanding of crop improvement methods, since exploiting natural or artificial polyploidy is effective for introducing beneficial traits into crops but can cause genetic instability.

Dr. Wolf earned his PhD in Botany from Washington State University, did postdoctoral research at UC Irvine, was a professor at Utah State University, and is now Professor and Chair at the University of Alabama in Huntsville. The research is funded by the US National Science Foundation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This series of experiments will begin to address the question of whether ferns are unable to downsize genomes as rapidly as flowering plants," says Dr Wolf.
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a 2019 scientific paper titled "Lateral transfers of large DNA fragments spread functional genes among grasses," published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Volume 116, no. 10, pages 4416-4425. The authors include Dunning, L.T., Olofsson, J.K., Parisod, C., Choudhury, R.R., Moreno-Villena, J.J., Yang, Y., Dionora, J., Quick, W.P., Park, M., Bennetzen, J.L., Besnard, G., Nosil, P., Osborne, C.P., and Christin, P.-A.

The study addresses whether lateral gene transfer (LGT) plays an important role in multicellular eukaryotes like plants, challenging the traditional view that vertical inheritance is paramount. The researchers assembled a chromosome-level genome for the grass Alloteropsis semialata, a species previously suspected of exhibiting two LGTs, and screened it against genomic data from 146 other grass species.

Key findings:
- Discovered 57 additional LGTs in the A. semialata nuclear genome, involving at least nine different donor species.
- These LGTs are clustered in 23 laterally acquired genomic fragments up to 170 kb long, accumulated during the diversification of Alloteropsis.
- The majority of the 59 total LGTs in A. semialata are expressed and added functions to the recipient genome.
- Functional LGTs were also detected in the genomes of five other grass species, showing the process is likely widespread in this globally important plant group.

Conclusion: LGT appears to represent a potent evolutionary force capable of spreading functional genes among distantly related grass species. The paper is open access under a CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0 license and available on the CGIAR (CGSpace) repository.
