SECONDARY ENDOSYMBIOSIS AND THE RISE OF PLASTID DIVERSITY As mentioned previously, primary plastids are found in glaucophytes, red algae and green algae (from which plants are derived). These groups represent a great deal of diversity and are collectively signiﬁcant ecologi-cally, but they only represent a fraction of eukaryotic phototrophs. Most algal lineages acquired their plas-tids through secondary endosymbiosis, which is the uptake and retention of a primary algal cell by another eukaryotic lineage (Delwiche 1999; McFadden 2001; Archibald & Keeling 2002; Stoebe & Maier 2002; Palmer 2003; Keeling 2004, in press; Archibald 2005; Gould et al. 2008). The plastids in most algal lineages can be attributed to this process, namely those of chlorarachniophytes and euglenids, which acquired plastids from green algae, and haptophytes, cryptomonads, heterokonts, dinoﬂagellates and api-complexans, which acquired a plastid from a red alga (ﬁgure 2). Overall, this secondary spread of plastids had a major impact on eukaryotic diversity, evolution and global ecology (Falkowski et al. 2004). Many of the lineages with secondary plastids have grown to dominate primarily production in their environment, and collectively they represent a signiﬁcant fraction of known eukaryotic diversity: it has been estimated that the lineage encompassing all the red algal second-ary plastids alone represents over 50 per cent of the presently described protist species (Cavalier-Smith 2004).
Our understanding of how such a process might have taken place is actually somewhat more clear than our understanding of how primary endosymbiosis might have played out, in part because the events were more recent, but more importantly because it hap-pened more than once so parallels and differences can be compared. As was the case for the cyanobacter-ium in primary endosymbiosis, the secondary endosymbiotic algae progressively degenerated until all that remained in most cases was the plastid, and one or two additional membranes around it. Essen-tially, no trace of mitochondria, ﬂagella, Golgi, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) or many other cellular features remain in these endosymbionts. In most lineages (see §4 for exceptions), the algal nucleus is completely absent as well, and any genes for plastid proteins that it once encoded have moved once again to the nuclear genome of the secondary host (it seems likely that many other genes also moved to that genome, but this has not been investigated very thoroughly). In general, it is thought that secondary endosymbiosis takes place through endocytosis, so the eukaryotic alga is taken up into a vacuole derived from the host endomembrane system (Delwiche 1999; McFadden 2001; Archibald & Keeling 2002; Keeling 2004; Archibald 2005; Gould et al. 2008).
After reduction, such a plastid would be predicted to be surrounded by four membranes, corresponding to (from the outside inward) the host endomembrane, the plasma membrane of the engulfed alga and the two membranes of the primary plastid (McFadden 2001; Archibald & Keeling 2002; Keeling 2004; Gould et al. 2008). Most secondary plastids are indeed surrounded by four membranes, and there is abundant evidence that the outermost membrane is derived from the host endomembrane system.
Indeed, in cryptomonads, haptophytes and hetero-konts, the outermost membrane is demonstrably contiguous with the host ER and nuclear envelope (Gibbs 1981). In other cases, the same situation is inferred from the way proteins are targeted (Foth et al. 2003; Gould et al. 2008; Bolte et al. 2009).
Many plastid proteins are encoded in the new host nucleus, and these are targeted to the plastid post-translationally, but the process requires an additional step compared with the analogous process in primary plastids. Recall that targeting in primary plastids typi-cally relies on the recognition of an N-terminal transit peptide by the TOC and TIC complexes on the outer and inner plastid membranes (McFadden 1999; Wickner & Schekman 2005; Hormann et al. 2007; Patron & Waller 2007; Gould et al. 2008). Secondary plastids are surrounded by additional membranes and are in effect situated within the endomembrane system of the secondary host (as opposed to the pri-mary plastid, which is situated in the cytosol of its host), so any protein expressed in the cytosol is not directly exposed to the plastid outer membrane and could not be imported by the TIC–TOC system alone (McFadden 1999; Gould et al. 2008; Bolte et al. 2009; Kalanon et al. 2009). This has led to an additional leg in the journey from the cytosol to the plastid, and because these plastids are located in the endomembrane of their host, travel to the plastid is initially through the secretory system. As a result, proteins targeted to secondary plastids have a more complex, bipartite leader, which consists of a signal peptide followed by a transit peptide (Patron & Waller 2007). The signal peptide is recognized by the signal recognition particle, which stops translation and directs the protein to the rough ER (RER), where translation resumes and the nascent protein crosses the membrane as it is elongated. How the protein crosses the next membrane is only just emer-ging in some groups (Hempel et al. 2007; Sommer et al. 2007; Bolte et al. 2009), and it is not yet certain if the same mechanism is used by all secondary plastids, but once exposed to the inner pair of membranes, the transit peptide may be ﬁnally recog-nized by the TOC and TIC complexes and import completed.
The origin of membranes in four-membrane secondary plastids presents few mysteries and corre-sponds well with what is known about protein trafﬁcking across those membranes. However, in euglenids and dinoﬂagellates, the secondary plastid is bounded by only three membranes (ﬁgure 2). This raised questions as to whether one membrane had been lost, and if so which one, or whether these plas-tids were derived by a different process. Speciﬁcally, it has been proposed that these plastids were acquired by myzocytosis, a feeding strategy whereby a predator attaches to a food cell and sucks its contents into a feeding vacuole, rather than engulﬁng the whole cell (Schnepf & Deichgraber 1984).
Myzocytosis is known in dinoﬂagellates and euglenids, and such a process could indeed explain the membrane topology, but it remains unclear how an alga taken up by 734 P. J. Keeling Review. Moreover, it is now abundantly clear that the three-membrane dinoﬂagellate plastid is orthologous to the four-membrane plastid in api-complexans (Moore et al. 2008; Keeling in press), so the three-membrane topology of dinoﬂagellate and euglenid plastids must be the result of some other con-vergent evolutionary pathway (Lukes et al. 2009). If the process of plastid origins is the same for three-and four-membrane secondary plastids (as must be the case in dinoﬂagellates), then which membrane was lost and why? There is no certain answer to this, but by a process of reduction it must have been the second membrane, corresponding to the plasma mem-brane of the engulfed alga. The rationale for this conclusion is that all other membranes are crossed by a known mechanism in protein targeting, and removing any one of them would have predictable and disastrous effects on trafﬁcking. For example, as the outermost membrane is part of the host endomem-brane system and protein trafﬁcking uses the ﬁrst steps in the secretion pathway to target plastid proteins to this compartment, the loss of this membrane would mean plastid-targeted proteins would be diverted to the secretory pathway. Similarly, the two inner mem-branes are involved in plastid function, and necessary to transit peptide recognition, so probably cannot be lost. In contrast, no satisfying explanation for why the second membrane is retained has been proposed (and we can therefore more readily imagine losing it), and the mechanism thought to be used to cross it in some groups is not clearly incompatible with loss (Bolte et al. 2009). This is not to say that the loss has not impacted targeting, because it has. Intrigu-ingly, the plastid-targeted proteins of both euglenids and dinoﬂagellates have targeting peptides that are different in some respects from those of other second-ary plastids (Sulli et al. 1999; Nassoury et al. 2003), and they share similar differences (Patron et al. 2005; Durnford & Gray 2006), despite having acquired their plastids independently from a green and red alga, respectively.
4. NUCLEOMORPHS Another exception that has emerged more than once is the retention of a relict nucleus of the secondary endo-symbiotic alga, structures called nucleomorphs (Gilson & McFadden 2002; Archibald 2007). In most cases, the secondary endosymbiont nucleus is completely lost, presumably owing to the movement of all genes necessary for the upkeep of the plastid to the nucleus of the new secondary host. In cryptomo-nads and chlorarachniophytes, however, this algal nucleus has persisted (ﬁgures 1 and 2) and has been the focus of much attention.
When these tiny structures were ﬁrst described using transmission elec-tron microscopy (TEM) (Greenwood et al. 1977; Hibberd & Norris 1984), the process of secondary endosymbiosis was not appreciated and the distri-bution of plastids correspondingly difﬁcult to understand. The demonstration that cryptomonad and chlorarachniophyte plastid compartments were associated with a eukaryotic nucleus and residual cytoplasm with 80S ribosomes (Ludwig & Gibbs 1989; Douglas et al. 1991; McFadden et al. 1994) was a galvanizing discovery that ushered in widespread acceptance that eukaryote–eukaryote symbiosis was an important part of plastid evolution.
Not surprisingly, attention soon turned to the gen-omes retained in nucleomorphs. As the cryptomonad plastid is clearly derived from a red alga and the chlor-arachniophyte plastid from a green alga, their nucleomorphs must have evolved independently from fully-ﬂedged algal nuclei, but they were soon found to share a number of superﬁcial similarities. In all species examined to date, the nucleomorph genome is composed of three small chromosomes, for a total genome size from as little as 373 kbp to over 650 kbp (Rensing et al. 1994; McFadden et al. 1997a; Gilson & McFadden 1999, 2002; Gilson et al.
2006; Archibald 2007; Silver et al. 2007). In nearly all cases, the rRNA operons are found as subtelomeric repeats on all six chromosome ends, although they face in opposite directions in some species (Gilson & McFadden 1996, 2002; Archibald 2007). Between these repeats, the chromosomes are ‘jam-packed’ with genes, the sequenced genomes have gene densities of about one gene per kilobase, the highest known density for a nuclear genome. This tight organization has apparently affected gene expression in nucleomorphs in both cryptomonads and chlorarachniophytes, so that there is now a high frequency of overlapping tran-scription: in Guillardia theta, nearly 100 per cent of characterized transcripts either begin in an upstream gene, terminate within or beyond a downstream gene, or both (Williams et al. 2005).
While these similarities certainly suggest that gen-omes in both lineages have been under similar pressures and constraints or been affected by similar modes of evolution, there are more differences the deeper one digs. Most importantly, there is no real pat-tern to the actual genes retained in the nucleomorphs.
When nucleomorphs were ﬁrst discovered, it was thought that they might harbour an extensive collec-tion of genes for plastid-targeted proteins, but in the complete genomes sequenced to date, plastid-targeted protein genes are relatively scarce: only 17 in Bigelowiella natans (Gilson et al. 2006) and 30 in the cryptomonads (Douglas et al. 2001; Lane et al. 2007) have been identiﬁed. Moreover, there is no signiﬁcant overlap in the identity of these genes, rather they seem to be two random subsets of possible plastid proteins (Gilson et al. 2006). Other interesting differences have been found in how these genomes have reacted to whatever process led to their severe reduction and compaction. For example, introns in cryptomonad nucleomorphs are not unusual in size or sequence, but they are extremely rare in number: the G. theta genome has only 18 introns (Douglas et al. 2001; Williams et al. 2005), and the nucleomorph of Hemiselmis andersenii has lost them altogether (Lane et al. 2007). In contrast, chlorarachniophyte nucleo-morph genes are riddled with introns: the B. natans genome retains over 800 identiﬁed introns, and most seem to be ancient introns conserved with green algae and other chlorarachniophytes (Gilson et al.
2006). These introns, however, have dramatically Review. The origin and fate of plastids P. J. Keeling 735 Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B (2010) reduced in size so that all known cases in B. natans are between 18 and 21 bp, and the majority are 19 bp, a situation more or less conserved in other chlorarachniophytes (Slamovits & Keeling 2009).
The majority of genes in nucleomorph genomes are housekeeping genes responsible for the maintenance and expression of the genome itself, although in no case is the complement of genes in a nucleomorph genome sufﬁcient for all necessary functions (Douglas et al. 2001; Gilson et al. 2006; Lane et al. 2007). Many genes are inferred to have moved to the host nucleus, and are presumably targeted back to the cytoplasm surrounding the nucleomorph (the periplastid compartment or PPC), or the nucleomorph itself.
PPC-targeted proteins are interesting from a protein trafﬁcking perspective, because in most secondary plastids there is little activity between the two pairs of membranes, and probably few genes targeted to this compartment. In cells with a nucleomorph, on the other hand, many genes appear to be targeted to this compartment and, as this is half way to the plastid, how they are targeted is an interesting question that could help resolve how proteins cross the second mem-brane (see above). The ﬁrst such genes to be identiﬁed were in the cryptomonad, G. theta, and the leaders were shown to include a signal peptide and a transit peptide (Gould et al. 2006a,b). Intriguingly, the transit peptides share a single common feature, which was the lack of a phenylalanine residue immediately down-stream of the signal peptide. This residue is part of a motif common to transit peptides of glaucophytes, red algae and all red-algal-derived plastids (Patron et al. 2005; Patron & Waller 2007). Adding a phenyl-alanine to this position of the PPC-targeted proteins led to their re-targeting to the plastid, suggesting that this position plays an important role in distinguishing PPC proteins from plastid proteins (Gould et al.
2006a,b), a function that seems to be directed by a derivative of the ERAD complex (Sommer et al.
2007; Bolte et al. 2009).
Interestingly, targeting to secondary green plastids does not rely on the F-residue (Patron et al. 2005; Patron & Waller 2007), so this information cannot participate even partially in the distinction between PPC- and plastid-targeting. Only two puta-tive PPC-targeted proteins have been identiﬁed in chlorarachniophytes, for the translation factors EFL and eIF1 (Gile & Keeling 2008). Once again, the tar-geting information on these proteins appears to consist of a signal peptide followed by a sequence with all the characteristics of a transit peptide.
Interestingly, the only difference between PPC-targeted and plas-tid-targeted protein leaders is the presence of an acid-rich domain at the C-terminus of the transit pep-tide (Gile & Keeling 2008). The B. natans genome is presently being sequenced, and will presumably yield a long list of PPC-targeted proteins whose targeting information, together with the ability to transform Lotharella amoebiformis (Hirakawa et al. 2008), will shed additional light on this problem.
The nucleomorphs of cryptomonads and chlorar-achniophytes are relatively well-studied components of a eukaryotic endosymbiont, and they have evolved along remarkably similar lines. But this does not mean such a path is inevitable. Indeed, in the tertiary endosymbiotic partnership between a diatom and dinoﬂagellates such as Kryptoperidinium and Durinskia (see below), the endosymbiont nucleus and its genome have not reduced at all, but grossly expanded (Kite et al. 1988). These endosymbionts are fully integrated in the host cell cycle, but are poorly studied at the mol-ecular level and it is not known if any genetic exchange has taken place. Because of their enormous size, the nuclei are not typically referred to as nucleomorphs, but in some ways the situation is similar to the argu-ments about the Paulinella chromatophore and whether it should be called a plastid: the interesting point is not so much the name, but that the organelle has followed a different evolutionary path than have those in cryptomonad and chlorarachniophyte endosymbionts.
5. HOW MANY TIMES HAVE PLASTIDS MOVED BETWEEN EUKARYOTES?
We know secondary endosymbiosis has happened on multiple occasions, because both green and red algal endosymbionts are known, but exactly how many times secondary endosymbiosis has taken place has been a subject of ongoing debate.
On the green side, the question is more or less settled. Secondary green algal plastids are known in euglenids and chlorarachniophytes, and there is no strong similarity between the two. Euglenids have three-membrane plastids and store paramylon in the cytosol, whereas chlorarachniophytes have four-membrane plastids with a nucleomorph and store beta-1-3-glucans in the cytosol (McFadden et al.
1997b; Leedale & Vickerman 2000; Ishida et al.
2007). The hosts are also different, and although the chlorarachniophytes have only recently found a home in the tree of eukaryotes with Cercozoa (Bhattacharya et al. 1995; Cavalier-Smith & Chao 1997; Keeling 2001; Nikolaev et al. 2004; Burki et al. 2009), it was clear early on that euglenids were similar to trypanosomes (Leedale & Vickerman 2000), and not chlorarachniophytes.
In keeping with this, early molecular phylogenies did not support a close relation-ship between the two groups. Nevertheless, it was proposed that their plastids shared a common ancestor, in the so-called Cabozoa hypothesis (Cavalier-Smith 1999). The rationale behind this hypothesis was that secondary endosymbiosis and the evolution of a protein-targeting system in particular is a complex process, and hypotheses for plastid evol-ution should severely limit the number of times this would have taken place. However, analysis of complete plastid genomes has refuted this proposal, because chlorarachniophytes and euglenid plastid genomes have now been shown to be speciﬁcally related to different green algal lineages (Rogers et al. 2007a; Turmel et al. 2009), and so could not have been derived from a single endosymbiosis (ﬁgure 2).
The evolution of secondary plastids from red algae is far more complex and a much greater number of lineages are involved. Secondary red algal plastids are found in cryptomonads, haptophytes, heterokonts, dinoﬂagellates and apicomplexans. Although these 736 P. J. Keeling Review. The origin and fate of plastids Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B (2010) organisms represent a great deal of plastid diversity (some have nucleomorphs, some are non-photosyn-thetic, some have three membranes, etc.), and although molecular phylogenies originally grouped neither nuclear nor plastid lineages together, again it was proposed that their plastids arose from a single common endosymbiosis, an idea known as the chro-malveolate hypothesis (Cavalier-Smith 1999).
In contrast to the Cabozoa hypothesis, data eventually emerged to support the chromalveolate hypothesis and, although still contentious, a variation on this hypothesis is gaining some general acceptance (ﬁgure 2). The evidence for this relationship and con-troversies surrounding it was recently reviewed elsewhere (Keeling in press), but as data are emerging quickly and because it does represent a major fraction of plastid diversity, the evidence will be summarized brieﬂy here.
Plastid gene phylogenies have supported the relationship of heterokonts, haptophytes and crypto-monads to the exclusion of what few red algal lineages have been sampled (Yoon et al.
2002; Hagopian et al. 2004; Khan et al. 2007; Rogers et al.
2007a), but the strange plastid genomes of apicomplex-ans and dinoﬂagellates have essentially excluded them from such analyses. In addition, two nucleus-encoded genes for plastid-targeted proteins, glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and fructose bisphosphate aldolase, have also supported the common origin of chromalveolate plastids because the chromalveolate genes have a unique evolutionary history that differs from homologues in other plastids (Fast et al. 2001; Harper & Keeling 2003; Patron et al. 2004). Nuclear gene phylogenies have typically not supported a mono-phyletic chromalveolate (e.g. Kim & Graham 2008), including analyses of some large multi-gene datasets (Patron et al. 2004; Burki et al. 2007, 2008). However, other large multi-gene analyses (e.g. Hackett et al. 2007; Hampl et al. 2009; Burki et al. 2009) have recovered a monophyletic chromalveolate, with one important provision: that it also includes Rhizaria. In the relatively short time since the monophyly of Rhizaria was discov-ered (Cavalier-Smith & Chao 1997; Keeling 2001; Archibald et al. 2002; Nikolaev et al. 2004), they have been considered a supergroup in their own right, but a string of large-scale analyses have consistently shown that they are closely related to alveolates and hetero-konts (Burki et al. 2007, 2008, 2009; Hackett et al.
2007; Hampl et al. 2009), and were recently shown to share a novel class of Rab GTPase (Elias et al. 2009).
If all of these observations are correct, it also means the ancestor of Rhizaria possessed the red algal plastid that is still present in many chromalveolates. This is interest-ing, not least because two rhizarian lineages are today photosynthetic: chlorarachniophytes and Paulinella, but they have acquired their plastids more recently and from different sources (see above). If Rhizaria are derived from an ancestrally photosynthetic chromalveolate, then these two lineages have reverted to phototrophy by entering into new symbioses (ﬁgure 2).
Although the single origin of all chromalveolate plastids remains in question, the ancestral state of two large and diverse subgroups has become much more clear in recent years.
First, many large multi-gene phylogenetic analyses, as well as the shared presence of a rare horizontal gene transfer in the plastid genome, have shown that cryptomonads and haptophytes are sisters (Rice & Palmer 2006; Burki et al. 2007, 2008, 2009; Hackett et al. 2007; Hampl et al. 2009; Okamoto et al. 2009). At the same time, they have been shown to be related to a number of more poorly studied lineages, including sev-eral that are non-photosynthetic (Okamoto & Inouye 2005; Not et al. 2007; Cuvelier et al. 2008; Burki et al.
2009; Okamoto et al.
2009).
This fast-growing group of increasing importance and diversity has recently been called the Hacrobia (Okamoto et al.
2009). The other group where the ancestral state is now well established is the apicomplexans and dinoﬂa-gellates. Since the discovery of the apicomplexan plastid, there has been a long-running debate over the ancestry of plastids in these two lineages, and indeed whether the apicomplexan plastid is derived from a red or green alga (Williamson et al. 1994; Ko ¨hler et al. 1997; Roberts et al. 1998; Keeling et al.
1999; Fast et al. 2001; Funes et al. 2002; Waller et al.
2003). This debate is a difﬁcult problem, because the plastid genomes of these two lineages are both highly derived and share almost no genes in common, so they are nearly impossible to compare directly (Keeling 2008). However, the discovery of Chromera velia, the photosynthetic sister to Apicomplexa (ﬁgure 1), changes this completely (Moore et al. 2008). Chromera forms a link between these two unusual lineages so that the initial characterization of molecular data (Moore et al. 2008) and now the complete sequence of its plas-tid genome (J. Janouskovec, A. Horak, M. Obernik, J. Lukes & P . J. Keeling 2009, unpublished data) com-pletely eliminate any basis for the green origin of the apicomplexan plastid, and ﬁrmly supports the presence of a plastid in the common ancestor of apicomplexans and dinoﬂagellates.
6. PLASTID LOSS AND CRYPTIC PLASTIDS One of the outcomes of the chromalveolate hypothesis has been an increased interest in the process of plastid loss and the prevalence of cryptic, non-photosynthetic plastids in heterotrophic lineages. This is because the early origin of the secondary red algal plastid central to the chromalveolate hypothesis requires that a number of currently non-photosynthetic lineages must have had photosynthetic ancestors. To under-stand the implications of this aspect of the hypothesis, it is necessary to consider several things carefully, in particular the difference between plastid loss and the loss of photosynthesis, and also how well we actually understand the distribution of cryptic plastids.
The difference between losing photosynthesis and losing a plastid may seem straightforward, but the dis-tinction is surprisingly often ignored.

args.key_excerpts: "Plastids and mitochondria each arose from a single endosymbiotic event and share many similarities in how they were reduced and integrated with their host. However, the subsequent evolution of the two organelles could hardly be more different: mitochondria are a stable fixture of eukaryotic cells that are neither lost nor shuffled between lineages, whereas plastid evolution has been a complex mix of movement, loss and replacement."
args.summary:
This is a review article by Patrick J. Keeling (Botany Department, University of British Columbia) published in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2010, vol. 365, pp. 729-748), examining the endosymbiotic origin, diversification, and fate of plastids. The article is part of a Theme Issue on "Evolution of organellar metabolism in unicellular eukaryotes."

Key points:

1. SINGLE ORIGIN OF PRIMARY PLASTIDS: Plastids and mitochondria each arose from a single endosymbiotic event (cyanobacterium and alpha-proteobacterium respectively). Primary plastids, surrounded by two membranes, are found in only three lineages: glaucophytes (retaining a relict peptidoglycan wall), red algae (5000-6000 species with chlorophyll a and phycobilisomes), and green algae (with chlorophyll a and b, starch storage in plastid, giving rise to land plants). Molecular phylogenies of concatenated genes strongly support the monophyly of these lineages, now called Plantae or Archaeplastida, with glaucophytes likely branching first. Plastid genomes have become a small fraction of cyanobacterial genome size, with protein targeting established through TOC/TIC complexes and transit peptides.

2. PAULINELLA AND POSSIBLE SECOND PRIMARY ORIGIN: Paulinella chromatophora, a testate amoeba in Cercozoa (Rhizaria), has acquired cyanobacterial endosymbionts (chromatophores) related to Synechococcus/Prochlorococcus. The chromatophore genome is ~1 Mbp with 867 genes (vs. ~3 Mbp/3300 genes in Synechococcus), reduced by loss of whole pathways rather than gene transfer seen in plastids. One gene (psaE) appears transferred to the host nucleus, but whether a protein-targeting system has evolved is uncertain. The debate over whether to call it an organelle affects how we think about organellogenesis.

3. SECONDARY ENDOSYMBIOSIS: Most algal lineages acquired plastids through secondary endosymbiosis (uptake of a primary algal cell). Green algal plastids were taken up by euglenids and chlorarachniophytes (independently, refuting the Cabozoa hypothesis). Red algal plastids were acquired by cryptomonads, haptophytes, heterokonts, dinoflagellates, and apicomplexans, hypothesized to derive from a single event in the ancestor of chromalveolates (including Rhizaria, per recent large multi-gene analyses). Secondary plastids typically have four membranes, with the outermost contiguous with host ER. Proteins use bipartite leaders (signal peptide + transit peptide). Euglenid and dinoflagellate plastids have three membranes, likely by loss of the second membrane.

4. NUCLEOMORPHS: Cryptomonads and chlorarachniophytes retain relict nuclei (nucleomorphs) of the secondary endosymbiont. Nuclear genomes are composed of three small chromosomes (373-650+ kbp) with the highest known gene density (~1 gene/kb). Only 17-30 plastid-targeted protein genes are retained, with no overlap between the two lineages. Cryptomonad nucleomorphs have very few introns, while chlorarachniophytes retain many ancient but tiny (18-21 bp) introns. The presence of a phenylalanine residue distinguishes PPC-targeted from plastid-targeted proteins.

5. PLASTID LOSS AND REPLACEMENT: Plastid loss is difficult to prove, with cryptic non-photosynthetic plastids being discovered. In some dinoflagellates, ancestral plastids have been replaced through tertiary endosymbiosis (with diatoms, haptophytes, cryptomonads) or serial secondary endosymbiosis (with a green alga). Two rhizarian lineages (chlorarachniophytes and Paulinella) appear to have reverted to phototrophy with new plastids of different origins. The discovery of Chromera velia, a photosynthetic sister to Apicomplexa, firmly establishes a red algal plastid in the common ancestor of apicomplexans and dinoflagellates. The distinction between losing photosynthesis and losing the plastid itself is important, as these have different likelihoods.

Phylogenomic Insights into the Origin of Primary Plastids 1 2 Iker Irisarri1,2,3,*, Jürgen F. H. Strassert1,4, Fabien Burki1,5 3 4 1 Department of Organismal Biology (Systematic Biology), Uppsala University, Norbyv. 5 18D, 75236 Uppsala, Sweden 6 2 Department of Biodiversity and Evolutionary Biology, Museo Nacional de Ciencias 7 Naturales, José Gutiérrez Abascal 2, 28006 Madrid, Spain 8 3 Current address: Department of Applied Bioinformatics, Institute for Microbiology 9 and Genetics, University of Göttingen, Goldschmidtstr. 1, and Campus Institute Data 10 Science (CIDAS), Göttingen, Germany 11 4 Department of Ecosystem Research, Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and 12 Inland Fisheries, Müggelseedamm 301, 12587 Berlin, Germany 13 5 Science For Life Laboratory, Uppsala University, 75236 Sweden 14 15 * Email: irisarri.iker@gmail.com 16 17 IRISARRI, STRASSERT, BURKI 2 Abstract 18 19 The origin of plastids was a major evolutionary event that paved the way for an 20 astonishing diversification of photosynthetic eukaryotes. Plastids originated by 21 endosymbiosis between a heterotrophic eukaryotic host and cyanobacteria, presumably 22 in a common ancestor of the primary photosynthetic eukaryotes (Archaeplastida). A 23 single origin of primary plastids is well supported by plastid evidence but not by nuclear 24 phylogenomic analyses, which have consistently failed to recover the monophyly of 25 Archaeplastida hosts. Importantly, plastid monophyly and non-monophyletic hosts 26 could be explained under scenarios of independent or serial eukaryote-to-eukaryote 27 endosymbioses. Here, we assessed the strength of the signal for the monophyly of 28 Archaeplastida hosts in four available phylogenomic datasets. The effect of 29 phylogenetic methodology, data quality, alignment trimming strategy, gene and taxon 30 sampling, and the presence of outlier genes were investigated. Our analyses revealed a 31 lack of support for host monophyly in the shorter individual datasets. However, when 32 analyzed together under rigorous data curation and complex mixture models, the 33 combined nuclear datasets supported the monophyly of primary photosynthetic 34 eukaryotes (Archaeplastida) and revealed a putative association with plastid-lacking 35 Picozoa. This study represents an important step towards better understanding deep 36 eukaryotic evolution and the origin of plastids. 37 38 Keywords: Archaeplastida, Bayesian, chloroplast, maximum likelihood, mixture 39 model, ortholog, outlier loci, paralog, protist 40 41 PHYLOGENOMICS OF PRIMARY PLASTID ORIGIN 3 The origin of plastids by endosymbiosis with cyanobacteria was a key evolutionary 42 event that allowed eukaryotes to perform oxygenic photosynthesis (i.e., 43 photoautotrophy). This innovation paved the way for an astonishing diversification of 44 micro- and macroscopic algae and land plants in all sunlit environments. Generally, 45 plastids have been viewed to originate from a single endosymbiotic event in a common 46 ancestor of three well-defined lineages: Glaucophyta, Rhodophyta (red algae), and 47 Chloroplastida (green algae and land plants), collectively known as Archaeplastida (Adl 48 et al. 2005) or Plantae (Cavalier-Smith 1998). These lineages harbor primary plastids, 49 i.e. derived by endosymbiosis directly from cyanobacteria, and thereafter will be 50 referred to as primary photosynthetic eukaryotes (PPE). Despite structural and genomic 51 differences, the plastids of Glaucophyta, Rhodophyta, and Chloroplastida share many 52 similarities such as the presence of a homologous protein transport apparatus, gene 53 content, and synteny blocks that have been interpreted as evidence supporting their 54 common origin (Cavalier-Smith 2000; McFadden and van Dooren 2004; Löffelhardt 55 2014; Mackiewicz and Gagat 2014). A more recent and independent symbiosis with 56 cyanobacteria is known to have given rise to chromatophores, plastid-like 57 photosynthetic organelles found in rhizarians of the genus Paulinella (Marin et al. 58 2005). 59 The genomic and structural similarities among primary plastids are consistent 60 with the monophyly of plastids generally recovered by phylogenies of plastid-encoded 61 genes (Baurain et al. 2010; Criscuolo and Gribaldo 2011; Ponce-Toledo et al. 2017; 62 Sánchez-Baracaldo et al. 2017). Unlike plastid phylogenies, resolving the relationship 63 among Archaeplastida host (nuclear) lineages has proven more difficult and currently 64 stands out as one of the major knowledge gaps in the eukaryotic Tree of Life (Burki et 65 al. 2020). This is because inferring the relationships among PPE necessarily involves 66 IRISARRI, STRASSERT, BURKI 4 resolving the affinities with other deep-branching eukaryotic groups lacking primary 67 plastids such as Cryptophyta, Haptophyta, or Picozoa; all notoriously difficult to place 68 in the eukaryotic tree (Burki et al. 2020). With a few exceptions (Price et al. 2019; 69 Strassert et al 2021), the majority of nuclear phylogenomic studies have not recovered 70 the monophyly of PPE (Hampl et al. 2009; Baurain et al. 2010; Parfrey et al. 2010; 71 Burki et al. 2012, 2016; Brown et al. 2013; Yabuki et al. 2014; Janouškovec et al. 72 2017), or did so with low statistical support (Burki et al. 2007, 2009), or using a very 73 sparse taxon sampling (Rodríguez-Ezpeleta et al. 2005, 2007a; Deschamps and Moreira 74 2009; Leebens-Mack et al. 2019). Recent studies reported contradicting Bayesian and 75 maximum likelihood trees regarding Archaeplastida monophyly (Brown et al. 2018; 76 Gawryluk et al. 2019; Strassert et al. 2019). Investigations also recovered a close 77 affinity of Rhodophyta with the newly discovered heterotrophic predatory lineage 78 Rhodelphidia (Gawryluk et al. 2019), or even the plastid-lacking Picozoa (Seenivasan et 79 al. 2013; Lax et al. 2018; Gawryluk et al. 2019). Importantly, we note that the majority 80 of these studies did not converge to a robust alternative to the monophyly of 81 Archaeplastida either, leading to the current situation of clear monophyly of plastids but 82 inconclusive relationships among host lineages. 83 While cell biological and genomic characters in primary plastids are more easily 84 explained under the hypothesis of a single endosymbiosis, the observed similarities 85 could at face value be the result of parallel or convergent evolution (Stiller 2014). In 86 fact, the monophyly of plastids is a necessary but insufficient condition to invoke a 87 single endosymbiosis in the ancestor of Archaeplastida. Alternative biological scenarios 88 can explain plastid monophyly when hosts are not monophyletic, including (i) serial 89 endosymbioses, (ii) the independent acquisition of plastids from closely-related (and 90 PHYLOGENOMICS OF PRIMARY PLASTID ORIGIN 5 perhaps now extinct) cyanobacterial lineages, or (iii) plastid losses (Mackiewicz and 91 Gagat 2014) (Supplementary Fig. 1; available https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.ffbg79cs1). 92 Here, we assessed the evidence for the monophyly of PPE by investigating the 93 signal and conflict in four available nuclear phylogenomic datasets. Even after 94 correcting for systematic biases, these datasets showed varying and unsupported 95 relationships. In search for the reasons of this lack of signal, we investigated the effects 96 of phylogenetic inference methods and models, gene sampling, taxon sampling, and the 97 presence of outlier loci. To overcome the limitations observed in the four source 98 datasets, we generated a series of curated combined datasets and investigated the effect 99 of data quality, systematic errors (model misspecifications), and the effect of alignment 100 trimming algorithms in recovering deep eukaryotic relationships. The overall poorer resolution of deep eukaryotic 458 relationships might be expected for summary coalescent methods that assume fixed 459 gene trees, due to the limited phylogenetic signal of individual loci at this level of 460 divergence. 461 462 Discussion 463 Resolving Recalcitrant Relationships in the Deep Phylogeny of Eukaryotes 464 IRISARRI, STRASSERT, BURKI 20 Resolving the backbone of the eukaryotic Tree of Life is a complex endeavor requiring 465 the inference of events dating back >1 Ga (Strassert et al. 2021). Decades of 466 phylogenetic research and the more recent burgeoning of phylogenomics have 467 progressively refined the shape of the tree, but some relationships have remained 468 contentious (Burki et al. 2020). One such contentious points is the relationships among 469 PPE and closely related lineages within Diaphoretickes. Here, we recovered consistent 470 phylogenetic relationships for PPE lineages only after combining individual datasets (in 471 particular more genes), careful data curation for the removal of paralogs and 472 contaminants, and the use of mixture models that better account for heterogeneous 473 evolutionary patterns. 474 None of the four original datasets under study could resolve the phylogenetic 475 affinities of PPE with confidence. Investigating subsets of shared taxa and genes across 476 the four datasets did not reveal specific taxa or gene combinations that recovered stable 477 PPE relationships. Heavily reducing taxon sampling to the 20 taxa shared by all four 478 datasets produced more similar trees, but these were still inconclusive regarding PPE 479 relationships (Fig. 2). Heavily reducing gene sampling to the 57 genes common to all 480 four datasets did not result in more similar trees (Fig. 2), suggesting increased stochastic 481 error with fewer loci. We found extensive gene conflict regarding PPE relationships, 482 which remained even after the identification and removal of several paralogs that 483 compromised phylogenetic accuracy (Fig. 3). In particular, the KAT dataset contained 484 plastid paralogs (Supplementary Figs. 6-11) that artificially inflated the support for 485 Archaeplastida due to the strong signal for plastid monophyly in plastid-encoded genes 486 (Baurain et al. 2010; Criscuolo and Gribaldo 2011; Ponce-Toledo et al. 2017; Sánchez-487 Baracaldo et al. 2017). The removal of the identified paralogs from KAT led to the loss 488 of the Archaeplastida monophyly recovered in the original dataset (Supplementary Fig. 489 PHYLOGENOMICS OF PRIMARY PLASTID ORIGIN 21 12). In BAU, the removal of one outlier locus (EF2) changed deep eukaryotic 490 relationships. Although we could not identify obvious problems of paralogy or 491 contamination in EF2, we observed a strong affinity between Glaucophyta and 492 Amorphea, in agreement with previous studies suggesting hidden paralogy or horizontal 493 transfer during the evolutionary history of this gene (Reeb et al. 2009; Atkinson and 494 Baldauf 2010). These results confirm previous reports that a handful of loci in 495 phylogenomic datasets can drive contentious relationships (Brown and Thomson 2017; 496 Shen et al. 2017; Siu-Ting et al. 2019). Therefore, carefully dissecting the signal and its 497 distribution in phylogenomic datasets is crucial to identify problematic loci. The 498 development of new approaches to outlier identification (Walker et al. 2020) and 499 automated pipelines for gene alignment curation (e.g., PhyloToL (Cerón-Romero et al. 500 2019) or PhyloFisher: https://pypi.org/project/phylofisher/) represent important 501 advances for assembling large and accurate eukaryotic phylogenomic datasets. 502 Given the limited signal of the original datasets, we tested whether the 503 combination of data improved the placement of PPE lineages. The combined datasets 504 showed higher internal consistency than any of the four source datasets (Supplementary 505 Fig. 16), which we interpret as evidence for stronger genuine phylogenetic signal. 506 Importantly, the strength of this signal was not associated with higher alignment 507 completeness metrics (sensu Wong et al. 2020). The combined datasets also showed 508 substantial conflict among genes with regards to PPE relationships (Supplementary Fig. 509 13) and deep eukaryotic relationships as a whole (Supplementary Fig. 17), although we 510 did not identify obvious issues of paralogy or contamination in the outlier loci. 511 Phylogenetic conflict measured as internode certainty was not preferentially associated 512 with short branches, as expected under predominance of incomplete lineage sorting 513 (Marcussen et al. 2014; Supplementary Fig. 18), suggesting that other sources of 514 IRISARRI, STRASSERT, BURKI 22 conflict, such as stochastic error or heterogeneous evolutionary patterns, are likely more 515 prevalent (Bryant and Hahn 2020). 516 The phylogenetic analysis of the combined datasets under better-fitting mixture 517 models converged to overall consistent topologies (Fig. 4). Mixture models can better 518 account for heterogeneous evolutionary patterns in the data thereby reducing the risks of 519 systematic errors (Rodríguez-Ezpeleta et al. 2007b; Philippe and Roure 2011; Wang et 520 al. 2018). Even though infinite profile mixtures (CAT) showed a better fit to the data 521 than empirical mixtures (C60), the current implementation of CAT-GTR in PhyloBayes 522 proved computationally challenging and failed to converge, as often seen in other 523 studies of deep eukaryotic relationships (Burki et al. 2016; Kang et al. 2017; Gawryluk 524 et al. 2019). In this respect, the development of more efficient implementations of 525 existing models (Dang and Kishino 2019) and new mixture models (Schrempf et al. 526 2020) should contribute to further resolving the eukaryotic Tree of Life. 527 528 Effect of Alignment Filtering Algorithms 529 To understand the effect of alignment filtering in resolving the eukaryotic tree, we 530 performed an empirical comparison between: (i) untrimmed data, (ii) the probabilistic 531 algorithm Divvier (Ali et al. 2019), and (iii) BMGE, a commonly used block trimming 532 method. In agreement with Tan et al. (2015), we found that untrimmed gene alignments 533 led to lower gene tree conflict (lower nRF to the concatenated tree) than block-trimmed 534 alignments (Supplementary Fig. 19a). Divvier, which was not assessed in Tan et al. 535 (2015), led to higher conflict than no trimming but less than block trimming. The 536 conflicts resulting from Divvier affected mostly longer genes (>400 aligned amino 537 acids; Supplementary Fig. 19c). We note that aggressive block trimming not only 538 increases gene tree conflict but can also affect tree topology and support values when 539 PHYLOGENOMICS OF PRIMARY PLASTID ORIGIN 23 hundreds of loci are concatenated (Supplementary Figs. 20–24). This is particularly the 540 case when the underlying phylogenetic signal is weak. In the case of PPE, block-541 trimmed concatenated alignments led Cryptista to branch with Chloroplastida + 542 Glaucophyta even when using complex mixture models (Supplementary Figs. 23, 26, 543 27). Instead, untrimmed and divvier-trimmed alignments consistently recovered the 544 monophyly of PPE (+ Picozoa) to the exclusions of Cryptista under the same mixture 545 models (Supplementary Figs. 24, 25, 28, 29). 546 547 Implications for Eukaryotic Evolution 548 Inferring stable PPE relationships was only possible after combining the four datasets 549 under study, the addition of newly discovered deep-branching lineages, careful data 550 curation, loose alignment trimming, and the application of complex mixture models. 551 Our analyses, based on a broad sampling of eukaryotic diversity, consistently recovered 552 the monophyly of PPE in agreement with some recent nuclear phylogenomic studies 553 (Brown et al. 2018; Lax et al. 2018; Gawryluk et al. 2019; Price et al. 2019; Strassert et 554 al. 2021) but in stark contrast with most earlier ones (Hampl et al. 2009; Baurain et al. 555 2010; Parfrey et al. 2010; Burki et al. 2012; Brown et al. 2013; Yabuki et al. 2014; 556 Janouškovec et al. 2017). In agreement with studies that recovered monophyletic PPE, 557 we found Cryptista to be the most likely sister lineage to Archaeplastida (Lax et al. 558 2018; Price et al. 2019), although the position of Picozoa remains inconsistent among 559 studies. A sister group relationship between Glaucophyta and Chloroplastida was 560 consistently recovered by all our analyses, as did many nuclear phylogenomic studies 561 (e.g., Burki et al. 2012, 2016; Brown et al. 2018; Lax et al. 2018; Gawryluk et al. 2019; 562 Price et al. 2019). This contrasts with the closer affinity of Chloroplastida and 563 Rhodophyta favored by many plastid phylogenies (Ponce-Toledo et al. 2017; Sánchez-564 IRISARRI, STRASSERT, BURKI 24 Baracaldo et al. 2017; Reyes-Prieto et al. 2018), even though a deeper branching of 565 Rhodophyta has also been recovered by plastid genes (Criscuolo and Gribaldo 2011; 566 Lang and Nedelcu 2012). An earlier divergence of Chloroplastida has also been 567 proposed based on plastid genes transferred to the nucleus during endosymbiosis 568 (Deschamps and Moreira 2009). Finally, our analyses confirmed the monophyly of 569 Rhodelphidia and Rhodophyta (Gawryluk et al. 2019) and were consistent regarding the 570 possible close affinity between Rhodophyta and Picozoa that has been sometimes — 571 although not always (Price et al. 2019) — observed (Burki et al. 2016; Lax et al. 2018). 572 573 Implications for the Origin of Primary Plastids 574 In addition to further resolving the tree of eukaryotes, the recovery of PPE monophyly 575 using nuclear data fills an important gap in our understanding of plastid origins. It is 576 commonly assumed that primary plastids originated once in the ancestor of 577 Archaeplastida (Reyes-Prieto et al. 2007; Gould et al. 2008; Löffelhardt 2014). This 578 hypothesis of a single endosymbiosis was initially based on the presence of a similar 579 double envelope surrounding both primary plastids and cyanobacteria and the homology 580 of the transit machinery for plastid protein import in all PPE. It also more easily 581 explains some similarities of plastid genomes, such as the presence of a conserved set of 582 genes and microsyntenic regions (Stoebe and Kowallik 1999), or the unusual tRNA-Leu 583 group I intron (Besendahl et al. 2000). Endosymbiotically-derived gene clusters (Ku et 584 al. 2015) and mosaic metabolic pathways (Reyes-Prieto and Bhattacharya 2007) have 585 been interpreted as additional evidences for a common origin. 586 Most of the evidence for a common origin are based on plastid data, but the 587 similarities in plastid genomes and cell biology could at face value also be explained by 588 alternative scenarios in which hosts are not necessarily monophyletic (Supplementary 589 PHYLOGENOMICS OF PRIMARY PLASTID ORIGIN 25 Fig. 1) (Mackiewicz and Gagat 2014). Our phylogenetic analyses of host (nuclear) 590 markers describe a set of conditions that previously prevented the recovery of consistent 591 relationships for PPE lineages, and clarify previous discrepancies between host and 592 plastid phylogenies. Thus, the host monophyly of PPE strongly favors the 593 Archaeplastida hypothesis of a single plastid origin in a common ancestor. Yet, our 594 analyses also supported the close affinity of Rhodophyta with two non-photosynthetic 595 taxa, Rhodelphidia and Picozoa (Fig. 5). The demonstration that the predatory genus 596 Rhodelphis (Rhodelphidia) shared a most recent common ancestor with Rhodophyta 597 provided fundamental insights on a possible mixotrophic behavior during early 598 Archaeplastida evolution (Gawryluk et al. 2019). However, because Rhodelphis has 599 most likely retained a non-photosynthetic cryptic plastid similar to that of red algae 600 (Gawryluk et al. 2019), its phylogenetic placement is not in contradiction with the 601 Archaeplastida hypothesis. The case of Picozoa as sister to the Rhodelphidia + 602 Rhodophyta clade is different, because so far, genomic and ultrastructural investigations 603 have failed to identify a plastid in this group (Yoon et al. 2011; Seenivasan et al. 2013). 604 If confirmed, the position of Picozoa would imply a scenario for the origin of primary 605 plastids that is more complex than traditionally assumed. At face value, Picozoa could 606 simply be secondarily plastid-lacking, but this possibility would require drastic 607 relocalization of plastid pathways (or bypassed entirely) to achieve independence from 608 the ancestral plastid. Importantly, complete loss of primary plastids has never been 609 reported, and is exceedingly rare in secondary plastid-containing lineages, having been 610 only confirmed in five parasitic lineages, all belonging to Myzozoa (Alveolata); two in 611 apicomplexans — Cryptosporidium (Zhu et al. 2000) and Gregarines (Janouškovec et 612 al. 2019; Mathur et al. 2019; Yazaki et al. 2021) — and in the dinoflagellate 613 Hematodinium (Gornik et al. 2015). The alternative to explain the position of Picozoa 614 IRISARRI, STRASSERT, BURKI 26 needs to invoke independent plastid acquisitions in Archaeplastida, either through 615 multiple primary endosymbioses (Stiller 2003), or secondary endosymbiosis (Kim and 616 Maruyama 2014). args.summary: This scientific paper by Irisarri, Strassert, and Burki investigates the origin of primary plastids through phylogenomic analysis, addressing the long-standing debate about whether primary photosynthetic eukaryotes (PPE/Archaeplastida) form a monophyletic group based on nuclear data. While plastid-based phylogenies consistently support Archaeplastida monophyly, nuclear phylogenomic analyses have failed to recover this relationship. The authors re-analyzed four published nuclear datasets (BAU, BRO, KAT, BUR) and found that none could resolve PPE relationships, with individual datasets showing conflicting results. They identified several issues including hidden paralogy (notably plastid paralogs in KAT that artificially inflated support for Archaeplastida monophyly, and the EF2 gene in BAU showing anomalous affinity between Glaucophyta and Amorphea). The researchers then constructed a larger combined dataset of 311 genes and 346 taxa with careful curation, including genomic data for two Rhodelphis species (Rhodelphidia). When analyzed under complex mixture models (LG+C60+G4), the combined datasets supported Archaeplastida monophyly with Picozoa as a putative associated lineage (sister to Rhodophyta + Rhodelphidia). Key findings include: (1) untrimmed alignments produced less gene tree conflict than aggressive block trimming (BMGE), which sometimes led Cryptista to incorrectly branch within Archaeplastida; (2) the monophyly of Rhodelphidia and Rhodophyta was confirmed; (3) Glaucophyta and Chloroplastida formed a consistent sister relationship in nuclear data (contrasting with plastid phylogenies favoring Chloroplastida + Rhodophyta); (4) Cryptista was the most likely sister lineage to Archaeplastida. The recovery of PPE monophyly strongly favors the Archaeplastida hypothesis of a single plastid origin in a common ancestor. However, the possible placement of Picozoa within or sister to this group raises questions, as no plastid has been identified in Picozoa. If confirmed, this would require either secondary plastid loss or more complex scenarios of independent plastid acquisition. Complete plastid loss is extremely rare in eukaryotes (only confirmed in five parasitic lineages within Myzozoa: Cryptosporidium, Gregarines, and Hematodinium).

## Abstract

The origin of plastids (chloroplasts) by endosymbiosis stands as one of the most important events in the history of eukaryotic life. The genetic, biochemical, and cell biological integration of a cyanobacterial endosymbiont into a heterotrophic host eukaryote approximately a billion years ago paved the way for the evolution of diverse algal groups in a wide range of aquatic and, eventually, terrestrial environments. Plastids have on multiple occasions also moved horizontally from eukaryote to eukaryote by secondary and tertiary endosymbiotic events. The overall picture of extant photosynthetic diversity can best be described as “patchy”: Plastid-bearing lineages are spread far and wide across the eukaryotic tree of life, nested within heterotrophic groups. The algae do not constitute a monophyletic entity, and understanding how, and how often, plastids have moved from branch to branch on the eukaryotic tree remains one of the most fundamental unsolved problems in the field of cell evolution. In this review, we provide an overview of recent advances in our understanding of the origin and spread of plastids from the perspective of comparative genomics. Recent years have seen significant improvements in genomic sampling from photosynthetic and nonphotosynthetic lineages, both of which have added important pieces to the puzzle of plastid evolution. Comparative genomics has also allowed us to better understand how endosymbionts become organelles.

**Keywords:** plastids; chloroplasts; genomics; phylogenomics; organelles, algae, protists; evolution

## Introduction

Algae are diverse and ecologically important organisms found across the eukaryotic tree of life, and they all have at least one thing in common—they are photosynthetic. Although their precise evolutionary paths vary, all canonical plastids are believed to be derived from the same endosymbiotic cyanobacterium. How do we know this? Simply put, it is in their DNA. The genes that remain within modern-day plastid genomes, along with those that have relocated to the nuclear genome, provide important clues as to how plastids evolved across different branches of the eukaryotic tree. The first plant plastid genomes were sequenced in the 1980s [(Ohyama et al. 1986](#evaa096-B75); [Shinozaki et al. 1986](#evaa096-B97)) and provided preliminary insight into their gene content and structure. Over 4,000 plastid genomes have now been sequenced from a wide diversity of photosynthetic and secondarily nonphotosynthetic eukaryotes. Together with nuclear genome sequences, these data have made it possible to investigate the “who, what, when, where, and how” of eukaryotic photosynthesis. Here, we review recent genomics-based advances in our understanding of how plastids arose and spread. With the immense amount of information now coming from genome sequencing projects, the potential for discovery and insight into these fundamental questions is unparalleled. What is emerging is a more complete and nuanced view of plastid evolution, one that is nevertheless still lacking in important details.

## The Origin of Plastids

A wealth of biochemical, molecular, and phylogenetic data support the notion that plastids evolved from endosymbiotic cyanobacteria on a single occasion (see [Kim and Archibald 2009](#evaa096-B49) and references therein for review). This landmark event is thought to have occurred at least ∼900 Ma (e.g., [Parfrey et al. 2011](#evaa096-B77); [Shih and Matzke 2013](#evaa096-B95)) in a common ancestor shared by land plants and green algae (Viridiplantae), red algae (Rhodophyta), and glaucophyte algae (Glaucophyta) ([fig. 1](#evaa096-F1)), giving rise to so-called “primary” plastids surrounded by two membranes. But although the phylogenetic information retained in plastid genomes clearly points to cyanobacteria as the source of the organelle, identifying the closest relative of plastids among present-day cyanobacteria has proven challenging. In attempting to address this question, researchers have analyzed the genes retained in plastid genomes as well as cyanobacterium-derived genes that migrated to the nuclear genome during and after the establishment of the organelle (see below). The picture has changed with the use of new analytical approaches and the discovery of new cyanobacterial lineages living in diverse environments.

### Fig. 1.

[Open in a new tab](figure/evaa096-F1/)
