--- SOURCE 2: Horizontal Transfer of Entire Genomes via Mitochondrial ... ---
URL: https://notablesdelaciencia.conicet.gov.ar/bitstream/handle/11336/2616/Rice2013.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper reports the complete mitochondrial genome sequence of Amborella trichopoda, a large shrub endemic to the rain forests of New Caledonia that is likely sister to all other angiosperms (diverging ~200 million years ago). The genome is enormous at 3.9 Mb (3,866,039 bp), assembled as five autonomously replicating circular chromosomes (3179, 244, 187, 137, and 119 kb). Remarkably, the genome contains approximately six genome equivalents of foreign mitochondrial DNA acquired from green algae, mosses, and other angiosperms, representing a striking example of horizontal gene transfer (HGT).

Key findings include:
- Four complete mitochondrial genomes were horizontally transferred: one from a moss (with architecture nearly identical to Physcomitrella and Anomodon) and three from green algae (donors A, B, C), plus a partial genome from a fourth green-algal donor (D). The green algal genomes likely came from the Coccomyxa subgroup of trebouxiophytes, possibly via lichens growing on Amborella.
- Approximately 753 kb of DNA was acquired from other angiosperms (about two genome equivalents), with donors identified including Santalales (parasitic plants, the major source), Fagales, Oxalidales, Ricinus communis, and Bambusa oldhamii. Some foreign tracts show evidence of serial angiosperm-to-angiosperm HGT.
- The genome also contains 138 kb of plastid DNA, mostly via intracellular gene transfer, with ~10 kb entering via foreign mitochondria.
- Of the 197 foreign mitochondrial protein genes, only 50 (25%) have full-length intact open reading frames, and most are pseudogenes; the majority of foreign genes are not functionally expressed. This makes Amborella mtDNA a striking example of neutral evolution and "junk DNA."

The authors propose a fusion-compatibility model: Amborella captured whole mitochondria from diverse green plants, followed by mitochondrial fusion (mechanistically limited to green plants) and genome recombination. They note that mitochondrial fusion in animals and fungi uses dynamin-related GTPases absent from green plants, suggesting a fundamentally different fusion mechanism in green plants. The ecological context—Amborella's heavy epiphyte load (mosses, lichens, other angiosperms), propensity to produce suckers from wounds (wounding may create new meristems that incorporate foreign mitochondria), and low rate of mitochondrial DNA loss—all contribute to the high level of foreign DNA. The transfers are likely millions of years old given extensive pseudogene decay but surprisingly intact retention of the whole-genome transfers.
</summary>

"We report the complete mitochondrial genome sequence of the flowering plant Amborella trichopoda. This enormous, 3.9 Mb genome contains six genome equivalents of foreign mitochondrial DNA, acquired from green algae, mosses, and other angiosperms. Many of these horizontal transfers were large, including acquisition of entire mitochondrial genomes from three green algae and one moss."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Gene transfer gone wild reveals driving force behind mitochondrial sex | EurekAlert! ---
URL: https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/695720

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a news release from Indiana University (via EurekAlert!) announcing groundbreaking research on horizontal gene transfer in the mitochondrial genome of Amborella trichopoda, a South Pacific shrub endemic to New Caledonia. The research, led by IU's Jeff Palmer and Danny Rice in collaboration with the U.S. Department of Energy, Penn State University, and the Institute of Research for Development in New Caledonia, uncovered the largest example of horizontal gene transfer (acquisition of foreign genes from other species) ever found in any organism. The study identified genes from multiple plant species in Amborella's mitochondrial genome, including the entire mitochondrial genomes of three green algae and one moss — marking the first time an organelle genome has captured entire foreign genomes (four total) and the first description of a land plant acquiring genes from green algae. The research demonstrates that mitochondrial fusion (merger of two mitochondria within a cell) drives mitochondrial gene transfer, and that incompatibility in fusion mechanisms between different phyla acts as a major barrier to unconstrained mitochondrial "sex" across the tree of life. Key findings include: (1) flowering plants and green algae, whose last common ancestor existed over a billion years ago, undergo mitochondrial fusion by the same mechanism, which differs from that of animals and fungi; and (2) Amborella retained the foreign DNA for tens of millions of years due to ecological exposure, developmental germline formation responses to wounding, and an exceptionally low rate of DNA loss. The study, "Horizontal Transfer of Entire Genomes via Mitochondrial Fusion in the Angiosperm Amborella," was published Dec. 20 in the journal Science, alongside two papers on Amborella's nuclear genomes. Funding came from the National Institutes of Health, National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy's Joint Genome Institute, and IU's METACyt Initiative (funded by the Lilly Endowment).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The research also shows, for the first time, that an organelle genome has captured an entire foreign genome, in this case, four of them. It is also the first description of a land plant acquiring genes from green algae., "The Amborella mitochondrial genome is like the old lady in the song who swallows a fly... the Amborella genome has swallowed whole mitochondrial genomes, of varying sizes, from a broad range of land plants and green algae. But instead of bursting from all this extra, mostly useless DNA, or purging the DNA, it's held on to it for tens of millions of years. So you can think of this genome as a constipated glutton... that has swallowed whole genomes from other plants and algae and also retained them in remarkably intact form for eons," said Jeff Palmer., "We found the first evidence that mitochondria of flowering plants and green algae, whose last common ancestor existed over a billion years ago, undergo fusion by the same mechanism. This mechanism appears to be different from that employed by animal and fungal mitochondria," said Danny Rice., Palmer said the new work provides "compelling evidence that mitochondrial fusion is the driving force for mitochondrial gene transfer and that incompatibility in the mechanism of mitochondrial fusion between different phyla – plants versus animals or fungi – provides the major barrier to unconstrained mitochondrial 'sex' across the evolutionary tree of life."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Mechanisms, detection, and impact of horizontal gene transfer in plant functional evolution ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12448838

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in The Plant Cell (2025) titled "Mechanisms, detection, and impact of horizontal gene transfer in plant functional evolution" by Lee Mariault, Camille Puginier, Jean Keller, Moaine El Baidouri, and Pierre-Marc Delaux (PMID: 40834228). The review explores the extent of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in the plant kingdom, focusing on mechanisms, detection methods, and evolutionary impact.

KEY FINDINGS ON PREVALENCE:
- HGT is significantly more common in plant genomes than previously assumed, involving transfers from bacteria, fungi, insects, and viruses
- Over 600 plant-to-plant HGT cases reported; more than 42% involve parasitic plants (Orobanchaceae and Convolvulaceae families) and their hosts, facilitated by haustorium contact
- More than 95% of plant-to-plant HGT events outside parasitic systems occurred within the Poaceae (grass) family
- Bacteria are the most frequent donors, with over 800 genes acquired from bacteria, particularly during origin of land plants and early divergence of seed plants
- Approximately 20 well-supported fungal-to-plant HGT events described, many involving endophytic Epichloë fungi
- Plant-to-insect HGT documented in whitefly Bemisia tabaci (25+ plant-derived genes, including a phenolic glucoside malonyltransferase gene)
- Viruses, particularly Caulimoviridae, found integrated in nuclear genomes of many plants

MECHANISMS OF HGT:
1. Genetic material exits donor nucleus via: transcription/mRNA export (mobile via plasmodesmata and phloem), double-strand breaks from genotoxic stress, apoptosis, or extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA, up to 400 kbp)
2. Transport to recipient via: haustoria (parasitic gateway), natural grafting (stock-scion contact), illegitimate pollination (heterospecific pollen in wind-pollinated grasses), or vectors (viruses, bacteria, nematodes, insects, fungi)
3. Integration requires nuclear import, with mRNA requiring reverse transcription (possibly via TE-associated reverse transcriptases or Caulimoviridae)

TRANSGENERATIONAL CONSIDERATIONS:
- HGT in vegetative tissues may be an evolutionary dead end unless germ cells arise from somatic cells (unlike animals)
- Vegetative/asexual reproduction (rhizomes, tubers, bulbs, runners, stolons, suckers, bulbils, epiphyllous buds) provides a plausible route for transgenerational inheritance of horizontally transferred genes
- Underground vegetative buds contact the rhizosphere, increasing exposure to foreign DNA

DETECTION METHODS:
- High sequence similarity between donor and recipient (higher than vertical orthologs)
- Phylogenetic incongruence with species phylogeny
- Patchy taxonomic distributions
- Detection constrained by a "window of HGT observation" defined by genetic divergence, transfer age, and gene fate
- Requires integration of multiple lines of evidence plus experimental validation to rule out contamination

CONCLUSION: Expanding phylogenomic scrutiny of the plant kingdom should reveal the full extent of HGT. In situ sequencing and combinations of synthetic biology and experimental evolution may allow catching ongoing HGT and testing functional relevance of such events.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Horizontal gene transfers (HGTs) have been observed across the tree of life. While their adaptive importance in bacteria is conspicuous, the occurrence of HGTs and their evolutionary significance in eukaryotes has only recently started to be considered."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Frontiers | Horizontal Gene Transfer Contributes to Plant Evolution: The Case of Agrobacterium T-DNAs ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2017.02015/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a mini review article published in Frontiers in Plant Science (24 November 2017) by Dora G. Quispe-Huamanquispe, Godelieve Gheysen, and Jan F. Kreuze (Ghent University, Belgium, and International Potato Center/CIP, Lima, Peru). The article examines horizontal gene transfer (HGT) and its contribution to plant evolution, focusing specifically on the transfer of Agrobacterium T-DNAs (tumor/root-inducing DNA segments) into plant genomes.

Key content:
- HGT is defined as acquisition of genetic material from another organism without being its offspring. It is common in prokaryotes (including antibiotic resistance, pathogenesis, metabolic pathways) but was historically thought rare in eukaryotes, though recent sequencing has revealed many examples. Examples in eukaryotes include bacteria/fungi/plant DNA in bdelloid rotifers, bacteria to insects, fungal carotenoid genes to pea aphids (affecting body color and predator susceptibility), bryophytes (hornworts) to ferns (the neochrome photoreceptor gene ~179 million years ago), and multiple transfers associated with the aquatic-to-terrestrial transition in mosses (Physcomitrella patens, 57 gene families from prokaryotes/fungi/viruses) and parasitic plants.
- The classical model: Agrobacterium is a plant pathogen that transfers T-DNA into host cells, causing crown galls or proliferating roots. Plant phenolics trigger virulence gene expression mediating T-DNA transfer. Key genes include iaaM/iaaH (auxin biosynthesis), rol (root loci) genes, and opine-related genes (Acs, mis, mas).
- HGT from Agrobacterium rhizogenes to Nicotiana: Cellular T-DNAs (cT-DNAs) were detected in Nicotiana glauca over three decades ago (White et al., 1983). N. glauca contains NgrolB, NgrolC, ORF13, ORF14, and mikimopine synthase sequences (NgmisL/NgmisR). Of 42 Nicotiana species screened, 15 contained rol genes. Deep sequencing of Nicotiana tomentosiformis revealed four cT-DNAs (TA, TB, TC, TD) from different Agrobacterium strains; the TB region contains an intact mannopine synthase 2' gene (mas2') highly expressed in roots of some N. tabacum cultivars.
- HGT to Linaria: cT-DNA sequences found in Linaria (sections Linaria and Speciosae), with two copies in Linaria vulgaris as imperfect direct repeats, originating from a mikimopine strain of A. rhizogenes. rolC is the most conserved gene but is not expressed in the tested tissues.
- HGT to Ipomoea (sweet potato): IbT-DNA1 and IbT-DNA2 were discovered in the sweet potato genome (Ipomoea batatas), representing the only known example of ancient HGT in a domesticated crop. IbT-DNA1 (~21,564 bp, inverted repeat) contains ORFs homologous to iaaM, iaaH, C-prot, and Acs; IbT-DNA2 contains ORFs related to ORF14, ORF17n, RolB/RolC, ORF13, and ORF18/ORF17n. These genes are transmitted to progeny and expressed, suggesting functional roles.
- Evolutionary impact: For a foreign gene to be retained, it must be integrated, survive genome rearrangements, enter the germline, and confer selective advantage. The rol genes are associated with root traits. In sweet potato, T-DNAs were discovered via small RNA sequencing, indicating RNA silencing suppresses their expression (since they are arranged as inverted repeats). TB-mas2' lost expression in N. tomentosiformis possibly due to silencing but is active in N. tabacum. No strong association was found between rolB/rolC and root yield parameters except at one location. The authors suggest using CRISPR-Cas9 knockout for functional analysis. In Nicotiana, Agrobacterium infected the group multiple times independently.
- Future perspectives: Screening of additional Ipomoea species will determine if T-DNA genes are confined to cultivated sweet potato or also present in wild relatives.

Citation: Quispe-Huamanquispe DG, Gheysen G and Kreuze JF (2017) Horizontal Gene Transfer Contributes to Plant Evolution: The Case of Agrobacterium T-DNAs. Front. Plant Sci. 8:2015. doi: 10.3389/fpls.2017.02015. Received 24 May 2017, accepted 13 November 2017, published 24 November 2017. Edited by Tatiana Matveeva (Saint Petersburg State University). Reviewed by Katharina Pawlowski (Stockholm University) and Nikolai Ravin (Russian Academy of Sciences). Open access under CC BY license.

SUMMARY:

**Main Topic:** The study investigates horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in parasitic plants, specifically within the Orobanchaceae family, which contains the full spectrum of parasitic capabilities. **Methods:** The team used a phylogenomic approach, analyzing transcriptomes of four Orobanchaceae species: the nonparasitic Lindenbergia and three parasites with increasing dependence—Triphysaria versicolor (facultative hemiparasite), Striga hermonthica (obligate hemiparasite), and Phelipanche aegyptiaca (obligate holoparasite). --- SOURCE 11: Evolution of the connectivity and indispensability of a transferable gene: the simplicity hypothesis ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12862-022-02091-w

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access research article published on 30 November 2022 in BMC Ecology and Evolution (Volume 22, article 140) by C. T. Jones, E. Susko, and J. P. Bielawski. The paper, "Evolution of the connectivity and indispensability of a transferable gene: the simplicity hypothesis," presents a theoretical model testing the "simplicity hypothesis" proposed by Novick and Doolittle (2020).

Key concepts:
- Connectivity: the number of interactions between a transferable gene (or its protein product) and host genes/gene products; higher connectivity reduces the likelihood of successful horizontal gene transfer (HGT) into new microbial hosts (per the complexity hypothesis).
- Indispensability: the degree to which a microbial host's viability depends on the transferable gene during a neutral (non-selective) environmental state.
- The simplicity hypothesis posits that connectivity may increase over time within a single population via gene-host coevolution (toward a more "sessile" state), but that differential rates of HGT colonization across populations may counter this and reduce connectivity over time (toward a more "itinerant" state), constituting an evolutionary trade-off.

Model and methodology:
- The model treats copies of a transferable gene (T) within microbial host populations as populations of genes undergoing birth (via HGT into naïve populations, impacted by connectivity) and death (via gene loss, impacted by indispensability).
- The study uses both a deterministic model based on the Price equation and stochastic computer simulations.
- Three key assumptions: (1) coevolution independently changes both connectivity and indispensability; (2) a collective of spatially segregated microbial populations exists (some hosting the gene, some naïve); (3) environments have two states—selective (gene provides fitness advantage) and neutral (no advantage).
- Key model parameters: beta (β) = opportunity to colonize naïve microbial populations via HGT; delta (δ) = probability of neutral environmental state.

Key results:
- When β = 0.06 (low HGT opportunity), the transferable gene persisted in only 2 populations by evolving toward a more sessile state (higher indispensability and connectivity), despite the absence of coevolution causing extinction.
- When β = 0.08 (higher HGT opportunity), the gene evolved toward a more itinerant state (lower indispensability and connectivity), with the metapopulation expanding from ~800 to nearly 9,000 populations.
- The evolutionary outcome transitions from sessile to itinerant between β = 0.06 and β = 0.08.
- The opportunity to enter new microbial populations via HGT can drive connectivity toward lower values, especially in unstable environments; lack of such opportunity in stable environments drives connectivity toward higher values.

Predictions and potential tests:
- A gene might evolve more sessile when there is a stable selective environment (δ ≈ 0) but little opportunity for HGT (β ≈ 0), as might be found in oligotrophic environments (open ocean, deep subsurface, polar ice caps) for genes conferring nutrient metabolism.
- A gene might evolve more itinerant when HGT opportunity is high (β > 0) and environmental exposure to selective pressures is intermittent (δ > 0), as might be found in pathogens episodically exposed to antimicrobial substances.
- Predictions could be tested by comparing genes of these types or by comparing transferable genes in species with broad versus narrow niche breadth.

Conclusion: The model suggests connectivity can evolve toward higher values (sessile, less transferable) or lower values (itinerant, more transferable) depending on ecological conditions, consistent with the simplicity hypothesis. However, the authors note that better understanding of gene-host coevolutionary dynamics in natural microbial systems is required before further conclusions can be drawn about the hypothesis's veracity.
</summary>

**Background and Hypotheses:** The paper addresses horizontal gene transfer (HGT) among prokaryotes. Previous research showed that operational genes (housekeeping functions) are frequently horizontally transferred, while informational genes (transcription, translation, and related processes) are rarely transferred. Two competing hypotheses were tested: (1) the continual horizontal transfer hypothesis—operational genes have been transferred continuously since prokaryote divergence, and (2) the early massive horizontal transfer hypothesis—one or a few massive gene exchanges occurred early in prokaryotic evolution before diversification.

**Methodology:** The researchers analyzed six complete prokaryotic genomes: Aquifex aeolicus, Escherichia coli, Synechocystis 6803, Bacillus subtilis, Methanococcus jannaschii, and Archaeoglobus fulgidus. They identified 312 orthologous gene sets (203 operational and 109 informational), with 144 reliable orthologs (88 operational, 56 informational) used for testing. Analyses included star sequence alignments, paralog rooting, three phylogenetic methods (Jukes-Cantor distances, maximum parsimony, and paralinear/logdet distances), and tree distance metrics including peripheral branch-transfer and prune-and-regraft distances.

**Key Results:** Three tests consistently supported the continual horizontal transfer hypothesis: (1) Paralog rooting showed significantly different root distributions between operational and informational trees (P<0.0039, χ²=13.35); (2) Operational trees had mean peripheral branch-transfer distance of 2.3 steps vs. 1.2 for informational trees (P<0.0003, χ²=23.0); (3) Prune-and-regraft distance analysis showed >40% of operational trees require 2+ transfers vs. <10% for informational trees (P<0.00007, χ²=19.08). Branch length analysis showed mean central branch lengths were significantly shorter for operational trees (0.071 ± 0.05) than informational trees (0.237 ± 0.05 substitutions per position), consistent with extensive horizontal transfer in operational genes, while peripheral branch lengths showed minimal rate differences.

**The Complexity Hypothesis:** The authors propose that informational genes are members of large, complex systems (e.g., translation requires ~100 coordinated gene products in E. coli), whereas operational genes typically interact with few products (e.g., thioredoxin-thioredoxin reductase complex). Using a simplified model where each required interaction has a 0.25 probability, a transferred ribosomal protein S5 would have success probability of 0.25⁶ (=0.00024), about 1,000 times less than a thioredoxin protein requiring one interaction. The authors suggest the operational gene component of prokaryotes can be viewed functionally as "a single global organism" due to the vast extent of horizontal transfer.

URL: https://ncse.ngo/evolution-biological-complexity

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in the Reports of the National Center for Science Education (Volume 26, No. 3, May-June 2006) by Finn Pond of Whitworth College, argues that naturalistic/evolutionary models can plausibly explain the origin of biological complexity, countering claims by "Intelligent Design" (ID) advocates. ID proponents, following Michael Behe's "irreducible complexity" argument (from Darwin's Black Box, 1996), contend that only an "intelligent agent" can generate the information content and complexity in biological systems. Behe argued the bacterial flagellum is irreducibly complex—a system where removing any part causes it to cease functioning, which cannot be produced by slight, successive modifications of a precursor system.

The paper reviews four naturalistic models:
1) Incremental additions model: An initially beneficial association of components becomes essential over time (e.g., RNase P, where RNA has catalytic activity alone at very low activity, but functions better with its protein partner; hammerhead ribozymes showing 10-20 fold increased activity in the presence of RNA-binding proteins).
2) Scaffolding model: "Redundant complexity" and superfluous components are lost, leaving tightly-matched components (analogous to building an arch with scaffolding; gene duplications and variant isoforms serve as examples).
3) Co-option model: Existing structures are recruited for new functions (e.g., the Krebs/citric acid cycle, where intermediate stages had functions apart from their role in the cycle; V(D)J gene splicing in vertebrate immune systems; butterfly eyespots, vertebrate limbs, complex leaves, and feathers).
4) Emerging complexity/self-organization model: Schneider's "ev" program simulated evolution via mutation and selection, demonstrating that Darwinian processes can generate new information (measured in bits via Shannon information theory) and irreducibly complex systems from a random genome.

The paper critiques William Dembski's responses (in No Free Lunch, 2002), who demanded "causal specificity" and objected to the "ev" program (Schneider eliminated the disputed rule and found the same results; David Wolpert, co-developer of the No Free Lunch Theorems, said Dembski applied the theorems inappropriately). Howard Van Till noted that hypotheses falling short of full causal specificity may still be highly plausible applications of partially understood mechanisms, and complained that ID tends to denigrate them as "just-so stories."

The paper also critiques Dembski's "specified complexity" criterion (probability of 10^-150 for design) and his application to the bacterial flagellum. Dembski's probability calculation treated the flagellum as a discrete combinatorial object assembling by pure chance—a scenario no biologist has ever proposed. Dembski failed to account for all relevant ways an event might occur, despite stating this was necessary.

The conclusion presents Kwang Jeon's 1966 experiment where amoebae cultures dying from bacterial infection eventually recovered, establishing a mutually obligate endosymbiosis (essentially a new cell organelle) through undirected natural processes—demonstrating that natural causes can generate irreducibly linked systems. The paper concludes that demanding a detailed chain of causality is unrealistic, and that calculating the probability of the flagellum assembling by pure chance to detect design is simply wrong.
</summary>

The study presents the first evidence of massive horizontal gene transfer in the animal kingdom—numerous chunks of foreign DNA from bacteria, fungi, and plants were discovered in the genome of the bdelloid rotifer Adineta vaga. While horizontal gene transfer is common in bacteria, it was previously unheard of on such a large scale in animals.

The study suggests that if bdelloids can incorporate foreign DNA from their environment, they could also pick up DNA from other bdelloids, which evolutionarily is almost as good as having sex.

The researchers propose a mechanism: bdelloids can survive total desiccation by entering a dehydrated suspended state, and during this phase both the rotifer and its food break down, potentially allowing foreign DNA to enter the germ line. During rehydration, DNA breakage is repaired and foreign DNA may become incorporated. This idea was inspired by earlier work (Gladyshev and Meselson, 2008) showing bdelloids are exceptionally good at recovering from ionizing radiation that shatters DNA. --- SOURCE 1: Massive horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes from ... ---
URL: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0408336102

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PNAS research article (published December 14, 2004, in volume 101, issue 51, pages 17747-17752) by Ulfar Bergthorsson, Aaron O. Richardson, Gregory J. Young, Leslie R. Goertzen, and Jeffrey D. Palmer, titled "Massive horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes from diverse land plant donors to the basal angiosperm Amborella."

STUDY PURPOSE: The researchers investigated whether plants could acquire multiple foreign genes through horizontal gene transfer (HGT), moving beyond the previously known cases of single-gene acquisition. They focused on Amborella trichopoda, a basal angiosperm (a monotypic genus of shrubs endemic to New Caledonia) that was already known to possess one horizontally acquired gene and showed signs of containing more.

METHODOLOGY: The team used PCR amplification with conserved primers (~100 primer pairs) to comprehensively sequence the mitochondrial protein gene set of Amborella, plus variable numbers of mitochondrial genes from 28 other diverse land plants. They also conducted maximum-likelihood and parsimony phylogenetic analyses, using the Shimodaira-Hasegawa (SH) test to assess whether phylogenetically anomalous gene placements suggestive of HGT were statistically significant. To rule out contamination, HGT cases were confirmed from multiple independent DNA preparations from four different sources of Amborella material.

KEY RESULTS:
- Of the 40 protein genes present in the ancestral angiosperm mitochondrial genome, 31 were recovered from Amborella.
- Of these 31 genes, 20 showed evidence of one or more cases of HGT, for a total of 26 foreign genes acquired.
- Most transfers came from other angiosperms (especially eudicots), while others came from nonangiosperms, including six striking cases of transfer from at least three different moss donors.
- The five sequenced angiosperm mitochondrial genomes (rice, Arabidopsis, Brassica, Beta, and others) showed no evidence of HGT.
- Most transferred genes are intact (functional or recently transferred), while nine are pseudogenes.
- Evidence suggests the transferred genes reside in the mitochondrial genome (not chloroplast or nuclear), based on RNA editing patterns characteristic of mitochondria, nucleotide substitution rates, and PCR abundance.
- The 11 remaining singleton genes appear to be of vertical descent, placing Amborella as sister to all other angiosperms.

DISCUSSION AND SIGNIFICANCE: Amborella mtDNA has sustained proportionately more HGT than any other eukaryotic, or perhaps prokaryotic, genome yet examined. The study suggests HGT incidence varies markedly between plants. The authors speculate that Amborella's environment—mid-elevation montane tropical rain forests in New Caledonia where the plant's leaves and stems are often covered with diverse epiphytes including mosses—could promote direct plant-to-plant HGT (similar to mechanisms proposed for parasitic plants). The authors note limitations of their PCR approach, including missing rRNA/tRNA genes, chloroplast-derived sequences, and intergenic DNA, and emphasize that only sequencing the complete Amborella mitochondrial genome can comprehensively census its horizontally acquired DNA. They cite the SH test as supporting 14 of the transfers, with divergent duplicates in plant mtDNA representing xenologs (horizontal products) rather than paralogs.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Results indicate that Amborella has acquired one or more copies of 20 of its 31 known mitochondrial protein genes from other land plants, for a total of 26 foreign genes, whereas no evidence for HGT was found in the five sequenced genomes."; "Most of the Amborella transfers are from other angiosperms (especially eudicots), whereas others are from nonangiosperms, including six striking cases of transfer from (at least three different) moss donors."; "Amborella mtDNA has sustained proportionately more HGT than any other eukaryotic, or perhaps even prokaryotic, genome yet examined."; "Clearly, then, the incidence of HGT varies markedly from one plant to another. One wonders how many other Amborella-type situations exist among the ≈255,000 species of flowering plants."; "We are lucky that, of all angiosperms, Amborella happens to be so rich in HGT, because its distinctive position at the base of angiosperms makes it relatively easy to detect with reasonable confidence transfers from other angiosperms, even with the scanty taxon sampling of this study."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Horizontal transfer of entire genomes via mitochondrial fusion ... ---
URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24357311

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PubMed abstract page for the scientific article "Horizontal transfer of entire genomes via mitochondrial fusion in the angiosperm Amborella" by Danny W Rice et al., published in Science on December 20, 2013 (Vol. 342, Issue 6165, pages 1468-73; PMID: 24357311; DOI: 10.1126/science.1246275). The study reports the complete mitochondrial genome sequence of the flowering plant Amborella trichopoda. This 3.9-megabase genome contains six genome equivalents of foreign mitochondrial DNA acquired from green algae, mosses, and other angiosperms. Notably, many transfers were large, including complete mitochondrial genomes from three green algae and one moss. The authors propose a fusion-compatibility model: Amborella captures whole mitochondria from diverse eukaryotes, followed by mitochondrial fusion (mechanistically limited to green plant mitochondria), then genome recombination. They suggest Amborella's epiphyte load, propensity to produce suckers from wounds, and low rate of mitochondrial DNA loss all contribute to its high foreign DNA content. Author affiliation: Department of Biology, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN. Funding came from NIH grant R01-GM-76012. Associated GenBank sequence data (KF754799-KF754802, KF798319-KF798355) are available. The article discusses MeSH topics including horizontal gene transfer, mitochondrial dynamics, membrane fusion, and plant genomes. There is a related commentary by K. Adams in the same Science issue (PMID: 24357306) and similar/cited articles on related topics including horizontal gene transfer involving chloroplasts.
</summary>

"We report the complete mitochondrial genome sequence of the flowering plant Amborella trichopoda. This enormous, 3.9-megabase genome contains six genome equivalents of foreign mitochondrial DNA, acquired from green algae, mosses, and other angiosperms." "Many of these horizontal transfers were large, including acquisition of entire mitochondrial genomes from three green algae and one moss." "We propose a fusion-compatibility model to explain these findings, with Amborella capturing whole mitochondria from diverse eukaryotes, followed by mitochondrial fusion (limited mechanistically to green plant mitochondria) and then genome recombination." "Amborella's epiphyte load, propensity to produce suckers from wounds, and low rate of mitochondrial DNA loss probably all contribute to the high level of foreign DNA in its mitochondrial genome."

SUMMARY:

This is an Academia.edu webpage for the 2004 paper "From the Cover: Massive horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes from diverse land plant donors to the basal angiosperm Amborella" by Ulfar Bergthorsson, published in Proceedings of The National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).

Key findings of the paper (from the abstract):
- The study focused on Amborella trichopoda, a basal angiosperm, because it was already known to possess one horizontally acquired gene and preliminary analyses suggested it contained several more.
- Researchers comprehensively sequenced the mitochondrial protein gene set of Amborella, sequenced a variable number of mitochondrial genes from 28 other diverse land plants, and conducted phylogenetic analyses including the five sequenced mitochondrial genomes of angiosperms.
- Results showed that Amborella has acquired one or more copies of 20 of its 31 known mitochondrial protein genes from other land plants, for a total of 26 foreign genes, while no evidence for HGT was found in the five sequenced genomes.
- Most Amborella transfers came from other angiosperms (especially eudicots), while others came from nonangiosperms, including six striking cases of transfer from at least three different moss donors.
- Most transferred genes are intact, consistent with functionality and/or recency of transfer.
- Conclusion: Amborella mtDNA has sustained proportionately more HGT than any other eukaryotic, or perhaps even prokaryotic, genome yet examined.

The page also includes related papers, most notably:
- "Widespread horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes in flowering plants" (Bergthorsson, Nature, 2003) showing HGT is evolutionarily frequent between distantly related flowering plants, occurring with gene duplication, recapture of genes lost through nuclear transfer, and chimaeric half-monocot/half-dicot genes.
- "Horizontal Transfer of Entire Genomes via Mitochondrial Fusion in the Angiosperm Amborella" (Science, 2013) reporting the complete 3.9 Mb Amborella mitochondrial genome containing six genome equivalents of foreign mitochondrial DNA from green algae, mosses, and other angiosperms, proposing a fusion-compatibility model.

However, in eukaryotes it is prevalent only in certain phagotrophic protists and limited largely to the ancient acquisition of bacterial genes." --- SOURCE 4: Gorgeous mosaic of mitochondrial genes created by horizontal transfer and gene conversion ---
URL: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1016295107

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research article published in PNAS (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) on November 29, 2010, by Weilong Hao, Aaron O. Richardson, Yihong Zheng, and Jeffrey D. Palmer (contributed by Palmer, received for review September 17, 2010). The paper reports the discovery of two lineages of plant mitochondrial genes exhibiting "gorgeous mosaicism" created through horizontal gene transfer (HGT) combined with repeated gene conversion between coresident native and foreign homologs.

Key findings:
- Two lineages of differentially mosaic mitochondrial genes were discovered: the atp1 gene in the genus Ternstroemia (Ericales) and the nad1/matR region in gingers (Hedychium and Boesenbergia of Zingiberaceae).
- The Ternstroemia atp1 genes are highly chimeric, with multiple (four or five) foreign regions interspersed with native regions across the three major clades, tracing back to a single initiating HGT event likely from Vaccinium (blueberry), inferred to have occurred 15-50 Myr ago between donor and recipient groups that diverged ~100 Myr ago.
- The ginger case involves HGT of the cd-4 intron region, occurring less than 26 Myr ago, with H-cis and H-trans copies in Hedychium both being chimeras of native ginger-derived and foreign eudicot-derived DNA.
- Gene conversion between native and foreign homologs was demonstrated for 5 of 17 cases of non-Amborella plant mitochondrial HGT examined.
- The paper proposes the duplicative HGT and differential gene conversion (DH-DC) model, which integrates HGT, ongoing gene conversion, and speciation to explain the diversification of mosaic genes.
- The mosaic genes also reflect prior conversions of two additional types: intramitochondrial retroprocessing (cDNA-mediated conversion) and interorganellar gene conversion between mitochondria and chloroplasts (across the ~2 billion year divergence between these organelles).
- Expression evidence (C-to-U RNA editing) confirms the mosaic genes are functional mitochondrial genes; only H-cis matR appears to be a pseudogene.
- Gene conversion introduced limited protein diversity (2-4 amino acid changes in Ternstroemia atp1; single changes in functional matR genes) but created substantial novel molecular variation, some potentially adaptive.

The article has 3,542 total views and 86 total citations (as of September 2026), with free access.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Here we report the discovery, in two lineages of plant mitochondrial genes, of novel gene combinations that arose by conversion between coresident native and foreign homologs." "These findings expand our appreciation of HGT and gene conversion as creative evolutionary forces, establish plant mitochondria as a premiere system for studying the evolutionary dynamics of HGT and its genetic reverberations." "We generalize these findings by developing a model for HGT-driven gene diversification, termed the duplicative HGT and differential gene conversion (DH-DC) model."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Horizontal gene transfer is more frequent with increased heterotrophy and contributes to parasite adaptation ---
URL: https://www.pnas.org/doi/abs/10.1073/pnas.1608765113

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research article published in PNAS (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) titled "Horizontal gene transfer is more frequent with increased heterotrophy and contributes to parasite adaptation." The article was published October 24, 2016, in Vol. 113, No. 45, pages E7010-E7019 (DOI: 10.1073/pnas.1608765113). It is available with free access and has received 102 total citations.

AUTHORS: The study was conducted by Zhenzhen Yang, Yeting Zhang, Eric K. Wafula, and 13 other researchers including Loren A. Honaas, Paula E. Ralph, Sam Jones, Christopher R. Clarke, Siming Liu, Chun Su, Huiting Zhang, Naomi S. Altman, Stephan C. Schuster, Michael P. Timko, John I. Yoder, James H. Westwood, and corresponding author Claude W. dePamphilis (cwd3@psu.edu). It was edited by David M. Hillis of the University of Texas at Austin and approved September 20, 2016.

KEY FINDINGS: The paper tests the hypothesis that parasitic plants are especially prone to horizontal gene transfer (HGT) because of their intimate feeding contacts with host plant tissues. HGT is the nonsexual transfer and genomic integration of genetic materials between organisms. While HGT is common in prokaryotes, it appears rare in eukaryotes, but parasitic plants may be exceptions.

RESEARCH METHODS: The researchers examined transcriptomes of three parasitic members of Orobanchaceae (a plant family containing species spanning the full spectrum of parasitic capabilities) plus the free-living Lindenbergia. After initial phylogenetic detection and extensive validation, they identified 52 high-confidence horizontal transfer events, often from lineages of known host plants. The number of HGT events increased in species with the greatest parasitic dependence.

KEY RESULTS: 
- 52 high-confidence HGT events were detected, exceeding 50 expressed and likely functional HGT events in one family of parasitic plants
- HGT reflected parasite preferences for different host plants
- HGT was much more frequent in plants with increasing parasitic dependency
- Analyses of intron sequences provided evidence for integration of genomic fragments far more often than retro-processed RNA sequences
- Purifying selection predominates in functionally transferred sequences, with a small fraction of adaptively evolving sites
- HGT-acquired genes are preferentially expressed in the haustorium (the feeding organ of parasitic plants)
- HGT was strongly biased toward expression and protein types likely to contribute to haustorial function, suggesting functional HGT of host genes plays an important role in adaptive evolution of parasites

DATA AVAILABILITY: Sequence data archived at NCBI BioProject (ID codes SRP001053 and SRP083761) and at ppgp.huck.psu.edu. Scripts and alignments submitted to github user "dePamphilis" under directory "HGT_PNAS_2016."

FUNDING: Supported by NSF Plant Genome Research Program Awards DBI-0701748 and IOS-1238057 (to J.H.W., C.W.d., M.P.T., and J.I.Y.), with additional support from the Plant Biology graduate program and the Genetics graduate program at Penn State University, National Institute of Food and Agriculture Project 131997 (to J.H.W.), and NSF Grant IOS-1213059 (to M.P.T.).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is the nonsexual transfer and genomic integration of genetic materials between organisms. In eukaryotes, HGT appears rare, but parasitic plants may be exceptions, as haustorial feeding connections between parasites and their hosts provide intimate cellular contacts that could facilitate DNA transfer between unrelated species."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Widespread impact of horizontal gene transfer on plant colonization of land ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms2148

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Nature Communications on October 23, 2012, titled "Widespread impact of horizontal gene transfer on plant colonization of land" by Jipei Yue, Xiangyang Hu, Hang Sun, Yongping Yang, and Jinling Huang. The study challenges the conventional belief that horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is rare in complex multicellular eukaryotes like plants.

**Key findings:**
- Genome analyses of the moss Physcomitrella patens identified 128 genes across 57 families that were acquired from prokaryotes, fungi, or viruses through HGT
- Of these, 18 gene families are present in both green algae and land plants (acquired before land plant origin), while 39 families were acquired during or after land plant origin
- 19 gene families are found only in P. patens and their putative donors, suggesting recent transfer
- The majority of acquired genes derive from miscellaneous bacterial lineages; ten families from fungi, and one each from archaea and viruses
- 35 of the identified gene families are also present in seed plants, indicating retention of beneficial acquired genes
- Land plants emerged from charophycean green algae about 480-490 million years ago

**Biological functions of acquired genes:**
The horizontally acquired genes are involved in:
- Xylem formation, plant defence, nitrogen recycling
- Biosynthesis of starch, polyamines, hormones (including auxin), and glutathione
- Arginase genes (derived from bacterial agmatinase) involved in polyamine biosynthesis
- Subtilase gene family (derived from a single bacterial HGT event) involved in protein degradation, lateral root formation, xylem differentiation, cuticle development, and stomata pattern formation
- Auxin biosynthesis genes (AAE18 and YUC3)
- Glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCL) for glutathione formation (plant disease resistance, stress defence, heavy metal detoxification)
- Purine degradation and nitrogen recycling genes
- DNA replication and repair genes

**Proposed HGT mechanism model:**
The authors propose two entry points for foreign genes into the moss genome: (1) spore germination and early gametophyte development stage, and (2) fertilization and early embryo development stage. This model applies to nonvascular and seedless vascular plants with unprotected or weakly protected zygotes. Mosses are effective in DNA transformation, enabling uptake of foreign DNA, which likely facilitated their establishment in hostile terrestrial environments. Mycorrhizal associations with fungi also provided opportunities for gene transfer.

**Methodology:**
Using the AlienG computational tool, 910 genes were identified as potentially of prokaryotic, fungal, or viral origin from P. patens annotated protein sequences. After removing 394 genes (short scaffolds or high cyanobacterial identity suggesting plastid origin), 128 genes of 57 families were confirmed as HGT-derived through phylogenetic analyses with bootstrap support of 80% or higher, with cautious measures to reduce false positives including comprehensive database construction and balanced taxonomic sampling.

**Conclusions:**
The findings suggest HGT had a critical role in the transition of plants from aquatic to terrestrial environments, and demonstrate that HGT is a dynamic process with foreign genes gradually accumulating over time. The study suggests that anciently acquired genes are more frequent in plants than commonly expected, and that HGT had a widespread and profound impact on the evolution of multicellular eukaryotes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In complex multicellular eukaryotes such as animals and plants, horizontal gene transfer is commonly considered rare with very limited evolutionary significance. Here we show that horizontal gene transfer is a dynamic process occurring frequently in the early evolution of land plants. Our genome analyses of the moss Physcomitrella patens identified 57 families of nuclear genes that were acquired from prokaryotes, fungi or viruses."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Widespread horizontal gene transfer between plants and ... ---
URL: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.08.25.505314.full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a bioRxiv preprint (DOI: 10.1101/2022.08.25.505314) titled "Widespread horizontal gene transfer between plants and their microbiota" by Shelly Haimlich, Yulia Fridman, Hitaishi Khandal, Sigal Savaldi-Goldstein, and Asaf Levy (from Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Technion-Israel Institute of Technology). It has since been published in ISME Communications (doi: 10.1093/ismeco/ycae073).

**Objective & Hypothesis:** The authors hypothesized that the spatial proximity and long-term relationships between plants and their microbiota promote cross-kingdom horizontal gene transfer (HGT). They tested this using Arabidopsis thaliana and its extensively sequenced microbiome.

**Methodology:**
- Compared A. thaliana genes against 582 fully sequenced commensal bacteria isolated from Arabidopsis (plant-associated, PA), covering 1,051 genomes total (including 441 non-plant-associated bacteria, plants, fungi, archaea, and other eukaryotes).
- Used BLASTP with threshold of at least 35% amino acid identity across at least 80% of both proteins.
- Filtered out 'trivial hits' shared with organelles (mitochondria and chloroplast, which originate in bacteria).
- Constructed gene trees from multiple sequence alignments to detect phylogenetic evidence of HGT (where gene trees and genome trees were inconsistent).

**Key Results:**
- Identified 767 Arabidopsis proteins mapped to 60,850 bacterial proteins as potential molecular mimicry candidates.
- Detected 180 unique cross-kingdom HGT events: 84 genes likely transferred from plants to bacteria, and 96 genes from PA bacteria to plants.
- Additionally found 161 genes transferred between PA bacteria and the eukaryotic domain (source unclear), 65 genes with unclear inheritance patterns, and 361 genes with no HGT patterns.
- Rejected DNA contamination by confirming no homologous pairs exceeded 76% amino acid identity.

**Functional Enrichment:**
- Genes transferred from plants to bacteria are enriched in secreted proteins, carbohydrate catabolism enzymes (pectin esterase, glycosidase), and include chitinases (CHI, AT2G43570), endo beta mannanase (XCD1), and pectin lyases (PME5) — enabling bacteria to exploit plant-derived sugars.
- Genes transferred from bacteria to plants are enriched in redox homeostasis and cytoplasmic proteins, including many auxin biosynthesis YUCCA genes and nucleoside metabolic processes. 69/96 (72%) of such genes are found in all dicots and monocots, suggesting ancient HGT events.

**Taxonomic Patterns:**
- Bacteroidetes were enriched as gene acceptors from plants, while Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria were depleted as either acceptors or donors.
- Rhizobiales and Hyphomicrobiales (Proteobacteria) and Micrococcales (Actinobacteria) showed significantly fewer HGT events than expected.
- In most cases the donor/acceptor taxonomy remained "unknown" (multiple phyla involved).

**Recent HGT Examples:**
- The plant CHI (chitinase) gene is present in only 7 PA Streptomyces genomes (patchy distribution), with protein structures very similar (RMSD=0.791).
- The bacterial DET2 homologue (steroid-5-alpha-reductase, key in brassinosteroid biosynthesis) is nearly specific to plant-associated Leifsonia genus (Actinobacteria), located downstream of a tRNA gene; protein structures highly similar (RMSD=0.727) despite less than 50% sequence identity.

**Functional Validation (Proof-of-Concept):**
- The authors tested whether the Leifsonia DET2 homologue (lfDET2) could functionally replace the Arabidopsis DET2 gene. Arabidopsis DET2 is 46% identical to Leifsonia Det2 (similar to identity shared with rice and barley homologues).
- Expression of lfDET2 (driven by 35S or Arabidopsis DET2 promoters) in the Arabidopsis det2 mutant background rescued the dwarf phenotype and root meristem defects, restoring normal plant growth.
- lfDET2 localized to the endoplasmic reticulum, matching atDET2 localization.

**Conclusion:** The results suggest cross-kingdom HGT is relatively frequent and shaped the genomes of plants and their microbiota by adding adaptive traits. The transferred genes likely participate in molecular mimicry between hosts and their commensal microbiomes. Key author correspondence: alevy@mail.huji.ac.il.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We detected 180 unique genes that were horizontally transferred between plants and their microbiota. Genes transferred from plants to their microbiota are enriched in secreted proteins that metabolize carbohydrates, whereas microbes transferred to plants genes that are enriched in redox homeostasis functions."
</key_excerpts>

This article, published in Nature Communications (2012 Oct 23; 3:1152, doi: 10.1038/ncomms2148), presents a study on the widespread impact of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) on plant colonization of land. **Functional significance:**
- Acquired genes are involved in essential or plant-specific activities including xylem formation, plant defence, nitrogen recycling, and biosynthesis of starch, polyamines, hormones (auxin), and glutathione.
- Notable examples include: land plant subtilases (derived from a single HGT event from bacteria, followed by rapid gene duplication), arginase (derived from bacterial agmatinase, involved in polyamine biosynthesis), phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPCase), FAD-linked oxidase, glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCL, first enzyme in glutathione formation), and auxin biosynthesis genes (AAE18 and YUC3 flavin monooxygenase).
- 35 gene families identified in P. patens are also present in seed plants, suggesting dynamic accumulation of foreign genes over time.

**Proposed HGT mechanism model:**
The authors propose a model for HGT in nonvascular and seedless vascular plants based on two entry points for foreign gene acquisition: (1) during spore germination and early gametophyte development (moss gametophytes are simple, undifferentiated, and in direct contact with soil), and (2) during fertilization and early embryo development (mosses conceal eggs in single-layered, hollow archegonia that are open during fertilization). The model predicts that organisms with unprotected or weakly protected zygotes are prone to HGT.

**Methods:**
Genome screening used the AlienG software package with P. patens annotated protein sequences. Candidates were validated through detailed phylogenetic analyses (maximum likelihood with PhyML 3.0 and distance methods), taxonomic distribution investigation, and inspection of rare genomic characters. A candidate was confirmed as horizontally acquired based on gene tree topology showing a green plant/donor clade with >80% bootstrap support, taxonomic distribution limited to donor groups, and unique shared domain structures/indels/amino acid residues.

**Funding:** NSF Assembling the Tree of Life (ATOL) grant (DEB 0830024) and the CAS/SAFEA International Partnership Program for Creative Research Teams. PMCID: PMC3493653, PMID: 23093189.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Here we show that horizontal gene transfer is a dynamic process occurring frequently in the early evolution of land plants. Our genome analyses of the moss Physcomitrella patens identified 57 families of nuclear genes that were acquired from prokaryotes, fungi or viruses."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 13: Widespread and frequent horizontal transfers of transposable elements in plants | Genome Research ---
URL: https://genome.cshlp.org/content/24/5/831

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article from Genome Research (published online before print, DOI: 10.1101/gr.164400.113) reporting the discovery of widespread and frequent horizontal transfers of transposable elements (TEs) in plants. 

**Study Design and Methods:**
- Conducted a computational search for LTR retrotransposons (LTR-RTs) among 40 sequenced angiosperm genomes representing 36 monocot and eudicot genera from major plant families
- Retrieved ~300,000 full-size elements, clustered into distinct families using an all-against-all BLAST comparison and SiLiX clustering software
- Applied detection thresholds of 90% sequence identity within monocot/dicot classes and 85% between classes (accounting for greater divergence time)
- Validated candidates through three criteria: patchy distributions in phylogenies, high sequence similarity between distantly related taxa, and phylogenetic incongruence between host and TEs
- Confirmed transfers via PCR amplification and sequencing for 22 of the identified HTTs

**Key Results:**
- 26 of 40 genomes (65%) harbor at least one case of horizontal TE transfer (HTT)
- Identified 32 cases of HTTs total: 1 between monocot and dicot species (palm tree/grapevine), 8 between distinct orders, and 23 between genera within the same family
- Transfers span highly diverged species pairs including palm/grapevine, tomato/bean, and poplar/peach
- All 32 families harbor LTR-RT gag-pol domains suggesting functionality; transferred elements remained transpositionally active post-transfer, with two cases (BG10, BG11) showing significant increases in copy number (transpositional bursts)
- Extrapolating from the data, the authors estimate more than 2 million HTTs (precisely 2,241,337) may have occurred among the 13,551 monocot and dicot genera within the last 3 million years

- A posteriori whole-genome comparisons also detected a previously identified class II transposon transfer between rice and millet (BG8), plus a second potentially horizontally transferred transposon

**Conclusions:**
- HTTs are very frequent and widespread among monocots and dicots, contradicting the long-held view that LTR-RTs are inherited exclusively vertically
- HTTs provide an escape route from TE silencing and elimination pathways, offering a possible explanation for the paradox of TE long-term survival in eukaryotic lineages despite their "selfish" and potentially deleterious nature
- The mechanisms and vectors of these transfers are not yet fully understood; parasitism is excluded as the sole cause since none of the species analyzed are parasitic
- The estimate exceeds by several orders of magnitude the number of HTTs previously documented in both plants and animals

--- SOURCE 15: Contribution of plant–bacteria interactions to horizontal gene transfer in plants ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper, published in Biotechnology & Biotechnological Equipment (Volume 35, Issue 1, 2021, pages 1587-1592), investigates the contribution of plant-bacteria interactions to horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in plants. The study was conducted by Hongsheng Cai, Yingying Liu, and Changhong Guo at Harbin Normal University and the Harbin Academy of Agricultural Sciences in China.

BACKGROUND: HGT is a major driver of adaptive evolution in prokaryotes, but its occurrence in eukaryotes (particularly as recipients) has been debated. The study hypothesized that bacterial-plant associations, given their close contact, are a major source of HGT in plants.

METHODS: The researchers used a comparative genomic approach, downloading genome sequences from NCBI. They selected 43 angiosperm genomes and 151 plant-associated bacteria to construct ortholog groups using OrthoFinder (2987 groups after filtering). Phylogenetic trees were constructed using RAxML, and HGT events were detected following methods adapted from Yang et al. Validation involved adding more taxa, BLAST searches against refseq databases, hidden Markov models, protein domain checks, and statistical analysis. HGTs were functionally annotated using the KEGG pathway database, and gene expression was analyzed in GENEVESTIGATOR.

RESULTS:
- 373 potential HGT events were identified (present in more than 2 species), with 90 confirmed as true events (27.27%-86.5% sequence similarity).
- Donor bacterial genera from Alpha-protobacteria, Beta-protobacteria, and Firmicutes (which include numerous plant-associated genera) were significantly enriched for HGT (p < 0.01), supporting the role of plant-bacterial interactions.
- The most enriched functional categories were metabolism of amino acids, cofactors/vitamins, and carbohydrates, plus genetic information processing. Nearly 83% of transferred genes coded for enzymes (oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases), with others including transporters, inhibitors, DNA-repair, and signaling proteins.
- A case example: Glyoxalase I (GlyI) transfer from bacteria to plants, confirmed by maximum likelihood and Bayesian phylogenetic analyses, leading to Ni/Co-dependent GlyI enzyme activity in plants.
- No clade- or species-specific HGTs were detected; all occurred anciently during the origin of angiosperm plants. Two transferred genes had >70% sequence similarity, likely representing relatively recent specific transfers (e.g., Agrobacteria).
- 309 "one-species" HGT events were identified and all were confirmed to be artifacts of sequencing error or inaccurate annotation (despite 40-100% sequence similarity).

CONCLUSIONS: The study confirmed that bacterial-plant interactions contribute to HGT from bacteria to plants. Both ancient transfer (during angiosperm origin) and recent specific transfer (e.g., Agrobacteria) occurred during plant evolution. The results can explain the discontinuity of HGT from prokaryotes to eukaryotes and suggest the "70% rule" (a key argument against eukaryotic HGT) should be re-evaluated.

FUNDING: Supported by The National Key Research and Development Program of China (2017YFD0101303), Heilongjiang Postdoctoral Fund (LBH-Z20160), and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (31770575, 31972507). No conflicts of interest were reported. The article is open access.
</summary>

In addition, we identified 309 'one-species' HGT events, and as expected, all the events could be accounted for as sequence errors or inaccurate annotations., We propose that both ancient transfer and recent specific transfer (e.g. Agrobacteria) occurred in the course of plant evolution.

--- SOURCE 20: role of horizontal gene transfer ---
URL: https://www.ars.usda.gov/ARSUserFiles/50620500/Publications/HCK/horizon.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (Annu. Rev. Phytopathol. 2000, by U. Liane Rosewich and H. Corby Kistler) examines the role of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in fungal evolution. The authors define HGT as stable transfer of genetic material between individuals not attributable to vertical (meiotic or mitotic) processes. They note that although HGT evidence in eukaryotes remains largely anecdotal, fungi may have experienced more HGT than other eukaryotes, making them well-suited model systems because HGT can be tested experimentally.

The authors outline indirect evidence for HGT, including character-state discordance between element and organismal phylogenies, high similarity between elements in distantly related organisms, irregular distribution patterns, habitat-associated gene sharing, and genomic inconsistencies (G+C content, codon usage). Alternative explanations (erroneous phylogenies, paralog comparisons, ancestral retention, introgressive hybridization) must be considered. Phylogenetic tests include bootstrapping, maximum likelihood, T-PTP tests, and incongruence length differences.

The review organizes potential HGT cases by element type:
1. PLASMIDS: Fungal plasmids (usually 1-21 kb, linear, often mitochondrial) show discordant phylogenies, random global distribution patterns (e.g., 7 Neurospora plasmid groups among 225 isolates), and experimental transfer. Horizontal transfer was demonstrated experimentally by co-culturing unrelated strains (e.g., pAI2 from Ascobolus immersus to Podospora anserina; kalilo between Neurospora species).
2. MYCOVIRUSES: Lacking an extracellular phase, these transfer via cytoplasmic mixing. Some RdRp similarities between distant species suggest possible HGT.
3. INTRONS: Group I introns (nuclear, mitochondrial, and rRNA) and group II introns (organellar only) can move via homing and transposition. The best-substantiated case involves horizontal transfer of a group I intron from fungi to the angiosperm Peperomia. The cox1 intron i4 of Agrocybe aegerita showed 90.5% amino acid identity with the homologous intron in P. anserina, strongly supporting recent HGT. Intron phylogenies are often incongruent with species phylogenies.
4. TRANSPOSABLE ELEMENTS: Sporadic distribution patterns (e.g., grasshopper retrotransposon in Magnaporthe grisea, Fot1 in Fusarium oxysporum) suggest HGT, though stochastic loss is an alternative explanation. Vectors (symbionts/parasites) are proposed but unproven.

The authors conclude that HGT in fungi may be a more important evolutionary factor than in other eukaryotes, particularly for introns and plasmids, which may need periodic horizontal transfer for long-term persistence.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In this review article we summarize reports of genetic exchanges between fungal populations and between fungi and other organisms that have been attributed to horizontal transfer mechanisms.", "We define HGT as the stable transfer of genetic material between individuals, not directly attributable to vertical, i.e. meiotic or mitotic, processes...", "Evidence for HGT in fungi and other eukaryotes is indirect. In most cases, HGT is invoked after unusual features of genetic elements have become evident, including (a) an inconsistency between the phylogeny of the genetic element in question and the traditionally accepted phylogeny of the organisms...", "Horizontal transfer of the linear mitochondrial plasmid pAI2 from the discomycete A. immersus to mitochondria of a plasmid-free strain of the pyrenomycete Podospora anserina was achieved experimentally by merely co-culturing these unrelated strains.", "In summary, our compilation of potential intron horizontal transmissions in fungi indicates that horizontal transfer of introns among fungi may be quite common."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution | Semantic Scholar ---
URL: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Horizontal-gene-transfer-in-eukaryotic-evolution-Keeling-Palmer/e752cd6145dc999140351f0334951a65465174b1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page describes a seminal 2008 review paper titled "Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution" by Patrick J. Keeling and Jeffrey D. Palmer, published in Nature Reviews Genetics (DOI: 10.1038/nrg2386). The paper has 1,313 citations and examines the growing number of well-supported cases of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) from both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, many with significant functional implications. Key trends highlighted include the important role of HGT in adaptation to specialized niches and the highly variable impact of HGT across different eukaryotic lineages.

The page also lists notable citing papers and references, including: the "weak-link model" of HGT in eukaryotes (Huang, 2013) proposing that unicellular and early developmental stages are entry points for foreign genes in multicellular eukaryotes; evidence from Bdelloid rotifers showing massive HGT with genes originating from bacteria, fungi, and plants (Gladyshev et al., 2008); massive HGT in Amborella trichopoda involving acquisition of hundreds of foreign mitochondrial genes (Richardson & Palmer, 2007); widespread horizontal transfer of mitochondrial genes in flowering plants (Bergthorsson et al., 2003); and the "complexity hypothesis" (Jain et al., 1999) explaining why operational genes are more frequently transferred than informational genes. HGT is shown to play important roles in eukaryotic adaptation to parasitism, pathogenesis, anaerobiosis, and nitrogen/iron limitation in marine environments, and there is evidence of HGT in metazoans (sponges, cnidarians, rotifers, nematodes, molluscs, arthropods).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The number of well-supported cases of transfer from both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, many with significant functional implications, is now expanding rapidly and major recent trends include the important role of HGT in adaptation to certain specialized niches and the highly variable impact of HGT in different lineages."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution ---
URL: http://www.ask-force.org/web/HorizontalGT/Keeling-HGT-Eukaryotic-Evolution-2008.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (Keeling & Palmer, Nature Reviews Genetics, Aug 2008) examines horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in eukaryotic evolution, arguing that its importance is often overshadowed by more extensive study of HGT in prokaryotes. The authors note that eukaryotes arose via the grandest HGT events — endosymbiosis giving rise to mitochondria and plastids — but ongoing HGT in eukaryotes has been under-appreciated due to overshadowing by bacterial studies, evidence coming largely from protists rather than animals, and the erroneous 2001 claim of substantial HGT in the human genome that chilled the field.

Key methodological point: The gold standard for identifying HGT is phylogenetic incongruence (strong conflict between gene and organism phylogenies), though this requires adequate taxonomic sampling. Detecting and evaluating HGT requires formal phylogenetic analysis; the 2001 claim of ~100 human genes from bacteria was debunked by such analysis.

Major findings and trends:
- Massive endosymbiotic gene transfer (EGT): Organellar genomes encode only a small fraction of their proteins; most organelle proteins are encoded by nuclear genes. EGT tempo has been highly punctuated, with bursts of transfer interspersed with periods of stasis. In striking contrast to angiosperms (where 16 of 40 mitochondrial-protein genes show recent EGT), animals show profound stasis — not one functional EGT across 600 million years of metazoan evolution.
- Protein import constrains transfer: Hydrophobic organelle proteins are hardest to import and assemble, locking animal mitochondria into a small, irreducible set of core genes.
- Bacterial endosymbiont transfers: Large tracts of Wolbachia DNA have moved to insect/nematode nuclear genomes; in one case an entire Wolbachia genome was found in a fruitfly genome.
- Prokaryote–eukaryote transfers vary enormously: estimates range from zero to hundreds of bacterial genes per genome. Rumen-dwelling ciliates acquired ~4% of genes from bacteria, approaching bacterial levels. Only one of dozens of sequenced animal genomes (human) has been analyzed, with no credible cases of bacterial HGT found.
- Adaptive functions: Anaerobic parasites and rumen ciliates are rich in transferred genes related to anaerobic metabolism; HGT supports adaptation to specialized niches (parasitism, anaerobiosis, soil life).
- Frequency is a complex function of opportunity (phagotrophy/"you are what you eat"), germ-line segregation, and other factors, varying by lineage.
- Bacterial transfers dominate detected cases partly due to detection bias (easy to spot given large evolutionary distance) but also real opportunity — bacterial populations and gene pools are far larger.
- Eukaryote–eukaryote transfers are underestimated due to poor sampling, confounding gene duplication, and lack of systematic searches, but many cases exist, including fungal toxin gene transfer (~70 years ago) and plastid-targeted protein transfers between algal groups.
- Organelle–organelle HGT: One extraordinary case of recent cytochrome b transfers among sympatric Mexican beetles; plant mitochondrial DNA is unexpectedly active in HGT while plastid and animal mitochondrial DNAs show none.
- Eukaryote–prokaryote transfers are rare but include tubulin genes in the bacterium Prosthecobacter, actin/profilin in Microcystis, and a eukaryotic FBA in Prochlorococcus/Synechococcus, presumably due to opportunity and intron barriers.

The article emphasizes that HGT in eukaryotes is now emerging at an increasing rate, accounts for many adaptively important traits, and has altered concepts of the genome, species, and the tree (or web) of life.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Extant eukaryotes arose by HGT on the grandest scale possible — the endosymbiosis and subsequent genetic integration of entire organisms that gave rise to the mitochondrion and the plastid."; "The gold standard for identifying HGT with confidence is phylogenetic incongruence — this occurs if there is strong conflict between the phylogenies of the gene and of the organism."; "By contrast, animals exhibit profound stasis in mitochondrial gene content: not one case of functional EGT has been reported across the 600 million years of metazoan evolution, despite sequencing of thousands of animal mitochondrial genomes."; "This has led to the 'you are what you eat' theory of HGT."; "Although we can safely generalize that overall levels of bacterial genes in nuclear genomes vary substantially among eukaryotes, too few 'whole' genomes have been examined to allow much insight into patterns, much less rates, of both horizontal transfer and loss of transferred genes."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution | Nature Reviews Genetics ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/nrg2386

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article titled "Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic evolution" by Patrick J. Keeling (University of British Columbia) and Jeffrey D. Palmer (Indiana University), published in Nature Reviews Genetics, Volume 9, pages 605–618 (2008). The article has over 35,000 accesses, 1,239 citations, and 182 Altmetric mentions.

MAIN TOPIC: The article examines horizontal gene transfer (HGT, also known as lateral gene transfer) — the non-sexual movement of genetic information between genomes — and its role in eukaryotic genome evolution. While HGT is more prevalent and better understood in prokaryotes, this review documents its significant impact on eukaryotic evolution.

KEY FINDINGS AND POINTS:
1. Definition: HGT is the non-sexual movement of genetic information between genomes, where incoming DNA/RNA can replace existing genes or introduce new genes.
2. HGT in eukaryotes has been overshadowed by its prevalence in bacterial genomes, but many cases involving eukaryotes have been documented. Its impact varies by lineage, and lineages most affected (like protists) are often the least studied at the genomic level.
3. Endosymbiosis has been extensive in eukaryotic evolution. Mitochondria and plastids (derived from endosymbiosis) contributed many genes to the nucleus, and subsequent endosymbioses allowed genes to move between eukaryotes. Persistent endosymbionts like Wolbachia are now recognized as major sources of DNA in host nuclei.
4. HGT without symbiosis is also common; most documented cases involve bacterial genes in eukaryotic nuclei. Bacteria may be the major source of new genes due to their abundance.
5. Eukaryote-to-eukaryote transfers may be more common than appreciated. Extensive gene exchange between mitochondrial genomes of plants provides the highest known levels of eukaryote–eukaryote transfer.
6. Transferred genes often have clear functional or ecological implications. For example, several highly derived anaerobes acquired metabolic genes from bacteria that contributed to their adaptation to anaerobic environments.
7. Ancient HGT events can serve as clues to organismal relationships, with several shared by major eukaryotic lineages (e.g., animals and fungi, or chromalveolates).
8. Recent transfers are more commonly observed than ancient ones, possibly indicating that transferred genes provide transient advantages but are frequently not retained long-term.
9. Major outstanding questions include: the fate of transferred genes over time, mechanisms of HGT, and what determines HGT's differential impact across lineages.

The article includes figures on eukaryotic evolution bifurcations/reticulations, sources of transferred genes ("you are what you eat, what you live on, what lives on you, and what lives in you"), and different kinds of transfer effects on gene phylogeny. The full content is behind a subscription paywall, though the abstract and key points are accessible.

Related articles referenced include "Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes: aligning theory with data" (2024), "A global survey of prokaryotic genomes reveals the eco-evolutionary pressures driving horizontal gene transfer" (2024), and "A compendium of horizontal gene transfers in Metazoa" (2026).

The reference list (over 57 references) covers foundational work on HGT including Doolittle's phylogenetic classification work, studies on endosymbiotic gene transfer from organelles to nuclei, Wolbachia genome integration in insects, HGT in parasitic protozoa and rumen ciliates, and large-scale genomic analyses of gene transfer in plants and animals.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Horizontal gene transfer (HGT; also known as lateral gene transfer) is the non-sexual movement of genetic information between genomes. Incoming DNA or RNA can replace existing genes, or can introduce new genes into a genome."
</key_excerpts>
